Lu You said: “Ride a donkey and enter the Jianmen in the drizzle.” Jianmen has been an impregnable pass for thousands of years, and there are many such impregnable passes in China. However, only the rain, donkey, dust in the journey and wine are able to dispel their power.

The heroic epic can also be spread in the world via words. Gu Yanwu said: “The History of the Han Dynasty is always hung in the ox horn.” Look, the powerful Han Dynasty that once could receive all criticisms and praise could only be swung by an ox horn. And the ox is walking down the mountain pass, at dusk, late in autumn.

A walk among the mountains and rivers reduces all great causes to the ordinary landscape, which can relax us a little. The human being should lay down all between the mountains and the rivers. In this way, we can also find the destination, for our value and our life.
Such a destination was once expressed accurately by Tao Yuanming: “The body is only entrusted to the mountains.”

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 一位年迈的老祖宗，没有成为挂在墙上的画像，没有成为写在书里的回忆，而是直到今天还在给后代挑水、送饭，这样的奇事你相信吗？
一匹千年前的骏马，没有成为泥土间的化石，没有成为古墓里的雕塑，而是直到今天还踯躅在家园四周的高坡上，守护着每一个清晨和夜晚，这样的奇事你相信吗？
当然无法相信。但是，由此出现了极其相似的第三个问题——
一个两千多年前的水利工程，没有成为西风残照下的废墟，没有成为考古学家们的难题，而是直到今天还一直执掌着亿万人的生计，这样的奇事你相信吗？
仍然无法相信，但它真的出现了。
它就是都江堰。
这是一个不大的工程，但我敢说，把它放在全人类文明奇迹的第一线，也毫无愧色。

世人皆知万里长城，其实细细想来，它比万里长城更激动人心。万里长城当然也非常伟大，展现了一个民族令人震惊的意志力。但是，万里长城的实际功能历来并不太大，而且早已废弛。都江堰则不同，有了它，旱涝无常的四川平原成了天府之国，每当中华民族有了重大灾难，天府之国总是沉着地提供庇护和濡养。有了它，才有历代贤臣良将的安顿和向往，才有唐宋诗人出川入川的千古华章。说得近一点，有了它，抗日战争时的中国才有一个比较稳定的后方。
它细细渗透，节节延伸，延伸的距离并不比万里长城短。或者说，它筑造了另一座万里长城。而一查履历，那座名声显赫的万里长城还是它的后辈。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 我去都江堰之前，以为它只是一个水利工程罢了，不会有太大的游观价值。只是要去青城山玩，要路过灌县县城，它就在近旁，就趁便看一眼吧。因此，在灌县下车，心绪懒懒的，脚步散散的，在街上胡逛，一心只想看青城山。
七转八弯，从简朴的街市走进了一个草木茂盛的所在。脸面渐觉滋润，眼前愈显清朗，也没有谁指路，只是本能地向更滋润、更清朗的去处去。
忽然，天地间开始有些异常，一种隐隐然的骚动，一种还不太响却一定是非常响的声音，充斥周际。如地震前兆，如海啸将临，如山崩即至，浑身骤起一种莫名的紧张，又紧张得急于趋附。
不知是自己走去的还是被它吸去的，终于陡然一惊，我已站在伏龙观前——眼前，急流浩荡，大地震颤。
即便是站在海边礁石上，也没有像这里这样强烈地领受到水的魅力。海水是雍容大度的聚汇，聚汇得太多太深，茫茫一片，让人忘记它是切切实实的水、可掬可捧的水。这里的水却不同，要说多也不算太多，但股股叠叠都精神焕发，合在一起比赛着飞奔的力量，踊跃着喧嚣的生命。
这种比赛又极有规矩，奔着奔着，遇到江心的分水堤，刷的一下裁割为二，直蹿出去，两股水分别撞到了一道坚坝，立即乖乖地转身改向，再在另一道坚坝上撞一下，于是又根据筑坝者的指令来一番调整……
也许水流对自己的驯顺有点恼怒了，突然撒起野来，猛地翻卷咆哮，但越是这样，越是显现出一种更壮丽的驯顺。已经咆哮到让人心魄俱夺，也没有一滴水溅错了方向。
水在这里，吃够了苦头，也出足了风头，就像一大拨翻越各种障碍的马拉松健儿，把最强悍的生命付之于规整，付之于企盼，付之于众目睽睽。
看云看雾看日出各有胜地，要看水，万不可忘了都江堰。

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 这一切，首先要归功于遥远的李冰。
四川有幸，中国有幸，公元前三世纪出现过一项并不惹人注目的任命：李冰任蜀郡守。
据我所知，这项任命与秦统一中国的宏图有关。本以为只有把四川作为一个富庶的根据地和出发地，才能从南线问鼎长江流域。然而，这项任命到了李冰那里，却从一个政治计划变成了一个生态计划。
他要做的事，是浚理，是消灾，是滋润，是灌溉。
他是郡守，手握一把长锸，站在滔滔江边，完成了一个“守”字的原始造型。
没有资料可以说明他作为郡守在其他方面的才能，但因为有过他，中国也就有了一种冰清玉洁的行政纲领。
中国后来官场的惯例，是把一批批杰出学者选拔为无所专攻的官僚，而李冰却因官位而成了一名实践科学家。
他当然没有在哪里学过水利。但是，以使命为学校，竭力钻研几载，他总结出治水三字经（“深淘滩，低作堰”）、八字真言（“遇弯截角，逢正抽心”），直到二十世纪仍是水利工程的圭臬。
他的这点学问，永远水气淋漓。而比他年轻的很多典籍却早已风干，松脆得难以翻阅。
他没有料到，他治水的韬略很快被偷换成了治人的谋略。他没有料到，他想灌溉的沃土都将成为战场。他只知道，这个人种要想不灭绝，就必须要有清泉和米粮。
他大愚，又大智。他大拙，又大巧。他以田间老农的思维，进入了最清澈的人类学思考。
他未曾留下什么生平故事，只留下硬扎扎的水坝一座，让人们去猜想。
人们到这儿一次次纳闷：这是谁啊？死于两千年前，却明明还在指挥水流。站在江心的岗亭前，“你走这边，他走那边”的吆喝声、劝诫声、慰抚声，声声入耳。
李冰在世时已考虑事业的承续，命令自己的儿子做三个石人，镇于江间，测量水位。李冰逝世四百年后，也许三个石人已经损缺，汉代水官重造高及三米的“三神石人”以测量水位。这“三神石人”其中一尊，居然就是李冰的雕像。
这位汉代水官一定是承接了李冰的伟大精魂，竟敢把自己尊敬的祖师放在江中用于镇水测量。他懂得李冰的心意，唯有那里才是其最合适的岗位。
石像终于被岁月的淤泥掩埋。二十世纪七十年代出土时，有一尊石像头部已经残缺，手上还紧握着长锸。有人说，这是李冰的儿子。
即使不是，我仍然把他看成是李冰的儿子。一位现代女作家见到这尊塑像怦然心动——“没淤泥而蔼然含笑，断颈项而长锸在握”，她由此向现代官场衮衮诸公诘问：活着或死了，应该站在哪里？
出土的石像现正在伏龙观里展览。人们在轰鸣如雷的水声中向他们默默祭奠。在这里，我突然产生了对中国历史的某种乐观：只要李冰的精魂不散，李冰的儿子会代代繁衍。轰鸣的江水，便是至圣至善的遗言。

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 看到了一条横江索桥。桥很高，桥索由麻绳、竹篾编成。跨上去，桥身就猛烈摆动。越是犹豫进退，摆动就越大。
在这样高的地方偷看桥下，一定会神志慌乱。但这是索桥，到处漏空，由不得你不看。一看之下，先是惊吓，后是惊叹。
脚下的江流，从那么遥远的地方奔来，一派义无反顾的决绝势头，挟着寒风，吐着白沫，凌厉锐进。我站得这么高还能感觉到它的砭肤冷气，估计是从雪山赶来的吧。但是，再看桥的另一边，它硬是化作许多亮闪闪的河渠，一片慈眉善目。人对自然力的调理，居然做得这么爽利。如果人类做什么事都这么爽利，地球早已是另一副模样。
都江堰调理自然力的本事，被近旁的青城山作了哲学总结。
青城山是道教圣地，而道教是唯一在中国土生土长的大宗教。道教汲取了老子和庄子的哲学，把水作为教义的象征。水，看似柔顺无骨，却能变得气势滚滚，波涌浪叠，无比强大；看似无色无味，却能挥洒出茫茫绿野，累累硕果，万紫千红；看似自处低下，却能蒸腾九霄，为云为雨，为虹为霞……
看上去，是人在治水；实际上，却是人领悟了水，顺应了水，听从了水。只有这样，才能天人合一，无我无私，长生不老。
这便是道。
道之道，也就是水之道，天之道，生之道。因此，也是李冰之道、都江堰之道。道无处不在，却在都江堰作了一次集中呈现。
因此，都江堰和青城山相邻而居，互相映衬，彼此佐证，成了研修中国哲学的最浓缩课堂。
那天我带着都江堰的浑身水气，在青城山的山路上慢慢攀登。忽见一道观，进门小憩。道士认出了我，便铺纸研墨，要我留字。我当即写下了一副最朴素的对子：
拜水都江堰，
问道青城山。
我想，若能把“拜水”和“问道”这两件事当作一件事，那么，也就领悟了中华文化的一大秘密。

sections.label: I
paragraphs: IMAGINE AN ANCESTOR from so far back we can’t work out which era they lived in, one who didn’t become notable enough for their portrait to hang on walls, or their name to appear in lesson books. Yet to this day, this person draws water and provides food for their descendants. Would you believe such a thing was possible?

Or let’s take a fine horse from the time of the first emperor that neither falls into mud and gets fossilized, nor becomes immortal in the form of an ancient tomb statue, but rather continues to trot back and forth today atop the highlands surrounding its homestead, watching over every dawn and nightfall, alert while abundant summers and bitter winters come and go. Would you believe such a thing was possible?
These are legends, or fairy tales, and of course impossible to believe. But from here, we derive a third question of a similar nature—

What about a water-engineering structure constructed more than two thousand years ago, that hasn’t crumbled away under the vicious assault of the west wind, nor turned into a knotty conundrum for archaeologists to puzzle over, but has continued to hold sway over the livelihoods of millions of people, and is destined to remain a permanent feature. Would you believe such a thing was possible?
Equally difficult to accept, yet such a thing exists in reality.
It is the Dujiangyan Irrigation System.
This isn’t a particularly large structure, but I reckon it could proudly claim a place in the first rank of the marvels of human civilization

Everyone on earth has heard of the Great Wall of China, but if you think about it, Dujiangyan is much more stirring than the Wall—which of course is magnificent, a demonstration of the astonishing willpower of an entire race. Yet the actual efficacy of the Great Wall was never that great, and it was obsolete a long time ago. Dujiangyan is different. Thanks to its existence, the Sichuan plains are no longer subject to an unpredictable regime of floods and droughts, and have become known as the “Heavenly Province,” a land of plenty. Whenever the Chinese people suffer a great tragedy, the Heavenly Province will be there, silently providing shelter and nourishment. Dujiangyan has provided a resting place and aspiration for generations of virtuous ministers and noble generals, has made possible the immortal verses of the Tang and Song Dynasties by poets who moved in and out of Sichuan. Moving closer in time, it was also Dujiangyan that gave China a stable rear position in the war against Japan.

Through a series of intricate movements, it causes water to deeply penetrate the land, gradually extending outward until its reach rivals that of the Great Wall. Or we could say that, looking both above and below ground, its construction was the equivalent of a second Great Wall. And examining the histories of both, it turns out this celebrated Wall actually came after Dujiangyan.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: BEFORE GOING TO DUJIANGYAN, I’d assumed it was a mere irrigation project, and therefore without too much value in terms of sightseeing. I only decided to take a look because the road to Qingcheng Mountain, where I was heading for a vacation, passed through Guan County Seat, and Dujiangyan was just nearby. Arriving in Guan County, I felt uninspired, my footsteps lethargic. I wandered listlessly through the streets, thinking only of getting to Qingcheng Mountain.

After several twists and turns, I left the unadorned city streets behind, entering a place of verdant grass and trees. I felt wetness on my face, and brightness shimmered before me. With no one to guide me, I instinctively walked towards the moisture and light.

Suddenly, the world grew strange. I was aware of a slight disturbance in the air, a noise that was both not too loud but somehow flooding the edges of my senses, as if an earthquake or tsunami or landslide were imminent. A strange tension filled my body, yet I was also anxious to connect with whatever lay ahead.

I can’t say if I walked forward of my own volition or was sucked in, but in any case I suddenly froze in shock, finding myself standing in front of the Dragon Taming Temple—and before my eyes was that turbulent flow, shaking the land itself.

Not even when standing on rocks by the ocean had I experienced the power of water so violently. Seawater is a graceful accumulation of volume, becoming so vast and deep as to eclipse the whole horizon, leading onlookers to forget it is still water, a substance you can cup in your hands. The water here was different—there wasn’t very much of it, but it was full of life as it leaped and doubled over, coming together then racing to spring apart with the utmost energy, bursting with exuberance.

This race was heavily regulated. The water sprinted along, and when it encountered the levee in the middle of the stream, it split itself into two and kept going, until both branches separately encountered a sturdy dam, whereupon they accommodatingly changed direction, hitting another dike and once more following the direction of the engineer, adjusting their course…

Perhaps the water flow was annoyed at its own obedience, abruptly growing wild, ferociously flipping over itself and roaring, but the more it churned, the more it seemed to display a magnificent control. Its howling was so intense our souls were completely gripped, yet not a single drop of water went the wrong way. In the dim arboreal light, this felt like a negotiation between humanity and nature that had been going on for thousands of years.

By this point, the water had endured its share of suffering and obstruction, like a marathon runner overcoming all kinds of obstacles with a single shove, sacrificing a most valiant life in the name of order, of hope, of public spectacle.
If you want to see clouds or mist or sunrises, there are well-known scenic spots you can visit. And if you want to observe water, you mustn’t leave Dujiangyan off your list.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: ALL OF THIS must primarily be credited to Li Bing, a man so distant from us that we cannot even make out his image.
The prosperity of Sichuan and of China, began with an unremarkable appointment in the third century BCE: Li Bing was made the Governor for the state of Shu in Sichuan.

As I understand it, this appointment had to do with the Qin state’s ambitions to unify China. Sichuan was initially intended as a base of operations from which troops could be dispatched, in order to advance from the southern line to seize the Yangtze River basin. When this order reached Li Bing, however, it transformed from a political scheme to an ecological one.
The work he decided to undertake included clearing the waterways, preventing disasters, moistening and irrigating the land.
Standing by the rushing water, he took a long shovel and sketched out a plan in the shape of the character shou (守), meaning “Governor,” his title.
We have no other data about his efficacy as Governor in other areas, but because of him, China developed an administrative apparatus as clear as ice and pure as jade.

After this, China’s usual practice when it came to bureaucracy was to dispatch outstanding scholars to posts in which they had no experience, whereas Li Bing’s position allowed him to become a practical scientist.

Naturally, he had never studied irrigation before, but using his mission as his school, he researched diligently for several years, finally developing his own water-engineering versions of the Three Character Classic (“Deep silted river, build low dams”) and Eight Character Mantra (“Where the river bends, dig through its heart”) that remained standard precepts of water engineering right up to the twentieth century.

His scholarship will forever have moisture running through it, whereas many thick tomes from who knows how many years after him have already become desiccated, so brittle their pages are impossible to turn.

Li Bing didn’t anticipate that his tactics for diverting water would be adopted as a stratagem for controlling the populace. He didn’t expect that the fertile land he’d hoped to irrigate would frequently become a battleground in time to come, its rice crops largely requisitioned as provisions for troops. All he knew was that if humanity wanted to prevent its own extinction, then it would require a source of clean water and grain.

He was enormously foolish, and also a genius. He was clumsy, and also extraordinarily dexterous. With the mindset of an old farmer in his fields, he found his way into the sharpest philosophies of anthropology.

He didn’t leave us any kind of life story, only the solid mass of the irrigation structure, leaving us to guess. People arrive in this place lost in bewilderment: just who was this person? He died more than two thousand years ago, yet continues to direct the flow of water today. Standing at the pavilions in the center of the river, listening to cries of “you go this way, he’ll go that way,” shouted admonishments, reassuring words. No one person could be so long-lived.

In his lifetime, Li Bing was already contemplating the continuation of his work. He ordered his son to construct three stone figures, to be fixed on the riverbed as indicators of the water level. About four hundred years after his death, perhaps because these stone figures had been damaged, a Han Dynasty Water Official ordered three three-meter high “Water Gods” to replace them. And among these new stone figures, one was actually a likeness of Li Bing.

The Han Dynasty official must have been the recipient of Li Bing’s mighty spirit to have had the audacity to place this revered figure from the past in the middle of the river to calm the flow and gauge the water level. He knew what Li Bing’s purpose was, and judged that this would be the most suitable position from which to carry out his work.

These stone statues were gradually buried by years of accumulated silt. When they were unearthed in the 1970s, one figure was missing its head, though its hand still clutched the long handle of a shovel. Some people conjecture that this must be Li Bing’s son. Even if it turned out not to be, I’d still see him as his son. A contemporary female writer was moved by this sight: “Buried in mud but still smiling warmly, a broken neck but still clutching a spade.” In this way, she asked of the imperious bureaucracy of the present day: whether alive or dead, where ought we to stand?

The excavated statues are now on display in the Dragon Taming Temple. In the midst of the cacophonous flow, visitors can pay silent obeisance to them. In this place, I suddenly developed a sort of optimism towards Chinese history: as long as Li Bing’s spirit remains intact, his sons will multiply, generation by generation. The thunderous water is the highest form of last words, a statement that resonates long after death.

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: I SAW A BRIDGE stretching high over the river, made of thick rope and bamboo strips. It started swaying fiercely as soon as I stepped onto it, and the more I hesitated, the greater was its movement.

Peering down from such a high vantage point would inevitably be unsettling, but this bridge was full of gaps, and there was no way to avoid seeing between them. Glancing below me, I felt first terror, and then wonder.

The gushing river beneath my feet had raced here from very far away, riding its momentum without a backward glance, clutching the icy wind, spitting white foam, rushing forward powerfully. Even at this height, I could sense its piercingly cold energy—I’m guessing it originated from the snowy hills. But then just at the other side of the bridge, it separated into glittering streams and rivulets, kindly eyes beneath frowning brows. To think human management of nature could take place so briskly. If humankind were so efficient in all its affairs, the earth would be a very different place.
Dujiangyan’s philosophy of harnessing the forces of nature could be summed up by the nearby Mount Qingcheng.

This mountain is a holy ground for Taoism, the only major religion indigenous to China. Taoism absorbed the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi, and uses water as a key image in its belief system. Water appears completely soft, yet can also possess great force, manifesting in surging waves that can overpower all before them; it seems colorless and flavorless, yet spreads itself before us as an endless green plain, sweeping ahead in victory, blazing with all shades and hues; it appears to seek the lowest level, yet can rise as vapor to the highest heavens, become clouds and rain, rainbows and fog; it seems formless, yet has the ability to be the savior of all living things, so we pray and long for it…

So while humankind apparently has control over water, all successful water systems actually depend on people understanding water, responding to it, obeying it. Only under these circumstances can the earth and humanity be one, without individual selfishness, thereby living forever.
This is the Tao, the path.

I believe that the “Tao” of Taoism is the path of water, of nature and humanity, of longevity. It is therefore also the path of Li Bing, of Dujiangyan. Tao is present everywhere, but in Dujiangyan it presents a unified appearance.

And so to have Dujiangyan and Mount Qingcheng next to each other, paralleling and validating each other, has created the most concentrated, most natural classroom in which to investigate Chinese philosophy.

That day, with Dujiangyan’s water vapor still about me, I slowly walked up Mount Qingcheng in silent contemplation Coming upon a Taoist temple, I went in for a short rest. Recognizing me, the priest brought out ink and paper for me to leave a few words. On the spot, I wrote a most simple couplet:
Paying respects to water at Dujiangyan,
Seeking the path on Mount Qingcheng.

And I thought, if we could only fully understand the millennia-old miracle of Dujiangyan, “paying respects to water” and “seeking the path” could be a single pursuit, and in this way, we’d have uncovered a great secret of Chinese culture.

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 莫高窟门外，有一条河。过河有一片空地，高高低低建着几座僧人圆寂塔。塔呈圆形，状近葫芦，外敷白色。我去时，有几座已经坍弛，还没有修复。只见塔心是一个个木桩，塔身全是黄土，垒在青砖基座上。夕阳西下，朔风凛冽，整个塔群十分凄凉。
有一座塔显得比较完整，大概是修建年代比较近吧。好在塔身有碑，移步一读，猛然一惊：它的主人，竟然就是那个王圆箓！
再小的个子，也能给沙漠留下长长的身影；再小的人物，也能让历史吐出重重的叹息。王圆箓既是小个子，又是小人物。我见过他的照片，穿着土布棉衣，目光呆滞，畏畏缩缩，是那个时代随处可以见到的一个中国平民。他原是湖北麻城的农民，在甘肃当过兵，后来为了谋生做了道士。几经转折，当了敦煌莫高窟的家。
莫高窟以佛教文化为主，怎么会让一个道士来当家？中国的民间信仰本来就是羼杂互融的，王圆箓几乎是个文盲，对道教并不专精，对佛教也不抵拒，却会主持宗教仪式，又会化缘募款，由他来管管这一片冷窟荒庙，也算正常。
但是，世间很多看起来很正常的现象常常掩盖着一个可怕的黑洞。莫高窟的惊人蕴藏，使王圆箓这个守护者与守护对象之间产生了文化等级上的巨大的落差。这个落差，就是黑洞。

我曾读到潘絜兹先生和其他敦煌学专家写的一些书，其中记述了王道士的日常生活。他经常出去化缘，得到一些钱后，就找来一些很不高明的当地工匠，先用草刷蘸上石灰把精美的古代壁画刷去，再抡起铁锤把塑像打毁，用泥巴堆起灵官之类，因为他是道士。但他又想到这里毕竟是佛教场所，于是再让那些工匠用石灰把下寺的墙壁刷白，绘上唐代玄奘到西天取经的故事。他四处打量，觉得一个个洞窟太憋气了，便要工匠们把它们打通。大片的壁画很快灰飞烟灭，成了走道。做完这些事，他又去化缘，准备继续刷，继续砸，继续堆，继续画。
这些记述的语气都很平静，但我每次读到，脑海里也总像被刷了石灰一般，一片惨白。我几乎不会言动，眼前一直晃动着那些草刷和铁锤。
“住手！”我在心底呼喊，只见王道士转过脸来，满脸困惑不解。我甚至想低声下气地恳求他：“请等一等，等一等……”但是等什么呢？我脑中依然一片惨白。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 一九○○年六月二十二日（农历五月二十六日），王道士从一个姓杨的帮工那里得知，一处洞窟的墙壁里面好像是空的，里边可能还隐藏着一个洞穴。两人挖开一看，嗬，果然一个满满实实的藏经洞！
王道士完全不明白，此刻，他打开了一扇轰动世界的门户。一门永久性的学问，将靠着这个洞穴建立。无数才华横溢的学者，将为这个洞穴耗尽终生。而且，从这一天开始，他的实际地位已经直蹿而上，比世界上很多著名博物馆馆长还高。但是，他不知道，他不可能知道。
他随手拿了几个经卷到知县那里鉴定，知县又拿给其他官员看。官员中有些人知道一点轻重，建议运到省城，却又心疼运费，便要求原地封存。在这个过程中，消息已经传开，有些经卷已经流出，引起了在新疆的一些外国人士的注意。
当时，英国、德国、法国、俄国等列强，正在中国的西北地区进行着一场考古探险的大拼搏。这个态势，与它们瓜分整个中国的企图紧紧相连。因此，我们应该稍稍离开莫高窟一会儿，看一看全局。
就在王道士发现藏经洞的前几天，在北京，英、德、法、俄、美等外交使团又一次集体向清政府递交照会，要求严惩义和团。恰恰在王道士发现藏经洞的当天，列强决定联合出兵——这就是后来攻陷北京，迫使朝廷外逃，最终又迫使中国赔偿四亿五千万两白银的“八国联军”。
时间，怎么会这么巧？
好像是北京东交民巷外国使馆里的一个决定，立即刺痛了一个庞大机体的神经系统。于是，西北沙漠中一个洞穴的门，霎时打开了。
更巧的是，仅仅在几个月前，甲骨文也被发现了。
我想，藏经洞与甲骨文一样，最能体现一个民族的文化自信。因此，必须猛然出现在这个民族即将失去自信的时刻。
即使是巧合，也是一种伟大的巧合。
遗憾的是，中国学者不能像解读甲骨文一样解读藏经洞了，因为那里的经卷已被悄悄转移。

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 产生这个结果，是因为莫高窟里三个男人的见面。
第一个就是“主人”王圆箓，不多说了。
第二个是匈牙利人斯坦因，刚加入英国籍不久，此时受印度政府和大英博物馆指派，到中国的西北地区考古。他博学、刻苦、机敏、能干，其考古专业水准堪称世界一流，却又具有一个殖民主义者的文化傲慢。他精通七八种语言，却不懂中文，因此引出了第三个人——翻译蒋孝琬。
蒋孝琬长得清瘦文弱，湖南湘阴人。这个人是中国十九世纪后期出现的买办群体中的一个。这个群体在沟通两种文明的过程中常常备受心灵煎熬，又两面不讨好。我一直建议艺术家们在表现中国近代题材的时候不要放过这种桥梁式的悲剧性典范。但是，蒋孝琬好像是这个群体中的异类，他几乎没有感受任何心灵煎熬。
斯坦因到达新疆喀什时，发现聚集在那里的外国考古学家们有一个共识，就是千万不要与中国学者合作。理由是，中国学者一到关键时刻，例如，在关及文物所有权的当口上，总会在心底产生“华夷之防”的敏感，给外国人带来种种阻碍。但是，蒋孝琬完全不是这样，那些外国人告诉斯坦因：“你只要带上了他，敦煌的事情一定成功。”
事实果然如此。从喀什到敦煌的漫长路途上，蒋孝琬一直在给斯坦因讲述中国官场和中国民间的行事方式。到了莫高窟，所有联络、刺探、劝说王圆箓的事，都是蒋孝琬在做。
王圆箓从一开始，就对斯坦因抱着一种警惕、躲闪、拒绝的态度。蒋孝琬蒙骗他说，斯坦因从印度过来，是要把当年玄奘取来的经送回原处去，为此还愿意付一些钱。
王圆箓像很多中国平民一样，对《西游记》里的西天取经故事既熟悉又崇拜，听蒋孝琬绘声绘色地一说，又看到斯坦因神情庄严地一次次焚香拜佛，竟然心有所动。因此，当蒋孝琬提出要先“借”几个“样本”看看时，王圆箓虽然迟疑、含糊了很久，但终于还是塞给了他几个经卷。
于是，又是蒋孝琬，连夜挑灯研读那几个经卷。他发现，那正巧是玄奘取来的经卷的译本。这几个经卷，明明是王圆箓随手取的，居然果真与玄奘有关。王圆箓激动地看着自己的手指，似乎听到了佛的旨意。洞穴的门，向斯坦因打开了。
当然，此后在经卷堆里逐页翻阅选择的，也是蒋孝琬，因为斯坦因本人不懂中文。
蒋孝琬在那些日日夜夜所做的事，也可以说成是一种重要的文化破读，因为这毕竟是千年文物与能够读懂它的人的第一次隆重相遇。而且，事实证明，蒋孝琬对中国传统文化有着广博的知识、不浅的根底。
那些寒冷的沙漠之夜，斯坦因和王圆箓都睡了，只有他在忙着。睡着的两方都不懂得这一堆堆纸页上的内容，只有他懂得，由他作出取舍裁断。
就这样，一场天下最不公平的“买卖”开始了。斯坦因用极少的钱，换取了中华文明长达好几个世纪的大量文物。而且由此形成惯例，各国冒险家们纷至沓来，满载而去。
有一天王圆箓觉得斯坦因实在要得太多了，就把部分挑出的文物又搬回到藏经洞。斯坦因要蒋孝琬去谈判，用四十块马蹄银换回那些文物。蒋孝琬谈判的结果，居然只花了四块就解决了问题。斯坦因立即赞扬他，说这是又一场“中英外交谈判”的胜利。
蒋孝琬一听，十分得意。我对他的这种得意有点厌恶。因为他应该知道，自从鸦片战争以来，所谓的“中英外交谈判”意味着什么。我并不奢望在他心底会对当时已经极其可怜的父母之邦产生一点点惭愧，而只是想，这种桥梁式的人物如果把一方河岸完全扒塌了，他们以后还能干什么？
由此我想，对那些日子莫高窟里的三个男人，我们还应该多看几眼。前面两个一直遭世人非议，而最后一个总是被轻轻放过。
比蒋孝琬更让我吃惊的是，近年来中国文化界有一些评论者一再宣称，斯坦因以考古学家的身份取走敦煌藏经洞的文物并没有错，是正大光明的事业，而像我这样耿耿于怀，却是“狭隘的民族主义”。
是“正大光明”吗？请看斯坦因自己的回忆：
深夜我听到了细微的脚步声，那是蒋在侦察，看是否有人在我的帐篷周围出现。一会儿他扛了一个大包回来，那里装有我今天白天挑出的一切东西。王道士鼓足勇气同意了我的请求，但条件很严格，除了我们三个外，不得让任何人得知这笔交易，哪怕是丝毫暗示。
从这种神态动作，你还看不出他们在做什么吗？

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 斯坦因终于取得了九千多个经卷、五百多幅绘画，打包装箱就整整花了七天时间。最后打成了二十九个大木箱，原先带来的那些骆驼和马匹不够用了，又雇来了五辆大车，每辆都拴上三匹马来拉。
那是一个黄昏，车队启动了。王圆箓站在路边，恭敬相送。斯坦因“购买”这二十九个大木箱的稀世文物，所支付给王圆箓的全部价钱，我一直不忍心写出来，此刻却不能不说一说了。那就是，三十英镑！但是，这点钱对王圆箓来说，毕竟比他平时到荒村野郊去化缘来的，多得多了。因此，他认为这位“斯大人”是“布施者”。
斯坦因向他招过手，抬起头来看看天色。
一位年轻诗人写道，斯坦因看到的，是凄艳的晚霞。那里，一个古老民族的伤口在流血。
我又想到了另一位年轻诗人的诗——他叫李晓桦，诗是写给下令火烧圆明园的额尔金勋爵的：
我好恨
恨我没早生一个世纪
使我能与你对视着站立在
阴森幽暗的古堡
晨光微露的旷野
要么我拾起你扔下的白手套
要么你接住我甩过去的剑
要么你我各乘一匹战马
远远离开遮天的帅旗
离开如云的战阵
决胜负于城下
对于斯坦因这些学者，这些诗句也许太硬。但是，除了这种办法，还有什么方式能阻拦他们呢？
我可以不带剑，也不骑马，只是伸出双手做出阻拦的动作，站在沙漠中间，站在他们车队的正对面。
满脸堆笑地走上前来的，一定是蒋孝琬。我扭头不理他，只是直视着斯坦因，要与他辩论。
我要告诉他，把世间文物统统拔离原生的土地，运到地球的另一端收藏展览，是文物和土地的双向失落、两败俱伤。我还要告诉他，借口别人管不好家产而占为己有，是一种掠夺……
我相信，也会有一种可能，尽管概率微乎其微——我的激情和逻辑终于压倒了斯坦因，于是车队果真被我拦了下来。
那么，接下来该怎么办呢？当然应该送交京城。但当时，藏经洞文物不是也有一批送京的吗？其情景是，没有木箱，只用席子捆扎，沿途官员缙绅伸手进去就取走一把。有些官员还把大车赶进自己的院子里精挑细选，择优盗取。盗取后又怕到京后点数不符，便把长卷撕成几个短卷来凑数搪塞。
当然，更大的麻烦是，那时的中国处处军阀混战，北京更是乱成一团。在兵丁和难民的洪流中，谁也不知道脚下的土地明天将会插上哪家的军旗。几辆装载古代经卷的车，怎么才能通过？怎样才能到达？
那么，不如叫住斯坦因，还是让他拉到伦敦的博物馆里去吧。但我当然不会这么做。我知道斯坦因看出了我的难处，因为我发现，被迫留下了车队而离去的他，正一次次回头看我。
我假装没有看见，只用眼角余光默送他和蒋孝琬慢慢远去，终于消失在黛褐色的山丘后面。然后，我再回过身来。
长长一排车队，全都停在苍茫夜色里，由我掌管。但是，明天该去何方？这里也难，那里也难，我左思右想，最后只能跪倒在沙漠里，大哭一场。哭声，像一匹受伤的狼在黑夜里嗥叫。

sections.label: 五
paragraphs: 一九四三年十月二十六日，八十二岁的斯坦因在阿富汗的喀布尔去世。
此时是中国抗日战争进行得最艰苦的日子。中国，又一次在生死关头被世人认知，也被自己认知。
在斯坦因去世的前一天，伦敦举行“中国日”活动，博物馆里的敦煌文物又一次引起热烈关注。
在斯坦因去世的同一天，中国历史学会在重庆成立。
我知道处于弥留之际的斯坦因不可能听到这两个消息。
有一件小事让我略感奇怪，那就是斯坦因的墓碑铭文：
马尔克·奥莱尔·斯坦因
印度考古调查局成员
学者、探险家兼作家
通过极为困难的印度、中国新疆、波斯、伊拉克之行，扩展了知识领域
他平生带给西方世界最大的轰动是敦煌藏经洞，为什么在墓碑铭文里故意回避了，只提“中国新疆”？敦煌并不在新疆，而是在甘肃。
我约略知道此间原因。那就是，他在莫高窟的所作所为，已经受到文明世界越来越严厉的谴责。
阿富汗的喀布尔，是斯坦因非常陌生的地方。整整四十年他一直想进去而未被允许，刚被允许进入，却什么也没有看到就离开了人世。
他被安葬在喀布尔郊区的一个外国基督教徒公墓里，但他的灵魂又怎么能安定下来？
直到今天，这里还备受着贫困、战乱和宗教极端主义的包围。而且，蔓延四周的宗教极端主义，正好与他信奉的宗教完全对立。小小的墓园，是那样孤独、荒凉和脆弱。
我想，他的灵魂最渴望的，是找一个黄昏，一个与他赶着车队离开时一样的黄昏，再潜回敦煌去看看。
如果真有这么一个黄昏，那么，他见了那座道士塔，会与王圆箓说什么呢？
我想，王圆箓不会向他抱怨什么，却会在他面前稍稍显得有点趾高气扬。因为道士塔前，天天游人如潮，虽然谁也没有投来过尊重的目光。而斯坦因的墓地前，永远阒寂无人。
至于另一个男人，那个蒋孝琬的坟墓在哪里，我就完全不知道了。有知道的朋友，能告诉我吗？

sections.label: I
paragraphs: A RIVER FLOWS past the entrance to the Mogao Grottoes. Across the river is a patch of land on which stand several structures of varying heights: the memorial stupas of deceased monks. They are round, resembling bottle gourds in silhouette, and painted white. When I visited, several of them had collapsed and not yet been restored. Each revealed a wooden pillar at the heart of the stupa, and around that yellow earth heaped atop a foundation of green bricks. By the light of the setting sun, as the icy north wind blew, this group of stupas appeared extremely desolate.

One of them was relatively intact, perhaps because it had been recently restored. Fortunately, it bore a plaque; when I stepped closer to read it, I was startled to discover that its owner was none other than Wang Yuanlu.

The smallest figure may cast a long shadow across the desert; the least significant individual, may cause history to heave a heavy sigh. Wang Yuanlu was a small figure, and also an insignificant individual. I have seen pictures of him—dressed in homespun padded clothes, a sluggish gaze, a cowering posture. He was the archetype of the Chinese commoner, such as could be seen everywhere during that era. Originally from a farming family in Macheng City, Hubei, he entered the army in Gansu, then subsequently decided to make his living as a Taoist priest. After several twists and turns, he was put in charge of the Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang.

These caves are a stronghold of Buddhist culture—so how could a Taoist priest have been put in charge of them? Well, China’s folk religions have always existed in harmony, mingling with and influencing one another. Wang Yuanlu was practically illiterate, neither particularly knowledgeable about Taoism nor opposed to Buddhism. He could conduct a religious ceremony, and knew how to supplicate and raise funds, so it was perfectly normal that he would be appointed to watch over this site of deserted caves and empty temples.

Yet in this world, many apparently normal situations often turn out to be concealing fearsome pitfalls. The startling contents of the Mogao Caves ended up creating a massive cultural disparity between their guardian, Wang Yuanlu, and the objects he was meant to be guarding. This disparity was such a black hole.

I’ve read books by Mr. Pan Jiezi and other Dunhuang specialists that described an ordinary day in the life of Abbot Wang. He often went out seeking alms, and after he’d raised sufficient money, would hire some not-particularly-skilled local craftsmen to whitewash the ancient wall paintings with straw brushes and lime, then take a hammer to the statues and bury the spirit officials and other figures in mud—all because he was a Taoist priest. But then he’d recall that this was, after all, a Buddhist site, and order those same workmen to whitewash the walls of the lower temple, then adorn them with a mural of Xuanzang fetching scriptures from the west in the Tang Dynasty. Finally, he’d look around, decide that all these little caves were too suffocatingly small, and have a passage smashed through linking them, so in short order vast areas of cave paintings were reduced to swirling dust. After he’d done all this, there’d come another round of alms, raising funds for more whitewashing, more smashing, more burying, more painting.

The tone of these accounts is fairly measured, but I cannot read them without my brain, too, becoming coated with lime, reduced to a patch of stark white. I become virtually incapable of speech, and before my eyes sway those straw brushes and metal hammers.

“Stop!” I scream in my heart, only to see Abbot Wang turn toward me, his face full of incomprehension. I’d even be ready to beg in a humble voice, “Please hold on a little, just wait…” But wait for what? My mind is a patch of stark white.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: ON JUNE 22, 1900 (the 26th day of the fifth month, by the Lunar calendar), Abbot Wang learned from a worker named Yang that one of the grottoes had a hollow-sounding wall, which meant it might conceal an inner cave. The two men pried it open, and—I say!—a library cache was revealed, crammed full of hidden scriptures.

Abbot Wang never fully understood how, at that moment, he was opening a door that would startle the world; an enduring branch of scholarship was established based on the contents of that cave, occupying countless top-ranking academics for their entire lives. In addition, from this day on, his actual position would rocket upwards, attaining a status even higher than the directors of many famous history museums. But he didn’t know this, and couldn’t possibly have known.

He grabbed a few of the scrolls and brought them to the head magistrate of the county to be appraised. The magistrate in turn showed them to his fellow officials, some of whom knew a little of such matters, and recommended that they be sent to the provincial capital. In the end, though, the expense of this move was thought too great, and it was requested that the scriptures be stored in their original site. As this process ground on, news was beginning to spread, and some of the scrolls had made their way into other hands, attracting the attention of some foreigners in Xinjiang.

At the time, Britain, Germany, France, Russia and the other great powers were engaged in a struggle for archaeological dominance in the northwest of China. This situation was closely connected to their desire to carve up China itself between them. And so, let us now take a moment’s leave of the Mogao Caves, stepping back to see the bigger picture.

In the few days before the abbot’s discovery, the diplomatic missions of Britain, Germany, France, Russia, America and so on in Beijing had been petitioning the Qing government en masse, requesting that the Boxers be severely punished for their rebellion. By coincidence, the day Abbot Wang found the secret cave is the day the Great Powers decided to raise an allied army—this was the so-called “Eight-Nation Alliance” that later invaded Beijing, forcing the imperial court to flee the capital, and finally compelled China to pay compensation of 450 million taels of silver—that is, one tael for every Chinese person.
Was this entirely by chance?

It seems as if when the embassies in Beijing’s Legation Quarter made the decision to attack China, a shock of pain was sent through the nervous system of a vast entity, causing the door to a cave in the northwestern desert to momentarily pop open.
Even more serendipitous, just a few months prior, jiaguwen bone script had also been discovered.

I believe the hidden manuscripts were like jiaguwen, the embodiment of a people’s cultural self-belief. And at the moment when we had lost almost all our self-confidence, these artifacts made an appearance when they were most needed.
Even if it was a coincidence, it was a noble coincidence.
Regrettably, Chinese scholars would be unable to analyze the cave scriptures in the same way they would study jiaguwen, because the ownership of those scrolls had already quietly changed hands.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: THIS OUTCOME was the result of three men meeting in the Mogao Grottoes.
The first was their “master,” Wang Yuanlu. We don’t need to say anything further about him.

The second man was the Hungarian Aurel Stein who, not long after acquiring British citizenship, was appointed by the Indian government and the British Museum to lead an expedition to the northwest region of China. He was erudite, hardworking, resourceful and capable, and his archaeological skills could be said to be among the best in the world, yet he also possessed the cultural arrogance of the colonialist. He spoke seven or eight languages, but not a word of Chinese—which necessitated the presence of the third person, the interpreter Jiang Xiaowan.

Jiang, a slender, etiolated man from Xiangyin in Hubei, was one of the class of compradors who had begun appearing in late nineteenth-century China. This group existed to facilitate communication between two civilizations, an often painful process that could leave the mediator with enemies on both sides. I have always urged our artists, when presenting material from China’s recent past, not to neglect the tragic examples of such bridging figures. Yet Jiang Xiaowan appears to have been an exception within his tribe, in that he seems to have endured almost no mental suffering in the course of his duties.

When Aurel Stein arrived in Kashgar, he found that all the foreign archaeologists held one piece of wisdom in common: never work with a Chinese scholar. Their reasoning was that when it came to the crucial moment, such as when the ownership of relics was in the balance, their latent “Chinese defense against foreigners” would rise to the surface, and they’d create all kinds of obstacles. Jiang Xiaowan, though, was not at all like this, and Stein was told by various people, “As long as you bring Jiang with you, the Dunhuang affair is sure to have a happy resolution.”

Sure enough, that’s how things turned out. All the long journey from Kashgar to Dunhuang, Jiang Xiaowan explained to Stein how Chinese bureaucracy worked, and how things were done among the common folk, knowledge that Stein came to believe was more important than anything he could have learned from several academic degrees. When they arrived at the Mogao Caves, the process of communicating with, probing, and finally persuading Wang Yuanlu was entirely in the hands of Jiang.

From the start, Wang Yuanlu was cautious, evasive and negative around Stein. Jiang lied to him, claiming Stein had just arrived from India with the aim of retrieving the scriptures brought over by Xuanzang back in the day, and with the aim of returning them to their original home—and he was willing to pay. Like many ordinary Chinese people, Wang Yuanlu knew and revered the story of the scriptures through the novel Journey to the West. Hearing Jiang’s vivid description, and seeing Stein repeatedly offer incense to Buddha with the utmost solemnity, Wang couldn’t help but be moved. And so, when Jiang suggested “lending” a few “samples” to Stein, Wang hesitated and obfuscated for a long time, but ultimately agreed to release a few scrolls.

Once again it was Jiang who stayed up all night, reading these scrolls by lamplight. He discovered that by sheer chance, they were indeed translations of the original scriptures brought back by Xuanzang. Wang had picked them at random from the pile, and they actually were connected to Xuanzang. At the news, Wang Yuanlu peered excitedly at his own fingers, as if witnessing a sign from Buddha. The door to the cave was now open to Aurel Stein.

Of course, the work of sifting through the pile of scrolls fell to Jiang too, because Stein couldn’t read Chinese. What Jiang did in those days and nights could be called an important cultural breakthrough—the momentous first encounter between these millennium-old artifacts and a person capable of understanding them. As later evidence shows, Jiang Xiaowan’s knowledge of China’s traditional culture was broad and deep-rooted.

Several cold desert nights passed. Long after Aurel Stein and Wang Yuanlu had fallen asleep, Jiang remained busy. His slumbering colleagues had no way of reading these mounds of paper, and only he could make the decision as to what was worth taking.

In this way, one of the most unjust transactions in the world began. Stein offered a minuscule sum of money in exchange for a vast number of Chinese artifacts dating back many, many centuries. With this precedent, adventurers from the other Great Powers would later begin arriving thick and fast, departing with equally impressive hauls.

There came a day when Wang felt Stein was demanding too much, and moved a portion of the scriptures back into the storage cave. Stein sent Jiang to talk to him, with an offer of forty horse-hoof silver ingots in exchange for their return. As a result of Jiang’s mediation, the matter was resolved with an expenditure of only four ingots. Stein effusively lauded Jiang for yet another successful round of “Sino-British diplomatic negotiations,” praise that caused Jiang to feel very pleased with himself. I find something particularly repulsive in his self-satisfaction. He certainly ought to have known, particularly after the Opium War, what “Sino-British diplomatic negotiations” hinted at. I don’t hold out any wild hopes that he might have felt the least bit of shame for his actions towards the already embattled land of his ancestors, but I have to wonder, when such individuals who make their living as bridges facilitate the utter looting of one river bank, what can they possibly hope to live on afterwards?

The way I see it, we should take a closer look at the three men who met in the Mogao Grottoes over those days. The first two have come in for a fair amount of criticism, whereas the third is usually passed over too lightly.

What I find even more startling is the way, in recent years, certain commentators in the world of Chinese culture have started asserting that Aurel Stein was not wrong to remove the Dunhuang scriptural artifacts in his role as an archaeologist, that this enterprise was honest and aboveboard, and that the unease I feel is no more than “narrow-minded nationalist ideology.”
Was this “honest and aboveboard?” Let’s look at Stein’s own recollection:

It was late at night when I heard cautious footsteps. It was Chiang [Jiang] who had come to make sure that nobody was stirring about my tent. A little later he returned with a big bundle over his shoulders. It contained everything I had picked out during the day’s work. The Tao-shih [abbot] had summoned up courage to fall in with my wishes, on the solemn condition that nobody besides us three was to get the slightest inkling of what was being transacted.
Isn’t it obvious, from the way they went about it, what they were really up to?

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: AUREL STEIN eventually made off with more than nine thousand scrolls, and more than five hundred drawings. It took seven days to pack these artifacts into twenty-nine large wooden trunks, more than the camels and horses he had brought with him could carry. He was forced to hire five large wagons, each pulled by three horses.

It was evening when the caravan got underway. Wang Yuanlu stood by the roadside, respectfully seeing them off. As for the actual amount of money Stein paid to “buy” these twenty-nine trunks of rare objects from Wang Yuanlu, I have so far not been able to bear writing it down, but it must be mentioned: about thirty English pounds, converted into silver! But to Wang Yuanlu, this was significantly more than he could ever have hoped to accumulate begging for alms in these remote villages. To his mind, “Sir Stein” was practicing dāna, or giving.
Stein waved farewell to him, then looked up at the sky.
A young poet once wrote that what Stein would have seen was the mournful splendor of twilight, the bleeding wound of an ancient civilization.
This puts me in mind of some lines by another young poet named Li Xiaohua, addressed to Lord Elgin who gave the order for the old Summer Palace to be burned down:
How I regret
Regret not being born a century sooner
That I may have stood locking eyes with you
In the eerie gloom of the ancient palace
The first rays of sun hitting this wilderness
Perhaps me taking up the white glove you flung down
Perhaps you catching the rapier I threw across
Perhaps us both mounted on battle steeds
Far away from flags and insignias
Away from battle formations
Dueling for victory beneath the city walls
These words might seem too harsh on scholars such as Stein, but apart from these methods, how else could we stop them?
I’m happy not to bear a sword, or even not to ride a horse, merely stand in the middle of the desert with my arms raised, blocking the path of their caravan.
The person who walks up to me, his face buried in smiles, must surely be Jiang Xiaowan. I turn my head and ignore him, staring directly at Aurel Stein instead, demanding to parley with him.

I tell Stein that to pluck the cultural artifacts of the world from their original sites and putting them on display on the other side of the world is a loss to both the lands they come from and the objects themselves, doing harm to both. I further point out that using the excuse of other nations being unable to take good care of their own possessions and so seizing them for yourself, is an act of cultural theft no different from the plundering of an invading army.
I like to believe the possibility exists, no matter how faint, that my passion and logic defeat Stein, and I do indeed cause the caravan to halt in its tracks.

In that case, what would the next step be? Naturally the artifacts would need to be delivered to the capital. But hadn’t a batch of the scrolls already been sent to Beijing? That’s true, but the reality is: there was no wooden trunk, they were merely wrapped in a straw mat, and along the way various officials and aristocrats reached their arms in and plucked some away for themselves, some even diverting the carriage into their own courtyards, the better to take their time making a selection, to ensure they stole only the very best. Then, afraid the shortfall would be noticed, they ripped some of the long scrolls into several shorter ones, in order to bolster the numbers.

The bigger problem is that China was at the time riddled with skirmishes and outbreaks of military violence, and Beijing was in even more anarchic. Between the flows of troops and refugees, no one knew whose flag would be plunged into the ground beneath their feet the next day. How could a few wagons full of ancient manuscripts hope to make it through this chaos? Would they ever arrive?

So fine, why not just call on Stein, and let him haul them back to the museum in London after all. But no, of course I wouldn’t do that. I know Stein is aware of my dilemma, because he keeps turning back to look at me.
I pretend not to notice, only watching him and Jiang Xiaowan slowly depart out of the corner of my eye. When they’ve finally vanished behind a dark brown hill, I turn around again.
The long, long caravan is standing there beneath the boundless night sky, entirely under my command. So where will we go tomorrow?
Every place I can think of is fraught with difficulty. I ponder the matter frantically, finally collapsing onto my knees on the desert floor, weeping furiously.
My sobs sound like the nighttime howls of an injured wolf.

sections.label: V
paragraphs: ON OCTOBER 26, 1943, the 80-year-old Aurel Stein passed away in Kabul, Afghanistan.
This was during the most bitter period of the Sino-Japanese war. Once more, China was acknowledged by others at a crisis of life and death, and also acknowledged that itself.
The day before Stein’s death, London held a “China Day,” and the Dunhuang artifacts in the museum once again came under scrutiny.
The day of his death, the Chinese Historical Society was founded in Chongqing.
I wonder whether Stein, on the boundary of worlds, was able to hear of these two items of news.
Another details startles me. These are the words engraved on Stein’s gravestone:
Mark Aurel Stein
Of the Indian Archaeological Survey
Scholar, Explorer, Author
By his arduous journeys in India, Chinese Turkistan, Persia and Iraq he enlarged the bounds of knowledge

The discovery of his that caused the greatest worldwide stir during his lifetime was the Dunhuang scripture library. Why is this deliberately left out of his epitaph, with only the mention of “Chinese Turkistan” (that is, Xinjiang)? Dunhuang is not in Xinjiang, but in Gansu.
I think I can guess at the reason: his actions in the Mogao Grottoes had already begun attracting more and more criticism from the civilized world.

Kabul would have been a very unfamiliar place to Stein. He’d wanted to travel to Afghanistan for forty years, but been refused permission many times to enter the country. When he finally gained admittance, he left the world a short while later, without having seen anything of the land he’d so longed to visit.

He was buried on the outskirts of Kabul, in a cemetery for Christian foreigners, but is his soul able to be at peace there? Up to this day, the area has been surrounded by poverty, war, and religious extremism. What’s more, the religious extremism spreading in all directions happens to be of a faith directly opposed to his own. That little graveyard must be so lonely, so weak and abandoned.
I think what his spirit must most desire is, on an evening like the one on which he departed at the head of a caravan, to return to Dunhuang.
If there really were to be such an evening, then when he saw Wang Yuanle’s stupa, what would he say to its owner?

I imagine that Abbot Wang would have no complaints to direct at him, but might perhaps be a little high-handed in his attitude. After all, throngs of tourists pass by the stupa every day, even if not one of them ever sends an admiring glance in his direction, while Stein’s grave is forever empty of visitors, deserted.
As for the third man, Jiang Xiaowan, I have no idea at all where his grave is. If anyone possesses this knowledge, please let me know?

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 公元三六六年，有一位僧人在敦煌东南方鸣沙山东麓的断崖上开始开凿石窟，后来代代有人继续，这就成了著名的莫高窟。
佛教在印度传播之初，石窟是僧人修行的场所，却不在里边雕塑和描绘佛像，要表现也只用象征物来替代，用得比较多的有金牛、佛塔、法柱等。后来到了犍陀罗时期，受到亚历山大大帝东征时带来的希腊雕塑家们的影响，开始开凿佛像石窟。因此，人们往往可以从那里发现希腊雕塑的明显痕迹。
这就是说，仅仅是佛像石窟，就已经把印度文明和希腊文明包罗在里边了。这些石窟大多处于荒山野岭之间，远远看去很不起眼，哪里知道里面所蕴藏的，却是两个伟大文明的精彩。
佛教从印度一进入中国，立即明白这是一个需要用通俗、形象的方式来讲故事的国度，因此在石窟造像艺术中又融入了越来越浓重的中华世俗文明。结果，以人类的几大文明为背景，一代代的佛像都在石窟里深刻而又通俗地端庄着，微笑着，快乐着，行动着，苦涩着，牺牲着。渐渐地，这一切都与中华历史接通了血脉，甚至成了一部由坚石雕刻的历史。
莫高窟，便是其中的典型。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 看莫高窟，不是看死了一千年的标本，而是看活了一千年的生命。
让人惊奇的是，历来在莫高窟周边的各种政治势力，互相之间打得你死我活，却都愿意为莫高窟做一点好事。
北魏的王室、北周的贵族都对莫高窟的建造起了很大的作用，更不必说隋代、初唐、盛唐时莫高窟的欢快景象了。连“安史之乱”以后占领敦煌的吐蕃势力，以及驱逐吐蕃势力的张议潮军队，本是势不两立的敌人，却也都修护了莫高窟。
五代十国时期的曹氏政权对莫高窟贡献很大，到宋代，先后占领这一带的西夏政权和蒙古政权，也没有对莫高窟造成破坏。莫高窟到元代开始衰落，主要是由于蒙古军队打通了欧亚商贸路线，丝绸之路的作用减弱，敦煌变得冷清了。
为什么那么多赳赳武将、权谋强人都会在莫高窟面前低下头来？我想，第一是因为这里关及人间信仰，第二是因为这里已经构成历史。宗教的力量和时间的力量足以让那些燥热的心灵冷却下来，产生几分敬畏。他们突然变得像个孩子，一路撒野下来，到这里却睁大了眼睛，希望获得宗教裁判和时间裁判。
在这个过程中，更值得关注的是全民参与。佛教在莫高窟里摆脱了高深的奥义，通俗地展现因果报应、求福消灾、丰衣足食、繁衍子孙等内容，与民众非常亲近。除了壁画和雕塑外，莫高窟还是当地民众举行巡礼斋会的活动场所，也是享受日常娱乐的游览场所。但是，这种大众化趋向并没有使它下降为一个乡村庙会，因为敦煌地区一直拥有不少高僧大德、世族名士、博学贤达，维系着莫高窟的信仰主体。
于是，在莫高窟，我常常走神。不明亮的自然光亮从洞窟上方的天窗中淡淡映入，壁画上的人群和壁画前的雕塑融成了一体，在一片朦胧中似乎都动了起来。在他们身后，仿佛还能看到当年来这里参加巡礼的民众，一群又一群地簇拥着身穿袈裟的僧侣。还有很多画工、雕塑家在周边忙碌。这么多人渐渐走了，又来了一批。一批一批构成一代，一代代接连不断。
也有了声音：佛号、磬钹声、诵经声、木鱼声、旌旗飘荡声、民众笑语声，还有石窟外的山风声、流水声、马蹄声、驼铃声。
看了一会儿，听了一会儿，我发觉自己也被裹卷进去了。身不由己，踉踉跄跄，被人潮所挟，被声浪所融，被一种千年不灭的信仰所化。
这样的观看是一种晕眩，既十分陶醉又十分模糊。因此，我不能不在闭馆之后的黄昏，在人群全都离去的山脚下独自徘徊，一点点地找回记忆、找回自己。
晚风起了，夹着细沙，吹得脸颊发疼。沙漠的月亮分外清冷，山脚前有一泓泉流，在月色下波光闪烁。总算，我的思路稍见头绪。

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 记得每进一个洞窟，我总是抢先走到年代标示牌前，快速地算出年龄，然后再恭敬地抬起头来。
年龄最高的，已经一千六百多岁，在中国历史上算是十六国时期的作品。壁画上的菩萨还是西域神貌，甚至还能看出从印度起身时的样子，深线粗画，立体感强，还裸着上身，余留着恒河岸边的热气。另一些壁画，描绘着在血腥苦难中甘于舍身的狠心，看上去有点恐怖，可以想见当时世间的苦难气氛。
接下来应该是我非常向往的魏晋南北朝了：青褐的色泽依然浑厚，豪迈的笔触如同剑戟。中原一带有那么多潇洒的名士傲视着乱世，此时洞窟里也开始出现放达之风，连菩萨也由粗短身材变得修长活泼。某些形象，一派秀骨清相，甚至有病态之美，似乎与中原名士们的趣味遥相呼应。
不少的场面中出现了各种乐器，我叫不全它们的名字。
有很多年轻的女子衣带飘飘地飞了起来，是飞天。她们预示出全方位舞动的趋势，那是到了隋代。一个叫维摩诘的居士被频频描绘，让人联想到当时一些士族门阀企图在佛教理想中提升自己。壁画上已经找不到苦行，只有华丽。连病态之美也消失了，肌肤变得日渐圆润。那些雕塑略显腿短头大，马背上的历练，使他们气定神闲。
整个画面出现了扬眉吐气般的欢乐，那只能是唐代。春风浩荡，万物苏醒，连禽鸟都是舞者，连繁花都卷成了图案。天堂和人间连在了一起，个个表情生动，笔笔都有创造。女性越来越占据主导地位，而且不管是菩萨还是供养人，都呈现出充分的女性美。由于自信，他们的神情反而更加恬静、素淡和自然。画中的佛教道场已经以净土宗为主，启示人们只要念佛就能一起进入美好的净土。连这种简明的理想，也洋溢着只有盛唐才有的轻快和乐观。
唐代画面中的那些世间人物，不管是盔甲将军、西域胡商，还是壮硕力士、都督夫人，都神采飞扬、炯炯有神。更难得的是，我在这些人物形象中分明看到了吴道子画派的某种骨力，在背景山水中发现了李思训、李昭道父子那一派的辉煌笔意。欢乐，就此走向了经典。走向了经典还在欢乐，一点也没有装腔作态。
除了壁画，唐代的塑像更是风姿无限，不再清癯，不再呆板，连眉眼嘴角都洋溢着笑意，连衣褶薄襞都流泻得像音乐一般。
唐代洞窟中的一切都不重复，也不刻板。我立即明白，真正的欢乐不可能重复，就像真正的人性容不得刻板。结果，唐代的欢乐诱发了长久的欢乐，唐代的人性贴合了永恒的人性，一切都融合得浑然一体。恍惚间，热闹的洞窟里似乎什么也没有了，没有画，没有雕塑，没有年代，也没有思考，一切都要蒸腾而去，但又哪里也不想去，只在这里，在洞窟，在唐代，在吴道子笔下。
突然，精神一怔，我看到了一个异样的作品，表现了一个尽孝报恩的故事。与一般同类故事不同，这个佛家弟子是要帮助流亡的父母完成复国事业。我心中立即产生一种猜测，便俯身去看年代标示牌——果然，创作于“安史之乱”之后。
“安史之乱”，像一条长鞭，哗啦一声把唐代划成了两半。敦煌因为唐军东去讨逆而被吐蕃攻陷，因此，壁画中帮助流亡父母完成复国事业的内容，并非虚设。
悲壮的意志刻在了洞壁上，悲惨的岁月却刻在了大地上，赫赫唐代已经很难再回过神来。此后的洞窟，似乎一个个活气全消。也有看上去比较热闹的场面，但是，模仿的热闹只能是单调。
在单调中，记得还有一个舞者背手反弹琵琶的姿态，让我眼睛一亮。
再看下去，洞窟壁画的内容越来越世俗，连佛教题材也变成了现实写生，连天国道场也变成了家庭宅院，连教义演讲也变成了说书人的故事会。当然这也不错，颇有生活气息，并让我联想到了中国戏剧史上的瓦舍和诸宫调。
唐宋之间，还算有一些呆滞的华丽；而到了宋代，则走向了一种冷漠的贫乏。对此，我很不甘心。宋代，那是一个让中国人拥有苏东坡、王安石、司马光、朱熹、陆游、李清照、辛弃疾的时代啊，在敦煌怎么会是这样？我想，这与河西走廊上大大小小的政权纷争有关。在没完没了的轮番折腾中，文化之气受阻，边远之地只能消耗荒凉。
到了元代，出现了藏传密宗的壁画，题材不再黏着于现实生活，出现了一种我们不太习惯的神秘和恐怖。但是笔触精致细密，颇具装饰性，使人想到唐卡。
这是一个民族之间互窥互征的时代，蒙古文化和西藏文化在这一带此起彼伏。倒是有一个欧洲旅行家来过之后向外面报告，这里很安定，他就是马可·波罗。
明清时期的莫高窟，已经没有太多的东西可以记住。

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 当我在夜色中这么匆匆回想一遍后，就觉得眼前这个看上去十分寻常的“小山包”，实在是一个奇怪的所在。
它是河西走廊上的一个博物馆，也是半部中国艺术史，又是几大文明的交会点。它因深厚而沉默，也许，深厚正是沉默的原因。
但是，就像世界上的其他事情一样，兴旺发达时什么都好说，一到了衰落时期，一些争夺行动便接连而至。
二十世纪二十年代莫高窟曾经成为白俄士兵的滞留地。那些士兵在洞窟里支起了锅灶，生火做饭，黑烟和油污覆盖了大批壁画和雕塑。他们还用木棒蘸着黑漆，在壁画上乱涂乱画。
这些士兵走了以后，不久，一群美国人来了。他们是学者，大骂白俄士兵的胡作非为，当场立誓，要拯救莫高窟文物。他们的“拯救”方法是，用化学溶剂把壁画粘到纱布上剥下墙壁，带回美国去。
为首的是两位美国学者，我要在这里记一下他们的名字：一位是哈佛大学的兰登·华尔纳，一位是宾夕法尼亚博物馆的霍勒斯·杰恩。
兰登·华尔纳带回美国的莫高窟壁画引起轰动，他非常后悔自己当初没有带够化学溶剂，因此又来了第二次。这次他干脆带来了一名化学溶剂的调配专家，眼看就要在莫高窟里大动手脚。
但是，他后来在回忆录里写道，这次在莫高窟遇到了极大的麻烦：
事态变得十分棘手，约有几十个村民放下他们的工作，从大约十五公里外的地方跑来监视我们的行动……以便有理由对我们进行袭击，或者用武力把我们驱逐出境。
结果，他们只是拍了一些遗迹的照片，什么也无法拿走。化学溶剂更是一滴也没有用。
后来华尔纳在美国读到一本书，是他第二次去莫高窟时从北京雇请一位叫陈万里的翻译写的。这才知道，那些村民所得到的信息正是这位翻译透露的。陈万里先生到敦煌的第二天，就借口母亲生病离开了华尔纳，其实是向村民通报美国人准备干什么了。
为此，我要向这位陈万里先生致敬。
一位名不见经传的普通知识分子，加上几十个他原先不可能认识的当地村民，居然在极短的时间内做成了这么一件大事。对比之下，我看那些不负责任的官员，以及那些助纣为虐的翻译，还怎么来寻找遁词？
陈万里先生不仅是翻译，还是一位医生和学者。中国另有一位姓陈的学者曾经说过一句话：“敦煌者，吾国学术之伤心史也。”这位陈先生叫陈寅恪，后来两眼完全失去了视力。
陈寅恪先生看不见了，我们还张着眼。陈万里先生和村民没有来得及救下的那些莫高窟文物，还在远处飘零。既然外人如此眼热，可见它们确实是全人类的精粹，放在外面也罢了。只是，它们记录了我们历代祖先的信仰和悲欢，我们一有机会总要赶过去探望它们，隔着外国博物馆厚厚的玻璃，长久凝视，百般叮咛。
莫高窟被那些文物拉得很长很长，几乎环绕了整个地球。那么，我们的心情也被拉长了，随着唐宋元明清千年不枯的笑容，延伸到整个世界。

sections.label: I
paragraphs: SOME OF THE GREATEST CIVILIZATIONS in the world resemble mighty folk we can imagine: the loftier their stature, as time goes on, the harder it is for them to lower themselves to interacting with and learning from others. So they stand tall with great dignity, and no matter how much they care about those around them, they’re unwilling to allow a desire for closeness to show in their expressions; quite the opposite, they are hypersensitive as to whether they’re receiving sufficient respect from the other party. In this way, with estrangement going unchallenged for millennia, many needless conflicts take place, perhaps even escalating into bloody wars characterized by both sides as “defending their honor.”
Civilization was meant to be an escape from such barbarism—so why has civilization’s own path now led it back to just such inhumanity? I don’t know what to say to this.
Yet there is a place in the world in which many of the world’s greatest civilizations were able to meet and communicate, and even partially connect with each other.

This place was called the “Western Regions” in ancient China, and consisted of present-day Western Gansu, Northern Qinghai and the entirety of Xinjiang. Whether it was the close-at-hand Indian and Persian civilizations, or else the farther off Mesopotamian or Greek ones, they all arrived in this spot. And needless to say, China’s own culture was very much present.
What drew these great civilizations to meet and intermingle in this one spot?

The attraction of this place was its distance from the political centers of all these empires, and with wilderness and desert all around, it would be neither necessary nor possible to bring large armies here. Troops of merchants, on the other hand, were able to slowly pass through on camel-back, a great development that every civilization had hoped for—and thus we have the Silk Road. Trade can also give rise to unhealthy conflict, but fortunately the Silk Road was also a path for many religious figures, which brought spiritual peace to this area. Which is not to say that religion itself cannot be a source of tension—fortunately, the predominant faith in this part of the world was Buddhism, the only widespread belief system in the world never to have started a religious war.

And so, almost by accident, this desolate patch of earth came to house a thriving cultural ecology: material civilization centered around the Silk Road, and spiritual civilization with Buddhism as its main conduit. This wasn’t enough to prevent battles between smaller individual states, but the major wars between the great empires could not possibly take place here.

Interestingly, I’ve learned that the minor skirmishes in this region were often tussles over a Buddhist grand master. They never lasted long, usually ending with the grand master in question saying, “Please stop fighting, I’ll come with you.”—thus putting a stop to the matter.

I love visiting this place, and do so at the slightest excuse. Standing in the sandy wastes, I hear the hoofbeats and camel bells of one or two thousand years ago, watching long-ago monks in cassocks walking slowly away. No matter how good and how vast a civilization, I muse, if it stays put in its original site, it will slowly but surely become fossilized. Only by its people traveling to such remote regions can these empires not feel the need to be dominant, but greet each other with a smile. This place could truly be said to be an open, light-filled space in which human civilization could develop.
And in this space, there are several famous roads, along which are several famous cities, one of which is Dunhuang.

In 366 AD, a priest began cutting a cave into the eastern face of Echoing Sand Hill, to the southeast of Dunhuang. Many generations continued the work after him, and the results are the famous Mogao Grottoes.

When Buddhism first began spreading in India, stone caves were where priests practiced their religion. They did not have statues or pictures of the Buddha, relying on symbolic objects instead: golden cows, pagodas, pillars. Later, during the time of the Gandhara Kingdom, thanks to the influence of the Greek sculptors brought by Alexander the Great during his eastern excursion, caves began to fill with Buddhist statues. Visitors to these grottoes today can clearly see the influence of Greek statuary.

So you see, even in the matter of Buddhist cave sculptures, the ancient Indian and Greek civilizations are already involved. These caves are mostly in remote, deserted hills that appear unimpressive from a distance. Who could guess that contained within them are the marvels of two great cultures?

Naturally, even more important is the dominant Chinese civilization. When Buddhism came into China, it understood that this was a country in which stories needed to be told with everyday language and imagery, and so the art of cave sculptures was brought into the ever-growing fold of Chinese folk culture. As a result, against a background of humanity’s major civilizations, generations of Buddhas appeared in these caves, profound yet prosaic, smiling, happy and active, yet also suffering and sacrificial. All of this entered the veins of Chinese history, setting it in stone.
The Mogao Grottoes are a prime example of this.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: TO SEE THE MOGAO CAVES is to witness not specimens that have been dead a thousand years, but a life that has flourished for a millennium.

What is startling is that although various political factions have struggled for power throughout history in this region, they were still, in the midst of their life-and-death struggles, willing to do a good deed for the grottoes.

The royal household of the Northern Wei and the aristocrats of the Northern Zhou both played a major part in the construction of the Mogao Caves, as did the officials and residents of Dunhuang itself during the Sui, early Tang, and middle Tang Dynasties, extending the vibrant fashions of the day into the joyous scenes in the caves. Even the Tibetan Tubo, who occupied Dunhuang after the An-Shi Rebellion, and the soldiers led by Zhang Yichao who drove out the Tubo, both participated in the maintenance of the grottoes, though they were otherwise firm enemies who opposed each other on all other matters. The Cao family who ruled Dunhuang during the period of Five Dynasties and Ten Nations, also made a large contribution. When it came to the Song Dynasty, this region was controlled by first the Western Xia and then the Mongols, and it’s a miracle that neither caused much damage to the Mogao Caves. The caves fell into decline in the Yuan dynasty, essentially because the Mongol regime provided many trade routes between Europe and Asia, lessening the importance of the Silk Road and leaving Dunhuang in a state of neglect.

Why would so many mighty generals and strong tacticians bow down before the Mogao Caves? I believe the first reason has to do with human religion, and the second with the existing history of the area. Both faith and time are powerful forces, a kind of silent power that would have been sufficient to cool down these hot-blooded souls, creating a sense of respect and awe. They would have become like children, and no matter how riotous they’d been on the way here, their eyes would have grown wide when they arrived, hoping to receive a favorable judgment from time and the gods.
As a result of this, the Mogao Grottoes were constantly being added to, restored and expanded, growing into a living entity that breathes, metabolizes, ages, and spawns new generations.

In the course of this process, most worthy of note is the participation of all people. In the Mogao Caves, Buddhism leaves behind its deeper mysteries, becoming simple and populist, emphasizing the ideas of reward or punishment for one’s actions, supplicating for blessings and avoiding disaster, being well-fed and clothed, and producing children and grandchildren—all of which resonated with the common folk. Apart from the statues and wall paintings, the caves were also where the Dunhuang residents carried out their rituals and fasts, and served as a classroom in which they could study Buddhist ceremonies, not to mention a venue they could visit for regular entertainment. Despite this movement toward mass-appeal, the faith never lowered itself to the level of a folk religion, such as those found in village temples in which gods were pleaded to and demons cast out. Dunhuang had always been home to quite a few senior monks, notable scholars and other worthies, who were able to uphold the core belief system of the Mogao Caves. They were the leaders of the people and the defenders of their culture.

I often find my mind wandering at the Mogao Grottoes. In the dim natural light that filters in from openings high up in the caves, the people in the cave paintings and the statues before them seem to merge, starting to move through the hazy gloom. Behind them are the crowds who came here back in the day to participate in religious ceremonies, throngs swarming around cassock-clad priests. When I look closely, there are still many painters and sculptors working away. Are they creating new works or restoring the existing ones? I can’t tell. As one group departs, a new one arrives. Each group is a new generation, and they succeed one another endlessly.

There are sounds too: the calling of the names of Buddha, chimes and cymbals, chanting scriptures, the tok-tok of wooden fish, flags flapping in the wind, human laughter, and also, from outside the caves, the mountain wind, flowing water, hoofbeats and camel bells.

After watching and listening for a while, I find myself swept into the scene. My body, no longer under my control, stumbles and is drawn into the crowds, covered in waves of sound, transformed by a faith that a thousand years couldn’t extinguish. My self has been crumbled into dust, and then even the dust is gone.

Looking upon this place is a kind of enchantment, leaving me completely intoxicated and confused. And so, when the caves are closed in the evening and the crowds have departed, I have no choice but to wander alone at the foot of the hill, retrieving my memories piece by piece, recovering my self.

The night wind starts up, bearing fine sand that stings when it hits my cheeks. Moonlight in the desert is especially clear and cold. A spring bubbles at the base of the hill, shimmering in this light. At last my thoughts are coherent once more.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: EACH TIME I VENTURE into a cave, I rush ahead to read the plaque stating when it was built and swiftly work out its age, before lifting my head with reverence.

The oldest of the Mogao Caves is 1,600 this year, dating back to the period of Sixteen Kingdoms. The Bodhisattvas in the wall paintings still have the features of the Western Region’s own gods, and you can spot the traces of their Indian origins—crude drawings with thick outlines and a solidity about them, the figures nude as if still in the heat of the Ganges River’s banks. Other drawings display a callous willingness to sacrifice lives during the bloody turmoil of the times; they are terrifying to look upon, suggestive of the hardship and bitterness of that era.

The next ones come from the Wei Jin Northern and Southern Dynasties, which I’ve always been attracted to: still deep brown and green shades, bold brushstrokes like a slashing halberd. At the time, China’s Central Plains would have been full of swaggering scholars looking on disdainfully at the sufferings of the world, and in these caves they would have manifested a new, forthright spirit, so even the Bodhisattva would have lost his stout figure, becoming willowy and full of vigor instead. Some illustrations have a kind of refined delicacy or even a diseased beauty, a distant echo revealing the tastes of those Central Plains scholars.
Quite a few of the pictures contain various musical instruments, not all of which I’m able to name.

Many of the young maidens are drifting into the air, their clothes flapping in the wind—they’re ascending to heaven. When a tendency toward depicting the utter joy of dance and movement begins, we’ve arrived at the Sui Dynasty. A lay Buddhist known as Vimalakirti is depicted over and over again, leading one to remember how several notable Monguor families attempted to modify their own desires within Buddhist ideals. Suffering is now absent from the drawings—they depict only splendor. Even the sickly beauties have vanished, replaced by ever more plump, smooth flesh. The statues are somewhat short in the leg and large in the head, perhaps drawing inspiration from the nomadic herding ecology to the north. The experience of long hours on horseback has given them an air of stillness and composure.

When a proud joyousness starts appearing in the paintings, I knew we’re in the Tang Dynasty. There is an atmosphere of springtime, of awakening life, and even the birds and beasts have become dancers, and the flower blossoms arrange themselves into pictures. Heaven and earth are one, and facial expressions grow vivid, each stroke of the brush full of creativity. Women start to occupy positions of leadership, and whether depicted making offerings or as Bodhisattvas, radiate a fully feminine beauty. With this self-confidence, their expressions are peaceful, quiet and natural. The Buddhist rituals shown are now centered around “pure land” practice, with the idea that chanting the name of Amitabha Buddha with total concentration will allow rebirth into a place of purity. Even this simple ideal is suffused with the light-hearted optimism that only became present in the Middle Tang period.

The people captured in the Tang era paintings, whether armored generals and Central Asian traders from the Western Regions, or mighty warriors, provincial governors and their wives, are all in high spirits, full of energy. What’s more precious is that, in the vigor of these figures, I can detect the spirit of Wu Daozi. Even the background scenery is influenced by the glorious brushwork of the father-and-son team Li Sixun and Li Zhaodao. At this point, the pure joy on display begins moving toward the classical, but even so continues to exist in a celebratory state, not putting on airs in the least.

Apart from the wall paintings, the Tang Dynasty statues also seem closer to flesh and blood, now imbued with a spirit of their own, no longer etiolated and stiff. Even their eyes and the corners of their lips carry a hint of a smile; even the creases and folds of their clothes flow as freely as music.

Nothing in the Tang Dynasty caves is repeated, nothing feels rigid. They make me understand in an instant that true happiness can contain no repetition, just as true humanity cannot admit rigidity. As a result, the Tang Dynasty’s joy has created everlasting joy, just as its humanity has joined the eternal human soul, becoming a single entity. As I stood, stunned, the bustling caves seemed to empty out—no paintings, no statues, no time, no thought, everything evaporated away but not going anywhere, only here, in the caves, in the Tang Dynasty, beneath the brush of Wu Daozi.

Suddenly, my mind cleared as I noticed a painting that didn’t seem to fit in with the rest—its subject was filial duty, and its narrative concerned, unusually, a young Buddhist man trying to help his exiled parents in their struggle for their nation to rise again. I immediately formed a conjecture in my mind, and bent to examine the plaque—and sure enough, this dated to just after the An-Shi Rebellion.

This insurrection, like a long whip, cleft the Tang Dynasty in two with a single stroke. Dunhuang had been captured by the Tubo as a result of Tang troops moving eastward to attack the enemy, and so this depiction of a son helping his displaced parents restore their country was not fabricated.

A strong, touching spirit was carved into that cave wall, while the tragedy of the age was engraved in the land itself. How impossible, at this point, for the mighty Tang Dynasty to recover. The caves created subsequent to this seemed to have the life force snuffed out of them. Some might present what appear to be vivacious scenes, but the artificial liveliness is merely unengaging.
Yet in the midst of this monotony, I still recall an image of a dancer reaching backward to play the pi-pa that caused my eyes to light up.

Moving onward, the cave paintings grow more and more secular, moving from Buddhist topics to real life, from ritual occasions to domestic scenes, and even from religious teaching to ordinary storytelling. Of course, there’s nothing wrong with this, and these pictures are full of the breath of life, which put me in mind of the Washe and Zhugongdiao styles of Chinese performance.

There was still some sluggish beauty here between the Tang and Song Dynasties, but during the time of the Song, the culture seemed to grow desolate and impoverished. I feel the injustice of this. The Song Dynasty was when China produced poets such as Su Dongpo, Wang Anshi, Sima Guang, Zhu Xi, Lu You, Li Qingzhao and Xin Qiji—so how could Dunhuang be so lacking in that department? I believe this might have to do with the many major and minor political disputes taking place along the Gansu Corridor at the time. In the midst of endless turmoil, the path of creativity is blocked, and border regions must languish in neglect.

In the Yuan Dynasty, themes from Tantric and Tibetan Buddhism begin to appear. The subject matter no longer sticks closely to real life, but is imbued with a mystery and terror unfamiliar to us. The brush strokes are fine and delicate, decorative as well as devotional, putting me in mind of Thangka paintings.

This was an age of cultural borrowing and influence, with Mongol and Tibetan influences taking turns to hold sway over this region. There was a European traveler who passed through during that time and reported to the outside world that this was a peaceful, settled place. His name was Marco Polo.
As for the Mogao Caves of the Ming and Qing Dynasties, there isn’t much worth remembering about them at all.

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: AS I HURRIEDLY THOUGHT through all this in the dusk, I realized that this cluster of hills before my eyes might appear perfectly normal, but in fact their very existence is peculiar.

They are a sort of museum of the Gansu Corridor, as well as a historical record of a good half of China’s artistic history, and also the meeting place of several great civilizations. They are unimaginably profound, and have been silent for a long time—and perhaps this silence is a product of the profundity, just as noise and commotion are usually indicators of shallowness.

And yet, as with everything else in the world, all was good while they were in the ascendance, but as soon as the decline set in, the plunder and appropriation began. Apart from the Mogao Library Cave incident that we have often lamented, the wall paintings and statues have also been a target.

This is when the Mogao Grottoes, originally a site where the Chinese civilization could have friendly encounters with other empires, became evidence of how unneighborly certain people could be toward the Chinese. If an object catches one’s eye and one wishes to take it, it’s only polite to at least acknowledge its owner. But who is the owner? That could only be the many, many people who created, maintained, decorated, carved, supported and officiated over the caves, not to mention their descendants, an enormous group and not lightly to be passed over.
No matter how poor or weak the owners might be, they are still the owners.
No matter how ignorant the owners might be, they are still the owners.
And besides, who is to say that the owner is completely ignorant?

In the 1920s, a band of White Russian soldiers escaped across the border and were interned by the authorities at the Mogao Grottoes. They set up boilers and lit cooking fires inside the caves, smearing dark smoke and grease over many of the decorated walls and statues. In addition, they also daubed wooden poles with black paint, and further defaced the frescoes with graffiti.

After the troops had left, a group of American scholars showed up. They cursed the White Russians for their mischief, and swore an oath on the spot that they would rescue the Mogao treasures. Their method of ‘rescue’ was to use a chemical solvent to transfer the wall paintings onto gauze, in order to transport them back to the United States.
This expedition was led by two American scholars, and I must record their names here: Langdon Warner of Harvard University, and Horace J. F. Jayne of the Pennsylvania Museum of Art.

The paintings that Langdon Warner brought to America from the Mogao Caves caused quite a stir. He regretted only that he hadn’t brought enough solvent with him the first time round, and shortly embarked on a second trip, this time in the company of an expert in mixing chemical solutions—it would appear he had plans for a massive raid on the caves.
However, as he later recorded, on this second trip to the Mogao Caves, he encountered a rather large obstacle:

The situation was one of extreme delicacy on account of the presence of a dozen villagers who had left their ordinary employments, some fifteen miles off, to watch our movements…to tempt us into a breach of the peace which would warrant an attack or forcible expulsion from the region.
As a result, they only managed to take some photographs of the relics, and had to leave with no physical relics whatsoever. Not one drop of chemical solvent got used in the end.
These villagers who’d come from fifteen miles away are the very “owners” that I mentioned before. To tell the truth, I’m extremely moved by their actions.

It was only later, after he’d returned to America, that Warner came across a book written by his interpreter on that second expedition, a man named Chen Wanli. Reading this, he learned that those villagers had been told of his plans by Chen himself. The day after their arrival at Dunhang, Chen Wanli claimed his mother was ill and took his leave of Warner, but actually rushed to inform the villagers of the American’s plans.
And so, I also have to express my respect for Mr. Chen Wanli.

An obscure member of the intelligentsia, plus a handful of local inhabitants he couldn’t possibly have known beforehand, were actually able to accomplish such a major coup within a short span of time! In this light, it’s hard to see what excuses those irresponsible officials could come up with, or those interpreters who were willing to lend a helping hand to the imperialists.

Mr. Chen Wanli was not just an interpreter, he was also a doctor and scholar. Another Chinese academic with the same surname once wrote the words, “Dunhuang is a sad history in our nation’s scholarship.” This was Chen Yinke, who later lost the sight in both his eyes.

Mr. Chen Yinke might have gone blind, but we have our eyes open wide. The artifacts that Mr. Chen Wanli and the villagers came too late to save are still drifting around the world. That other people were so desperate to get their hands on them is proof that they are indeed among the finest objects produced by humanity. So let them go into the outside world, then. And yet, they record the beliefs and experiences of generations of our ancestors, and whenever we’re able to, we rush off to visit them—only to find ourselves gazing at them through the thick glass of some foreign museum, as they call to us in every possible way.

The Mogao Grottoes have been expanded by those artifacts, so much that they now almost wrap around the planet. And our hearts, too, have been stretched, following a smile that has not withered for a thousand years, through the Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing, expanding to encompass the entire world.

sections.label: main
paragraphs: 沙漠中也会有路的，但这儿没有。
远远看去，有几行歪歪扭扭的脚印。
顺着脚印走吧？不行，被人踩过了的地方反而松得难走。只能用自己的脚，去走一条新路。回头一看，为自己长长的脚印高兴。不知这行脚印，能保存多久？
挡眼是几座巨大的沙山。只能翻过它们，别无他途。上沙山实在是一项无比辛劳的苦役。刚刚踩实一脚，稍一用力，脚底就松松地下滑。用力越大，陷得越深，下滑也越加厉害。才踩几脚，已经气喘，不禁恼怒。
我在浙东山区长大，在幼童时已经能够欢快地翻越大山。累了，一使蛮劲，还能飞奔峰巅。这儿可万万使不得蛮劲。软软的细沙，也不硌脚，也不让你磕撞，只是款款地抹去你的全部气力。你越发疯，它越温柔，温柔得可恨至极。无奈，只能暂息雷霆之怒，把脚底放松，与它厮磨。
要腾腾腾地快步登山，那就不要到这儿来。有的是栈道，有的是石阶，千万人走过了的，还会有千万人走。只是，那儿不给你留下脚印——属于你自己的脚印。来了，那就认了吧，为沙漠行走者的公规，为这些美丽的脚印。
心气平和了，慢慢地爬。沙山的顶越看越高，爬多少它就高多少，简直像儿时追月。
已经担心今晚的栖宿。狠一狠心，不宿也罢，爬！再不理会那高远的目标了，何必自己惊吓自己。它总在的，看也在，不看也在，那么，看又何益？
还是转过头来打量一下自己已经走过的路吧。我竟然走了那么长，爬了那么高！脚印已像一条长不可及的绸带，平静而飘逸地画下了一条波动的曲线，曲线一端，紧系脚下。
完全是大手笔，不禁钦佩起自己来了。
不为那越来越高的山顶，只为这已经画下的曲线，爬。
不管能抵达哪儿，只为已耗下的生命，爬。
无论怎么说，我始终站在已走过的路的顶端——永久的顶端，不断浮动的顶端，自我的顶端，未曾后退的顶端。
沙山的顶端是次要的。爬，只管爬。
脚下突然平实，眼前突然空阔，怯怯地抬头四顾——山顶还是被我爬到了。
完全不必担心栖宿，西天的夕阳还十分灿烂。
夕阳下的绵绵沙山是无与伦比的天下美景。光与影以最畅直的线条进行分割，金黄和黛赭都纯净得毫无斑驳，像用一面巨大的筛子筛过了。日夜的风，把风脊、山坡塑成波荡，那是极其款曼平适的波，不含一丝涟纹。
于是，满眼皆是畅快，一天一地都被铺排得大大方方、明明净净。色彩单纯到了圣洁，气韵委和到了崇高。
为什么历代的僧人、信众、艺术家要偏偏选中沙漠沙山来倾注自己的信仰，建造了莫高窟、榆林窟和其他洞窟？站在这儿，我懂了。我把自身的顶端与山的顶端合在一起，心中鸣起了天乐般的梵呗。
刚刚登上山脊时，已发现山脚下尚有异象，舍不得一眼看全。待放眼鸟瞰一过，此时才敢仔细端详。那分明是一湾清泉，横卧山底。
动用哪一个藻饰词，都会是对它的亵渎。只觉它来得莽撞，来得怪异，安安静静地躲藏在本不该有它的地方，让人的眼睛看了很久还不大能够适应。再年轻的旅行者，也会像慈父心疼女儿一样叫一声：这是什么地方，你怎么也跑来了！
是的，这无论如何不是它来的地方。要来，该来一道黄浊的激流，但它是这样清澈和宁谧。或者，来一个大一点的湖泊，但它是这样纤瘦和婉约。按它的品貌，该落脚在富春江畔、雁荡山间，或是从虎跑到九溪的树荫下。
漫天的飞沙，难道从未把它填塞？夜半的飓风，难道从未把它吸干？这里可曾出没过强盗的足迹，借它的甘泉赖以为生？这里可曾蜂聚过匪帮的马队，在它身边留下一片污浊？
我胡乱想着，随即又愁云满面。怎么走近它呢？我站立峰巅，它委身山底。向着它的峰坡，陡峭如削。此时此刻，刚才的攀登，全化成了悲哀。
向往峰巅，向往高度，结果峰巅只是一道刚能立足的狭地。不能横行，不能直走，只享一时俯视之乐，怎可长久驻足安坐？上已无路，下又艰难，我感到从未有过的孤独与惶恐。
世间真正温煦的美色，都熨帖着大地，潜伏在深谷。君临万物的高度，到头来只构成自我嘲弄。我已看出了它的讥谑，于是亟亟地来试探下削的陡坡。
人生真是艰难，不上高峰发现不了它，上了高峰又不能与它亲近。看来，注定要不断地上坡下坡、上坡下坡。
咬一咬牙，狠一狠心。总要出点事了，且把脖子缩紧，歪扭着脸上肌肉把脚伸下去。一脚，再一脚，整个骨骼都已准备好了一次重重的摔打。
然而，奇了，什么也没有发生。才两脚，已出溜下去好几米，又站得十分稳当。不前摔，也不后仰，一时变作了高加索山头上的普罗米修斯。
再稍用力，如入慢镜头，跨步若舞蹈，只十来下，就到了山底。
实在惊呆了：那么艰难地爬了几个时辰，下来只是几步！想想刚才伸脚时的悲壮决心，哑然失笑。康德说，滑稽是预期与后果的严重失衡，正恰是这种情景。
来不及多想康德了，亟亟向泉水奔去。
一湾不算太小，长可三四百步，中间最宽处相当一条中等河道。水面之下，漂动着丛丛水草，使水色绿得更浓。竟有三只玄身水鸭，轻浮其上，带出两翼长长的波纹。真不知它们如何飞越万里关山，找到这儿。水边有树，不少已虬根曲绕，该有数百岁高龄。
总之，一切清泉静池所应该有的，这儿都有了。至此，这湾泉水在我眼中又变成了独行侠——在荒漠的天地中，全靠一己之力，张罗出了一个可人的世界。
树后有一陋屋，正迟疑，步出一位老尼，手持悬项佛珠，满脸皱纹布得细密而宁静。
她告诉我，这儿本来有寺，毁于二十年前。我不能想象她的生活来源，讷讷地问，她指了指屋后一条路，淡淡说：会有人送来。
我想问她的事情自然很多，例如，为何孤身一人长守此地？什么年岁初来这里？终是觉得对于佛家，这种追问过于钝拙，掩口作罢。目光又转向这脉静池，答案应该都在这里。
茫茫沙漠，滔滔流水，于世无奇。唯有大漠中如此一湾，风沙中如此一静，荒凉中如此一景，高坡后如此一跌，才深得天地之韵律、造化之机巧，让人神醉情驰。
以此推衍，人生、世界、历史，莫不如此。给浮嚣以宁静，给躁急以清冽，给高蹈以平实，给粗犷以明丽。唯其这样，人生才见灵动，世界才显精致，历史才有风韵。
因此，老尼的孤守不无道理。当她在陋室里听够了一整夜惊心动魄的风沙呼啸时，明晨，即可借明净的水色把耳根洗净。当她看够了泉水的湛绿时，抬头，即可望望灿烂的沙壁。
山，名为鸣沙山；泉，名为月牙泉。皆在敦煌境内。

en.title: A Secret Spring in the Sand

sections.label: main
paragraphs: ROADS EXIST even within the desert, although there are none here.
From a distance, several winding trails of footprints can be seen.

Follow the footprints? But no, tracks that others have already walked on are loose and difficult to find one’s footing on. Climbing a dune feels like more work than any other activity. As soon as one foot finds a grip, a little too much force sends it sliding as the ground crumbles beneath you. The more strength you use, the deeper you sink and the faster you slide. Only a few steps are enough to leave your breath ragged and your spirits frayed.

I grew up in the hill district of Zhedong, and by early childhood was already able to happily climb tall peaks. Even when I was tired, a burst of energy was enough to propel me to the top. But in this place now, a burst of energy wouldn’t be advisable. The soft, fine sand allows you to neither stamp down hard nor kick against it, and all the while it absorbs your energy at its leisure. The more frenzied you grow, the more tender it becomes, so tender as to attract your utmost loathing. Helplessly, you can only suppress your growing rage, soften your stride, and adapt yourself to it.

If you were hoping to leap up a hill in a series of bounds, you should have gone somewhere else. There are places with stone steps or planks set into the slope, ones that ten million people have climbed and ten million more will climb. The only thing is, these hills won’t accept your footprints—the marks that belong to you alone. Since you’re here, just accept that’s how things are—for the sake of the rules that govern all who walk in the desert, for the sake of those beautiful footprints.

My heart calms down, and I slowly climb upwards. The top of the dune seems to grow higher each time I look at it, and the further I climb the taller it grows, reminding me of how I used to chase the moon as a child.

I’m worried about finding a lodging for the night, but I harden my heart—so what if I don’t find a place to sleep? Keep climbing! Forget about that distant objective—no point frightening myself. It will be there whether I look at it or not, so what’s the point of gazing up?

Instead, I turn back to study the distance I’ve already traversed. Have I really covered so much ground and climbed so high? My footsteps are an unimaginably long silk ribbon, calmly drifting away, sketching a fluid line, one end of which is firmly attached to my feet.
This is the calligraphy of a master. I can’t help admiring myself.
Never mind that ever-taller peak. For the sake of the undulating line, climb.
Never mind if you ever get anywhere. For the life you’ve already squandered, climb.
No matter how you look at it, I’ve always stood at the summit of a road that’s already been trodden—that eternal summit, the endlessly shifting summit, the summit of myself that has never retreated.
The summit of the sand dune is secondary now. Climb, just climb.
My feet suddenly feel stable, and my vision grows clear. I tentatively raise my head and look around—and here I am, I’ve reached the peak.
No need to worry about finding a place to sleep yet, the sun is still dazzling, low in the western sky.

The soft dunes beneath the setting sun form the most beautiful landscape. Light and shadow cut into each other in the straightest possible lines, golden yellow and ocher both so pure and unblemished it looks as if they’ve passed through a giant sieve. The wind that blows day and night has sculpted the ridge and slopes into surging waves, but waves so calm and smooth that there isn’t a wrinkle to be found on them.

And so, everything before my eyes is free of care, earth and sky arranged with absolute openheartedness and clarity. The colors are so pure as to be sacred, the atmosphere so still it approaches the sublime.

Why have so many generations of priests, believers and artists come to the desert hills to throw themselves into their faith, creating the Mogao Grottoes, the Yulin Caves, and all these other structures? Standing here, I understand. I have melded the summit of my self and the summit of this dune, and my heart fills with the chanting of Buddhist prayers that bring a heavenly joy.
