As I step onto the ridge, I sense a strange vision at the foot of the hill, but can’t bring myself to take it in all at once. Instead I scan the landscape, getting a bird’s eye view, before zooming in on this detail. It is clearly a spring, nestling beneath the hill.

No matter what elegant phrases I apply, I would only desecrate it. I feel only that it’s shown up so abruptly, so oddly, hiding quietly in a place that should never have contained it, impossible for human eyes to adjust to its presence even after staring for some time. Even the youngest traveler would find himself shouting, like a loving father to his daughter: What kind of place is this, how could you have come all the way here?

Yes, no matter what, this isn’t a place it should have come to. If anything, it should be a murky yellow torrent, not something this pure and still. Or else, it should have come as a bigger lake, not this slender, graceful thing. By the looks of it, it should have shown up by the scenic Fuchun River or Yandang Mountains, or else run from Tiger Springs to the shady trees of Nine Creeks.

The air is full of wind-borne sand grains—have they never filled it in? Have the violent midnight winds never sucked it dry? Have bandits ever left their footprints here, relying on it to sustain themselves? Have marauders on horseback never gathered here, leaving filth beside it?

As my mind wanders, clouds of worry come back to me. How can I get closer to that spring? I’m at the peak, and it’s at the foot of this hill. The slope leading down to it is precipitous as a knife-edge. At this moment, the climb I’ve just achieved is completely transformed into tragedy.

Aiming for the summit, yearning for the heights, I’ve arrived here to find a narrow scrap of ground barely large enough to stand on. I can’t walk ahead or sideways, only enjoy a moment of gazing downwards. Remaining here would be impossible. There’s no way to go higher, and descending is fraught with difficulty. I feel an unprecedented loneliness and terror.

All the charm of the world that possesses true warmth is firmly affixed to the land, concealed in its deep valleys. When humanity claims dominion over all living things, we only succeed in mocking ourselves. I can see the ridicule here—and so eagerly test my footing on that steep slope.

Existence can be so difficult. You can’t see it without ascending to the heights, but at the summit you can’t be close to it. It looks like I’m fated to endlessly climb up and down the hill, up and down the hill.

I grit my teeth and harden my heart. Something is about to happen. I pull my neck in, arrange my face in a grimace, and extend my legs forward. One foot, then the other. My entire skeleton is prepared to take a hard beating.

And the strange thing is, nothing happens at all. In just two steps, I’ve slid several yards downhill, and am standing firmly again. Not tilting forward or leaning back. For a moment I am Prometheus atop the Caucasus.
Just a touch more effort and I slip into slow motion, taking huge strides like a dancer, and in just ten leaps I am at the foot of the hill.

This is astonishing: hours of hard climbing to reach the top, a few paces to get back down again! Recalling the heroic resolve with which I stretched my legs earlier, I laugh silently. Kant said that comedy was the result of a serious mismatch between expectation and result, and this is exactly where I find myself.
But no time for more thoughts of Kant. I dash towards the spring.

This isn’t too small a body of water, maybe three or four hundred paces long. At its widest point, in the middle, it’s about the breadth of a medium-sized river. Beneath the water surface, clumps of grass wave, giving the lake a rich green hue. Three reddish-black ducks are gliding by, creating two long lines in their wake. I have no idea how they flew over thousands of miles of enclosing mountains and discovered this spot. There are trees by the waterside, their roots gnarled and twisted, suggesting they must be centuries old.

All in all, this spring-fed lake has everything it needs. In my eyes, this oasis is a lone warrior—in the vastness of the desert waste, relying on no one but itself, it has carved out a pleasant space for itself.
Behind the trees is a simple hut. As I hesitate, an old nun emerges from it, a string of prayer beads dangling from her hand, her face densely, calmly covered in wrinkles.

She tells me that there was once a temple here, but it was destroyed twenty years ago. I can’t imagine where her sustenance comes from, but when I stammeringly ask, she points to the road behind her and says, simply: Someone delivers it.

Naturally, I have many other questions for her, such as: Why did you choose to live here, all alone? How old were you when you first arrived here? But such curiosity always seems foolish and clumsy before Buddhist devotees, and I hold my tongue. Gazing back at the peaceful lake, I realize the answers are already there.

The empty desert and flowing water are not in themselves miracles. Only finding such water in the arid land, such stillness amongst sandstorms, such a scene in the midst of desolation, such a fall from the highest peak—only then can we sense the rhythms, the ingenious design, the great plan behind nature, leaving us utterly intoxicated.

I deduce, therefore, that this must also be true of human existence, the world, all of history. Allow clamor to grow quiet, anxiety to cool, restlessness to settle, coarseness to melt into beauty. Only in this way can human existence fill with intelligence, the world appear exquisite and history show its grace.

And so this nun’s lonely vigil is not without sense. After spending a night in her hut listening to the heart-stopping howls of wind and sand, her ears can be washed clean by the lapping waves the next morning. When she has gazed her fill at the clear waters, she can raise her head and look at the dazzling walls of sand. This hill is named Echoing Sand Hill; this lake is called Crescent Lake. Both are within the borders of Dunhuang county.

paragraphs: 在中国古代，文官兼有文化身份和官场身份。在平日，自己和别人关注的大多是官场身份。但奇怪的是，当峨冠博带早已零落成泥，崇楼华堂也都沦为草泽之后，那一杆竹管毛笔偶尔涂画的诗文，却有可能镌刻山河、雕镂人心，永不漫漶。
我曾有缘，在黄昏的江船上仰望过白帝城，在浓冽的秋霜中登临过黄鹤楼，还在一个除夕的深夜摸到了寒山寺。我的周围人头济济，可以肯定，绝大多数人的心头，都回荡着那几首不必引述的古诗。
人们来寻景，更来寻诗。这些诗，他们在孩提时代就能背诵。孩子们的想象，诚恳而逼真。因此，这些城，这些楼，这些寺，早在心头自行搭建。
待到年长，当他们刚刚意识到有足够脚力的时候，也就给自己负上了一笔沉重的宿债，焦渴地企盼着对诗境实地的踏访，为童年，为想象，为无法言传的文化归属。
有时候，这种焦渴，简直就像对失落的故乡的寻找，对离散的亲人的查访。
文人的魔力，竟能把偌大一个世界的生僻角落，变成人人心中的故乡。他们薄薄的青衫里，究竟藏着什么法术呢？
今天，我冲着王维的那首《渭城曲》，去寻阳关了。出发前曾在下榻的县城向老者打听，回答是：“路又远，也没什么好看的。这雪一时下不停，别去受这个苦了。”我向他鞠了一躬，转身钻进雪里。
一走出小小的县城，便是沙漠。除了茫茫一片雪白，什么也没有，连一个褶皱也找不到。在别地赶路，总要每一段为自己找一个目标，盯着一棵树，赶过去，然后再盯着一块石头，赶过去。在这里，睁疼了眼也看不见一个目标，哪怕是一片枯叶、一个黑点。于是，只好抬起头来看天。
从未见过这样完整的天，一点儿没有被吞食、被遮蔽，边沿全是挺展展的，紧扎扎地把大地罩了个严实。
有这样的地，天才叫天；有这样的天，地才叫地。在这样的天地中独个儿行走，侏儒也变成了巨人；在这样的天地中独个儿行走，巨人也变成了侏儒。
天竟晴了，风也停了，阳光很好。没想到沙漠中的雪化得这样快，才片刻，地上已见斑斑沙底，却不见湿痕。
天边渐渐飘出几缕烟迹，并不动，却在加深。疑惑半晌，才发现，那是刚刚化雪的山脊。
地上有一些奇怪的凹凸，越来越多，终于构成了一种令人惊骇的铺陈。我猜了很久，又走近前去蹲下身来仔细观看，最后得出结论：那全是远年的坟堆。
这里离县城已经很远，不大会成为城里人的丧葬之地。这些坟堆被风雪所蚀，因年岁而塌，枯瘦萧条，显然从未有人祭扫。它们为什么会有那么多，排列得又是那么密呢？只可能有一种理解：这里是古战场。
我在望不到边际的坟堆中茫然前行，心中浮现出艾略特的《荒原》。这里正是中华历史的荒原：如雨的马蹄，如雷的呐喊，如注的热血。中原慈母的白发，江南春闺的遥望，湖湘稚儿的夜哭。故乡柳荫下的诀别，将军咆哮时的怒目，丢盔弃甲后的军旗。随着一阵烟尘，又一阵烟尘，都飘散远去。
我相信，死者临死时都是面向朔北敌阵的；我相信，他们又很想在最后一刻回过头来，给熟悉的土地投注一个目光。于是，他们扭曲地倒下了，化作沙堆一座座。

这繁星般的沙堆，不知有没有换来史官们的几行墨迹？堆积如山的中国史籍，写在这个荒原上的篇页还算是比较光彩的，因为这儿是历代王朝的边远地带，担负着保卫华夏疆域的使命。所以，这些沙堆还铺陈得较为自在，这些篇页也还能哗哗作响。就像眼下单调的土地一样，出现在这里的历史命题也比较单纯。在中原内地就不同了。那儿没有这么大大咧咧铺陈开来的坦诚，一切都在花草掩映中发闷，无数不知为何而死的冤魂，只能悲愤懊丧地深潜地底，使每片土地都疑窦重重。相比之下，这片荒原还算荣幸。
远处已有树影。疾步赶去，树下有水流，沙地也有了高低坡斜。登上一个坡，猛一抬头，看见不远的山峰上有荒落的土墩一座，我凭直觉确信，这便是阳关了。
树愈来愈多，开始有房舍出现。这是对的，重要关隘所在，屯扎兵马之地，不能没有这一些。转几个弯，再直上一道沙坡，爬到土墩底下，四处寻找，近旁正有一碑，上刻“阳关古址”四字。
这是一个俯瞰四野的制高点。西北风浩荡万里，直扑而来，踉跄几步，方才站住。脚是站住了，却分明听到自己牙齿打战的声音，鼻子一定是立即冻红了的。呵一口热气到手掌，捂住双耳用力蹦跳几下，才定下心来睁眼。
这儿的雪没有化，当然不会化。所谓古址，已经没有什么故迹，只有近处的烽火台还在，这就是刚才在下面看到的土墩。土墩已坍了大半，可以看见一层层泥沙，拌和着一层层苇草。苇草飘扬出来，在千年之后的寒风中抖动。
向前俯视，是西北的群山，都积着雪，直伸天际。我突然觉得自己是站在大海边的礁石上，那些山全是冰海冻浪。
王维的笔触实在是温厚。对于这么一个阳关，他仍然不露凌厉惊骇之色，而只是文静淡雅地写道：“劝君更尽一杯酒，西出阳关无故人。”他瞟了一眼渭城客舍窗外青青的柳色，看了看友人已打点好的行囊，微笑着举起了酒壶——再来一杯吧，阳关之外，也许就找不到可以这样对饮畅谈的老朋友了。
这杯酒，友人一定是毫不推却、一饮而尽的。
这便是唐人风范。他们多半不会声声悲叹，执袂劝阻。他们的目光放得很远，他们的人生道路铺展得很广。告别是经常的，步履是放达的。这种神貌，在李白、高适、岑参那里，焕发得越加豪迈。由此联想到，在南北各地的古代造像中，唐人造像一看便可识认，形体那么健美，目光那么平静，笑容那么肯定，神采那么自信。
在欧洲看蒙娜丽莎的微笑，你立即就能感受，这种恬然的自信只属于那些真正从中世纪的梦魇中苏醒、对前路挺有把握的艺术家们。这些艺术家以多年的奋斗，执意要把微笑输送进历史的魂魄。而更早就具有这种微笑的唐代，却没有把它的自信延续久远。阳关的风雪，竟越见凄迷。
王维诗画皆称一绝，莱辛等西方哲人反复论述过的诗与画的界限，在他是可以随脚出入的。但是，长安的宫殿只为艺术家们开了一个狭小的边门，只允许他们以文化侍从的身份躬身而入。这里，不需要艺术闹出太大的人文局面，不需要对美有太深的人性寄托。
于是，九州的文风渐渐刻板。阳关，再也难以享用温醇的诗句。西出阳关的文人越来越少，只有陆游、辛弃疾等人一次次在梦中抵达，倾听着穿越沙漠冰河的马蹄声。但是，梦毕竟是梦，他们都在梦中死去。
即便是土墩、石城，也受不住见不到诗人的寂寞。阳关坍弛了，坍弛在一个民族的精神疆域中。它终成废墟，终成荒原。身后，沙坟如潮；身前，寒峰如浪。谁也不能想象，这儿，一千多年之前曾经验证过人生旅途的壮美、艺术情怀的宏广。
这儿应该有几声胡笳和羌笛的，如壮汉啸吟，与自然浑和，却夺人心魄。可惜它们后来都不再欢跃，成了兵士们心头的哀音。既然一个民族都不忍听闻，它们也就消失在朔风之中。
回去吧，时间已经不早，怕还要下雪。

sections.label: main
paragraphs: IN ANCIENT CHINA, government officials had both a cultural and bureaucratic status, the latter being the identity they and others generally focused on. The strange thing is, long after the idea of the scholar-bureaucrat had been trampled into the dirt, their grand halls and mansions sunk into the mud, the verses they’d occasionally scrawl with their bamboo-handled brushes have continued to hold images of mountains and rivers, which are inscribed deep into the human heart with a clarity that will not be washed away.

I have been fortunate enough to have gazed upon White Emperor City from a river boat one evening, climbed Yellow Crane Tower amidst autumn frosts, and groped my way to Cold Mountain Temple late one New Year’s Eve. On each occasion I was surrounded by people, and it is certain that, in most of their minds, these ancient poems were resonating, so familiar they don’t need to be quoted.

The crowds may have come for the scenery, but even more in search of poetry. And these poems are the ones they would have begun memorizing and reciting as infants. Children’s imaginations are vivid and sincere. As a result, certain cities, mansions, and temples are constructed within our minds long before we set eyes on them.

Much later in life, as they realize their legs are strong enough, they take on a heavy long-term debt: a fierce thirst to step into these poetic scenes, for the sake of childhood, or imagination, or a sense of cultural belonging that cannot be put into words. At times, this thirst resembles searching for a lost homeland, or seeking out long-lost family members.
Writers have the magical ability to turn a neglected corner of this vast world into a homeland found in everyone’s heart. What is this sorcery, found up the sleeves of the scholar’s green jacket?

On this day, at the instigation of Wang Wei’s poem “Song at Weicheng,” I went in search of the Southern Pass. Before setting off, I asked an old chap at the county town where I’d passed the night for his advice. His response was, “It’s far away, and there’s nothing to see there. It’s snowing non-stop right now—don’t put yourself through that.” I bowed to him, and turned to step out into the blizzard.

Immediately outside the little town was a desert. Apart from the borderless white snowstorm, there was nothing at all, not even a wrinkle in the blankness. When trekking elsewhere, I always pick out a landmark for each stretch of the journey, staring at a tree and hurrying toward it, then a rock for the next little bit. In this place, even stretching my eyes so wide open they hurt, I couldn’t see a single distinguishing feature, not even a withered leaf or speck on the ground. And so, I could only lift my head and gaze at the sky.
I had never seen such a complete sky, not one bit of it eaten away or hidden. Its perimeter was firmly attached all the way round, so it securely covered the great earth.

Only on such land could the sky be called the sky; and only beneath such a sky could the earth be called the earth. Walking alone like this between heaven and earth, even a pygmy would be transformed into a giant, and so would a giant be reduced to a pygmy.

The weather finally grew clear, and the wind stopped. Now the sun made a fine appearance. I’d never imagined desert snow could melt this quickly; in just a few moments, streaks of sand were visible again, not even damp.
A few wisps of smoke drifted out against the horizon, not moving, but growing thicker. After a moment’s confusion, I realized these were mountain ridges, appearing as the snow melted off them.

There were a series of odd bumps in the ground, more and more of them, until they’d built up an alarming pattern. After a great deal of conjecture, I knelt to examine them, and finally deduced that they were burial mounds from the distant past.

This was quite some distance from the town, and it seemed unlikely that folk would have come all the way out here for their funerals. These mounds had been nibbled at by wind and snow, and were close to collapse due to their antiquity, shriveled and desolate. It was clear that these graves had not been tended. And why were there so many of them, and squashed so tightly together? There could only be one explanation: I had stumbled upon a battlefield.

Wandering amongst the burial heaps that seemed to stretch forever, T. S. Eliot’s “The Waste Land” drifted into my mind. This place truly was the wasteland of Chinese history: hoofbeats like raindrops, shouts like thunder, a cascade of hot blood. The white hairs of a loving mother in the Central Plains, the impossibly distant spring in Jiangnan, an infant crying in the night in Hunan. A final parting below the willow trees of home, the rage-filled eyes of the bellowing general, an army’s flag during a chaotic retreat. One plume of smoky dust, then another, and the wind blows all away.

I believe that as these men prepared to die, facing the barbarian hordes from beyond the Great Wall, they yearned to look back one last time at the familiar land behind them. And so they twisted and writhed as they fell, creating these mounds of sand.

Who knows whether these sand heaps, like a skyful of stars, led to a few lines of ink from the court historians? In the mountains of Chinese historical records, those written on the page of this wasteland are some of the most splendid, because this is a remote region that, dynasty after dynasty, was trusted with the important duty of protecting the territories of Cathay. These sand mounds can rest easy, while these pages turn freely. Just as the land here is monotonous and unvaried, the historical topics that arise here are pure. Matters are different in the Central Plains. You couldn’t find such blazing honesty there, in that region where everything is stifled, concealed beneath grass and flowers. Numberless vengeful souls, their deaths unaccounted for, can only cling to the earth, mired in rage and grief, causing every patch of soil to become laden with doubt. By comparison, this wasteland here seems fortunate.

There were the silhouettes of trees in the distance. I trotted over quickly, and found water flowing beneath the trees, while the sand rose and fell in peaks and valleys. Climbing up a slope, I looked up to see a derelict earthen structure had appeared close by, on the peak of a hill. My instincts told me that this was surely the Southern Pass.

There were more and more trees here, and houses began appearing too. Of course, with an important pass nearby, there’d have to be somewhere to stable horses and garrison troops. After a few more turns and a path leading up a sandy slope, I found myself beneath the structure. I searched the surrounding area, finally stumbling upon a plaque on which were carved the words “Ancient Site of the Southern Pass.”

This was an excellent vantage point with views in all directions. The northwest wind swept in mightily, causing me to stumble a few paces before I found my footing. Although I was still, I could clearly hear my teeth chattering, and my nose must have been red from the cold. I puffed warm air into my palms, clasped them over my ears and jumped up and down, before I finally felt able to open my eyes wide.

The snow here had not melted, of course. This might be a designated ancient site, but there were no ruins here, apart from the fire beacon tower—the earthen structure I’d seen from lower down. This was half-collapsed, partly covered in dirt and sand, with clumps of reed-grass waving in the icy winds as they have done for thousands of years.
Directly ahead were the mountains of the northwest, all covered with snow, reaching to the edge of the sky. I felt as if I were on the shore of a vast ocean, and they were frozen waves.

Wang Wei’s brushstrokes were warm and generous. Writing of the Southern Pass, he didn’t mention its desolation or terror, but calmly, elegantly said, “I urge my friend to have one last cup of wine/Westward beyond the Southern Pass, there are no familiar faces.” Wei glanced outside the window of the Weicheng Inn at the green willow tree, then saw that his friend had finished packing, and smilingly raised the wine flask—one more for the road. Once you get through the Southern Pass, you may not find another old buddy to drink and chat with.
I’m sure his friend didn’t refuse that cup of wine, but drank it gladly.

This is how things were done in the Tang Dynasty. I doubt they’d have sighed in sorrow or plucked at each other’s sleeves. They’d both have looked far ahead, seeing the long road of their lives spread out before them. Saying goodbye was just a normal part of the journey, and then their footsteps would take them far afield. In the work of Li Bai, Gao Shi and Cen Shen, this spiritual attitude shone even more boldly. From here I am reminded of ancient statues found both in the north and south, the instantly recognizable form of Tang sculpture: such elegant physiques, such calm eyes, such certain smiles, such self-confident souls.

Looking at the Mona Lisa’s smile, you immediately sense that such nonchalant self-possession could only come from a painter who’d truly awakened from the nightmare of the Middle Ages, and who was confident of the path ahead. Such artists had to struggle for many years, fighting to deliver that smile into the soul of history. The Tang Dynasty, which had such a smile in an even earlier era, was unable to send its confidence far into the future. The wind and snow around the Southern Pass now seemed desolate.

Wang Wei was a master of both painting and poetry. European philosophers such as Gotthold Ephraim Lessing have long debated the boundary between these two art forms, a line Wang Wei easily stepped across. Yet the palace at Chang’an only had a narrow side door for artists, and they had to enter bowing and scraping, in the role of cultural chamberlains. In this place, there was no need to have art creating too much of a cultural impact, nor to place too many of humanity’s hopes in beauty.

And so, the literary style of China gradually hardened. The Southern Pass would struggle to find such tender verses lavished upon it. Fewer literary figures went westward beyond the Southern Pass, only a few such as Lu You and Xin Qiji arrived here in their dreams, hearing the sound of hoofbeats passing through the desert and icy rivers. But a dream is a dream, and in the end they all died within their dreams.

Even a stone city or earthen building cannot withstand the loneliness of not encountering poets. Here was the Southern Pass falling apart, an unraveling within the spiritual domain of a nation. It would finally become rubble, and then a wasteland. Behind it, a sea of sandy graves; before it, an ocean of frozen waves. No one would be able to imagine that a thousand years ago, this place embodied the magnificence of human existence, and the grandeur of the artistic temperament.

Here, we should have a few notes of the bamboo flute, a rousing call to arms, in keeping with the natural surroundings but stirring to the human soul. What a pity that later on, these were no longer a cause for joy, but rather the mournful tones in every soldier’s heart. As an entire people can no longer bear to listen, it should vanish with the northern wind.
Time to go back. It was getting late, and I was afraid it might snow again.

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 一个中国古代文人不管漂泊何处，晚年最大的向往就是回归故乡。这事到了近代那些具有世界历史视野的学者那里就不一样了，他们会以一生的学养把时间和空间浓缩，然后拄着拐杖站在书房的窗口看着远方。他们在想：如果生命能够重来一次，我最希望投生何处？
我很想知道几位大学者对这个问题的答案，排在第一的是英国历史学家汤因比（Arnold Joseph Toynbee）。因为正是他洋洋洒洒的著作，最早让我了解了世界各地的不同历史形态。
但是，他已经去世三十多年，似乎并没有留下这方面的答案。我，只能在他的著作中猜测。猜测了几处，都没有把握。
终于，我突然知道，他曾经在一次对话中，留下了答案。
他说，如果生命能够重来一次，他希望生活在中国古代的西域。因为，那是一个文化会聚的福地。
他所说的西域，是指中国新疆塔里木河、叶尔羌河一带。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 我每次去新疆，总会想起汤因比的选择。
西域，这是一个伟大的地名。汉武帝派张骞“通西域”，是这位帝王，也是整个汉代对世界历史的杰出贡献。从此，人类各大文明在那里发生了最大规模的汇集、交流和融合。
本来，无论是印度文明、波斯文明、巴比伦文明、阿拉伯文明，还是再远一点的埃及文明、希腊文明、罗马文明等等，都自成规模、自享尊荣，很难放得下架子来与其他文明主动融合，除非用战争的方式来收纳别人。因此，各大文明都在万分警惕地防范着来自别处的铁骑战火。但是，商品流通的诱惑太大了，旅行者口中的描述太吸引人了，因此，彼此都悄悄地产生了一种不约而同的渴望：要找一个地方，展开各大文明之间的非战争交往。
这个地方需要具备两个条件：一，必须是一个地广人稀的所在，离各大文明的首府都比较遥远，使谁也感受不到威胁；二，所有的旅行团队最想靠近的那个文明，有一种让大家放心的宽容精神。
能够满足这两个条件的地方，在古代世界的地面上只有一个，那就是西域。于是，在天山、昆仑山和塔里木盆地之间的茫茫大漠，终于成了各大文明沟通的巨大平台。看似最缺少文化的地方，变成了最热闹的文化集市。一场场古代的世博会、交易会、嘉年华，不断地在西域开幕又闭幕，闭幕又开幕。
这么一想，觉得汤因比对那里的选择，实在很有道理。
古代由西域通向整个亚洲腹地，有北疆的草原之路和南疆的丝绸之路。丝绸之路又分南、北两路，然后在一个地方汇合，翻越帕米尔高原而继续前去。两条丝绸之路的汇合处，是西域开发最早的城郭叫“疏勒”，也就是现在中国最西的城市喀什，又叫喀什噶尔。
这是历来所有的旅行家、探险家、行脚僧、商贸者都必须停步的地方。不管是出去还是进来，都已经承受过严酷的生死考验，而前面，可能是帕米尔，也可能是塔克拉玛干，考验更大。因此，要在这里收拾一下好不容易捡回来的一条命，然后重新豁命前行。
对很多人来说，这里是生命的最后一站；对另一些人来说，这又是豪迈壮行的新起点。不管是终点还是起点，都是英雄们泼酒祭奠之处。喀什的每一寸空气，都熔铸过男子汉低哑的喉音。
世界在这里渴望着被一次次走通，而高原在这里却显得寸步难行。一位高大的当地汉子在昆仑山脚下对我说：“在这里，地远路险，从有些村子到乡里去，骑毛驴也要走七天。一个妻子最高的愿望是去一趟县城，丈夫不让，说这么漂亮的女人走那么久，怎么还回得来？几十年后丈夫去世，妻子也走不动了。”
但是，这些妻子和丈夫都看到了，总有一些人从他们村边走过。是去乡里吗？是去县城吗？难道，还有更远的地方？
最近，我和妻子又一次去了喀什。一路上饱满的感觉无与伦比，我只想重复多年前说过的一句话：如果你想研究的历史不是一般的历史而是“大历史”，如果你想从事的文学不是一般的文学而是“大文学”，那么，请务必多去西域，多去新疆，多去喀什。

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 两千多年前张骞通西域的时候，已经发现喀什有非常像样的商贸市场。后来，出任汉朝“西域都护”的班超，又曾把这里当做安定西域的大本营，他自己一住就是十几年。
班超在这里的时候，当地民众在精神文化上还停留于萨满巫术的原始自然宗教。但是，就在班超走后不久，一件重大的文化事件把这里裹卷进去了：印度的佛教开始向中国大规模传播，这里成了一条最主要的走廊。
对于佛教东传这件事，我一直认为是人类文化史上的一个特大事件。原因是，作为被传入一方的中国大地，自从诸子百家之后已经实现了超浓度的精神自足，似乎一切思维缝隙都已填满，怎么可能如此虔诚地接受万里关山之外一种全然陌生的文明呢？但是，由于印度文明和中华文明的双向高贵，又痛又痒的防范心理居然被一步步克服。首感痛痒的地方，应该就在喀什。首度克服的地方，应该也在喀什。
磨合了两百年，到了公元四世纪，这儿已经成了一个佛教繁盛之地，留下的古迹和事迹都很多。例如，那位在中国佛教史上贡献堪比玄奘的鸠摩罗什，就曾在十二岁时到这里学习小乘佛教长达两年，后来也在这里，遇到了精通大乘佛教的来自莎车的王子参军兄弟二人，开始转向大乘佛教，并终生传习。而莎车，现在也属喀什地区。尽管喀什的佛教主流一直是小乘，鸠摩罗什不得不离开，但这儿是他的精神转型地。
在鸠摩罗什之后不久，法显西行取经也经过这里，惊叹这里的法会隆重。后来玄奘取经回来时经卷落水破损，也曾在这里停留一段时间补抄。
在公元九世纪至十三世纪的喀喇汗王朝时期，喀什表现了很高的文化创造能力，向世界贡献了第一部用纯粹回鹘文写成的长篇叙事诗《福乐智慧》和精心巨著《突厥语大词典》。这是两部极重要的维吾尔文化经典，跟着它们，还有不少优秀的著作产生。喀什，因创建经典而闪现出神圣的光彩。
其实，伊斯兰教在公元七世纪传入中国时，也以喀什为前沿。在这里落地生根几百年后，才向北疆传播。喀什地区的伊斯兰教文物不胜枚举，因为直到今天这儿的主要信仰还是这个宗教。千余年来天天被虔诚的仪式滋润着，即便是遗迹也成了生活，因此看上去都神采奕奕。
据到过这里的欧洲旅行家马可·波罗记述，基督教的一个教派聂斯托利派即中国所称“景教”，在这里也不乏信奉者，而且礼拜完满，尽管这个教派早在公元五世纪已在罗马被取缔。对此，作为意大利人的马可·波罗就很敏感。同样，在古代波斯早被取缔的祅教（即拜火教），在这一带的民间也曾风行，致使《南唐书》说疏勒地区“俗奉祅神”。
总之，几千年来，喀什不仅是商品贸易的集散地，而且也是精神文化的集散地。集散范围很大，近至中亚、南亚，远至西亚、欧洲。如果说，西域是几大文明的交汇中心，那么，喀什则是中心的中心。
这个地位，自古以来一直具有，却只是默默地存在于各国商人心中。到了十九世纪，世界在空间和时间上获得新的自觉，喀什的重要性再一次被广泛瞩目。当时很多全球顶级的学者都坚信，这一带必定留下了诸多文明的重大脚印，因此都不远万里纷纷赶来。正如日本探险家橘瑞超所说的那样：“这是中亚地区政治、商业的中心，自古以来就为世人所知，至今到中亚旅行的人，没有不介绍喀什的。”
翻阅那时的世界考古学著作就可以发现，喀什，在东方学研究中，已经成了一个怎么也避不开的常用名词。
到十九世纪末、二十世纪初，中国内忧外患，水深火热，差一点被列强彻底瓜分了。但是，即使到了这个时候，一个以亚洲腹地为目标的考古学家如果没有来过喀什，还是会像一个毕业生的文凭上没有盖过校长的签名印章。
历史，很容易被遗忘，却又很难被彻底遗忘。在那些迷乱的夜晚，正当一批批外来的酒徒在沙丘上狂欢喧嚣的时候，他们脚下，沙丘寂寞一叹，冷然露出某个历史大器的残角，似乎在提醒他们，这是什么地方。

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 一八八一年四月，俄国驻喀什领事馆开张，本来这很正常，但奇怪的是，领事馆里有六十名哥萨克骑兵。这些骑兵每天早晚两次列队穿越市区的大广场到城东河边操练，还向围观的人群表演刀术、马术、射击术。俄国驻喀什的领事很有学问，名叫彼得罗夫斯基，一个英国学者曾这样描述他：
彼得罗夫斯基是个能干、傲慢、狡猾而精于诱惑的家伙，任职的二十一年间对中国官员使尽了阴谋恐吓、威胁、利诱、收买、强迫之伎俩。他的目的便是将新疆最西部的绿洲从中国瓜分出去，使俄国得以控制通往印度后门的战略性山口。
（珍妮特·米斯基：《斯坦因考古与探险》）
俄国要控制通往印度的后门，显然是在挑衅英国。当时，英国不仅在印度实行殖民统治，而且已经控制了昆仑山、兴都库什山、阿姆河以南的多数地区，怎么会允许俄国来插手？因此，后起的英国驻喀什总领事馆占地面积，是俄国领事馆的整整两倍，而且也比英国自己在乌鲁木齐的领事馆豪华很多。一位英国记者写道：
在大英帝国与沙皇俄国争夺中亚的五十多年大角逐中，喀什一直是大英帝国最前沿的一个阵地。在那场大角逐中，大英帝国为了在亚洲取得政治和经济的主导权，与沙皇俄国进行过漫长而又扑朔迷离的争斗。在大英帝国驻喀什领事馆上飘扬的那面英国国旗，是印度到北极之间唯一的一面。
（彼得·霍布科克：《一个外交官夫人对喀什的回忆》）
就在那队哥萨克骑兵和那面英国国旗天天都在喀什对峙的时候，一些心在千年之前的学者也来到了这座城市。斯文·赫定来了，并从这里出发，发现了千年前的古城丹丹乌里克，又考察了塔里木河和罗布泊的迁徙遗址。斯坦因也来了，顺着斯文·赫定的成果进一步发现了“希腊化的佛教艺术”犍陀罗的遗存，又发现了楼兰遗址……这一系列文物，从不同方向展示了这片土地在古代无与伦比的重要性。
“在古代无与伦比的重要性”，可分为两类。第一类是随着古代的结束而结束，第二类却可以延伸到现代。西域发现的文物，大多属于第二类。它们像古代智者留下的一排排巨大的数学公式，证明着几个大空间之间的必然联系，以及把这种必然联系打通的实际可能。因此，就在这些西域考古大发现之后，历史学家威尔斯作出判断：“直到今天我才开始明白，塔里木河流域比约旦河流域和莱茵河流域更为重要。”

正是这种判断，使得喀什城里那队哥萨克骑兵和那面英国国旗更加抖擞起来。两国的领事，都会殷勤地接待那些考古学家，希望他们为帝国的现代野心提供更多的古代理由。但是，从种种记录来看，那些考古学家对于两位领事除了感谢之外并不抱有太多的尊敬。他们毕竟深谙历史，比眼前披着外交套装的情报政客更知道轻重。他们来到沙漠深处，只要见到一点点古代的痕迹就会急速地跪下双腿，用双手轻轻地扒挖，细细地拂拭。很久很久，还跪在那里。
如果仅仅从动作上看，考古学家，是在代表现代人跪身谢恩。
无言的大地，有多少地方值得我们跪身，又有多少地方需要我们谢恩。

sections.label: 五
paragraphs: 在中华文明的诸多“老祖宗”中，在形态和气度上最让人震撼的，是西域，包括喀什。
这个说法也许会使别的“老祖宗”侧目，那实在对不起了，但我实在不是随口赞誉。请想一想，天山、昆仑山和塔克拉玛干大沙漠，这几宗真正的天下巨构，只须窥得其中任何一角，就足以让世人凝神屏息。但在这里，却齐齐地排列在一起、交接在一起、呼应在一起，这会是什么景象？
一连串无可超越的绝境，一重重无与伦比的壮美，一系列无法复制的伟大，包围着你，征服着你，粉碎着你，又收纳着你。你失去了，好不容易重新找回，却是另一个你。
在天山、昆仑山面前，其他“老祖宗”所背靠的三山五岳，就有点像盆景了。在塔克拉玛干大沙漠面前，其他“老祖宗”所吟咏的大漠孤烟、长河落日，也有点太孩子气了。

到喀什，不能按照内地休闲的习惯，选择那些人群密集的旅游景点。应该选择的，是乔戈里峰、慕士塔格冰川和奥依塔克冰川、红其拉甫口岸、亚克艾日克烽火台，以及散布处处的千年胡杨林和夕阳下的沙漠。我和妻子则非常着迷莎车的《十二木卡姆》，每次都听得情醉神驰。难怪躲得那么僻远的它，早已被堂皇地列入世界非物质文化遗产名录。它让我联想到，在隋唐年间轰动长安的疏勒乐和龟兹乐。不错，在中国古代最伟大王朝的雄伟和声中，占据极高引领地位的，大多是西域乐舞。
由此想到，在喀什之外，新疆还有不少西域名胜值得一再拜访，例如龟兹（现在的库车）、于阗（现在的和田）、高昌、交河等地。有足够体力的，还可以狠狠心去一下楼兰、米兰、尼雅遗址。
在叶尔羌河畔，一位本地官员已经摆好了毛笔和宣纸，要我题写几个字，准备刻在山壁上。我问他写哪几个字，他说——
昆仑第一城
我说：“你们这儿，随口一说就气势非凡。”
写完，我的目光越过灿如火阵的胡杨林，再越过层层叠叠的绕山云，远眺昆仑山上的天路。那条天路，通向西藏阿里地区。突然发现，在连绵的雪峰之上，竟然冒出缕缕白烟，飘向蓝天。难道，那里还有人间的生活？
“那么高的云层之上，怎么会有白烟？”我问。
主人说，那不是白烟，而是高天风流吹起了山顶积雪。
原来如此。但转念一想，我刚刚的疑惑，历代旅行者也一定产生过。他们猜测着，判断着，时不时低头看路，又时不时抬起头来。没有人烟的地方何来人烟？他们多半找不到人询问，带着疑惑离开，然后又回头，看了又看。
那么，这神奇的“白烟”，也就成了一面面逗引远方客人的白色旗幡。
想到这里我笑了，心想汤因比先生向往西域的来世之魂，现在一定已经顺着这白色旗幡找到归宿，乐滋滋地安顿了下来。

sections.label: I
paragraphs: NO MATTER HOW FAR an ancient Chinese writer traveled, his greatest dream was to return home. However, it is completely different for scholars with the world-historical views of modern times. They would concentrate time and space in their lifetime of cultivation, then walk with a cane to the window of their study and stare into the distance. They would think: where would be my favorite birthplace if I could have my life again?

I have a strong desire to know the answers of some great scholars to this question. The first one is Arnold Joseph Toynbee, an historian from England. Just from his voluminous works, I came to understand the different historic morphologies in the world at the earliest time.
However, he has been dead for more than thirty years, and seems not to leave any answer about it. I can only guess from his works. There are several places, but I am not very sure.
Finally, I know all at once. He disclosed the answer in a conversation.
He said that if he could have his life again, he hoped to live in the West Regions in China, for that was a blessed place for cultural integration.
The West Regions, he said, refers to the area of Tarim River and Yarkand River in Xinjiang, China.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: EVERY TIME I GO TO XINJIANG, I always think of Toynbee’s choice.

The West Regions is really a great name. Emperor Wudi assigned Zhang Qian to “connect the West Regions.” It was this emperor and the overall Han Dynasty that made great contributions to world history. Hence, major civilizations at the greatest scale of assembly, exchange, and integration were here.

Originally, Indian, Persian, Babylon, and Arabic civilizations, or slightly farther back, Egyptian, Greek, and Roman civilizations, could form their own values and enjoy their own glories, but it was very difficult for them to integrate with other civilizations actively, unless taking others through war. Therefore, various major civilizations were cautious and intent on warding off the cavalries and wars from other places. However, commodity circulation was a great lure, and descriptions by travelers were very attractive, so a desire was generated invariably and secretly among them: to find a place and develop peaceful contacts between major civilizations.

Two conditions were necessary. First, it had to be a vast territory with a sparse population, remote from the capital of each civilization, where no one could feel threatened. Second, the civilization that all of the traveling representatives wanted to get close to had to possess the spirit of tolerance that makes people at ease.

There was only one place that could satisfy those two conditions in the ancient world, and that is the West Regions. Thus the vast desert between Mount Tianshan, Mount Kunlun and Tarim Basin finally became a huge platform for the major civilizations of the world to communicate on. The place with a seeming lack of culture became the liveliest culture bazaar. One after another exposition, trade fair, and carnival in ancient times opened and flourished and closed in the West Regions continuously.
Thinking about it for a while, I decided that Toynbee’s selection was very reasonable.

In ancient times, the West Regions could lead to the whole interior of Asia, including the grassland road in northern Xinjiang and the Silk Road in southern Xinjiang. The Silk Road could be divided into South Road and North Road, which were integrated at one place, climbing over the Pamir Mountains and continuing forward. The junction of the two Silk Roads was the city wall developed earliest in the West Regions, whose name was “Shule,” and which is the westernmost city in China today—Kashgar.

This was a place where all travelers, explorers, Buddhists, and merchants had to stop. No matter going out or in, they all suffered this harsh testing ground, but they faced greater tests before, maybe the Pamir, maybe the Takla Makan Desert. Therefore, they purged their souls, picked themselves up, and prepared to risk their lives on the road again.

For many people, this was the last station for their lives; for others, this was the new starting point, filled with generousness, fortifying them for their subsequent departure. Whether as terminal or starting point, here was a place for heroes’ pouring wine and sacrificing. Every inch of air in Kashgar bore the dumb guttural sounds of such men.

The world yearned for the connection from here time and time again, but the plateau here was difficult to be climb over. At the foot of Kunlun Mountain, a tall local man told me: “Here the road is remote and dangerous. It takes seven days from some villages to the town, even by donkey. The greatest wish of a wife was to go to the town, but her husband did not allow. He thought that his wife was so beautiful, how could she come back again after walking such a long way? Several decades later, her husband died, but she was too old to go to the town.”
However, these wives and husbands all saw that some persons always walked through their villages. Did they go to the township? Did they go to the county? Or even a much farther place?

Recently, I and my wife went to Kashgar again. Such plump feeling along the way was incomparable. I just want to repeat the words said years before: if the history you want to study is not the common kind but the “great history,” if the literature you want to engage in is not the common kind but the “great literature,” please go to the West Regions, go to Xinjiang, and go to Kashgar.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: WHEN ZHANG QIAN OPENED the West Regions more than two thousand years ago, he found that Kashgar had a very decent commercial market. Later, Ban Chao, of the “Protectorate of the West Regions” in Han Dynasty, made it the supreme headquarters for maintaining the West Regions, and he even lived there ten years.

When Ban Chao came here, the spiritual culture of the local people remained the primitive natural religion of shaman witchcraft. However, soon after he left there was a significant cultural event: Buddhism from India began to spread to China on a massive scale, and this became its primary corridor.

As for Buddhism’s eastward spread, I have always believed it was a very significant event in the history of human culture. The reason: as it spread to China, it achieved an integral, self-sufficient concentration of spirit. Since a hundred schools of thought contended in the Han Dynasty, it seemed that all their minds had been filled up, and so how could they receive such a completely unknown civilization devoutly outside Mount Guan from thousands of miles away? However, thanks to the mutual dignity of Indian and Chinese civilizations, the psychology of painful precaution was finally overcome step by step. Kashgar must have been the first place to feel such pain, and the first place to overcome it.

After two hundred years, or the fourth century AD, this was already a place of prosperous Buddhist culture, with many historical sites and deeds. For example, Kumarajiva, whose contributions to Chinese Buddhist history were as great as Xuanzang, came here when he was twelve years old and studied Hinayana for two years; also here, he met Wangzi and Canjun from Shache, who mastered Mahayana, and so he turned to Mahayana and passed that on all through his life. Shache now belongs to Kashgar, too. Although the main Buddhism in Kashgar was always Hinayana, and Kumarajiva had to leave, it would always be the place for his spiritual transformation.

Soon after Kumarajiva left, Fa Hien came here for the scriptures and proclaimed the grand Dharma assembly here. Later, with regard to the scriptures retrieved by Xuanzang, he also stayed here for a period to copy some scriptures damaged by water.

During the Karakhanid Empire in the ninth to thirteenth centuries AD, surpassing culturally creative capability was shown in Kashgar, including the long narrative poem “Kutadgu Bilig,” the first work written with pure Uighur script, and the elaborate Turkic Dictionary, which were crucially important Uygur culture classics. Following them were many excellent works. Kashgar shines with sacred glory in the creation of classics.

In fact, Kashgar was also the front line of Islam’s introduction to China in the seventh century AD; Islam did not spread to the north and Xinjiang until setting down its roots in Kashgar for hundreds of years. The cultural relics of Islam there are too numerous to mention, for its main belief up to today was Islam. Over thousands of years, it was nourished by devout rites every day, and the ruins also shared in this life, so all would brim with energy and vitality.

According to the records of Marco Polo, a traveler from Europe, the Nestorians, one of the religious sects of Christianity, named as “Nestorianism” in China, included many adherents here, and its religious services continued in a satisfactory manner, though it had been banned by Rome in the fifth century AD. About such matters, the Italian Marco Polo was very sensitive. Also, Zoroastrianism, long banned by Persia in ancient times, was very popular in the civil society of this region; even the Book of Southern Tang reported that “Zoroastrianism is embraced” in Shule area.

In general, Kashgar was a clearinghouse not only for the commodity trades, but also for spiritual culture over thousands of years. It had a large range that included Central Asia, South Asia, West Asia, and faraway Europe. If the West Regions was the integration center of major civilizations, Kashgar was the center of the center.

The place had existed since ancient times, but only quietly in the hearts of traveling merchants. In the nineteenth century, the world gained new consciousness of that realm, and so the significance of Kashgar again aroused widespread attention. At that time, many of the leading scholars in the world firmly believed that many significant cultural footprints must have been left there, so they traveled thousands of miles and came to Kashgar. As Tachibana Zuicho, an explorer from Japan, said: “Here is the political and commercial center in Central Asia, known by the world long before. Now all people who travel to Central Asia will certainly appreciate Kashgar.”
When looking over archeological works in the world, you find that Kashgar has become a commonly used noun that cannot be avoided in Orientalism research.

In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, domestic strife and foreign aggression troubled China greatly; added to those deep distresses, China was almost completely partitioned by the Great Powers. However, even at such a time, an archeologist who was sent to innermost Asia but never came to Kashgar was like a graduate whose diploma had never been stamped with the signature and seal of the president.

History is easy to forget, but is difficult to forget it entirely. In those wanderers’ nights, when batches of foreign tipplers rejoiced at the sandhill, the sandhill under their feet sighed desolately and coldly revealed the scrap of historical ruins, which seemed to remind them what this place was.

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: IN APRIL 1881, the Russian consulate in Kashgar was established. It was a commonplace post originally, but strangely enough, sixty Cossack cavalries were quartered there. These cavalries crossed the large square in the city to the riverbank of the east city for practice, twice in the morning and evening every day, and also performed swordplay, equestrian feats, and marksmanship for the crowds. The consul in the Russian consulate was quite learned, and his name was Petrovskiy. A British scholar describes him as follows:

Petrovskiy, efficient, arrogant, cunning and skillful in ensnarement, used every means including conspiracy, intimidation, threat, inducement, bribe and compulsion with Chinese officials during the twenty-one years of his tenure. His aim was to partition the oasis in the westernmost Xinjiang of China, so that Russia would be able to control the strategic mountain pass to the Indian postern.
—Janet Miskiw, Archeology and Exploration of Stein

Russia’s expectation to control the postern to India was clearly a provocation to England. At that time, besides implementing colonial rule in India, England also controlled Kunlun Mountain, the Hindu Kush, and majority of districts south of Amu Darya. How could it allow the intervention of Russia? Therefore, the later British consulate general in Kashgar occupied twice the floor area of Russia’s, and it was even much grander than its consulate in Urumchi. A British journalist wrote:

During over fifty years of great competition and fighting for Central Asia between the British Empire and Tsarist Russia, Kashgar was always a forefront position for the British Empire. In that competition, the British Empire carried out a long and complicated battle with Tsarist Russia, so as to obtain dominance of the politics and economy in Asia. That British flag waving on the British consulate in Kashgar was the only one between India and the North Pole.
—Peter Holbrook, Reminiscence of a Diplomatist Wife to Kashgar

During the confrontation between Cossack cavalries and the British flag in Kashgar, every day scholars of the past thousands of years also came to this city. Sven Hedin came, and setting off from here, he found the ancient city—Dandan Oilik, thousands of years old—and investigated the migration sites of Tarim River and Lop Nur. Along with the achievements of Sven Hedin, Stein also came and found the remains of the Gandhara—“Hellenistic Buddhism art”—and the Loulan ruins. Such a series of relics showed the incomparable significance of this land from ancient times in many different ways.

This “incomparable significance” can be divided into two kinds. The first kind ends with ancient times while the second kind extends to modern times. Most cultural relics found in the West Regions are of the second kind. Just like rows of huge mathematical formulae left by the ancient sages, they are proving the necessary connection between major spaces, and the practical possibility of opening up such necessary connections. After the archeological discoveries in the West Regions, the historian Wales made a judgment: “I begin to know as of today that the Tarim River is much more important than the Jordan River basin and Rhine Valley.”

It was just such judgment that roused the Cossack cavalries and the British in Kashgar. The consuls from the two countries would receive those archeologists affably, and seek for them to provide more ancient reasons for the modern ambitions of their separate empires. However, the archeologists had little respect for those two consuls. After all, they knew the history very well and understood the severity of their tasks compared with the politics of these diplomats. They went deep into the desert and would drop to their knees if they saw even a little ancient trace, scrabbling it gently and wiping it off carefully with their hands. They knelt there for a long time.
In this way the archaeologists knelt and gave thanks on behalf of all modern people. On this dumb earth, many places are worth kneeling down at, and many places are worth giving thanks for.

sections.label: V
paragraphs: AMONG MANY “ANCESTORS” in Chinese civilization, the place with the most stunning geography is the West Regions, including Kashgar.

Such words may lead to sidelong glances by other “ancestors,” and I am very sorry about that, but in fact I do not give such praise lightly. Consider Mount Tianshan, Kunlun Mountain, and Taklimakan Desert, real-world structures; just a glimpse of any corner is sufficient to make the people hold their breath. However, here they are arranged together, connected together, and echoing together neatly. What a scene.

A series of unsurpassable impasses, a layer of incomparable magnificence, and a flow of unique greatness surrounds you, conquers you, smashes you, but accepts you nonetheless. You are lost and found again, but it is not the same you.

Facing Mount Tianshan and Kunlun Mountain, high mountains backed by other “ancestors” are just like the bonsai. Facing Taklimakan Desert, the lonely smoke in the desert and the river sunsets chanted about by other “ancestors” are mere childishness.

If you come to Kashgar, you should not select the usual crowded tourist attractions, but the Chogori, Muztagata Mountain, Oytag Glacier, Khunjerab Pass, Yakeailike beacon tower, the millennial euphratica poplar forest that spreads everywhere, and the desert at sunset. I and my wife are fascinated with the music of the Twelve Muqam in Shache, which makes us yearn for it in our hearts every time. It is no wonder that it is declared one of the world’s intangible cultural heritages though hidden far away. It makes me think of the Shule music and Qiuci music that caused a sensation in Chang’an during the Sui and Tang Dynasties. Among the grand harmonies of the greatest ancient dynasties in China, it is the music and dance from the West Regions that occupy the leading position.

In fact, besides Kashgar, many other West Region attractions in Xinjiang are worth visiting repeatedly, such as Qiuci (now Kuqa), Khotan (now Hotan), Gaochang, Jiaohe, etc. If you have sufficient energy, you can visit Loulan, Milan, and the Niya ruins.

By the Yarkand River, a local officer had already placed the brush and Xuan paper in the proper arrangement, to let me inscribe some words and prepare to engrave them in the mountainside. I asked him what words to write, and he said, “Top City in Kunlun.”
I said, “Everwhere here is magnificent.”

After I finished it, my view spanned the euphratica forest, glowing like a row of flames, the layers of clouds, and the heavenly road on Kunlun Mountain. That road led to the Ali District in Tibet. Suddenly I saw plumes of white smoke rising into the blue sky from the snowy peak. Could there be someone living there?
“How can white smoke appear among such high clouds?” I asked.
The master said it was not white smoke, but the snowcap being blown by the wind.

So that was it. Yet on second thought, my doubts have been shared by travelers in past times. They were guessing and judging, looking down the road sometimes, and raising their heads again. How can a place without people have white smoke? They probably could not ask it of anyone, and so stayed in doubt, but then looked back again.
In this way, such magical “white smoke” becomes the white banners and flags tantalizing the faraway guests.
I smiled, and thought that the soul of Mr. Toynbee, yearning for the West Regions, now must find its destination among the white banners and settle down delightedly.

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 我们这些人，对清代总有一种复杂的情感阻隔。记得很小的时候，历史老师讲到“扬州十日”、“嘉定三屠”时，眼含泪花，这是清代的开始；而讲到“火烧圆明园”、“戊戌变法”时又有泪花了，这是清代的尾声。年迈的老师一哭，孩子们也跟着哭。清代历史，是小学中唯一用眼泪浸润的课程。从小种下的怨恨，很难化解得开。

老人的眼泪和孩子们的眼泪拌和在一起，使这种历史情绪有了一种最世俗的力量。我小学的同学全是汉族，没有满族。因此很容易在课堂里获得一种共同语言，好像汉族理所当然是中国的主宰，你满族为什么要来抢夺呢？抢夺去了能够弄好倒也罢了，偏偏越弄越糟，最后几乎让外国人给瓜分了。于是，在闪闪泪光中，我们懂得了什么是汉奸、什么是卖国贼、什么是民族大义、什么是气节。我们似乎也知道了中国之所以落后于世界列强，关键就在于清代后期的腐败无能，而辛亥革命的启蒙者们重新点燃汉人对这个清朝的仇恨，提出“驱除鞑虏，恢复中华”的口号，又是多么有必要、多么让人解气。清朝终于被推翻了，但至今在很多中国人心里，它仍然是一种冤孽般的存在。

年长以后，我开始对这种情绪产生警惕。因为无数事实证明：在我们中国，许多情绪化的社会评判规范，虽然堂而皇之地传之久远，却包含着极大的不公正。我们缺少人类普遍意义上的价值启蒙，因此这些情绪化的社会评判规范大多是从封建正统观念引申出来的，带有很大盲目性。先是姓氏正统论，刘汉、李唐、赵宋、朱明……在同一姓氏的传代系列中所出现的继承人，哪怕是昏君、懦夫、色鬼、守财奴、精神失常者，都是合法而合理的；而外姓人氏若有觊觎，即便有一千条一万条道理，也站不住脚，真伪、正邪、忠奸全由此划分。由姓氏正统论扩而大之，就是民族正统论。这种观念要比姓氏正统论复杂得多，你看辛亥革命的闯将们与封建主义的姓氏正统论势不两立，却也需要大声宣扬民族正统论，便是例证。
汉族当然非常伟大，没有理由要受到外族的屠杀和欺凌。问题是，不能由此而把汉族等同于中华，把中华历史的正义、光亮、希望全部压在汉族一边。与其他民族一样，汉族也有大量的污浊、昏聩和丑恶，它的统治者曾一再地把整个中国历史推入死胡同。在这种情况下，历史有可能做出超越汉族正统论的选择，而这种选择又未必是倒退。
为此，我要写写承德的避暑山庄。清代的史料成捆成扎，把这些留给历史学家吧，我们，只要轻手轻脚地绕到这个消夏的别墅里去偷看几眼也就够了。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 承德的避暑山庄是清代皇家园林，又称“热河行宫”、“承德离宫”，虽然闻名史册，但久为禁苑，又地处塞外，历来光顾的人不多。我去时，找了山庄背后的一个旅馆住下。那时正是薄暮时分，我独个儿走出住所大门，对着眼前黑黝黝的山岭发呆。查过地图，这山岭便是避暑山庄北部的最后屏障，就像一把罗圈椅的椅背。在这张罗圈椅上，休息过一个疲惫的王朝。
奇怪的是，整个中华版图都已归属了这个王朝，为什么还要把这把休息的罗圈椅放到长城之外呢？清代的帝王们在这张椅子上面南而坐的时候都在想些什么呢？
月亮升起来了，眼前的山壁显得更加巍然怆然。北京的故宫把几个不同的朝代混杂在一起，谁的形象也看不真切；而在这里，远远地、静静地、纯纯地、悄悄地，躲开了中原王气，藏下了一个不羼杂的清代。它实在使我产生了一种巨大的诱惑，从第二天开始，我便一头埋到了山庄里边。

山庄很大，本来觉得北京的颐和园已经大得令人咋舌了，它竟比颐和园还大整整一倍，据说装下八九个北海公园是没有问题的。我想不出国内还有哪个古典园林能望其项背。山庄里面，除了前半部有层层叠叠的宫殿外，是开阔的湖区、平原区和山区。尤其是山区，几乎占了整个山庄的八成，这让游惯了别的园林的人很不习惯。园林是用来休闲的，何况是皇家园林，大多追求方便平适，有的也会堆几座小山装点一下。哪有像这儿的，硬是圈进莽莽苍苍一大片真正的山岭来消遣？这个格局，包含着一种需要我们抬头仰望、低头思索的审美观念和人生观念。
山庄里有很多楹联和石碑，上面的文字大多由皇帝们亲自撰写。他们当然想不到多少年后会有我们这些陌生人闯入他们的私家园林来读这些文字。这些文字是他们写给后辈继承人看的。我踏着青苔和蔓草，辨识和解读着一切能找到的文字，连藏在山间树林中的石碑都不放过。一路走去，终于可以有把握地说：山庄的营造，完全出自一代政治家在精神上的强健。
首先是康熙。他是走了一条艰难而又成功的长途才走进山庄的，到这里来喘口气，应该。

他一生的艰难都是自找的。他的父辈本来已经给他打下了一个很完整的江山，他八岁即位，十四岁亲政，年纪轻轻一个孩子，坐享其成就是了，能在如此辽阔的疆土、如此兴盛的运势前做些什么呢？他稚气未脱的眼睛，竟然疑惑地盯上了两个庞然大物：一个是朝廷中最有权势的辅政大臣鳌拜，一个是自恃当初领清兵入关有功、拥兵自重于南方的吴三桂。平心而论，对于这样与自己的祖辈、父辈都有密切关系的重要政治势力，有几人能下得了决心去动手？但康熙却向他们，也向自己挑战了。他，十六岁上干净利落地除了鳌拜集团，二十岁开始向吴三桂开战，花八年时间的征战取得彻底胜利。
他等于把到手的江山重新打理了一遍，使自己从一个继承者变成了创业者。他成熟了，眼前几乎已经找不到什么对手，但他还是经常骑着马，在中国北方的山林草泽间徘徊，这是他祖辈崛起的所在，他在寻找着自己的生命和事业的依托点。
他每次都要经过长城。长城多年失修，已经破败。对着这堵历代帝王切切关心的城墙，他想了很多。他的祖辈是破长城进来的，没有吴三桂也绝对进得了，那么长城究竟有什么用呢？堂堂一个朝廷，难道就靠这些砖块去保卫？但是如果没有长城，我们的防线又在哪里呢？他思考的结果，可以从一六九一年他的一份上谕中看出个大概。
那年五月，古北口总兵官蔡元向朝廷提出，他所管辖的那一带长城“倾塌甚多，请行修筑”，康熙竟然不同意，他的上谕是：
秦筑长城以来，汉、唐、宋亦常修理，其时岂无边患？明末我太祖统大兵长驱直入，诸路瓦解，皆莫能当。可见守国之道，唯在修德安民。民心悦则邦本得，而边境自固，所谓“众志成城”者是也。如古北、喜峰口一带，朕皆巡阅，概多损坏，今欲修之，兴工劳役，岂能无害百姓？且长城延袤数千里，养兵几何方能分守？
说得实在是很有道理。

康熙希望能筑起一座无形的长城。对此，他有硬的一手和软的一手。硬的一手是在长城外设立“木兰围场”，每年秋天，由皇帝亲自率领王公大臣、各级官兵一万余人去进行大规模的“围猎”，实际上是一种声势浩大的军事演习，这既可以使王公大臣们保持住勇猛、强悍的人生风范，又可顺便对北方边境起一个威慑作用。“木兰围场”既然设在长城之外的边远地带，离北京就很有一点距离，如此众多的朝廷要员前去秋猎，当然要建造一些大大小小的行宫，而热河行宫就是其中最大的一座。
软的一手是与北方边疆的各少数民族建立起一种常来常往的友好关系，他们的首领不必长途进京也能有与清廷交谊的场所。而且还为他们准备下各自的宗教场所，这也就需要有热河行宫和它周围的寺庙群了。
总之，软硬两手最后都汇集到这一座行宫、这一个山庄里来了，说是避暑，说是休息，意义却又远远不止于此。把复杂的政治目的转化为一片幽静闲适的园林、一圈香火缭绕的寺庙，这不能不说是康熙的大本事。
康熙几乎每年立秋之后都要到“木兰围场”参加一次为期二十天的秋猎，一生共参加了四十八次。每次围猎，情景都极为壮观。先由康熙选定逐年轮换的狩猎区域，然后就搭建一百七十多座大帐篷为“内城”、二百五十多座大帐篷为“外城”，城外再设警卫。第二天拂晓，八旗官兵在皇帝的统一督导下集结围拢。在上万官兵的齐声呐喊下，康熙一马当先，引弓射猎，每有所中便引来一片欢呼。然后，扈从大臣和各级将士也紧随康熙射猎。
康熙身强力壮，骑术高明，围猎时智勇双全，弓箭上的功夫更让王公大臣由衷惊服，因而他本人的猎获就很多。
晚上，营地上篝火处处，肉香飘荡，人笑马嘶，而康熙还必须回到帐篷里批阅每天疾驰送来的奏章文书。
康熙一生打过许多著名的仗，但在晚年，他最得意的还是自己打猎的成绩，因为这纯粹是他个人生命力的验证。一七一九年康熙自“木兰围场”行猎后返回避暑山庄时，曾兴致勃勃地告谕御前侍卫：
朕自幼至今，凡用鸟枪弓矢获虎一百三十五，熊二十，豹二十五，猞猁狲十，麋十四，狼九十六，野猪一百三十二，哨获之鹿数百，其余围场内随便射获诸兽不胜记矣。朕曾于一日内射兔三百一十八，若庸常人，毕世亦不能得此一日之数也。
这笔流水账，他说得很得意，我们读得也很高兴。身体的强健和精神的强健是连在一起的，须知中国历史上多的是病恹恹的皇帝，他们即便再“内秀”，却何以面对如此庞大的国家？
由于强健，他有足够的精力处理复杂的西藏事务和蒙古事务，解决治理黄河、淮河和疏通漕运等大问题，而且大多很有成效，功泽后世。由于强健，他还愿意勤奋地学习，结果不仅武功一流，“内秀”也十分了得，成为中国历代皇帝中特别有学问，也特别重视学问的一位。

谁能想得到呢，这位清朝帝王竟然比明代历朝皇帝更热爱汉族传统文化。大凡经、史、子、集、诗、书、音律，他都下过一番工夫，其中对朱熹哲学钻研最深。他亲自批点《资治通鉴纲目大全》，还下令访求遗散在民间的善本珍籍加以整理，大规模组织人力编辑出版了卷帙浩繁的《古今图书集成》和字典辞书，文化气魄铺天盖地。直到今天，我们研究中国古代文化还离不开那些重要的工具书。在他倡导的文化气氛下，涌现了一大批优秀的文史专家。在这一点上，很少有哪个年代能与康熙朝相比肩。

以上讲的还只是我们所说的“国学”，可能更让现代读者惊异的是他的“西学”。因为即使到了现代，在我们印象中，国学和西学虽然可以沟通，但在同一个人身上深谙两边的毕竟不多。然而早在三百年前，康熙皇帝竟然在北京故宫和承德避暑山庄认真研究了欧几里得几何学，经常演算习题，又学习了法国数学家巴蒂的《实用和理论几何学》，并比较它与欧几里得几何学的差别。他的老师是当时来中国的一批西方传教士，但后来他的演算比传教士还快。以数学为基础，康熙又进而学习了西方的天文、历法、物理、医学，与中国原有的这方面知识比较，取长补短。在自然科学问题上，中国官僚和外国传教士经常发生矛盾，康熙从不袒护中国官僚，也不主观臆断，而是靠自己认真学习，几乎每次都作出了公正的裁断。
这一切，居然与他所醉心的“国学”互不排斥，居然与他一天射猎三百一十八只野兔互不排斥，居然与他一连串重大的政治行为、军事行为、经济行为互不排斥！
我并不认为康熙给中国带来了根本性的希望，他的政权也做过不少坏事，如臭名昭著的文字狱之类。我想说的只是，在中国历代帝王中，这位少数民族出身的帝王具有异乎寻常的生命力，他的人格比较健全。

有时，个人的生命力和人格会给历史留下重重的印记。与他相比，明代的许多皇帝都活得太不像样了，鲁迅说他们是“无赖儿郎”，的确有点像。尤其让人生气的是明代万历皇帝（神宗）朱翊钧，在位四十八年，亲政三十八年，竟有二十五年时间躲在深宫之内不见外人的面，完全不理国事，连内阁首辅也见不到他，不知在干什么。他聚敛的金银如山似海，但当辽东起事、朝廷束手无策时问他要钱，他死也不肯拿出来，最后拿出一个无济于事的小零头，竟然都是因窖藏太久变黑发霉、腐蚀得不能见天日的银子！这是一个失去了人格支撑的心理变态者，但他又集权于一身，明朝怎能不垮？他死后还有后代继位，但明朝已在他的手里败定了。康熙与他正相反，把生命从深宫里释放出来，在旷野、猎场和各个知识领域挥洒，避暑山庄就是他这种生命方式的一个重要吐纳点。

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 康熙与晚明帝王的对比，避暑山庄与万历深宫的对比，当时的汉族知识分子当然也感受到了，心情比较复杂。
开始，大多数汉族知识分子都坚持抗清复明，甚至在赳赳武夫们纷纷掉头转向之后，一群柔弱的文人还宁死不屈。文人中也有一些著名的变节者，但他们往往也承受着深刻的心理矛盾和精神痛苦。
我想这便是文化的力量。一切军事争逐都是浮面的，而事情到了要摇撼某个文化生态系统的时候才会真正变得严重起来。
一个民族、一个国家、一个人种，其最终意义不是军事的、地域的、政治的，而是文化的。当时江南地区好几次重大的抗清事件，都起于“削发”之事，即汉人历来束发而清人强令削发，甚至到了“留头不留发，留发不留头”的地步。头发的样式看来事小，却关及文化生态。结果，是否“毁我衣冠”的问题成了“夷夏抗争”的最高爆发点。

这中间，最能把事情与整个文化系统联系起来的是文化人，最懂得文明和野蛮的差别，并把“鞑虏”与野蛮连在一起的也是文化人。老百姓的头发终于被削掉了，而不少文人还在拼死坚持。著名大学者刘宗周住在杭州，自清兵进杭州后便绝食，二十天后死亡；他的门生、另一位著名大学者黄宗羲投身于武装抗清行列，失败后回余姚家乡事母、著述；又一位著名大学者顾炎武，武装抗清失败后便开始流浪，谁也找不着他，最后终老陕西……这些宗师如此强硬，他们的门生和崇拜者们当然也多有追随。
但是，事情到了康熙那儿却发生了一些微妙的变化。文人们依然像朱耷笔下的秃鹰，以“天地为之一寒”的冷眼看着朝廷，而朝廷却奇怪地流泻出一种压抑不住的对汉文化的热忱。开始大家以为是一种笼络人心的策略，但从康熙身上看，好像不完全是。
他在讨伐吴三桂的战争还没有结束的时候，就迫不及待地下令各级官员以“崇儒重道”为目的，向朝廷推荐“学问兼优、文辞卓越”的士子，由他亲自主考录用，称做“博学鸿词科”。
这次被保荐、征召的共一百四十三人，后来录取了五人。其中有傅山、李颙等人被推荐了却宁死不应考。傅山被人推荐后又被强抬进北京，他见到“大清门”三字便滚倒在地，两泪直流。如此行动举止，康熙不仅不怪罪，反而免他考试，任命他为“中书舍人”。他回乡后不准别人以“中书舍人”称他，但这个时候说他对康熙本人还有多大仇恨，大概谈不上了。
李颙也是如此，受到推荐后称病拒考，被人抬到省城后竟以绝食相抗，众人只得作罢。这事发生在康熙十七年，康熙本人二十五岁。没想到二十五年后，年过半百的康熙西巡时还记得这位强硬的学人，要召见他；李颙没有应召，但心里毕竟已经很过意不去了，派儿子李慎言做代表应召，并送自己的两部著作《四书反身录》和《二曲集》给康熙。这件事带有一定的象征性，表示最有抵触的汉族知识分子也开始与康熙和解了。

与李颙相比，黄宗羲是大人物了。康熙对黄宗羲更是礼仪有加，多次请黄宗羲出山未能如愿，便命令当地巡抚到黄宗羲家里，把黄宗羲写的书认真抄来，送入宫内以供自己拜读。这一来，黄宗羲也不能不有所感动。与李颙一样，自己出面终究不便，由儿子代理，黄宗羲让自己的儿子黄百家进入皇家修史部门，帮助完成康熙交下的修《明史》的任务。你看，即便是原先与清廷不共戴天的黄宗羲、李颙他们，也觉得儿子一辈可以在康熙手下好生过日子了。这不是变节，也不是妥协，而是一种文化生态意义上的开始认同。既然康熙对汉文化认同得那么诚恳，汉族文人为什么就完全不能与他认同呢？

黄宗羲不是让儿子参加康熙下令编写的《明史》吗？编《明史》这事给汉族知识界震动不小。康熙任命了大历史学家徐元文、万斯同、张玉书、王鸿绪等负责此事，要他们根据《明实录》如实编写，说“他书或以文章见长，独修史宜直书实事”。他还多次要大家仔细研究明代晚期破败的教训，引以为戒。汉族知识界要反清复明，而清廷君主竟然亲自领导着汉族的历史学家在冷静研究明代了。这种研究又高于反清复明者的思考水平，那么，对峙也就不能不渐渐化解了。《明史》后来成为整个二十四史中写得较好的一部，这是直到今天还要承认的事实。
当然，也还余留着几个坚持不肯认同的文人。例如，康熙时代浙江有个叫吕留良的学者，在著书和讲学中还一再强调孔子思想的精义是“尊王攘夷”。这个提法，在他死后被湖南一个叫曾静的落第书生看到了，很是激动，赶到浙江找到吕留良的儿子和学生几人，筹划反清。
这时康熙也早已过世，已是雍正年间，这群文人手下无一兵一卒，能干成什么事呢？他们打听到川陕总督岳钟琪是岳飞的后代，想来肯定能继承岳飞遗志来抗击外夷，就派人带给他一封策反的信，眼巴巴地请他起事。
这事说起来已经有点近乎笑话。岳飞抗金到那时已隔着整整一个元朝、整整一个明朝，清朝也已过了八九十年，算到岳钟琪身上都是多少代的事啦，居然还想着让他凭着一个“岳”字拍案而起，中国书生的昏愚和天真就在这里。
岳钟琪是清朝大官，做梦也没有想到过要反清，接信后虚假地应付了一下，却理所当然地报告了雍正皇帝。雍正下令逮捕了这个谋反集团，又亲自阅读了书信、著作，觉得其中有好些观点需要自己写文章来与汉族知识分子辩论。他认为有过康熙一代，已有足够的事实证明清代统治者并不差，可为什么还有人要对抗清廷？于是这位皇帝亲自编了一部《大义觉迷录》颁发各地，而且特免肇事者曾静等人的死罪，让他们专到江浙一带去宣讲。

雍正的《大义觉迷录》写得颇为诚恳。他的大意是：不错，我们是夷人，我们是“外国”人，但这是籍贯而已，天命要我们来抚育中原生民，被抚育者为什么还要把华、夷分开来看？你们所尊重的舜是东夷之人、文王是西夷之人，这难道有损于他们的圣德吗？吕留良这样著书立说的人，将前朝康熙皇帝的文治武功、赫赫盛德都加以隐匿和诬蔑，实在是不顾民生国运只泄私愤了。外族入主中原，可能反而勇于为善，如果著书立说的人只认为生在中原的君主不必修德行仁也可享有名分，而外族君主即便励精图治也得不到褒扬，外族君主为善之心也会因之而懈怠，受苦的不还是中原百姓吗？
雍正的这番话带着明显的委屈情绪，而且是给父亲康熙打抱不平，也真有一些动人的地方。但他的整体思维显然比不上康熙，口口声声说自己是“外国”人、“夷人”，在一些前提性的概念上把事情搞复杂了。他的儿子乾隆看出了这个毛病，即位后把《大义觉迷录》全部收回，列为禁书，杀了被雍正赦免的曾静等人，开始大兴文字狱。
除了华、夷之分的敏感点外，其他地方雍正倒是比较宽容、有度量，听得进忠臣贤士们的尖锐意见和建议，因此在执政的前期，做了不少好事，国运可称昌盛。这样一来，即便存有异念的少数汉族知识分子也不敢有什么想头，到后来也真没有什么想头了。其实本来这样的人已不可多觅，雍正和乾隆都把文章做过了头。真正第一流的大学者，在乾隆时代已经不想做反清复明的事情。
乾隆靠着人才济济的智力优势，靠着康熙、雍正给他奠定的丰厚基业，也靠着他本人的韬略雄才，做起了中国历史上福气最好的大皇帝。承德避暑山庄，他来得最多，总共逗留的时间很长，因此他的踪迹更是随处可见。乾隆也经常参加“木兰秋猎”，亲自射获的猎物也极为可观，但他的主要心思却放在边疆征战上，避暑山庄和周围的外八庙内记载这种征战成果的碑文极多。
这种征战与汉族的利益没有冲突，反而弘扬了中国的国威，连汉族知识界也引以为荣，甚至可以把乾隆看成是华夏圣君了。但我细看碑文之后却产生一个强烈的感觉：有的仗迫不得已，打打也可以，但多数战争的必要性深可怀疑——需要打得这么大吗？需要反复那么多次吗？需要杀得如此残酷吗？
好大喜功的乾隆把他的所谓“十全武功”雕刻在避暑山庄里乐滋滋地自我品尝，这使山庄回荡出一些燥热而又不祥的气氛。在满、汉文化对峙基本上结束之后，这里洋溢着的是中华帝国的自得情绪。

一七九三年九月十四日，一个英国使团来到避暑山庄，乾隆以盛宴欢迎，还在山庄的万树园内以大型歌舞和焰火晚会招待，避暑山庄一片热闹。英方的目的是希望乾隆同意他们派使臣常驻北京，在北京设立洋行，希望中国开放贸易口岸，在广州附近拨一些地方让英商居住，又希望英国货物在广州至澳门的内河流通时能获免税和减税的优惠。本来，这是可以谈判的事，但对于居住在避暑山庄、一生喜欢用武力炫耀华夏威仪的乾隆来说，却不存在任何谈判的可能。
他给英国国王写了信，信的标题是“赐英吉利国王敕书”。信内对一切要求全部拒绝，说：“天朝尺土俱归版籍，疆址森然，即岛屿沙洲，亦必划界分疆，各有专属”，“从无外人等在北京城开设货行之事”，“此与天朝体制不合，断不可行”。至今有人认为这几句话充满了爱国主义的凛然大义，与以后清廷签订的卖国条约不可同日而语。对此我实在不敢苟同。
本来康熙早在一六八四年就已开放海禁，在广东、福建、浙江、江苏分设四个海关欢迎外商来贸易。过了七十多年，乾隆反而关闭其他海关只许外商在广州贸易。外商在广州也有许多可笑的限制，例如，不准学说中国话、买中国书，不许坐轿，更不许把妇女带来，等等。我们闭目就能想象清廷对外国人的这些限制是出于何种心理规定出来的。
康熙向传教士学西方自然科学，关系不错，而乾隆却把天主教给禁了。
乾隆在避暑山庄训斥外国帝王的朗声言辞，在历史老人听来，不太顺耳了。这座园林已掺杂进某种凶兆。

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 我在山庄松云峡乾隆诗碑的西侧，读到了他儿子嘉庆写的一首诗。嘉庆即位后经过这里，看到父亲那些得意扬扬的诗作后不禁长叹一声：父亲的诗真是深奥，而我这个做儿子的却实在觉得肩上的担子太重了！（“瞻题蕴精奥，守位重仔肩。”）
嘉庆一生都在面对内忧外患，最后不明不白地死在避暑山庄。
道光皇帝继嘉庆之位时已近四十岁，没有什么才能，只知艰苦朴素，穿的裤子还打过补丁。这对一国元首来说可不是什么佳话。朝中大臣竞相模仿，穿了破旧衣服上朝，一眼看去，这个朝廷已经没有多少气数了。
父亲死在避暑山庄，畏怯的道光也就不愿意去那里了，让它空关了几十年。他有时想想也该像祖宗一样去打一次猎，打听能不能不经过避暑山庄就可以到“木兰围场”，回答说没有别的道路，他也就不去打猎了。像他这么个可怜巴巴的皇帝，似乎本来就与山庄和打猎没有缘分；鸦片战争已经爆发，他忧愁的目光只能一直注视着南方。
避暑山庄一直关到一八六○年九月，突然接到命令，咸丰皇帝要来，赶快打扫。咸丰这次来时带的银两特别多，原来是来逃难的，英法联军正威胁着北京。咸丰这一来就不走了，东走走西看看，庆幸祖辈留下这么个好地方让他躲避。他在这里又批准了好几份丧权辱国的条约，但签约后还是不走，直到一八六一年七月十七日死在这儿，差不多住了近一年。
咸丰一死，避暑山庄热闹了好些天，各种政治势力围着遗体进行着明明暗暗的较量。一场被历史学家称为“辛酉政变”的行动方案在山庄的几间屋子里制订。然后，咸丰的灵柩向北京起运了，刚继位的小皇帝也出发了，浩浩荡荡。避暑山庄的大门，又一次紧紧地关住了。而在这支浩浩荡荡的队伍中间，很快站出来一个二十七岁的青年女子，她将统治中国数十年。
她就是慈禧，离开了山庄后再也没有回来。不久她又下了一道命令，说热河避暑山庄已经几十年不用，殿亭各宫多已倾圮，只是咸丰皇帝去时稍稍修治了一下，现在咸丰已逝，众人已走，“所有热河一切工程，着即停止”。
这个命令，与康熙不修长城的谕旨前后辉映。康熙的“长城”也终于倾塌了，荒草凄迷，暮鸦回翔，旧墙斑驳，霉苔处处，而大门却紧紧地关着。
关住了那些宫殿房舍倒也罢了，还关住了那么些苍郁的山、那么些晶亮的水。在康熙看来，这儿就是他心目中的清王朝，但清王朝把它丢弃了。被丢弃了的它可怜，丢弃了它的清王朝更可怜，连一把罗圈椅也坐不到了，恓恓惶惶，丧魂落魄。
后来慈禧在北京重修了一个颐和园，与避暑山庄“对峙”。塞外朔北的园林不会再有对峙的能力和兴趣，它似乎已属于另外一个时代。热河的雄风早已吹散，清朝从此阴气重重、劣迹斑斑。
当新的一个世纪来到的时候，一大群汉族知识分子向这个政权发出了毁灭性声讨。避暑山庄，在这个时候是一个邪恶的象征，老老实实躲在远处，尽量不要叫人发现。

sections.label: 五
paragraphs: 清王朝灭亡后，社会震荡，世事忙乱。直到一九二七年六月二日，大学者王国维先生在颐和园投水而死，才让全国的有心人肃然沉思。
王国维先生的死因众说纷纭，我们且不管它，只知道这位汉族文化大师拖着清代的一条辫子，自尽在清代的皇家园林里，遗嘱为“五十之年，只欠一死；经此世变，义无再辱”。
他不会不知道明末清初为汉族人是束发还是留辫之争曾发生过惊人的血案，他不会不知道刘宗周、黄宗羲、顾炎武这些大学者的慷慨行迹，他更不会不知道按照世界历史的进程，社会巨变乃属必然。但是，他还是死了。
我赞成陈寅恪先生的说法，王国维先生并不是死于政治斗争、人事纠葛，而是死于一种文化：
凡一种文化值衰落之时，为此文化所化之人，必感苦痛，其表现此文化之程量愈宏，则其所受之苦痛亦愈甚；迨既达极深之度，殆非出于自杀无以求一己之心安而义尽也。
（《王观堂先生挽词并序》）
王国维先生实在无法把文化与清廷分割开来。在他的书架里，《古今图书集成》、《康熙字典》、《四库全书》、《红楼梦》、《桃花扇》、《长生殿》、乾嘉学派、纳兰性德都历历在目，每一本、每一页都无法分割。在他看来，在他身边陨灭的，不仅仅是一个政治意义上，而且更是一个文化意义上的古典时代。
他，只想留在古典时代。
我们记得，在康熙手下，汉族高层知识分子经过剧烈的心理挣扎已开始与朝廷建立文化认同，没有想到的是，当康熙的事业破败之后，文化认同还未消散。为此，宏才博学的王国维先生要以生命来祭奠它。他没有从心理挣扎中找到希望，死得可惜又死得必然。
知识分子总是不同寻常，他们总要在政治、军事的折腾之后表现出长久的文化韧性。文化变成了他们的生命，只有靠生命来拥抱文化了，别无他途。明末以后是这样，清末以后也是这样。
文化的极度脆弱和极度强大，都在王国维先生纵身投水的扑通声中呈现无遗。
王国维先生到颐和园这也还是第一次，是从一个同事处借了五元钱才去的。颐和园门票六角，死后口袋中尚余四元四角。他去不了承德，也推不开山庄紧闭的大门。
今天，我面对着避暑山庄的清澈湖水，却不能不想起王国维先生的面容和身影。我轻轻地叹息一声：一个风云数百年的朝代，总是以一群强者英武的雄姿开头，而打下最后一个句点的，却常常是一些文质彬彬的凄怨灵魂。
秋雨注：这篇文章发表于一九九三年，后来被中国评论界看成是全部“清宫电视剧”的肇始之文。“清宫电视剧”拍得不错，但整体历史观念与我有很大差别。我对清代宫廷的看法，可参见本书另一篇《宁古塔》。

sections.label: I
paragraphs: PEOPLE LIKE US have a complicated emotional reaction regarding the Qing Dynasty. As a child, I remember my history teacher’s eyes would begin to fill with tears as he spoke of the “Ten Days in Yangzhou” or “The Three Jiading Massacres,” because they marked the start of the Qing Dynasty. He would also weep when it came time to talk about the “Burning of the Old Summer Palace” or “The Hundred Days’ Reform” in the dying days of the Qing. Seeing our elderly teacher crying, naturally us kids began sobbing too. These were the only tears I shed during the whole of elementary school. A grudge put in place this early on is difficult to get rid of.

When the tears of old people and children mingle, a historical atmosphere is created with a most tangible power. My classmates in elementary school were all Han Chinese, with not a single Manchu amongst them. It was therefore easy to fall into a common vocabulary in the classroom, as if it were completely natural that the Han should be the rulers of China, and why would you Manchus come try to snatch it away from us? If you’d grabbed it and made it better, that would have been one thing, but you made the country worse and worse, until by the end it was practically being carved up by foreigners. With tears falling freely, we learned what it was to be a traitor, what it meant to sell off your country to the highest bidder, what nationalism was, and the definition of integrity. We seemed to understand that the reason China had fallen behind and was no longer a world power, was all because of the Qing Dynasty, until the instigators of the Xinhai Rebellion lit the fuse of the Han people’s anger against the regime, raising the slogan “Expel the Manchus and Restore China”—a necessary, cathartic movement. And so the Qing Dynasty was overturned, but even till this day, it lurks in the hearts of many Chinese people, like a form of retribution.

When I grew up, I became wary of this mindset. Countless events have shown that in China, many societal judgments are emotionally based, and while they may have been imposed on generation after generation, they contain vast injustices within them. We lack the enlightened values of common humanity. These emotionally charged values are often derived from the orthodoxies of feudal times, and so have huge blind spots. There’s the idea of continuity by surname—Liu in the Han Dynasty, Li in the Tang, Zhao in the Song, Zhu in the Ming—and as long as each successor has the right surname, it doesn’t matter if they’re an incompetent ruler, a coward, a pervert, a miser, or someone with mental difficulties; their right to take over is seen as preordained, and if someone with an outsider’s surname were to try to muscle in, a thousand and one reasons could be found why they didn’t have a leg to stand on, their name being the sole determiner of truth or falsehood, goodness or evil, loyalty or treachery. Expanding this mindset, we arrive at tribalism—a way of thinking with a bit more complexity than the former, as we see in the rupture during the Xinhai Revolution, when the generals and the feudalists clashed over surname orthodoxy, but were forced to loudly proclaim that they ultimately supported this chauvinism.

The Han are, of course, a very noble people, and have never deserved the slaughter or humiliation inflicted by outsiders. But we can’t therefore equate the Han tribe with Chinese culture, and credit them with all the righteousness, brilliance and hope of Chinese history. As with all other communities, the Han had their share of corruption, muddled thinking, and ugly behavior, and at one point their proponents were trying to shove the whole of Chinese history down a dead end. In these circumstances, history made the choice of transcending Han orthodoxy, which does not necessarily represent a retreat.

And so, I’d like to write a little about a mountain house in Chengde. The history of the Qing Dynasty is tangled and knotted, and I will leave it to the historians to unravel. Let us instead move lightly over to this summer villa, where a few quick glances will satisfy us.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: THE CHENGDE MOUNTAIN RESORT BELONGED to the Qing Imperial family, and was also known as the Hot River Palace and the Chengde Distant Residence. Although this is a famous historical site, it was a forbidden building for a long time, as well as being located beyond the Great Wall, so there have never been very many visitors here. After arriving, I checked into a hotel behind the villa. It was twilight when I stepped out alone through the main lobby, and stood gazing at the dark bulk of the mountains before me. Looking at the map, this range was the final barrier to the north of the resort, like the back of a round-framed chair. An exhausted dynasty rested on this chair.

The strange thing was, with the entirety of China at the disposal of the dynasty, why locate this place of rest beyond the Great Wall? What did the Qing Emperors ponder as they sat in this seat, facing south?

As the moon rose, the slopes before me grew even more majestic and melancholy. Beijing’s Forbidden Palace muddles several different dynasties together so their outlines are blurred; in this place, so distant, so still, so pure, so quiet, the authority of the Central Plains was concealed, and the Qing Dynasty reposed here unmixed with other influences. All of this exerted an enormous pull on me, and I resolved that from the next day, I would devote my time to the villa.

The palace was huge. The size of Beijing’s Summer Palace had already left me stunned, and this place was actually twice as big. You could probably fit eight or nine Beihai Parks in here. I can’t think of a single ancient garden anywhere in China that comes close to this. After the various palaces gathered at the front of the property, the premises opened out into lakes, plains and hills. The hills, in particular, seemed to occupy eight-tenths of the land, an unusual proportion for those of us used to the layout of other parks. Landscaped gardens are presumably intended for relaxation, particularly imperial ones, and mostly aim for convenience and ease. Some scatter a few hillocks around for ornamentation, but nothing like this, a vast, desolate stretch of actual mountain range—what kind of recreation would this provide? Such a vista commands us to raise our heads and behold it in its entirety, and then look back down and contemplate its aesthetics and our outlook on life.

Also within the grounds were many couplets on stone tablets, many of them inscribed personally by the various Emperors. Of course, they never imagined that many decades later, strangers like us would be barging into their private gardens and reading these words, written with their successors and descendants in mind. Treading across moss and thick grass, I pieced together and read what text I could find, even seeking out the stone tablets deep within the hilly woods. As I walked, I could finally pronounce with confidence: the construction of this mountain villa was the result of a generation of politicians’ psychological strength.
The first of these was Emperor Kangxi. He walked a long, arduous road before succeeding. He walked into the villa to draw breath—as well he should.

All the challenges of his life were self-imposed. His father’s generation had already presented him with a most complete set of mountains and rivers. He ascended the throne at the age of eight, and began governing at fourteen. Although just a child, he had no need to do anything but stay put. What more could he achieve, already possessing such sweeping territories, such enormous good fortune? Yet his barely mature eyes were fixed mistrustfully on two powerful figures: the most powerful of his regents, Oboi, and the arrogant general Wu Sangui, who’d initially led the Qing troops into China, and held great authority over his forces. In fairness, how many people would be determined enough to strike against important political figures with such close relationships to one’s own forebears? But Kangxi did battle with them, and also with himself. At sixteen, he felled the entire Oboi clan in one clean blow. At twenty, he launched an attack on Wu Sangui, spending eight years on this conflict before securing a decisive victory.

This was equivalent to him reevaluating the lands under his command, turning himself from an inheritor to a creator. He was an adult now, and could see no opponents before him, yet still frequently rode his horse through the forests and grasslands of the north, from where his ancestors rose up, searching for a resting point for his own life and endeavors.

On every trip, he passed by the Great Wall, now neglected for many years and looking distinctly dilapidated. He thought a great deal about this structure that had been so important to generations of Emperors. His ancestors had broken through the Wall to enter this country, and would have managed to do so even without the leadership of Wu Sangui. So what use was this Wall, then? Could such a mighty dynasty really need a pile of bricks to protect it? Yet without the Wall, where would our line of defense be? The results of his contemplation can be seen in an imperial edict dating from 1691.

That May, the Commander-in-Chief of the forces at Gubeikou, Cai Yuan, pointed out to the court that the stretch of wall under his charge was “riddled with collapsed sections” and requested that “repair work be carried out.” Kangxi, remarkably, disagreed, and his edict was:

Ever since the Qin built the Wall, the Han, Tang and Song have often maintained it, but where are the threats to our borders now? At the end of the Ming, my ancestors led an army and broke through, clearing all roads before them, overcoming all obstacles. We can see, then, that in order to protect the kingdom, all that requires maintenance is our virtue and the peace of the people. If the people are happy, the land will be secure. The only way to reinforce our borders is by heeding the saying “the will of the people creates the wall.” Places such as Gubei and Xifengkou we have patrolled and inspected, and while there is much damage, if we wish to repair this, it will inevitably require forced labor, which would surely be detrimental to the people. In any case, the Great Wall stretches for thousands of li—how many soldiers would we require to properly defend it?
All of which is perfectly reasonable.

Kangxi wished to construct an intangible Great Wall. To this end, he was harsh with one hand and gentle with the other. The hard aspect established the “Mulan Hunting Reserve” beyond the Great Wall, and personally led the aristocracy and ministers, not to mention more than ten thousand soldiers of all ranks, on a large scale “enclosed hunt” every fall. In practice, this was a large-scale military training exercise, enabling the aristocrats and government officials to maintain a intrepid, valiant mode of being, while incidentally carrying out a little saber-rattling toward the northern border. As the Mulan Hunting Reserve was in the area outside the Great Wall, it was some little distance from Beijing, and with so many important courtiers involved in the fall hunt, naturally some temporary palaces were required to accommodate them. The Hot River Palace was the largest of these.

The softer aim was to become good friends with the various minority tribes along the northern border regions, setting up frequent exchanges with them, creating sites where the leaders of these communities could meet Qing officials without making the long journey to the capital. He also made sure they each had their own places of worship, which was another reason for the existence of the Hot Water Palace and its surrounding temples.

In the end, both these tactics converged on a single palace, this mountain resort. While its stated purpose was to escape the heat of summer or to provide a place of rest, the significance of this building went far beyond that. It’s hard to deny that Kangxi’s great achievement was to transform the complexities of political motives into a peaceful, serene garden, and temples filled with tendrils of incense smoke.

Almost every year, as soon as fall arrived, Kangxi was obliged to head to Mulan Hunting Reserve to take part in a twenty-day autumn hunt—over his lifetime, he participated in forty-eight of these. The proceedings would always be magnificent. First, Kangxi would select the hunting zone—it changed every year—and then an “inner city” of 170 tents would be raised, with 250 around these as the “outer city,” and a ring of guardsmen beyond that. At dawn the next morning, armies of the Eight Banners would gather under the command of the Emperor, more than ten thousand of them cheering loudly as they rode forth, with Kangxi at their head, bows at the ready, hurrahs greeting every fresh kill. Later, Emperor would also lead a retinue of minsters and generals on a hunt.

Kangxi was strong and vigorous, with excellent horseback skills. He had both the courage and intelligence needed in a formidable huntsman. His prowess with the bow left the watching aristocrats and officials in awe, and his tally of kills at each expedition was always spectacular.

At night, campfires would be dotted across the land, the aroma of roasting meat rising from them amid laughter and horses neighing, while Kangxi was obliged to retire to his tent, where he would read through the court reports delivered each day.

Emperor Kangxi fought many famous battles over the course of his life, but in his later years, he remained proudest of his achievements while hunting, because they alone were a proof of his vitality. In 1719, Kangxi returned from a Mulan hunt and excitedly told his bodyguard:

Since I was a child, with my musket or bow and arrow, I’ve killed 135 tigers, 20 bears, 25 leopards, 10 lynxes, 14 river deer, 96 wolves, and 132 wild boar. My men have bagged several hundred deer, and countless other beasts that we shot around the reserve. In one day, I shot 318 rabbits. That’s more than normal people kill in their entire lifetime.

He seems terribly proud of this account, and it brings us joy to read it. Physical strength and vigor of the spirit go together—yet you should know that Chinese history has been populated with feeble, sickly Emperors who, no matter how “quietly intelligent” they might have been, would surely have found it tricky to govern such a vast country.

Kangxi’s good constitution gave him all the energy he needed to deal with the fiendish situations in Tibet and Mongolia, to bring the Yellow River and Huai River under control, to solve the problem of transporting goods by the waterways—most of which he handled very successfully, with results that continued to benefit future generations. He also had the energy to study constantly, resulting in a “quiet intelligence” to add to his military prowess. Of all the Chinese emperors, he was the most learned, and also the one who valued learning the most.

Who could have imagined that this Qing Dynasty Emperor would turn out to be even more passionate about traditional Han culture than any of the Ming? Whether it was scriptures, histories, the writings of Confucius, anthologies, poems, letters or tomes, he’d put effort into studying them, particularly in analyzing the philosophy of Zhu Xi. He personally annotated A Mirror for the Wise, and sent out orders for rare books in possession of the common people to be acquired and restored. He set in motion the massive task of compiling and publishing the enormous Imperial Encyclopedia and a dictionary, infusing the nation with a literary atmosphere. To this day, when researching ancient Chinese culture, we’re still very dependent on these reference books. With his support, there was a flourishing of literature and history scholarship, and very few other eras could compete with the renaissance that Kangxi presided over.

The above only covers what we’ve already talked about, “national studies,” but there was also a subject startling even to modern readers—”Western studies.” Our impression today is that Chinese and Western studies have some common ground, but few people really have a deep knowledge of both. Yet three hundred years ago, in both Beijing’s Forbidden City and the Chengde Villa, Kangxi made a serious study of Euclid’s theories of geometry, often working his way through practice problems, and also analyzing the French mathematician Pardies’ Practical and Theoretical Geometry, comparing his methods to those of Euclid. His teachers were missionaries who’d come to China from the West, but he was soon able to perform calculations faster than they did. With mathematics as his foundation, Kangxi began studying Western ideas of astronomy, calendar science, physics, and medicine, expanding China’s base of knowledge in these areas, gaining new concepts and patching up gaps. When it came to the natural sciences, the Chinese bureaucrats frequently clashed with the missionaries, and on these occasions Kangxi neither defended the Chinese side nor made assumptions about who might be right, but diligently worked through the problem for himself, and almost every time made a fair judgment

All of this was, remarkably, compatible with the “national studies” that intoxicated him, the hunting habit that saw him shoot 318 wild rabbits in a single day, and the important political, military, and economic projects he undertook.

I don’t believe that Kangxi brought a fundamental new hope to China—his regime was responsible for plenty of evil deeds, such as the notorious Literary Inquisition. All I’m saying is that in the history of Chinese emperors, this one from a minority tribe possessed extraordinary vitality, and his character was better formed than most.

There are times when a person’s life force and character can leave a deep imprint on history. Compared to Kangxi, many of the Ming Emperors were very badly behaved, and Lu Xun was not wrong to describe them as “a pack of feckless chaps.” The one who makes me most angry is the Wanli Emperor, (Shenzong) Zhu Yijun. He held power for forty-eight years, the first ten under a regent. For twenty-five of these, he buried himself deep in the palace, refusing to see any outsiders and neglecting affairs of state completely, so that even the ministers of his cabinet were unable to meet him. I don’t know what he was doing all that time. He accumulated mountains of wealth, but when there were problems on the Liaodong Peninsula and the court, at a loss for funds, begged him for money, he refused to hand any over, finally releasing only a pittance that did no good for the situation at hand—silver pieces covered in mold, having been kept in storage too long! This was a thoroughly debased individual, yet all power resided in his person—how could the Ming Dynasty not collapse, after this? Although he was succeeded after his death, he had already caused the destruction of the Ming. Kangxi was the exact opposite, releasing the energy of his life from the palace out into the wilderness, the hunting fields, and various schools of knowledge. And the Mountain Resort at Chengde was an important breathing space for him.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: KANGXI’S DIFFERENCE FROM WANLI, the Chengde Resort versus Wanli’s palace retreat—these comparisons were keenly felt by ethnic Han intellectuals, leading to complicated emotions.

To start with, a majority of the Han intelligentsia were in favor of overthrowing the Qing and restoring the Ming, and long after the valiant military men had retreated, the frail scholars were still clinging firmly to this idea. Although there were a few well-known literary figures who later recanted, even they suffered deep psychological conflict and spiritual torment.
I believe this is the power of culture. Military affairs can only be on the surface, but it is only when a cultural shift is underway that matters become serious.

A people, a country, a race—in the end, these are defined not by armies, or territory, or politics, but by culture. Many of the biggest anti-Qing rebellions in the Jiangnan district were the result of “head-shaving” incidents. For the Han, who’d traditionally kept their hair long, having it forcibly cut off by the Manchus was such an affront that it led to stand-offs in which they were forced to choose between keeping their hair or keeping their heads. Hairstyles might not seem like a particularly significant subject, but they have to do with cultural existence. And so, a question of dress became one of the flashpoints in the clash between Han and non-Han.

In the middle of this, the people best-equipped to place matters in their cultural context are cultural figures themselves, who understand the difference between civilization and barbarism, and it was also these who connected the Manchu “Tartars” with uncivilized behavior. The peasants finally had their hair shaved off, while quite a few scholars resisted fiercely. The famous academic Liu Zongzhou went on a hunger strike after Qing forces entered his home city of Hangzhou, and died twenty days later. His pupil Huang Zongxi, another well-known scholar, threw himself into armed resistance against the Qing; when he was defeated, he returned to his hometown to take care of his mother and focus on his writing. Yet another well-known scholar, Gu Yanwu, began wandering the country after his own attempts at armed resistance against the Qing failed. No one could ever track him down, and he ended up spending his old age in Shaanxi. All these great scholars were strong and full of integrity; many of their students and followers naturally took them as role models.

When it came to Kangxi’s reign, though, there were some subtle shifts. Writers had, like the bald eagle depicted by Zhu Da, a clear-eyed view of “heaven and earth united by frost”—glaring piercingly at the court, while the court seemed strangely unable to hold back its passion for Han culture. At first everyone assumed this was a tactic to win hearts and minds, but no one observing Kangxi’s conduct could believe this was completely the case.

Even in the midst of sending troops to deal with Wu Sangui, he was already hurrying to send out orders to his ministers that, with the objective of “revering Confucianism and revering Taoism,” he wanted them to recommend scholars of “excellent all-round knowledge and ability with words” whom he would personally examine, in order to nominate an especially learned elite.

In total, 143 individuals were nominated and summoned, of which ultimately five were chosen. These included people such as Fu Shan and Li Yong, who refused to respond to the call. Fu Shan had to be forcibly brought to Beijing, where he saw the three-character “Great Qing Gate” and flung himself to the ground, tears streaming from his eyes. Not only did Kangxi not punish him for this behavior, but actually allowed him to bypass the exam, conferring directly upon him the title of “Gentleman of Chinese Letters.” Fu Shan refused to let anyone address him by this name after he’d returned home, but it’s difficult to maintain that he still held as great a grudge against Kangxi himself at this point.

Li Yong, similarly, refused to take the exam—by feigning illness. After being hauled to the capital, he went on a hunger strike in protest, and they had to let him go. This happened in the seventeenth year of Kangxi’s reign, when Kangxi was only twenty-six years old. Twenty-five years after this, the now-fifty-something Kangxi went on a journey to survey the West, and actually remembered this stubborn scholar, summoning him to an interview. Li Yong refused to go, but must have felt some awkwardness about this, because he sent his son Li Shenyan instead to represent him, and to present Kangxi with two of his books: Records of Reflections on the Four Great Texts and Collected Erqu. This had a symbolic meaning, showing that even the most resistant Han intellectuals were beginning to thaw toward Kangxi.

Compared to Li Yong, Huang Zongxi was a much more important figure, and Kangxi treated him with even more ceremony, frequently inviting him to meet, only to be rebuffed. Finally, he sent local patrols to Huang Zongxi’s home, ordering them to copy out all his books, with the copies being sent back to the palace for his perusal. This must have left Huang Zongxi feeling, at the least, a little moved. Like Li Yong, he claimed to be unable to make a personal appearance, and sent his son in his place. Huang Baijia ended up working for the Emperor, compiling historical records, helping Kangxi complete his grand project of creating a History of the Ming. So we see how even someone strongly against the Qing was willing to allow his son to spend a lifetime under the command of Kangxi. This wasn’t recantation or compromise, but merely the beginning of a shift in cultural identity.
