I just knew to step forward; my feelings spread everywhere, and I wrote much every day, so much so I forgot the purpose of my journey.

Traveling in Europe, I could also read a lot of information in various places. I read the Medici in Florence, Havel in Prague, Njáls in Iceland. I was fascinated. I was farther and farther away from Chinese civilization.

Until now, on the night train in northern Europe, when I came back to my own mind. There were no other passengers except me. I alone accounted for a fully equipped bedroom. Outside the windows were stretches of snow and the name of the area was not found on the map again. Such a long way, such a long night, a great strangeness in the movement. I settled down and began to sort out the feelings of comparison with Chinese civilization.

Europe had too many images and scattered topics, so it was difficult to concisely summarize the logical comparison with China. I could only give up the generalization, reserve the sensibility, and remember the images with contrasting values. Taking out two sheets of paper from the luggage, I wrote more than thirty more, but figured that might be too many. So I deleted some and finally left seven contrasting images:
A line of letters;
A section of a cemetery;
A part of a chart;
A castle;
A group of idlers;
A stone;
A blue flag.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: A LINE OF LETTERS, first.
That line of letters was in Florence, Italy. M-E-D-I-C-I, on the street, wall, and even on the ground, the name of the Medici family.

According to the conventional view of Chinese culture, wealthy nobles of high rank were mostly obstacles for historical progress and the objects of social revolution. However, we were surprised by the Medici family.

The simple fact was, without the Renaissance, the modernization of the world could not be envisaged; without Florence, the Renaissance could not be envisaged; without the Medicis, Florence and the Renaissance could not be envisaged.

The Medici family built a new center of culture at a key moment in history, provided through wealth and power as a background for a convergence of masters of humanist art, and constituted a challenging but demonstratively strong presence in the region. History was marching away from the Middle Ages in this case, with heavy footsteps and deep footprints. The mold of Dante was worshipped, and traces of Michelangelo and Leonardo da Vinci were everywhere; the statue of David stood there proudly, and man’s glory had begun to illuminate the hard stone-paved narrow alleyways. Although no profound modern thinking was generated in Florence, the city had laid the foundation for modern Europe.

In China’s transitional historical period, a benign convergence of power, wealth, and cultural resources was always hard to find. Social reformers in China thought mostly of their deprivation, and such deprivation might even embrace justice, but it was easily downgraded in Chinese historical transformations of the time.

Cultural resources were of primary importance. The Medici family did particularly well in this respect. They did not grasp the right of cultural creation firmly in their own hands for charity, but to search for the true creators with the most devout attitude. Their discovery, cultivation, fostering, and protection of generations of artists gave an emotional energy to new ideas and made a new era beautiful.
People in this city followed the Medicis for a long time, and the Medicis always followed the art masters, which catalyzed a collective ascension of humanity.

In the progress and transformation of China, we were likely to seek quick success but ignore the establishment of new spiritual and cultural foundations, and perhaps think that was necessary at the expense of culture. Actually, the key to success for social transformation was the concentration of power, wealth, and cultural resources to create a new culture.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: A SECTION of a cemetery.

I mean the cemeteries for Fichte and Hegel in Berlin, Germany. In fact, a lot of scholars’ graves are available for sightseeing in Europe, along with many former residences and statues, there so that future generations can appreciate the souls of wise men.

We were also intellectuals, but the German peers were much purer than their Chinese counterparts, achieving magnificence in their purity. Even the most excellent Chinese writers in history were closely connected to the power structure, so that even escape and rebellion became a kind of reverse coupling. Therefore, their words and deeds when “going into society” deconstructed independent cultural thoughts, while their words and deeds “going out of society” were characterized by an intention. Until today, the excitement of the Chinese scholar-politician still hovered between solitude and a bookworm’s detachment, an excitement illusory and false.

German scholars rarely faced such a situation, even though Goethe’s taking in high officials at Weimar could not help but affect the creation of Faust. Hegel’s huge aesthetic and philosophical framework could not be full-time work. He served as the president of Berlin University, a big administrative position, but he also adhered strictly to the objective of Wilhelm von Humboldt, the founder of the university, to implement full academic freedom and not allow administrative interference.
Kant, with much freer thoughts than Hegel, was secluded in a village all his life, thinking about the mysteries of the universe and man.

However, Kant was also against the lofty appearance of intellectuals pretending to reject society and stay out of the public. He put forward a standard of conduct for intellectuals by taking the French Enlightenment as an example: “to be rational in all public areas.” This was exactly the Chinese intellectuals’ Achilles’ heel. Even our esteemed senior intellectuals left very little spiritual wealth for the “public domain.”
Therefore, the cemeteries and the former residences of China’s intellectuals were always very deserted.

An outstanding example of contemporary European intellectuals, I thought, was Vaclav Havel, who was president of the Czech Republic for over ten years. In his beautiful Prague, I had locked myself up in the hotel for several days, reading his works from recent years. His main ideas were written in the fourth part of Havel, No Regret, and I wish more and more Chinese readers could read them carefully.

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: A PART of a chart.

The chart was in a museum in Lyon, France, listing the creations and inventions of this city during the nineteenth century. I looked at it three times, and each item directly promoted the modernization of all humanity, from textile machinery to cinematography, as many as a dozen.

This was just Lyon. How many would the whole of France have? But I also saw that until the end of the nineteenth century, both French officials and intellectuals were in deep reflection: compared to the inventions in the United States and Germany, France was far behind!
This chart reminds us that Chinese had no justification to lie, gloating about the “four great inventions” far away in time.

Due to its longtime enclosure, China mostly did not participate in the creation of modern human civilization, and knew little about the rapidly changing conditions of creation in the Western world. As the result, the main components of modern life were almost never of Chinese invention, until today. What was intolerable was that our children were not bothered by it, and still immersed themselves in some “quintessence of Chinese culture.” This situation intensified cultural conservatism and seriously hampered the pace of innovation.

Some scholars in the West spoke highly of China’s early inventions, which was often misread by us. Therefore, I once reminded my compatriots by using the History of Ancient Chinese Science and Technology, written by Mr. Joseph Needham when at Oxford University:

I hoped that Chinese readers did not forget the environment in which he wrote this work, only to look for the unidirectional comfort from me while thinking that human progress was completely benefited by inventions in ancient China. When [Needham] wrote this book, the United Kingdom was still continuously creating “the firs”: The first bottle of penicillin, the first vacuum tubes, the first radar, the first computer, the first TV set…even recently, they had also released the news of the first cloned sheep and the first test-tube baby. In such waves of creation, the British actually completed the inventions of ancient China, in a way much integrated than that of the Chinese themselves, which was really smart. If we were so complacent due to this, it was really shortsighted.

sections.label: V
paragraphs: THAT CASTLE.
I mean the Royal Windsor Castle in the United Kingdom, as well as Eton College nearby.

Chinese civilization originally believed in the doctrine of the mean, but it was deeply affected by French radicalism during the national crisis in modern China. From the French Revolution to the Paris Commune, the passionate declamations and struggles infected many Chinese reformers. By contrast, China did not accept the United Kingdom’s path of moderate and gradual improvement.

Later, they did not even know which system France eventually settled on, but the radicals had proven incapable of further growth. Even in peacetime, they still worshipped violence, including verbal attacks.

The radicalism was easily celebrated as praiseworthy idealism. Even through the disaster of the extreme radical “cultural revolution,” there were still lots of people who saw “fierce bashing” as the basic cultural pattern. In fact, such radicalism had already led to enormous consequences in the injuring of social vitality, the destruction of civil rituals, and the deprivation of human rights and humanitarianism, which was not only detrimental to contemporaries, but also their descendants.
I had already thought about this issue, but I was not fully convinced emotionally until entering Windsor Castle and Eton College for a look in the late autumn season.
I wrote:

The path of moderate and gradual improvement in the United Kingdom might be easily criticized as not profound. However, when thinking carefully, you may find that they did the right things for social development; the thresholds for civilization’s progress were all crossed by them, and the notions of modern society had also been formed by them. Then, what more could you say?

Less bloody, less harsh, and with less Germanic thought, but only following, only feeling all the way, repressing the experience, bypassing the obstacles, they selected a less consuming but rapid development road—such social behavior has been proved by history to have been a remarkable path.

sections.label: VI
paragraphs: ANOTHER POINT of comparison was the ubiquitous groups of leisurely crowds along the road.

Throughout Europe, crowds of people can always be seen with a beer or a cup of coffee in their hands, lounging at small tables beside the road. They eat little, but sit for a long time, some chatting and others reading newspapers. Occasionally they raise their head and look at the street, with calm eyes, complacent and decent.
This also constituted an obvious contrast with Chinese society.

I discussed this issue with some friends in Italy. Many Chinese immigrants already lived in Europe, and my Italian friends admired them but also wondered about them. What they admired was that the Chinese not only stood firmly through their toil around the clock, but also accumulated considerable wealth; what they wondered about was the fact that they almost had no leisure or vacation time, so people did not understand their purpose. The Chinese said it was for their children, but their children repeated this pattern after growing up.

To be fair, I could understand their behavior. They had lived in poverty for a long time, and later there was a lack of security even when out of poverty, so they could not fail to work hard to accumulate wealth.
The problem was when such endless hard work blindly evolved into psychological inertia because of group behavior, and the biggest crisis of blindness was the shunning of the public space and society.

When I was in Rome, I noticed that most people were away on public holidays and the place was almost empty, which led me to think about their socially important differences with Chinese civilization. I wrote:

The Chinese were hardworking and occasionally took a vacation, but only for better work in the future; the Europeans, conversely, believed that hard work in ordinary times was largely for the sake of a vacation. For only on vacation could people could stop the chores, suspend their anxiety, return to their bodies, and reappear the family relationships. In other words, people said goodbye to alienation and restored their humanity. Such notions melted away the individual rights and return to nature in the West, so it was easily accepted by the people and was ubiquitous among them.

Readers knew that my respect was not for the vacation itself, but for what “made people say goodbye to alienation and restore their humanity.” This was the fundamental question of life, which was also likely to be obscured by blind pragmatic inertia. Therefore, leisure could also be sober, whereas the busy life was also likely to be confused. The Chinese civilizations focused on practical rationality, but not the ultimate reflection, with little care for the humanist ideal in the path of economic development. In this regard, Europe always kept me alert. For example, some countries in northern Europe had a slow economic development pace in recent years, mostly because they implemented more radical social welfare policies, giving leisure a wide range of possibilities.
To this end, I wrote a few words in Stockholm, Sweden:
I learned to summarize a series of logical relationships here:
The realization that social security relied on common welfare;
The realization that common welfare relied on economic development;
The realization that economic development relied on market competition;
The realization that market competition relied on normal order;
The realization that normal order relied on social responsibility;
The realization that social responsibility relied on civic duty.
Therefore, property must be reflected in obligations, and freedom must be reflected in responsibility; these were the cultural ethics of a modern economy.
Here, I understood that the country under rapid development should not laugh at the Swedish model that seems to be slow and leisurely.

From a narrow view, those leisurely crowds on the streets of Europe could be regarded with special respect. Did Chinese rapidly accumulating wealth ever think of their future social model? Unlimited wealth is within a limited life, so where will you be when the dusk of life finally falls?

sections.label: VII
paragraphs: NEXT, THAT STONE.
In Iceland, I saw a large stone in the Thingvellir volcano, called the “legal stone.”

It was cold there when I went, but I stood in the cold air for a very long time. At the beginning, it was the place where Vikings voluntarily accepted legal arbitration, so I saw it just out of curiosity. But standing there, I thought of a great blind vein of Chinese civilization, and spent a few days later writing a number of articles after returning to Reykjavik.

The great blind vein of Chinese civilization was the martial spirit. The popularity of the martial arts and its movies proved the potential strength of such a vein. It always started with family revenge for reasons of justice. Its behavior was straightforward and heroic, with the worship of the “hero personality.” However, such a blind vein ignored the law of nature, which therefore led to a serious barrier between Chinese civilization and modern society. Countless facts proved that the “hero character” easily turned into the “mob character” and poisoned the society.
Facing the “legal stone” in Thingvellir, Iceland, I found how Nordic heroes took hundreds of years to painfully replace their yardsticks for measuring honor and rewrite the hero’s feelings.

The result of such replacing and rewriting was to put down the sword and oath and listen to the sentence of the law and church bells, which was different from the issue of “amnesty” encountered by heroes in China. If “amnesty” was also used here, it meant amnesty by law and religion. I wrote:

The rising up of many men was supposed to claim social justice, but obtained greater injustice, which could be found everywhere, so the enmity stories became common in Eastern and Western societies. There were no rules save hoped-for rules; even under the most just law, they could not calm their hearts. This was just the risk of spirit that was hard to pass through but that had to be passed through for humanity, for only through such risk could human beings really set foot on the path of civilization.

What I paid much attention to was the struggling process of Northern Europe’s heroes when going through the spiritual risk, which was detailed in the Njáls saga. In contrast, “social justice” in Chinese heroes was always unidirectional and revengeful, so its relationship was always opposite and conflicted with the law.

The Njáls saga states that “the heroes of heroes” Nyall and Gunnar saw both revenge-based old honor and reason-based new honor, and they saw that a villain was the new legal representative. However, they were still willing to give their lives to the new honor and law, and endure the jeers.
Such characters could not be found in contemporary Chinese stories and were even more difficult to find later.
Therefore, I considered the “legal stone” as an important comparison point.

What happened here made Scott, Wagner, Ernest Hemingway, and Borges very excited, but due to the dangerous seas and wasteland, they failed to go to Iceland and have a look. I was lucky enough to come, and thought about Chinese culture here.

sections.label: VIII
paragraphs: The last main comparison point was that blue flag.

This blue flag, the flag of the European Union, could be found everywhere in Europe, but it flew more authoritatively in the lobby of the EU headquarters in Brussels. Only forty kilometers away from the EU headquarters was the Waterloo battlefield where modern European history was rewritten. Such close proximity left me shocked.

Immortal feats and heroes always drew attention on the battlefields of Waterloo and many others. Eyes were always on the last winner’s flag rising in the fiery smoke. However, Europe had finally told us that the flag rising at last flew regardless of the outcome, the states, or the nation, but the was a Union flag, at one with the color of the blue sky.
We Chinese had already been aware of this reality, but the profound meaning embedded in it was still indifferent to us.

The wars between nation-states in Europe were particularly impressive. From ancient to modern times, most of the most legendary and cruel chapters in world history happened among the nation-states in Europe. In this regard, a more ambitious conscience existed in Europe to oppose such impulses.

By nature, Chinese civilization carried with it a broad expanse of world consciousness. The concept of nation-state derived from a time of internal strife and external threats. In our time, when China finally strode into the international community, it could show the bearing of a society with open horizons, but might also revert to a narrow mind due to fierce competition.
So, I thought there was something that should be addressed to Chinese culture from European soil:

Kant believed that human reason concluded that the mankind would overcome confrontation and move toward harmony; each country would also regulate its behavior and gradually establish a benign League of Nations, and eventually establish the worldwide and significant “universal legislative civil society.” This is the idea that became the theoretical basis of later European integration.

I certainly preferred Kant, for his transnational greatness and the foresight behind his rigorous thinking. National sovereignty had its share of rationality, but the blood and fire of Europe had already proved that excessive nationalism was the curse of mankind. Common principles of human civilization must be the ultimate guide. Any noble nation was supposed to be the maker, practitioner, and advocator of these common principles.
Europe’s cultural conscience, including Goethe and Hugo, whom I particularly admired, also took this position.

Facts had proved and would continue to prove that many evil deeds often hid behind the banners of “nation” and “country.” We should get past these banners, expose the huge undercurrent of anti-humanity, anti-society, anti-life, anti-order, and anti-intelligence to the light of day, and defeat it together. Otherwise, mankind will face a series of common disasters. As we have seen, the vast majority of disasters today have no ethnic or national boundaries.
This was my “last lecture” in Europe.

sections.label: IX
paragraphs: THE INVESTIGATION IN EUROPE was certainly not as horrific as the last visits to North Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia, but not as safe as one would expect.

The separatist group in the north of Spain created negative events constantly, as we were reminded every day when staying there; “Neo-Nazis” in Germany focused on foreigners, so we were again on alert; in Naples, in the south of Italy, we were told that even if you just ate a meal in the street while parking, half the car’s wheels might be unloaded when you went back again. A local person said: “In this district, at least half the people have been in prison,” which might be somewhat exaggerated, but the shrill police siren of police chasing gangsters often sounded in our ears. Wanderers from all over the world could be found in Europe, so thefts often occurred.

A great theft occurred in Paris, when several big boxes in our car were stolen. When we thought about it later, we recalled that the driver we hired was not familiar with the traffic conditions in the city. He was likely a member of the theft group, and deliberately did not lock the door after our stop.

In Amsterdam, the windows of our cars were smashed in different parking lots, several laptops disappeared, and even my digital camera went missing, including precious investigation photos. We reported it at the police station, but the police said quietly that the marijuana-smokers might do anything when they had no money, and such cases happened every day and were never solved.

So even though I found the weakness of Chinese civilization by taking European civilization as a coordinate of comparison, European civilization itself troubled me a lot. Many human catastrophes were mutually intermixed; various dangers I saw in the Middle East and South Asia also had a significant presence in Europe. Even in Toulouse, France, which we thought the most peaceful city, we experienced a big explosion. Unfortunately, the excellent European had lost sensitivity and concern for disasters in other parts of the world, and lacked the capacity to respond to the crisis around him. I wrote:

Several generations of Oriental intellectuals treated European civilization with admiration and followed its views, but as a result, sentimental and superficial feelings based on misunderstandings were generated. This tendency was also growing in Europe. With the history no longer painful, the time no longer burdened mission, and the memory no longer weighted with responsibility, Europe might go into a kind of lost daze.

The journey to Europe made me doubt the idea of French philosopher Alexandre Kojeve as elaborated in The End of History by Francis Fukuyama. In this view, Europe had assimilated various systems from Christian civilization to the French Revolution, defeated many opponents, and entered the terminal state of history due to material plenty, individual freedom, systemic democracy, and social stability. Although local conflicts would exist in the future, the overall trend was consumption and games in the context of globalization.

I thought that this view was a kind of escape into its own value system, and a kind of deliberately chosen ignorance of the crisis, rancor, terrorism, and violence that actually existed. This mindset in Europe would also bring a great deal of insecurity, because when a civilization cannot face up to the outside world, it cannot face up to its own history, which only weakens its body as a result.
Facing such a situation, we should derive more general thoughts when learning about European civilization, but could not continue to admire and followed its views as cultural predecessors.

Chinese civilization varied greatly from European civilization. However, they are all referred to as “civilizations,” so they must deal with common enemies, which are the strength of all noncivilizations, such as terrorism, the nuclear arms race, environmental pollution, natural disasters.

On this point I disagreed with Professor Samuel Huntington, for he only pointed out the conflicts possibly generated between various civilizations. In fact, the most fundamental conflict in the twenty-first century has been between civilization and noncivilization. In our time guarding the whole of civilization is the imminent path.

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 此刻我正在西太平洋的一条小船上，浑身早已被海浪浇得透湿。一次次让海风吹干了，接着又是劈头盖脑的浪，满嘴咸苦，眼睛渍得生疼。
我一手扳着船帮，一手抓着缆绳，只咬着牙命令自己，万不可哆嗦。只要一哆嗦，绷在身上的最后一道心理防卫就会懈弛，那么，千百顷的海浪海风会从汗毛孔里涌进，整个生命立即散架。
不敢细想现在所处的真实位置，只当作是在自己熟悉的海域。但偶尔心底又会掠过一阵惊悚，却又不愿承认：这是太平洋中最深的马里亚纳海沟西南部，海底深度超过珠穆朗玛峰的高度。按世界地理，是在“狭义大洋洲”的中部，属密克罗尼西亚（Micronesia）。最近的岛屿，叫雅浦（Yap），那也是我们晚间的栖宿地。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 最深的海，海面的状况有点特别。不像海明威所写的加勒比海，不像海涅所写的北海，也不像塞万提斯所写的地中海。海水的颜色，并非一般想象的深蓝色，而是黑褐色，里边还略泛一点紫光。那些海浪不像是液体，而有凝固感。似乎刚刚由固体催动，或恰恰就要在下一刻凝固。
不远处也有一条小船，看它也就知道了自己。一会儿，那小船似乎是群山顶上的圣物，光衬托着它，云渲染着它，我们须虔诚仰视才能一睹它的崇高。但它突然不见了，不仅是它，连群山也不见了，正吃惊，发现不远处有一个巨大深渊，它正陷落在渊底，那么卑微和渺小，似乎转眼就要被全然吞没。还没有回过神来，一排群山又耸立在半天了，那群山顶上，又有它在天光云影间闪耀。
如此极上极下，极高极低，却完全没有喧嚣，安静得让人窒息，转换得无比玄奥。
很难在小船上坐住，但必须坐住，而且要坐得又挺又直。那就只能用双手的手指，扣住船帮和缆绳，像要扣入它们的深处，把它们扣穿。我在前面刚刚说过，在海船中万不可哆嗦，现在要进一步补充，在最大的浪涛袭来时，连稍稍躲闪一下也不可以。一躲闪，人就成了活体，成了软体，必然会挣扎，会喊叫，而挣扎和喊叫在这里，就等于灭亡。
要做到又挺又直，也不可以有一点儿走神，必须全神贯注地拼将全部肢体，变成千古岩雕。面对四面八方的狂暴，任何别的身段、姿态和计策都毫无用处，只能是千古岩雕。哪怕是裂了、断了，也是千古岩雕。
我是同船几个人中的大哥，用身体死死地压着船尾。他们回头看我一眼都惊叫了：怎么整个儿都成了黑色？
被海水一次次浇泼，会让衣服的颜色变深，这是可以解释的，但整个人怎么会变黑？
我想，那也许是在生命的边涯上，我发出了加重自己身体分量的火急警报，于是，生命底层的玄铁之气、墨玉之气全然调动并霎时释出。古代将士，也有一遇强敌便通体迸发黑气的情景。
不管怎么说，此刻，岩雕已变成铁铸，真的把小船压住在狂涛之间。

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 见到了一群海鸟。
这很荒唐。它们飞到无边沧海的腹地，究竟来干什么？又怎么回去？最近的岛屿也已经很远，它们飞得到那里吗？
据说，它们是要叼食浮游到海面的小鱼。但这种解释非常可疑，因为我看了那么久，没见到一只海鸟叼起过一条小鱼，而它们在狂风中贴浪盘旋的体力消耗，又是那么巨大。即使叼到了，吞噬了，体能又怎么平衡？
它们，到底为了什么？
一种牺牲的祭仪？一种求灭的狂欢？或者，我心底一笑：难道，这是一群远行到边极而自沉的“屈原”？
突然想到儿时读过的散文《海燕》，高尔基写的。文章中的海燕成了一种革命者的替身，居然边飞翔边呼唤，“让暴风雨来得更猛烈些吧！”我海旅既深，早已怀疑，高尔基可能从来没有坐着小船来到深海远处。他的“暴风雨”，只是一个陆地概念和岸边概念。在这里，全部自然力量浑然一体，笼罩四周，哪里分得出是风还是雨，是暴还是不暴，是猛烈还是不猛烈？
在真正的“大现场”，一切形容词、抒情腔都显得微弱可笑。这里的海鸟，不能帮助任何人写散文，不能帮助任何人画画，也不能帮助任何人创作交响乐。我们也许永远也猜不透它们翅膀下所夹带的秘密。人类常常产生“高于自然”的艺术梦想，在这里必须放弃。

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 我们的船夫，是岛上的原住民。他的那个岛，比雅浦岛小得多。
他能讲简单的英语，这与历史有关。近几百年，最先到达这些太平洋小岛的是西班牙人，这是欧洲人在“地理大发现”时代的半道歇脚点。德国是第二拨，想来远远地拾捡殖民主义的后期余晖。再后来是太平洋战争时期的日本和美国了，这儿成了辽阔战场的屯兵处。分出胜负后，美国在这里留下了一些军人，还留下了教会和学校。
“每一拨外来人都给岛屿带来过一点新东西。这个走了，那个又来了。最后来的是你们，中国人。”船夫笑着说。
船夫又突然腼腆地说，据岛上老人传言，自己的祖辈，也来自中国。
是吗？我看着他的黑头发、黑眼珠，心想，如果是，也应该早已几度混血。来的时候是什么年代？几千年前？几百年前？
我在研究河姆渡人和良渚人的最终去向时，曾在论文中一再表述，不排斥因巨大海患而远航外海的可能。但那时，用的只能是独木舟。独木舟在大海中找到岛屿的概率极小，但极小的概率也可能遗留一种荒岛血缘，断断续续延绵千年。
这么一想，突然产生关切，便问船夫，平日何以为食，鱼吗？
船夫的回答令人吃惊，岛上居民很少吃鱼。主食是芋头，和一种被称为“面包树”的果实。
为什么不吃鱼？回答是，出海打鱼要有渔船，一般岛民没有。他们还只分散居住在林子中的简陋窝棚里，日子非常原始，非常贫困。
少数岛民，有独木舟。
独木舟？我又想起了不知去向的河姆渡和良渚。
“独木舟能远行吗？”我们问。
“我不行。我爸爸也不行。我爷爷也不行。我伯伯也不行。亲族里只有一个叔叔，能凭着头顶的天象，从这里划独木舟到夏威夷。只有他，其他人都不行了。”船夫深深叹了一口气，像是在哀叹沧海豪气的沦落。
“一个人划独木舟，能到夏威夷？”这太让人惊讶了。那是多少日子，多少海路，多少风浪，多少险情啊。
“能。”船夫很有把握。
“那也能到中国吧？”
“能。”他仍然很有把握。

sections.label: 五
paragraphs: 那海，还是把我妻子击倒了。
她在狂颠的小船上倒还从容，那天晚上栖宿在岛上，就犯了病。肠胃功能紊乱，狂吐不止，浑身瘫软，不得动弹。
栖宿的房舍，是以前美国海军工程兵建造的，很朴素，还干净。妻子病倒后，下起了大雨。但听到的不是雨声，而是木质百叶窗在咯吱吱地摇撼，好像整个屋子就要在下一刻粉碎。外面的原始林木又都在一起呼啸，让人浑身发毛。什么“瓢泼大雨”、“倾盆大雨”等等说法，在这里都不成立。若说是“瓢”，那“瓢”就是天；若说是“盆”，那“盆”就是地。天和地在雨中融成了一体，恣肆狂放。
一位走遍太平洋南部和西部几乎所有大岛的历险家告诉我，这儿的雨，减去九成，只留一成，倾泻在任何城市，都会是淹腰大灾。他还说，世间台风，都从这儿起源。如此轰隆轰隆的狂暴雨势，正是在合成着席卷几千公里的台风呢！
这一想，思绪也就飞出去了几千公里，中间是无垠的沧海巨涛。家，那个我们常年居住的屋子，多么遥远，遥远到了无法度量。在这个草莽小岛上，似乎一切都随时可以毁灭，毁灭得如蚁蝼，如碎草，如微尘。我的羸弱的妻子，就在我身旁。
她闭着眼，已经很久颗粒未进，没有力气说话，软软地躺着。小岛不会有医生，即使有，也叫不到。彻底无助的两条生命，躲在一个屋顶下，屋顶随时可以掀掉，屋顶外面的一切，完全不可想象。这，就是古往今来的夫妻。这，就是真实无虚的家。
我和妻子对家的感受，历来与故乡、老树、熟路关系不大。每次历险考察，万里大漠间一夜夜既不同又相同的家。漂移中的家最能展示家的本质，危难中漂移最能让这种本质刻骨铭心。
总是极其僻远，总是非常陌生，总是天气恶劣，总是无法开门，总是寸步难行，总是疲惫万分，总是无医无药，总是求告无门。于是，拥有了一个最纯净的家，纯净得无限衰弱，又无限强大。

sections.label: 六
paragraphs: 大自然的咆哮声完全压过了轻轻的敲门声，然而，不知在哪个间隙，还是听到了。而且，还听出了呼叫我们的声音，是汉语。
赶快开门。一惊，原来是那位走遍了太平洋南部和西部几乎所有大岛的海洋历险家。他叫杨纲，很多年前是北京一名年轻的外交官，负责过南太平洋国家的交往。多次往返，就沉浸在那里了，又慢慢扩展到西太平洋。因喜爱而探寻，因探寻而迷恋，他也就辞去公职，成了一名纵横于大洋洲的流动岛民。
不管走得多远，心里却明白，一个中国人在病倒的时候最需要什么。他站在门前，端着一个小小的平底铁锅，已经熬了一锅薄薄的大米粥，还撒了一些切碎的青菜在大米粥里。
我深深谢过，关上门，把小铁锅端到妻子床前。妻子才啜两口，便抬头看我一眼，眼睛已经亮了。过一会儿，同行的林琳小姐又送来几颗自己随身带的“藿香正气丸”。妻子吃了就睡，第二天醒来，居然容光焕发。
青菜大米粥，加上藿香正气丸，入口便回神，这就是中国人。
这就牵涉到了另一种“家”，比在风雨小屋里相依为命的“家”要大得多。但这个“家”更是流荡的，可以流荡到地球上任何地方。中国有一个成语叫“四海为家”，听起来气象万千，可惜这“四海”两字，往往只是虚词。这些年才慢慢发现，把这两个字走实的中国人，并不太少。他们心中的那个“家”，与国内很多人老挂在口边的所谓“常回家看看”的那个“家”，全然不同。
对我和妻子来说，我们的家，是一个漫无边际的大海，又是一个抗击风浪的小岛。“家”的哲学意义，是对它的寻常意义的突破。因此，这次居然走得那么远。是的，越远，越要来。

sections.label: 七
paragraphs: 这个岛上，多年来已经住着一个中国人，他叫陈明灿。作为唯一的中国人住在这么一个孤岛上，种种不方便可想而知，但他一直没有要离开的意思。我想只有一个理由，那就是他实在太爱海、太爱岛了。他也是那种在本性上“四海为家”的人，没有海，就没有他的家。
老家，在广东河源。他曾漂流到太平洋上另一个岛屿帕劳生活了十年，后来又来到了这里。他现在无疑是岛上的“要人”了，开了一个小小的农场，陆续雇来了五个中国职工。酋长有事，也要找他商量。
他居住的地方，是一间可以遮蔽风雨的简单铁皮棚屋，养着几只家禽，放着一些中国食物。他装了一根天线，能接收到香港凤凰卫视，因此见到我便一顿，立即认出来了。在太平洋小岛上听一位黑黝黝的陌生男子叫一声“秋雨老师”，我未免一惊，又心里一热。
在岛上还遇到了一对中国的“潜水夫妻”，那就比陈明灿先生更爱海了。全世界不管什么地方只要有良好的潜水点，他们一听到就赶去，像是必须完成的功课，不许缺漏。去年在非洲塞舌尔的海滩，他们一听说这里有上好的珊瑚礁，就急忙赶过来了。丈夫叫李明学，辽宁铁岭人。我一听铁岭，就聊了几句熟人赵本山。妻子是沈阳人，叫张欣，我一听这个名字，又聊了几句熟人潘石屹，他太太也是这个名字。
李明学、张欣夫妇原本都有很好的专业，在上海工作。但是他们在读了不少有关“终极关怀”的古今文本之后，开始怀疑自己上班、下班的日常生态，强烈向往起自由、自在、开阔、无羁的生活，于是走向了大海。在大海间，必须天天挑战自己的生命，于是他们又迷上了挑战。
“我先在海岸边看他潜水，自己不敢潜。后来觉得应该到水下去陪他。从马尔代夫开始学，终于，等到用完了二十个气瓶，我也潜得很自如了。”张欣说。
“这么多年总是一起潜水，必须是夫妻。”张欣突然说得很动情，“潜水总会遇到意外，例如，一个人气瓶的气不够了，潜伴就要立即用自己的气瓶去援助。如果不是夫妇，首先会考虑自身安全。我丈夫喜欢在水下拍摄各种鲨鱼，这也有很大危险，我必须长时间守在他身边，四处张望着。只有夫妻，才耐得下这个心。”
“世上的潜水夫妻，天天生死相依，一般都没有孩子，也没有房子。脑子中只想着远方一个个必须去的潜水处。欧洲有好几个，更美的是南美洲。阿根廷、巴西、玻利维亚、厄瓜多尔、哥伦比亚，都有潜水者心中的圣地。对中国潜水者来说，近一点的是东南亚，马来西亚、印尼、菲律宾、泰国，都有。澳大利亚也有很好的潜水处。我们中国海南岛的三亚也能潜，差一点。”
她用十分亲切的语调讲述着全世界的潜水地图，就像讲自己的家，讲自己庞大的亲族。

sections.label: 八
paragraphs: 两个月前，这个海岛上来了另一对夫妻，住了一个月就走了，与我们失之交臂。他们对海的痴迷，我听起来有点惊心动魄。
丈夫是比利时人，叫卢克（Luc），妻子是美籍华人，叫贾凯依（Jackie）。他们居然在不断航行的海船上住了整整二十五年！
靠岸后当然也上岸，做点谋生的事，但晚上必定回到船上。从一个海岸到另外一个海岸，每次航行一般不超过半个月，为的是补充淡水和食物。在航行途中，晚上两人必须轮流值班，怕气象突变，怕大船碰撞，怕各种意外。
由于走遍世界，他们船上的设备也在年年更新，卫星导航、电脑、冰箱，都有了。但在茫茫大海中，在难以想象的狂风巨浪间，他们二十五年的航行，与那个凭着天象划独木舟的土著大叔，没有太多区别。
渺小的人，一个男人和一个女人，走了一条坚韧的路，而且是水路，海路，一条永远不可知的路，当然也是一条惊人的生命之路，忠贞的爱情之路，人类的自雄之路。
我们能设想这二十五年间，日日夜夜在狭小的船上发生的一切吗？我觉得，人类学、伦理学、文学、美学，都已经被这样的夫妻在晨曦和黄昏间，轻轻改写。
我看到了贾凯依的照片，果然是一个中国人，相貌比年龄更为苍老。那是狞厉的空间和时间，在一个中国女性身上留下的隆重印痕。
很多航海者告诉我，夫妻航海，年年月月不分离，听起来非常浪漫，其实很难坚持，首先离开的必定是妻子，因为任何女性都受不了这种生活。因此，这对能在大海上坚持二十五年的夫妻，关键性的奇迹，在于这位中国女性。
看着照片，我想起一路上所见的那一批批爱海、爱岛爱到了不可理喻的中国人。因此我必须说，中国文化固然长期观海、疑海、恐海、禁海，而对无数活生生的中国人来说，则未必。他们可以入海、亲海、依海，离不开海。文化和生命，毕竟有很大不同。
其实，从河姆渡、良渚开始，或者更早，已有无数从中国出发的独木舟，在海上痴迷。可惜，刻板的汉字，与大海不亲。伟大的航海家郑和葬身在哪个海域、哪个海岸？居然也没有清晰记载。中国的一半历史，在海浪间沉没了。慵懒的巷陌学者，只知检索着尘土间的书本。那些书本上，从未有过真实的大海，也没有与大海紧紧相融的中国人的生命。
幸好到了一个可以走出文字、走出小家的时代。终于有一批中国人惊动海天，也唤醒了中国文化中长久被埋没的那种生命。
在密克罗尼西亚的日日夜夜，妻子几次看着我说：“早该有一条船……”
我知道她这句话后面无穷无尽的含义。
我说：“必须是海船。”
她一笑，说：“当然。”

sections.label: I
paragraphs: I WAS ON A BOAT IN THE WESTERN PACIFIC, and was already drenched by the waves from head to toe. I was dried by the sea winds time and time again, but again assaulted by the waves, with a full mouth of bitter salt water, and my eyes hurt.

One of my hands pulled the gunwale, and the other hand grabbed the rope; I gritted my teeth and told myself not to shiver. Just a shiver could release the last psychological defense in your body, and admit thousands of hectares of sea breezes into your pores, making your whole life fall apart immediately.

I dared not think about the actual location I was in, and only looked at the familiar waters. However, occasionally a thrill would pass through my heart, even if I was still unwilling to admit it: this was the deepest place in the world, the southwest of the Marianas Trench in the Pacific, its depth even greater than the height of Mount Everest. According to world geography, this was in the middle of “narrow Oceania,” belonging to Micronesia. The nearest island, Yap, was where we stayed at night.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: THE DEEPEST OCEAN WAS UNIQUE, unlike the Caribbean written of by Hemingway, the North Sea of Heine, or the Mediterranean of Cervantes. The color of the sea was far beyond dark blue, but rather dark brown, with a little purple in it. The waves were not like liquid, but had a sort of solidity.

A boat was not far away, and you could know yourself when seeing it. After a moment, the boat seemed to be the holy article on the top of a mountain, set off by light and rendered by the clouds, and we could not enjoy its sublime beauty until we looked up at it devoutly. It suddenly disappeared, even the mountains beneath it; we were so astonished—a huge pit was found not far away and it was just now falling to its bottom, so humble and small, and seemed to be swallowed up in a flash. Before you could recover, a row of mountains stood there for a long time, the top of which was shining in the bright clouds.
So quiet, so breathtaking, its rhythm was very profound.

It was hard to sit in the boat, but I had to sit in it quite straight. Then, I could only use my fingers of both hands to hold the gunwale and cables, as if to clasp tightly to its mass. I said above that even a shiver was not allowed in the ship, but on top of that, when the biggest wave struck, even a dodge was forbidden. Once dodging, the one could become the living body and the soft body, so struggle and shouting were unavoidable, which could mean death.

You must stay straight and upright, and alert, and must turn all your limbs into eternal rock carvings. Facing fury from all sides, any other posture, gesture, and strategy was useless, only the endurance of the ancient rock carvings. Even if they were cracked or broken, they were still of ancient rock.
In the ship, I was the eldest and held down the stern with my body. They turned back to look at me, screaming: how did the entire person become all black?
When one is splashed by the seawater time and time again, the clothes may become darker and darker, which could be explained, how did an entire person turn black?

In my opinion, I found an emergency measure to increase my body weight at the edge of life, so the dark steel and black jade vigor at the pit of life were totally mobilized and released in an instant. The ancient soldiers also had exuded black vigor when encountering a nemesis.
Anyway, at that moment, the rock carvings had been transformed into cast iron, and pushed the boat between the waves.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: I SAW A FLOCK OF BIRDS.
This was absurd. What were they doing, flying to the hinterlands of the boundless sea? How did they get back again? Even the nearest island was far away; could they fly there?

It was said that they ate the small fish floating on the surface. However, such an explanation was very suspicious, for I had been looking for a long time and no bird had picked up even a little fish, and yet their physical output in the strong wind and waves was so great. Even if they ate the fish, how could they maintain physical fitness?
What on earth were they for?
Is it a kind of sacrificial ritual? A kind of extinction carnival? Or, I smiled in my heart: were they a group of “Qu Yuan” going to the very boundary and sinking down?

Suddenly, I thought of Gorky’s Petrels, which I had read in my childhood, in which the petrels became a substitute for revolutionaries, calling while flying, “Let the storm come a bit more fiercely!” With my rich sea experience, I had long suspected that Gorky might have never come far out to sea in a boat. His “storm” was just concepts of the land and the shore. Here all natural forces unified as a whole, covering everything. How could the wind or rain, storm or non-storm, or violence or nonviolence, be distinguished?

In the true “big scene,” all adjectives and lyrics seem weak and ridiculous. Seabirds here could not help anyone write essays, could not help anyone paint, and could not help anyone write symphonies. We might never make out the secret carried under their wings. Humans often have artistic dreams “higher than nature,” but they must be given up here.

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: OUR BOATMAN WAS A NATIVE of an island much smaller than Yap.

He could speak a little English, which was related to the island’s history. Over the past hundreds of years, the people who first reached the Pacific Islands were the Spanish; this was the halfway stopping point for Europeans in the times of “the great geographical discoveries.” Germany was the second, wanting to pick up the late twilight of colonialism from afar. Then during the Pacific War, Japan and the United States came, and the island became a vast battlefield troop station. After the war, the United States left some soldiers here, as well as the church and school.

“Every batch of strangers had brought something new to the island. Coming and going again. You Chinese were the last batch,” the boatman said with a laugh. He suddenly said with a blush that according to old rumors on the island, his ancestors were also from China.
Were you? I looked into his dark hair, dark eyes, and thought, if he was, he should have been mixed blood already. When did they come here? Thousands of years ago? Or hundreds of years ago?

When researching the ultimate fate of the Hemudu and Liangzhu people, I had repeatedly expressed in the paper that the possibility of open-sea voyages could not be excluded. Then, however, they could only use canoes. It was extremely improbable to find an island in the sea by canoe, but that extremely small probability might also leave a trace of a bloodline on a desert island that might continue for a long time.
I asked the boatman, what was his typical dinner, fish?
But his answer was surprising: the islanders rarely ate fish; instead, their staples were taro and the fruit grown on something called “bread tree.”
Why not eat fish? The answer was that a fishing boat was needed when going to sea, but the islanders had none. They were scattered in crude shacks in the forest, very poor. A few islanders, canoeing.
Canoes? I again thought of the Hemudu and Liangzhu disappearing without a trace.
“The canoe can go far away?” I asked.

“I cannot do it. My dad, my grandfather, and my uncle cannot, either. Only an uncle in the family, with the sky above, canoed from here to Hawaii. Only he can, and others not.” The boatman took a deep sigh, as if to bemoan the degradation of sea pride.
“A man can canoe to Hawaii?” This surprised me so much. How many days, how many seaways, how many storms, how many dangers might be encountered?
“Yes.” The boatman was very sure.
“Could he also canoe to China?”
“Of course.” He was still quite sure.

sections.label: V
paragraphs: THE SEA knocked down my wife finally.
She was still calm on the jolted boat, but fell ill that night on the island. She vomited violently, was limp and motionless.

The premises were built by United States Navy engineers, and were simple and clean. When my wife fell ill, it was beginning to rain heavily. But what we heard was not the rain, but the slightly creaking shake of wooden blinds, as if the entire room would be crushed in the next moment. The trees outside were howling in the wind, making any man very scared. The terms “heavy rain,” “heavy downpour,” and so on could not be used here. If we said “heavy rain,” it was just the sky; if we said “heavy downpour,” it was just the earth. The sky and earth formed a whole in this rain, wild and unrestrained.

One adventurer traveling almost all the big islands in the south and west Pacific told me that just 10 percent of the rain here would flood any city and cause great disasters. He also said that typhoons all originated from here. Such a rumbling rain was compounding the typhoon that swept over thousands of kilometers!

My thoughts had also flown thousands of kilometers, and their middle was a boundless sea. The house we lived in throughout the years was so far away it could not be calculated. In this uncultivated small island, it seemed that everything could be destroyed at any time, turned into a nonentity, chopped grass, and dust. My frail wife was right beside me.

Her eyes were closed, she did not eat anything for a long time, and she had no strength to speak of, just laying there. The island did not have a doctor, and even if there were, we could not have called him or her. Two completely helpless lives hid under a roof, but the roof was ready to be pulled off at any time; the scenes outside were unthinkable. This was a couple through all the ages. This was the true virtual home.

For my wife and me, our family feeling always had little to do with the hometown, old trees, and familiar routes. At each time of adventure, there was investigation and conflicts but also the same home in the desert night after night. The drifting home could be the best way to show the nature of home, and the drift in the distress could be the best way to make such nature unforgettable.

Always extremely remote destinations, always very strange, always inclement weather, always the closed door, always difficult to move, always tired enough, always unaided by medical drugs, and always unassisted. Thus we possessed one of the most pure homes, infinitely frail but mighty enough.

sections.label: VI
paragraphs: THE ROAR OF NATURE drowned out the gentle knock on the door, but I heard it finally during a pause. Also, the voice calling us was Chinese.

I hurried to open the door. Surprisingly, it was the adventurer who traveled almost all the big islands. His name was Yang Gang, who many years ago was a young diplomat in Beijing, responsible for communication with South Pacific countries. After many visits, he immersed himself there and slowly expanded his path to the Western Pacific. Due to his love for the region, he explored it, due to that exploring, he resigned from office, and became a mobile islander in Oceania. No matter how far away he was, he understood the urgent need when a Chinese person fell ill. He stood at the door, holding a small flat-bottomed wok with thin rice gruel and some chopped vegetables sprinkled on it.

I thanked him deeply, shut the door, and put a small wok before my wife. After only taking a little, she looked at me with bright eyes. After a few moments, Miss Lin Lin, who accompanied us, sent some “Huoxiang zhengqi pills.” My wife went to sleep after eating, and when she woke up the next day, she was radiant.
Vegetable rice gruel and Huoxiang zhengqi pills will help you recover quickly. That is Chinese.

This involved another kind of “home,” larger than the “home” in the storm hut. However, this “home” was more mobile, extending even to any place on earth. In China there was a phrase “settle down anywhere within the four seas,” which sounds grandiose, but “four seas” here is only a functional word. Over the years, I slowly found that Chinese who did so were not small in number. The “home” in their minds was absolutely different from the “home” in the “coming back home often” said by many old people.

For my wife and me, our home was a boundless sea, and also a small island fighting against waves. The philosophical significance of “home” thus broke through from its ordinary meaning. Therefore, we went very far this time. Yes, though it was far away, we must come here.

sections.label: VII
paragraphs: ON THIS ISLAND A CHINESE MAN had lived for many years, called Chen Mingcan. For such a Chinese person living on such a desert island, all sorts of inconveniences could be imagined, but he did not want to leave. I thought there was only one reason, that he really loved the sea, really loved the island. He was the one who “settled down everywhere” by his nature; no sea, no home.

His hometown was in Heyuan, Guangdong Province. He had drifted to another Pacific island, Palau, and lived there for ten years, and then came here. He now was no doubt the “VIP” on the island, ran a small farm, and hired five Chinese workers in succession. The tribal chief would also talk to him if having the need for something.

He lived in a simple tin shack, keeping a flock of poultry, together with some Chinese food. He had installed an antenna and could receive Hong Kong Phoenix TV; I recognized it at once when I saw it. On the Pacific island, listening to “Teacher Qiuyu” named by a strange dark man, I was surprised, and then felt very comforted.

China’s “diving couple” was also on the island, and they loved the sea more than Mr. Chen Mingcan. As long as there were good diving spots around the world, they would go there, as if it were homework they must complete, without any omission. Last year, they went to the beach in Seychelles; when they heard there were good reefs, they hurried there. The husband was Li Mingxue, from Tieling, Liaoning. We chatted together about our acquaintance Zhao Benshan. His wife was from Shenyang, named Zhang Xin; I talked about Pan Shiyi, and the name of his wife was the same.

Li Mingxue and Zhang Xin originally had very good professional careers in Shanghai. However, after reading a lot of books about “ultimate concerns,” they began to doubt their own daily works ecology, and strongly yearned for the free, uncontrolled, open, and unmanaged life, so they went to sea. In the ocean, they had to challenge their own lives every day, and they were fascinated by the challenge.

“First, I saw him diving on the coast, but I dared not. Then I thought I should accompany with him underwater. I began to learn to dive in Maldives, and finally it became very easy after finishing twenty gas cylinders,” Zhang Xin said.

“Diving together for so many years, we must be husband and wife.” Zhang Xin, suddenly very emotional, said, “Accidents are unavoidable when diving—for example, one tank of gas is running out, and the diving buddy must assist the other one with his or her own cylinders immediately. If they were not a couple, each would consider their own safety at first. My husband likes to shoot sharks underwater, which brings great risks, so I have to keep with him for a long time and look around. Only couples have such patience.

“Diving couples in the world are dependent on each other every day, and generally they have no children or home. The only thing in their brains are the diving spots in the distance. There are several in Europe and those in South America are much more beautiful. Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Ecuador, and Colombia are all holy lands in the hearts of divers. For divers in China, Southeast Asia is a closer spot, like Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Australia also has very good diving spots. Sanya in Hainan Island of China is also one, but not very ideal.”
She presented the world diving maps in a very cordial tone, just like she was talking about her own family.

sections.label: VIII
paragraphs: TWO MONTHS AGO, another couple came here, but they went away just a month later, and we failed to meet them. Their obsession with the sea might be a little dramatic, in my opinion.
The husband was Belgian, called Luc, and his wife was a Chinese-American, called Jackie Jia. They lived for twenty-five years straight on a sailboat!

Of course, they would go from shore to shore to make a living, but at night they got back on the boat. From one coast to the other coast, the sailing time was generally not more than half a month, in order to replenish the fresh water and food. During the night voyages, they had to take turns on duty, to prevent weather catastrophes, ship collisions, and other accidents.

With their travel around the world, the equipment on their ship was also being updated annually, including satellite navigation, computer, refrigerator, and all the rest. But in the vast sea, between the unimaginable storms, they sailed for twenty-five years, which was not much different than that uncle canoeing by astronomical phenomena.

Such small human beings, a man and a woman, took a tough road, the waterway, the sea route, an unknowable path, an amazing way of life, a road to faithful love, and one to strengthen themselves as human beings.

Could we imagine the things that happened in that small boat day and night over twenty-five years? I thought anthropology, ethics, literature, and aesthetics had been rewritten gently by such couples between their dawns and dusks.
I saw the photos of Jackie Jia, really a Chinese, but looked older than her age. That was the grand impression left on a Chinese woman by the ferocity of space and time.

Many mariners had told me that the voyaging couples would not separate from each other, which sounded very romantic, but it was hard to stick to, and the wife must be the first one to leave, because no woman could bear such a life. Therefore, the key miracle of this couple who could go twenty-five years on the sea was this Chinese woman.

Looking at the picture, I thought of those groups of Chinese who loved the ocean and loved the island so much. So I must say that within Chinese culture, a long period of sea-watching, doubting, fearing, and prohibition existed, but for innumerable Chinese themselves, it was not that way. They could go into the sea, live with the sea, rely on the sea, and be inseparable from the sea. Culture and life, after all, were very different.

In fact, starting from the Hemudu and Liangzhu, or even earlier, there had been numerous canoes sent out from China and an obsession with the sea. Unfortunately, the inflexible characters were not intimate with the sea. The waters and shore where the Great Navigator Zheng He died were not clearly recorded. Half of Chinese history sank in the waves. Scholars taking the lazy route only knew to retrieve the book of dust. Those books never touched a real sea, or the lives of Chinese people tightly integrated with the sea.

Fortunately, times were reached that left behind the characters and small homes; finally, a group of Chinese had perturbed the ocean, and also wakened that life that had long been buried in Chinese culture.
In Micronesia, days and nights, my wife looked at me and said, “There should be a boat…”
I knew the infinite meaning behind it.
I said, “It must be a ship.”
She smiled and said, “Of course.”

zh.title: 谢家门孔
intro: 说明：
在经历了“中国之旅”和“世界之旅”之后，《文化苦旅》现在进入第三部分——“人生之旅”。
考古学家在寻找一个个远古“文化”的时候，其实是在寻找人的最初痕迹。文化在发达之后，根子上仍然是生命的痕迹。我在前面写到的那么多古迹，中国的，世界的，也都有无数高贵的生命在支撑。
高贵的生命要创造文化，必然会经历坎坷。因此，我所说的“苦旅”，并不是指旅行之苦，而是指创造之苦。由创造之苦连接成了人生旅途，这便是文化的宿命。
我只能以自己最熟悉的一些文化创造者为例，来说明问题。谢晋、巴金、黄佐临、陈逸飞……曾经是上海文化的骄傲代表。他们在不长的时间内齐刷刷地谢世了，留下一个惶恐而荒凉的上海，也留下一个惶恐而又荒凉的我。因此，我也要顺便写写朋友们离开后的自己。朋友们的经历和我自己的经历加在一起，大体能说明“文化苦旅”的本质是什么。
历来总有读者问我为什么那么突出这个“苦”字，为什么在这个嬉闹的时代如此不合时宜，那就请读读下面这几篇文章吧。

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 直到今天，谢晋的小儿子阿四，还不知道“死亡”是什么。
大家觉得，这次该让他知道了。但是，不管怎么解释，他诚实的眼神告诉你，他还是不知道。
十几年前，同样弱智的阿三走了，阿四不知道这位小哥到哪里去了，爸爸对大家说，别给阿四解释死亡；
两个月前，阿四的大哥谢衍走了，阿四不知道他到哪里去了，爸爸对大家说，别给阿四解释死亡；
现在，爸爸自己走了，阿四不知道他到哪里去了，家里只剩下了他和八十三岁的妈妈，阿四已经不想听解释。谁解释，就是谁把小哥、大哥、爸爸弄走了。他就一定跟着走，去找。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 阿三还在的时候，谢晋对我说：“你看他的眉毛，稀稀落落，是整天扒在门孔上磨的。只要我出门，他就离不开门了，分分秒秒等我回来。”
谢晋说的门孔，俗称“猫眼”，谁都知道是大门中央张望外面的世界的一个小装置。平日听到敲门或电铃，先在这里看一眼，认出是谁，再决定开门还是不开门。但对阿三来说，这个闪着亮光的玻璃小孔，是一种永远的等待。
他不允许自己有一丝一毫的松懈，因为爸爸每时每刻都可能会在那里出现，他不能漏掉第一时间。除了睡觉、吃饭，他都在那里看。双脚麻木了，脖子酸痛了，眼睛迷糊了，眉毛脱落了，他都没有撤退。
爸爸在外面做什么？他不知道，也不想知道。
有一次，谢晋与我长谈，说起在封闭的时代要在电影中加入一点人性的光亮是多么不容易。我突然产生联想，说：“谢导，你就是阿三！”
“什么？”他奇怪地看着我。
我说：“你就像你家阿三，在关闭着的大门上找到一个孔，便目不转睛地盯着，看亮光，等亲情，除了睡觉、吃饭，你都没有放过。”
他听了一震，目光炯炯地看着我，不说话。
我又说：“你的门孔，也成了全国观众的门孔。不管什么时节，一个玻璃亮眼，大家从那里看到了很多风景，很多人性。你的优点也与阿三一样，那就是无休无止地坚持。”

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 谢晋在六十岁的时候对我说：“现在，我总算和全国人民一起成熟了！”那时，“文革”结束不久。
“成熟”了的他，拍了《牧马人》、《天云山传奇》、《芙蓉镇》、《清凉寺的钟声》、《高山下的花环》、《最后的贵族》、《鸦片战争》……那么，他的艺术历程也就大致可以分为两段，前一段为探寻期，后一段为成熟期。探寻期更多地依附于时代，成熟期更多地依附于人性。

一切依附于时代的作品，往往会以普遍流行的时代话语，笼罩艺术家自身的主体话语。谢晋的可贵在于，即使被笼罩，他的主体话语还在顽皮地扑闪腾跃。其中最顽皮之处，就是集中表现女性。不管外在题材是什么，只要抓住了女性命题，艺术也就具有了亦刚亦柔的功能，人性也就具有了悄然渗透的理由。在这方面，《舞台姐妹》就是很好的例证。尽管这部作品里也带有不少时代给予的概念化痕迹，但“文革”中批判它的最大罪名，就是“人性论”。
谢晋说，当时针对这部作品，批判会开了不少，造反派怕文艺界批判“人性论”不力，就拿到“阶级立场最坚定”的工人中去放映，然后批判。没想到，在放映时，纺织厂的女工已经哭成一片，她们被深深感染了。“人性论”和“阶级论”的理论对峙，就在这一片哭声中见出了分晓。
但是，在谢晋看来，这样的作品还不成熟。让纺织女工哭成一片，很多民间戏曲也能做到。他觉得自己应该做更大的事。“文革”使他获得了浴火重生的机会。“文革”以后的他，不再在时代话语的缝隙中捕捉人性，而是反过来，以人性的标准来拷问时代了。
对于一个电影艺术家来说，“成熟”在六十岁，确实是晚了一点。但是，到了六十岁还有勇气“成熟”，这正是二三十年前中国最优秀知识分子的良知凸现。也有不少人一直表白自己“成熟”得很早，不仅早过谢晋，而且几乎没有不成熟的阶段。这也可能吧，但全国民众都未曾看到。谢晋是永远让大家看到的，因此大家与他相陪相伴地不成熟，然后一起成熟。
这让我想起云南丽江雪山上的一种桃子，由于气温太低，成熟期拖得特别长，因此收获时的果实也特别大，大到让人欢呼。
“成熟”后的谢晋让全国观众眼睛一亮。他成了万人瞩目的思想者，每天在大量的文学作品中寻找着既符合自己切身感受、又必然能感染民众的描写，然后思考着如何用镜头震撼全民族的心灵。没有他，那些文学描写只在一角流传；有了他，一座座通向亿万观众的桥梁搭了起来。
于是，由于他，整个民族进入了一个艰难而美丽的苏醒过程，就像罗丹雕塑《青铜时代》传达的那种象征气氛。
那些年的谢晋，大作品一部接着一部，部部深入人心，真可谓手挥五弦，目送归鸿，云蒸霞蔚。
就在这时，他礼贤下士，竟然破例聘请了一个艺术顾问，那就是比他小二十多岁的我。他与我的父亲同龄，我又与他的女儿同龄。这种辈分错乱的礼聘，只能是他，也只能在上海。
那时节，连萧伯纳的嫡传弟子黄佐临先生也在与我们一起玩布莱希特、贫困戏剧、环境戏剧，他应该是我祖父一辈。而我的学生们，也已成果累累。八十年代“四世同堂”的上海文化，实在让人难以忘怀。而在这“四世同堂”的热闹中，成果最为显赫的，还是谢晋。他让上海，维持了一段为时不短的文化骄傲。
从更广阔的视角来看，谢晋最大的成果在于用自己的生命接通了中国电影在一九四九年之后的曲折逻辑。不管是幼稚、青涩、豪情，还是深思、严峻、浩叹，他全都经历了，摸索了，梳理了。
他不是散落在岸边的一片美景，而是一条完整的大河，使沿途所有的景色都可依着他而定位。他是一脉彩色的光缆，为很多并不彩色的历史过程提供了审美可能。
我想，当代中国的电影艺术家即便取得再高的国际成就，也不能轻忽谢晋这个名字，因为进入今天这个制高点的那条崎岖山路，是他跌跌绊绊走下来的。当代艺术家的长辈，都从他那里汲取过美，并构成遗传。在这个意义上，谢晋不朽。

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 谢晋聘请我做艺术顾问，旁人以为他会要我介绍当代世界艺术的新思潮，其实并不。他与我最谈得拢的，是具体的艺术感觉。他是文化创造者，要的是现场设计，而不是云端高论。
我们也曾开过一些研讨会，有的理论家在会上高谈阔论，又明显地缺少艺术感觉。谢晋会偷偷地摘下耳机，出神地看着发言者。发言者还以为他在专心听讲，其实他很可能只是在观察发言者脸部的肌肉运动状态和可以划分的角色类型。这好像不太礼貌，但高龄的他有资格这样做。
谢晋特别想说又不愿多说的，是作为文化创造者的苦恼。
我问他：“你在创作过程中遇到的最大苦恼是什么？是剧作的等级，演员的悟性，还是摄影师的能力？”
他说：“不，不，这些都有办法解决。我最大的苦恼，是遇到了不懂艺术的审查者和评论者。”
他所说的“不懂艺术”，我想很多官员是不太明白其中含义的。他们总觉得自己既有名校学历又看过很多中外电影，还啃过几本艺术理论著作，怎么能说“不懂艺术”呢？
其实，真正的艺术家都知道，这种“懂”，是创造意义上而不是学问意义上的。
那是对每一个感性细节小心翼翼的捧持，是对每一个未明意涵恭恭敬敬地让它保持未明状态，是对作品的有机生命不可稍有割划的万千敏感，是对转瞬即逝的一个眼神、一道光束的震颤性品咂，是对那绵长多变又快速运动的镜头语汇的感同身受，以及感同身受后的气喘吁吁、神驰心飞。
用中国传统美学概念来说，这种“懂”，不“隔”。而一切审查性、评论性的目光，不管包含着多少学问，都恰恰是从“隔”开始的。
平心而论，在这一点上，谢晋的观点比我宽容得多。他不喜欢被审查却也不反对，一直希望有夏衍、田汉这样真正懂艺术的人来审查。而我则认为，即使夏衍、田汉这样的艺术家再世，也没有权利要谢晋这样的艺术家在艺术上服从自己。
谢晋那些最重要的作品，上映前都麻烦重重。如果说，“文革”前的审查总是指责他“爱情太多，女性话题太多，宣扬资产阶级人性论太多”，那么，“文革”后的审查者已经宽容爱情和女性了，主要是指责他“揭露革命事业中的黑暗太多”。
有趣的是，有的审查者一旦投身创作，立场就会发生天翻地覆的变化。我认识两位职业审查者，年老退休后常常被一些电视剧聘为顾问，参与构思。作品拍出来后，交给他们当年退休时物色的徒弟们审查，他们才发现，这些徒弟太不像话了。他们愤怒地说：“文化领域那么多诽谤、伪造、低劣都不审查，却总是盯着一些好作品不依不饶！”后来他们扪心自问，才明白自己大半辈子也在这么做。
对于评论，谢晋与他的同代人一样，过于在乎，比较敏感，容易生气。
他平生最生气的评论，是一个叫朱大可的上海评论者所揭露的“谢晋模式”。忘了是说“革命加女人”，还是“革命加爱情”。谢晋认为，以前的审查者不管多么胡言乱语，也没有公开发表，而这个可笑的“谢晋模式”，却被很多报纸刊登了。
他几乎在办公室里大声咆哮：“女人怎么啦？没有女人，哪来男人？爱情，我在《红色娘子军》里想加一点，不让；《舞台姐妹》里也没有正面爱情。只有造反派才批判我借着革命贩卖爱情，这个朱大可是什么人？”
我劝他：“这个人没有什么恶意，只是理论上幼稚，把现象拼凑当作了学问。你不要生气，如果有人把眼睛、鼻子、嘴巴的组合说成是脸部模式，你会发火吗？”
他看着我，不再说话。但后来，每次研讨会我都提议让朱大可来参加，他都不让。而且，还会狠狠地瞪我一眼。
直到有一天，朱大可发表文章说，有一个妓女的手提包里也有我的《文化苦旅》，引起全国对我的讪笑。谢晋也幸灾乐祸地笑了，说：“看你再为他辩护！”
但他很快又大声地为我讲话了：“妓女？中外艺术中，很多妓女的品德，都比文人高！我还要重拍《桃花扇》，用李香君回击他！”
我连忙说：“不，不。中国现在的文艺评论，都是随风一吐的口水，哪里犯得着你大艺术家来回击？”
“你不恨？”他盯着我的眼睛，加了一句，“那么多报纸。”
“当然不恨。”我说。
他把手拍在我肩上。

sections.label: 五
paragraphs: 在友情上，谢晋算得上是一个汉子。
他总是充满古意地反复怀念一个个久不见面的老友，怀念得一点儿也不像一个名人；同时，他又无限兴奋地结识一个个刚刚发现的新知，兴奋得一点儿也不像一个老者。他的工作性质、活动方式和从业时间，使他的“老友”和“新知”的范围非常之大，但他一个也不会忘记，一个也不会怠慢。
因此，只要他有召唤，或者，只是以他的名义召唤，再有名的艺术家也没有不来的。
有时，他别出心裁，要让这些艺术家都到他出生的老家去聚合，大家也都乖乖地全数抵达。就在他去世前几天，上海电视台准备拍摄一个纪念他八十五岁生日的节目，开出了一大串响亮的名单，逐一邀请。这些人中的任何一个，在一般情况下是“八抬大轿也抬不动”的，因为有的也已年老，有的非常繁忙，有的片约在身，有的身患重病。但是，一听是谢晋的事，没有一个拒绝。当然，他们没有料到，生日之前，会有一个追悼会……
我从旁观察，发觉谢晋交友，有两个原则：一是拒绝小人，二是不求实用。这就使他身边的热闹中有一种干净。相比之下，有些同样著名的老艺术家永远也摆不出谢导这样的友情阵仗，不是他们缺少魅力，而是本来要来参加的人想到同时还有几双忽闪的眼睛也会到场，便借故推托了。有时，好人也会利用小人，但谢晋不利用。
他对小人的办法，不是争吵，不是驱逐，而是在最早的时间冷落。他的冷落，是炬灭烟消，完全不予互动。听对方说了几句话，他就明白是什么人了，便突然变成了一座石山，邪不可侵。转身，眼角扫到一个朋友，石山又变成了一尊活佛。
一些早已不会被他选为演员和编剧的老朋友，永远是他的座上宾。他们谁也不会因为自己已经帮不上他的忙，感到不安。西哲有言：“友情的败坏，是从利用开始的。”谢晋的友情，从不败坏。
他一点儿也不势利。再高的官，在他眼中只是他的观众，与天下千万观众没有区别。但因为他们是官，他会特别严厉一点。我多次看到，他与官员讲话的声调，远远高于他平日讲话，主要是在批评。他还会把自己对于某个文化高官的批评到处讲，反复讲，希望能传到那个高官的耳朵里，一点儿不担心自己会不会遇到麻烦。
有时，他也会发现，对那个高官的批评搞错了，于是又到处大声讲：“那其实是个好人，我过去搞错了！”
对于受到挫折的人，他特别关心，包括官员。
有一年，我认识的一位官员因事入狱。我以前与这位官员倒也没有什么交往，这时却想安慰他几句。正好上海市监狱邀请我去给几千个犯人讲课，我就向监狱长提出要与那个人谈一次话。监狱长说，与那个人谈话是不被允许的。我就问能不能写个条子，监狱长说可以。
我就在一张纸上写道：“平日大家都忙，没有时间把外语再推进一步，祝贺你有了这个机会。”写完，托监狱长交给那个人。
谢晋听我说了这个过程，笑眯眯地动了一会儿脑筋，然后兴奋地拍了一下桌子说：“有了！你能送条子，那么，我可以进一步，送月饼！过几天就是中秋节，你告诉监狱长，我谢晋要为犯人讲一次课！”
就这样，他为了让那个官员在监狱里过一个像样的中秋节，居然主动去向犯人讲了一次课。提篮桥监狱的犯人，有幸一睹他们心中的艺术偶像。那个入狱的官员，其实与他也没有什么关系。
四年以后，那个人刑满释放，第一个电话打给我，说他听了我的话，在里边学外语，现在带出来一部五十万字的翻译稿。然后，他说，急于要请谢晋导演吃饭。谢导那次的中秋节行动，实在把他感动了。

sections.label: 六
paragraphs: 我一直有一个错误的想法，觉得拍电影是一个力气活，谢晋已经年迈，不必站在第一线上了。我提议他在拍完《芙蓉镇》后就可以收山，然后以自己的信誉、影响和经验，办一个电影公司，再建一个影视学院。简单说来，让他从一个电影导演变成一个“电影导师”。
有这个想法的，可能不止我一个人。
我过了很久才知道，他对我们的这种想法，深感痛苦。
他想拍电影，他想自己天天拿着话筒指挥现场，然后猫着腰在摄影机后面调度一切。他早已不在乎名利，也不想证明自己依然还保持着艺术创造能力。他只是饥渴，没完没了地饥渴。在这一点上他像一个最单纯、最执着的孩子，一定要做一件事，骂他，损他，毁他，都可以，只要让他做这件事，他立即可以破涕为笑。
他当然知道我们的劝说有点道理，因此，也是认认真真地办电影公司，建影视学院，还叫我做“校董”。但是，这一切都不能消解他内心的强烈饥渴。
他越来越要在我们面前表现出他的精力充沛、步履轻健。他由于耳朵不好，本来说话就很大声，现在更大声了。他原来就喜欢喝酒，现在更要与别人频频比赛酒量了。
有一次，他跨着大步走在火车站的月台上，不知怎么突然踉跄了。他想摆脱踉跄，挣扎了一下，谁知更是朝前一冲，被人扶住，脸色发青。这让人们突然想起他的皮夹克、红围巾所包裹着的年龄。
不久后一次吃饭，我又委婉地说起了老话题。
他知道月台上的踉跄被我们看到了，因此也知道我说这些话的原因。
他朝我举起酒杯，我以为他要用干杯的方式来接受我的建议，没想到他对我说：“秋雨，你知道什么样的人是真正善饮的吗？我告诉你，第一，端杯稳；第二，双眉平；第三，下口深。”
说着，他又稳又平又深地一连喝了好几杯。
是在证明自己的酒量吗？不，我觉得其中似乎又包含着某种宣示。
即使毫无宣示的意思，那么，只要他拿起酒杯，便立即显得大气磅礴，说什么都难以反驳。
后来，有一位热心的农民企业家想给他资助，开了一个会。这位企业家站起来讲话，意思是大家要把谢晋看作一个珍贵的品牌，进行文化产业的运作。但他不太会讲话，说成了这样一句：“‘谢晋’这两个字，不仅仅是一个人名，而且还是一种有待开发的东西。”
“东西？”在场的文化人听了都觉得不是味道。
一位喜剧演员突然有了念头，便大声地在座位上说：“你说错了，谢晋不是东西！”他又重复了一句，“谢晋不是东西！”
这是一个毫无恶意的喜剧花招，全场都笑了。
我连忙扭头看谢晋导演，不知他是生气而走，还是蔼然而笑。没想到，我看到的他似乎完全没有听到这句话，只是像木头一样呆坐着，毫无表情。我立即明白了，他从这位企业家的讲话中才知道，连他们也想把自己当作品牌来运作。
“我，难道只能这样了吗？”他想。
他毫无表情的表情，把我震了一下。他心中在想，如果自己真的完全变成了一个品牌，丢失了亲自创造的权利，那谢晋真的“不是东西”了。
从那次之后，我改变了态度，总是悉心倾听他一个又一个的创作计划。
这是一种滔滔不绝的激情，变成了延绵不绝的憧憬。他要重拍《桃花扇》，他要筹拍美国华工修建西部铁路的血泪史，他要拍《拉贝日记》，他要拍《大人家》，他更想拍前辈领袖的女儿们的生死恩仇、悲欢离合……
看到我愿意倾听，他就针对我们以前的想法一吐委屈：“你们都说我年事已高，应该退居二线，但是我早就给你说过，我是六十岁才成熟的，那你算算……”
一位杰出艺术家的生命之门既然已经第二度打开，翻卷的洪水再也无可抵挡。
这是创造主体的本能呼喊，也是一个强大的生命要求自我完成的一种尊严。

sections.label: 七
paragraphs: 他在中国创建了一个独立而庞大的艺术世界，但回到家，却是一个常人无法想象的天地。
他与夫人徐大雯女士生了四个小孩，脑子正常的只有一个，那就是谢衍。谢衍的两个弟弟就是前面所说的老三和老四，都严重弱智，而姐姐的情况也不好。
这四个孩子，出生在一九四六年至一九五六年这十年间。当时的社会，还很难找到辅导弱智儿童的专业学校，一切麻烦都堆在一门之内。家境极不宽裕，工作极其繁忙，这个门内天天在发生什么？只有天知道。
我们如果把这样一个家庭背景与谢晋的那么多电影联系在一起，真会产生一种匪夷所思的感觉。每天傍晚，他那高大而疲惫的身影一步步走回家门的图像，不能不让人一次次落泪。不是出于一种同情，而是为了一种伟大。
一个错乱的精神旋涡，能够生发出伟大的精神力量吗？谢晋作出了回答，而全国的电影观众都在点头。
我觉得，这种情景，在整个人类艺术史上都难以重见。
谢晋亲手把错乱的精神旋涡，筑成了人道主义的圣殿。我曾多次在他家里吃饭，他做得一手好菜，常常围着白围单、手握着锅铲招呼客人。客人可能是好莱坞明星、法国大导演、日本制作人，但最后谢晋总会搓搓手，通过翻译介绍自己两个儿子的特殊情况，然后隆重请出。
这种毫不掩饰的坦荡，曾让我百脉俱开。在客人面前，弱智儿子的每一个笑容和动作，在谢晋看来就是人类最本原的可爱造型，因此满眼是欣赏的光彩。他把这种光彩，带给了整个门庭，也带给了所有的客人。
他自己成天到处走，有时也会带着儿子出行。我听谢晋电影公司总经理张惠芳女士说，那次去浙江衢州，坐了一辆面包车，路上要好几个小时，阿四同行。坐在前排的谢晋过一会儿就要回过头来问：“阿四累不累？”“阿四好吗？”“阿四要不要睡一会儿？”……过几分钟就回一次头，没完没了。
每次回头，那神情，能把雪山消融。

sections.label: 八
paragraphs: 他万万没有想到，他家后代唯一的正常人，那个从国外留学回来的典雅君子，他的大儿子谢衍，竟先他而去。
谢衍太知道父母亲的生活重压，一直瞒着自己的病情，不让老人家知道。他把一切事情都料理得一清二楚，然后穿上一套干净的衣服，去了医院，再也没有出来。
他恳求周围的人，千万不要让爸爸、妈妈到医院来。他说，爸爸太出名，一来就会引动媒体，而自己现在的形象又会使爸爸、妈妈吃惊。他一直念叨着：“不要来，千万不要来，不要让他们来……”
直到他去世前一星期，周围的人说，现在一定要让你爸爸、妈妈来了。这次，他没有说话。
谢晋一直以为儿子是一般的病住院，完全不知道事情已经那么严重。眼前病床上，他唯一可以对话的儿子，已经不成样子。
他像一尊突然被风干了的雕像，站在病床前，很久，很久。
他身边，传来工作人员低低的抽泣。
谢衍吃力地对他说：“爸爸，我给您添麻烦了！”
他颤声地说：“我们治疗，孩子，不要紧，我们治疗……”
从这天起，他天天都陪着夫人去医院。
独身的谢衍已经五十九岁，现在却每天在老人赶到前不断问：“爸爸怎么还不来？妈妈怎么还不来？爸爸怎么还不来？”
那天，他实在太痛了，要求打吗啡，但医生有犹豫。幸好有慈济功德会的志工来唱佛曲，他平静了。
谢晋和夫人陪在儿子身边，那夜几乎陪了通宵。工作人员怕这两位八十多岁的老人撑不住，力劝他们暂时回家休息。但是，两位老人的车还没有到家，谢衍就去世了。
谢衍是二○○八年九月二十三日下葬的。第二天，九月二十四日，杭州的朋友就邀请谢晋去散散心，住多久都可以。接待他的，是一位也刚刚丧子的杰出男子，叫叶明。
两人一见面就抱住了，号啕大哭。他们两人，前些天都哭过无数次，但还要找一个机会，不刺激妻子，不为难下属，抱住一个人，一个经得起用力抱的人，痛快淋漓、回肠荡气地哭一哭。
那天谢晋导演的哭声，像虎啸，像狼嚎，像龙吟，像狮吼，把他以前拍过的那么多电影里的哭，全都收纳了，又全都释放了。
那天，秋风起于杭州，连西湖都在呜咽。
他并没有在杭州长住，很快又回到了上海。这几天他很少说话，眼睛直直地看着前方。有时也翻书报，却是乱翻，没有一个字入眼。
突然电话铃响了，是家乡上虞的母校春晖中学打来的，说有一个纪念活动要让他出席，有车来接。他一生，每遇危难总会想念家乡。今天，故乡故宅又有召唤，他毫不犹豫地答应了。他给驾驶员小蒋说：“你别管我了，另外有车来接！”
小蒋告诉张惠芳，张惠芳急急赶来询问，门房说，接谢导的车，两分钟前开走了。
春晖中学的纪念活动第二天才开始，这天晚上他在旅馆吃了点冷餐，没有喝酒，倒头便睡。这是真正的老家，他出走已久，今天只剩下他一个人回来。他是朝左侧睡的，再也没有醒来。
这天是二〇〇八年十月十八日，离他八十五岁生日，还有一个月零三天。

sections.label: 九
paragraphs: 他老家的屋里，有我题写的四个字：“东山谢氏”。
那是几年前的一天，他突然来到我家，要我写这几个字。他说，已经请几位老一代书法大家写过，希望能增加我写的一份。东山谢氏？好生了得！我看着他，抱歉地想，认识了他那么多年，也知道他是绍兴上虞人，却没有把他的姓氏与那个遥远而辉煌的门庭联系起来。
他的远祖，是公元四世纪那位打了“淝水之战”的东晋宰相谢安。这仗，是和侄子谢玄一起打的。而谢玄的孙子，便是中国山水诗的鼻祖谢灵运。谢安本来是隐居会稽东山的，经常与大书法家王羲之一起喝酒吟诗，他的侄女谢道韫也嫁给了王羲之的儿子王凝之，而才学又远超丈夫。谢安后来因形势所迫再度做官，这使中国有了一个“东山再起”的成语。
正因为这一切，我写“东山谢氏”这四个字时非常恭敬，一连写了好多幅，最后挑出一张，送去。
谢家，竟然自东晋、南朝至今，就一直住在东山脚下？别的不说，光那股积累了一千六百年的气，已经非比寻常。
谢晋导演对此极为在意，却又不对外说，可见完全不想借远祖之名炫耀。他在意的，是这山、这村、这屋、这姓、这气。但这一切都是秘密的，只是为了要我写字才说，说过一次再也不说。
我想，就凭着这种无以言表的深层皈依，他会一个人回去，在一大批远祖面前画上人生的句号。

sections.label: 十
paragraphs: 此刻，他上海的家，只剩下了阿四。他的夫人因心脏问题，住进了医院。
阿四不像阿三那样成天在门孔里观看。他几十年如一日的任务是为爸爸拿包、拿鞋。每天早晨爸爸出门了，他把包递给爸爸，并把爸爸换下的拖鞋放好。晚上爸爸回来，他接过包，再递上拖鞋。
好几天，爸爸的包和鞋都在，人到哪里去了？他有点奇怪，却在耐心等待。突然来了很多人，在家里摆了一排排白色的花。
白色的花越来越多，家里放满了。他从门孔里往外一看，还有人送来。阿四穿行在白花间，突然发现，白花把爸爸的拖鞋遮住了。他弯下腰去，拿出爸爸的拖鞋，小心放在门边。
这个白花的世界，今天就是他一个人，还有一双鞋。

en.title: Peephole of Family Xie
intro: AFTER THE “CHINA TOUR” AND “WORLD TOUR,” the third part of A Bittersweet Journey Through Culture—the “life journey”—was begun.

When the archeologists found ancient “cultures,” they in fact were looking for the original traces of human beings. After the culture was greatly developed, the life trace remained in its root. So many historic sites I described before, at home and abroad, were supported by countless magnificent lives.

Twists and turns must be experienced when a noble life creates the culture. Therefore, A Bittersweet Journey Through Culture did not mean suffering in the journey, but in the creation. The life journey connected by the sufferings of creation was just the fate of culture.

I could list some culture creators I am familiar with to illustrate this problem. Xie Jin, Ba Jin, Huang Zuolin, and Chen Yifei…they were all proud representatives of Shanghai culture. Theyall passed away within a short time, just leaving a fearful and dreary Shanghai, and a fearful and desolate me. Therefore, I also wanted to write about my own state after the departure of my friends. The combination of my friends’ experiences and mine, the nature of a “bitter sweet journey,” could be told in general.
Readers often asked me why I always highlighted the “bitter,” so outdated in this era of playfulness. Then please read the following articles.

sections.label: I
paragraphs: UNTIL TODAY, the youngest son A Si of Xie Jin still did not know what “death” was.
Everyone felt that he should know by this time. However, no matter how they explained it, his honest eyes always told you he still did not know.
A dozen years ago, A San, with a mental handicap, had gone away. A Si did not know where his little brother had gone, but his father, while he told it to everyone, never explained it to A Si.
Two months ago, the elder brother of A Si, Xie Yan, had gone away. He did not know where his brother had gone, but his dad told everyone, never explaining it to A Si.

Now, his father had gone. A Si did not know where his father had gone, but only he and his eighty-three-year-old mother were left at home. A Si did not want an explanation again. The person who explained was just the person who brought his little brother, big brother, and father away. He must go and find them.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: WHEN A SAN WAS HERE, Xie Jin said to me: “Look at his eyebrows, so sparse, for they were grinded on the peephole all day long. As long as I go out, he cannot leave until I come back.”

The peephole Xie Jin mentioned was known as the “cat’s eye,” and everyone knew that it was the small device at the center of gate to look at the outside world. When listening to the knock or bell, we often take a look from here at first, recognize who it is, and then decide whether to open the door. But as for A San, the shining glass eyelet was always an insistent wait.

He did not allow himself to have an iota of laxness, for his father might show up there at any time, and he could not miss the first time. Except for sleeping and eating, he was there to watch. His feet were numb, his neck was painful, his eyes were darkened, and his eyebrows fell off, but he did not retreat.
What did his dad do outside? He did not know, and did not want to know.
Once, Xie Jin and I had a long talk, and talked about the difficulty of adding a little humanity to film in that closed-off time. I suddenly free-associated and said, “Director Xie, you’re A San!”
“What?” He looked at me strangely.
I said, “You were like A San. Find a hole on the closed door, and then stare at it fixedly for light and kinship. Except for sleeping and eating, you never give up.”

He was shocked, and looked at me with a piercing gleam, without saying a word. Again, I said: “Your door hole has become the door hole of a national audience. Regardless of the season, a glass hole could help us see a lot of scenery and a lot of human nature. Just like A San, you were also endlessly insistent.”

sections.label: III
paragraphs: WHEN HE WAS SIXTY YEARS OLD, Xie Jin said to me: “Now, I’ve finally matured together with all the people!” This was shortly after the Cultural Revolution.

After he had “matured,” he shot The Wrangler, Legend of Tianyun Mountain, Hibiscus Town, Bell of Purity Temple, Wreaths at Foot of Mountain, The Last Aristocrats, and The Opium War. His work could be roughly divided into two sections: the exploring period, then the maturity period. The first period was more based on the times, while the latter period was more dependent on human nature.

The works of his maturity tended to cover the subject words of the artist over the popular language in the era. The valuable point of Xie Jin was that, even if he was concealing himself, his subject words still fluttered and jumped mischievously. His most mischievous point was to focus on women. No matter what the external subject matter, as long as the women’s propositions were seized, the art also had strength and gentleness, and a quiet penetration of humanity. Stage Sisters is a good example. Although this work also carried some traces of the concepts of the times, the greatest charge in the Cultural Revolution was the “theory of human nature.”

Xie Jin said that the criticism meetings were driven a lot by this work at that time; the rebels feared the inadequacy of the criticism “on human nature” in the literary circle, so they reviewed it with the workers who “were with the firmest standpoint” for criticism. Unexpectedly, when shown the film, the women workers in the textile mills cried heavily; they were impressed. The theoretical confrontation between “human nature” and “class theory” had cried itself out.

However, from the view of Xie Jin, this was not yet maturity. To make women textile workers cry, lots of folk operas could achieve that, too. He felt he should do something greater. From the Cultural Revolution on, he led a new life. He had no longer seized humanity from the discourse of the times, but in fact tortured the times with the standard of humanity.

For a film artist, it was indeed a bit late to mature at the age of sixty. However, it highlighted the conscience of Chinese top intellectuals twenty or thirty years ago that they could still have the courage to mature at the age of sixty. There were many who had asserted their earlier “maturity,” not only earlier than Xie Jin, but also almost without an immature stage. It might be so, but the public had never seen it. Xie Jin was forever seen by us, so together with us he got through his immaturity and maturity stages.

This reminded me of a peach grown on a snowy mountain in Lijiang of Yunnan Province. Due to the low temperature, its maturation period was extremely long, so the fruits harvested were particularly large, and ripe enough.

Xie Jin, after “maturity,” lit up the eyes of national audiences. He became a remarkable thinker. Every day, in a large number of literary works, he looked for descriptions in line with his own personal experience, while also connecting with the public, and then he thought about how to use the camera and shake the hearts of the whole nation. Without him, the literary descriptions could only be kept in a corner; it was he who built the bridges to the millions of people.
Therefore, with him, the whole nation experienced a revival process, difficult but beautiful, just like the symbolic atmosphere conveyed in Rodin’s sculpture The Age of Bronze.
All those years, Xie Jin filmed a lot of great works, one after another, winning popular support and an excellent career, so colorful and flourishing.

At the same time, he courteously hired an art consultant on a part-time basis, myself, more than twenty years younger than he. He was the same age as my father, while I was his daughter’s age. This cordial invitation could only be from him and only in Shanghai.

At that time, even, Mr. Huang Zuolin, a disciple of George Bernard Shaw, also put on plays by Brecht, together with us, poor theatre, and environmental theater, and he was of my grandfather’s generation. My students had also been fruitful. Shanghai “four generations” culture in the 1980s was really unforgettable. Among them, the most prominent was still Xie Jin. He maintained the reputation of Shanghai with a long period of proud cultural achievement.

From a broader perspective, the greatest achievement of Xie Jin was to get through the tortuous logic that set in after 1949 with his own life intact. No matter the childishness, immaturity, pride, or the pondering, and the severe and deep sadness, he had all gone through it all, however he could.

His was the wonderful view all along scattered points on the shore, but of a complete river, so that the landscape all along the way could be framed in accordance with him. He was able to fulfill the aesthetic possibilities of lots of historical processes normally without too much color.

No contemporary Chinese filmmaker could ignore the name of Xie Jin even if achieving greater international success, for it was Xie Jin who stumbled and tripped up the rugged mountains to the commanding heights of today. The older contemporary artists had all learned from his beauty and inherited it. In this sense, Xie Jin was immortal.

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: XIE JIN HIRED ME as his artistic consultant. Others might think he would want me to introduce new trends in contemporary world art, but in fact no. What we talked about most was the specific artistic sense. He was a creator of culture, requiring site design rather than harangues.

We had held a number of seminars, in which some theorists talked but obviously lacked artistic feeling. Xie Jin would secretly take off his headphones and look at the speaker, fascinated. The speaker thought he was attentive, but in fact he was probably watching the facial muscle movement of the speaker and the role type he could be categorized into. It seemed not very polite, but he was entitled to do so.
What Xie Jin wanted to express but was reluctant to discuss much was the distress of a culture creator.
I asked him, “What is the biggest distress you encounter during the creation? Is it the level of drama, the actors’ perception, or ability of cameramen?”
He said, “No, no, these have solutions. My biggest trouble is meeting the reviewers and commentators who do not understand art.”

“Do not understand art,” he said, I thought that many officials did not quite understand what it all meant. They always figured they had graduated from famous universities, seen many Chinese and foreign movies, and learned several artworks, so how could you say they “do not understand art”?
In fact, only the real artists knew that such kind of “understanding” referred to the created meaning rather than the learned meaning.

The careful focus on each perceptual detail. The great sensitivity without the slightes omission to the organic life of the work. The understanding of the constantly and quickly changing visual vocabulary, as well as the breathless yearning for that understanding.

Within the traditional Chinese aesthetic concept, this kind of “understanding” would not be “separated”—but all reviews and critical views precisely began from such a “separation” no matter how much knowledge was contained in the tradition.

To be fair, at this point Xie Jin’s viewpoint was far more tolerant than mine. He did not like to be reviewed but had not opposed them, and always hoped for art reviews by Xia Yan and Tian Han, who really knew the art. However, I believed that even if Xia Yan and Tian Han could be reborn, they had no right to ask Xie Jin and the like to obey them in the art.

So many important works by Xie Jin encountered lots of problems before their screenings. If we said that the reviews before Cultural Revolution were always accusing him of “too much love, too many female topics, and too much promotion of “bourgeois human nature,” then the reviews after the Cultural Revolution had forgiven his love and female topics but mostly accused him of “too much revelation of the dark side in the revolutionary cause.”

What was interesting was that once joining the process of creation, some reviewers reversed themselves. I knew of two professional reviewers often hired as consultants by some television shows after they retired, who became involved in the conception of the shows. After their work was finished, they submitted it to their students for reviews, but they discovered that the apprentices were scandalous toward them. They said angrily: “So much slander, forgery, and inferiority in the cultural field were not reviewed, but always these excellent works!” Later, asking themselves about that, they suddenly understood what they had done for most of their lives.
Of course, with regard to any remark, Xie Jin, like his contemporaries, was too caring, sensitive, and touchy.

The comment that angered him the most was from Zhu Dake, a commentator from Shanghai, who categorized the “Xie Jin mode.” I had forgotten whether it was to say “revolution plus woman” or “revolution plus love.” Xie Jin believed that no matter how raving the previous review had been, it was not published, but this ridiculous “Xie Jin mode” had been published in many newspapers.

He almost shouted in the office: “What is wrong with women? Where is man from if not woman? I wanted to add a little element of love to the Red Detachment of Women, which he did not allow; positive love was also prohibited in Stage Sisters. Only the rebels will criticize me about the marketing of love through revolution. Who was Zhu Dake?”

I argued, “He has nothing malicious, just childish theories, so he regards the medley phenomenon as knowledge. Do not be angry again. If someone describes the facial pattern as the combination of eyes, nose, and mouth, will you get angry?”
He looked at me and stopped talking. But later I proposed that Zhu Dake participate in the seminar; he did not allow it and he even glared at me.

Until one day, Zhu Dake said in an article that in the handbag of a prostitute was also my Bittersweet Journey Through Culture, which made the national public laugh at me. Xie Jin also gleefully smiled and said, “Continue to defend him!”

But he soon spoke loudly for me: “Prostitute? In the arts in Chinese and foreign countries, their morality is much higher than the literati! I also remade The Peach Blossom Fan, to fight back against him with Li Xiangjun!”
I quickly said, “No, no. Current literary criticism in China is all spit in the wind. Need you, a major artist, fight back?”
He stared at me. “You don’t hate…so many newspapers?”
“Certainly not,” I said.
He put his hand on my shoulder.

sections.label: V
paragraphs: AS FOR FRIENDSHIP, Xie Jin was wholly committed. He always missed his old friends whom he had not seen for a long time, and was not a typical celebrity; he made new friends excitedly, like he did when he was still young. His job, activity level, and working time greatly expanded the scope of his “old friends” and “new friends,” but he would never forget or neglect any of them.
Therefore, when he summoned one, or just called their name, even the much more famous artists would come.

Sometimes he had the surprising idea of getting together in his hometown, and all his friends would arrive there. Just a few days before his death, a Shanghai TV station prepared to shoot a film of his eighty-fifth birthday program, and listed the big roll call of invitations one by one. Any one of these people could not generally be invited no matter how ceremonious the occasion, for some had become old, some were very busy, some were working, and some suffered serious illness. However, no one refused when hearing it was about Xie Jin. But no one expected that there would be a memorial service before his birthday.

I observed from the sidelines and found that Xie Jin had two principles when making friends: one was a denial of any scheming friendships, while the second one was that friendship was not for practical use, which made for a kind of purity in his lively surroundings. By contrast, some artists equally old and famous would never enjoy friendship like Director Xie, not because they lacked charm, but because people asked to participate would decline with some excuse, and betray avaricious reasons. Sometimes the good guy would make use of the villain, but Xie Jin would not.

His approach to the villain was not to quarrel, or expel, but to neglect within the shortest time. His neglect was through withdrawal without any interaction. After listening to a few words, he knew what kind of person was before him, and suddenly he turned into a stone mountain, and the evil could not invade. When he turned around and met a friend, this stone mountain would again turn into a living Buddha.

Some old friends would not be selected as actors and writers but would always be his guests. They did not feel uneasy, for they could not help him any longer. The Western philosophers said: “The corruption of friendship begins from the utilization.” The friendship of Xie Jin would never become corrupt.

He was not a snob. In his eyes even high officials were only an audience, no different from tens of millions of other viewers in the world. But since they were officials, he would be particularly harsh. I had seen that his tone when talking with officials was much more elevated than his usual speech, primarily in criticism. He would also extend his criticism to some culture official again and again, hoping to be heard by that officer, but he was not at all worried about them making trouble.
Sometimes he would discover that the criticism of some official was a mistake, so he would say everywhere: “He is actually a nice guy. I made a mistake in the past!”
As for frustrated people, he would show great care to them, including officials.

An official I knew was in jail for a year once because of some matter. I did not have any contact with the official before, but this time I wanted to soothe him with a few words. Just at that time, Shanghai Municipal Prison invited me to lecture to thousands of inmates, so I asked the warden for a chance to talk with that person. However, he told me that was not allowed. I asked if I could write a note, and he finally agreed.

I wrote on a piece of paper: “We were very busy in normal times and had no chance to further promote foreign languages. Congratulations to you on this opportunity.” Then I delivered it to that person via the warden.

Once listening, Xie Jin thought for a while with a smiled, then patted the table excitedly: “I’ve got it! You can take note, so then I can go further and send the mooncake! In a few days is the Mid-Autumn Festival. You tell the warden, I want to lecture to inmates!”

So gave a lecture to let that official have a decent Mid-Autumn Festival in prison. The inmates in Tilanqiao Prison could have the honor of glimpsing their idols. The official in prison, in fact, had no relationship with him.
