黄佐临先生曾小声地对我说：“夏衍气量大一点，对我还可以。于伶先生和他的战友，包括‘文革’结束后出任宣传部长的王元化先生等等，就比较坚持他们地下斗争时的原则，对我比较冷漠。”
除了这笔历史旧账之外，他还遇到了一个更糟糕的环境。一九四九年之后的中国戏剧界，论导演，一般称之为“北焦南黄”。“北焦”，是指北京艺术剧院的焦菊隐先生。由于当时北京集中了不少文化高端人士，文化气氛比较正常，焦菊隐先生与老舍、曹禺、郭沫若等戏剧家合作，成果连连。而“南黄”，也就是上海的黄佐临先生，却遇到了由上海最高领导柯庆施和他在宣传、文化领域的干将张春桥、姚文元等人组成的“极左思潮征候群”。
我听谢晋导演说，有一次柯庆施破例来看黄佐临新排的一台戏，没等看完，就铁青着脸站起身来走了，黄佐临不知所措。
还有一次，黄佐临导演了一台由工人作者写的戏，戏很一般，但导演手法十分精彩，没想到立即传来张春桥、姚文元对报纸的指示：只宣传作者，不宣传导演。
于是，当“北焦”红得发“焦”的时候，“南黄”真的“黄”了。
黄佐临在承受了一次次委屈之后，自问：“我的委屈来自何方？”答案是：“我怎么又在乎政治了！”
于是，他找回了从英国回来后的那份尊严。“不管他们怎么说，我还是回到艺术。”
黄佐临退出了人们的视野。上海的报纸，更愿意报道北京的焦菊隐，更愿意报道越剧、沪剧、淮剧，这些实在有待于黄佐临先生指点后才有可能脱胎换骨的地方戏曲。
真正国际等级的艺术巨匠在做什么？想什么？匆匆的街市茫然不知，也不想知道。
正在这时，由政治狂热和自然灾害共同造成的大饥荒开始了。上海，一座饥饿中的城市，面黄肌瘦。
在饥荒中，还会有像样的艺术行为吗？谁也不敢奢想。
完全出乎人们的意料，一九六二年四月二十五日，北京的一份报纸发表了黄佐临先生的长文《漫谈“戏剧观”》。虽然题目起得很谦虚，但这是一座现代世界戏剧学上的里程碑。突然屹立在人们眼前，大家都缺少思想准备。
这篇文章所建立的思维大构架，与当时当地的文化现实完全格格不入，却立即进入了国际学术视野。
这正像，狮王起身，远山震慑，而它身边的燕雀鱼蛙却完全无感。
须知，当时的多数中国文人，还在津津乐道阶级斗争。如果要说戏剧观，也只有无产阶级和资产阶级两种，并已经简称为“香花”和“毒草”。因此，对于黄佐临先生用浅显白话文写出来的文字，读起来却非常隔阂了。
那么，我不能不以国际学术标准来审视他当时的理论成就了。
一、以“造成幻觉”和“打破幻觉”来概括人类戏剧史，是一种化繁为简的高度提炼，属一流理论成果。
二、借用法国柔琏“第四堵墙”的概念来划分“幻觉”内外，使上述提炼获得了一个形象化的概念依托，精确而又有力度。
三、以打破“幻觉”和“第四堵墙”来引出布莱希特，使这位德国戏剧家的“创新功能”上升为“历史断代功能”。
四、以斯坦尼斯拉夫斯基、布莱希特、梅兰芳来标志二十世纪人类的三个戏剧观，理论气度广远，道前人所未道，却非常切合戏剧实际。提出至今，国际上未见重大异议。
五、以三大戏剧观过渡到“写意戏剧观”，是一个重大的美学创造。现在，已经成为戏剧界一种通用的工作用语。这在现代文艺的理论建设上，是一个奇迹。
鸟瞰世界，概括世界，又被世界接受，这样的理论成果，历来罕见。
记住了，一九六二年四月二十五日，这是天上的哲学之神、艺术之神都在低头注视中国、注视上海的日子。
我实在想不起，几十年来，全中国的艺术理论，不，全中国的所有文化理论，有哪一项成果，能超过它。
我问过很多文化人、理论家。他们想了好久，找了好久，排了好久，最后都摇头，说：“确实找不到一项。”
那么，我又要提醒大家，就在这个日子的两个星期之后，一九六二年五月九日，上海的另一位文化巨匠巴金，将有一个发言，题为《作家的勇气和责任心》，一针见血地指出了阻碍中国文学发展的主要障碍是“棍子”。实践证明，那是对“文革”灾难的预言。
一九六二年的晚春季节，上海显得那么光辉。大创建、大发现、大判断、大预言，居然一起出现。
光辉之强，使整整半个世纪之后的今天还觉得有点刺眼，因此大家故意视而不见，就像从来没有发生过这样的事一样。
若问今日媒体：五十年前，这个城市出现过什么值得记忆的文化人物和文化事件？答案可能是两首广泛宣传的歌曲，三段市井听熟的唱词，一堆人人皆知的明星。当然，还可能排出几个据称博学、却不屑写文章发表自己见解的教授。不管再怎么排，也挨不到黄佐临的文章，巴金的发言。

sections.label: 五
paragraphs: 黄佐临先生在“文革”中的遭遇，我不想多说。理由是，他自己也不想多说。
对这类事情我早有经验：受苦最深的人最不想说，说得最多的人一定受苦不多，说得高调的人一定是让别人受了苦。
在不想说的人中，也有区别。在我看来，同样是悲剧，巴金把悲剧化作了崇高，而黄佐临则把悲剧化作了喜剧。或者说，巴金提炼了悲剧，黄佐临看穿了悲剧。看穿的结果，是发笑。
他的几个女儿都给我讲过他在“文革”中嘲弄造反派歹徒，而对方却不知道被嘲弄的很多趣事。有几次讲的时候他在场，但他不仅没有搀和，反而轻轻摇头阻止。
不管怎么说，他对那场灾难的最终思维成果是非常严肃的，那就是对知识分子心灵的拷问。“文革”结束后不久，他到北京，导演了布莱希特名作《伽利略传》（与陈颙合作）。
当时，为了拨乱反正，全国科学大会刚刚召开，知识分子在业务上应该有驰骋的空间了，但他们在精神上能不能建立尊严？《伽利略传》及时地提出了这个问题，一时震动了整个京城。
人们说，从来没见过一部戏能够在关键时刻如此摇撼人们的灵魂深处。又说，这是“科学大会”的续篇，只不过这个“大会”在全国知识分子的心底召开。
“北焦”已逝，“南黄”北上，京城一惊，名不虚传！
从北京回上海之后，黄佐临先生决心加紧努力，在“写意戏剧观”的基础上推进“民族演剧体系”的建设。他如饥似渴地学习和探索，从事一个个最前卫的艺术实验，几乎让人忘了，他已经快要八十岁。
那年月，我见过很多“劫后余生”的前辈学者，温厚老成，令人尊敬，但思维都已严重滞后。没有一个能像黄佐临先生那样，依然站在国际艺术的第一线，钻研各种新兴流派，生命勃发，甚至青春烂漫。
那时候的他，变得比过去任何时候都“帅”，浑身上下都散发着一种无与伦比的光辉。
他的女儿黄蜀芹导演说，一位中年的前苏联女学者尼娜告诉她：“哎呀，我简直是爱上你爸爸了，很少见到像他这样高贵、有气质的！”尼娜看来是真的爱上了，因此到处对别人这样宣称，终于传到了黄佐临先生耳朵里。他回应道：“那好啊，中苏友好有指望了！”
老年男子变“帅”，一定是进入了一个足以归结一生的美好创造过程。
我在《霜冷长河》一书中对“老年是诗的年岁”的判断，主要来自于对他的长期观察。
当时，我的每一部学术著作出版，他都会在很短时间内读完。我曾经估计，他可能更能接受我的《世界戏剧学》、《中国戏剧史》这样的书，却未必能首肯《观众心理学》（初版名《戏剧审美心理学》）。因为《观众心理学》几乎否认了自古以来一系列最权威的艺术教条，只从观众接受心理上寻找创作规则。这对前辈艺术家来说，有一种颠覆性的破坏力。没想到，这部书出版才一个月，他的女儿交给我一封他写的长信。
他在信里快乐地说：“读完那本书才知道，自己一辈子都在摸索着观众心理学。这情景，莫里哀在《贵人迷》里已经写到，那个一心想做贵族的土人花钱请老师来教文学，知道不押韵的文章叫散文，终于惊叹道：原来我从小天天都在讲散文！”
他说：“我就是那个土人，不小心符合了观众心理学。”然后，他又在几个艺术关节上与我作了详尽探讨。
这样的老者太有魅力了，我怎么能不尽量与他多交往呢？
他也愿意与我在一起。就连家里来了外国艺术家，或别人送来了螃蟹什么的，他都会邀我去吃饭。他终于在餐桌上知道我能做菜，而且做得不错，就一再鼓动我开一个“余教授餐厅”，专供上海文化界。他替我“坐堂”一星期，看生意好不好，如果不太好，他再坐下去。
后来，他又兴致勃勃地给我讲过一个新构思的“戏剧巡游计划”。选二十台最好的戏，安排在二十辆大货车上做片段演出，一个城市、一个城市轮着走。他每次讲这个计划的时候，都会激动得满脸通红。
他说，剧场是死的，车是活的，古希腊没有机动车，我们现在有了，以前欧洲不少城市也这么做过。但是，当我一泼冷水，说根本选不出“二十台最好的戏”，他想一想，点了点头，也就苦恼了。这个过程多次重复，使我相信，大艺术家就是孩子。
交往再多，真正的“紧密合作”却只有一次，时间倒是不短。
那是上世纪八十年代中期的事吧，上海文化界也开始要评“职称”了。这是一件要打破头的麻烦事，官员们都不敢涉足。其实他们自己也想参评，于是要找两个能够“摆得平”的人来主事。这两个人，就是黄佐临先生和我。
经过多方协调，他和我一起被任命为“上海文化界高级职称评审委员会”的“双主任”。我说，不能“双主任”，只能由黄佐临先生挂帅，我做副主任。但黄佐临先生解释说，他也是文化界中人，而我则可以算是教育界的，又在负责评审各大学的文科教授，说起来比较客观。因此，“双主任”是他的提议。
在评审过程中，黄佐临先生的品格充分展现。他表面上讲话很少，心里却什么都明白。
例如，对于一九四九年之后历次政治运动中的“整人干将”，不管官职多高，名声多大，他都不赞成给予高级职称。有一个从延安时代过来的“院长”，很老的资格，不小的官职，也来申报。按惯例，必然通过，但评审委员会的诸多委员们沉默了。黄佐临先生在讨论时只用《哈姆雷特》式的台词轻轻说了一句：“搞作品，还是搞人？这是个问题。”过后投票，没有通过。
上海文化界不大，有资格申报高级职称的人，大家都认识。对于其中那些“文革”中的造反派首领和积极分子，怎么办？黄佐临先生说：“我们不是政治审查者，只评业务。但是，艺术怎么离得开人格？”
我跟着说：“如果痛改前非，业务上又很强，今后也可以考虑。但现在，观察的时间还不够。”因此，这样的人在我们评的第一届，都没有上去。
对于“革命样板戏”剧团的演员，黄佐临先生觉得也不必急着评，以后再说。“那十年的极度风光，责任不在他们。但他们应该知道，当时他们的同行们在受着什么样的煎熬，不能装作没看见。”他说。
对于地方戏曲的从业人员，黄佐临先生和我都主张不能在职称评定上给予特殊照顾。他认为，这些名演员已经拥有不少荣誉，不能什么都要。这是评定职称，必须衡量文化水准和创新等级。
我则认为，上海的地方戏曲在整体上水准不高，在风格上缺少力度。那些所谓“流派”，只是当年一些年轻艺人的个人演唱特点，其中有不少是缺点。如果我们的认识乱了，今后就会越来越乱，说不定会把缺点当作“遗产”来继承。
那年月，文化理智明晰，艺术高低清楚，实在让人怀念。出乎意料的是，当时被我们搁置的那些人，现在有不少已经上升为“艺术泰斗”、“城市脊梁”。我估计，黄佐临先生的在天之灵又在朗诵《哈姆雷特》了：
“泰斗，还是太逗？这是个问题。”
“脊梁，还是伎俩？这又是个问题。”
就在那次职称评定后不久，国家文化部在我所在的上海戏剧学院经过三次“民意测验”，我均排名第一，便顺势任命我出任院长。
黄佐临先生听说后，立即向媒体发表了那著名的四字感叹：可喜，可惜！
上海电视台的记者祁鸣问他：“何谓可喜？”
他说：“‘文革’十年，把人与人的关系都撕烂了。这位老兄能在十年后获得本单位三次民意测验第一，绝无仅有，实在可喜。文化部总算尊重民意了，也算可喜。”
记者又问：“何谓可惜？”
他说：“这是一个不小的行政职务，正厅级，但只适合那些懂一点艺术又不是太懂、懂一点理论又不是太懂的人来做。这位老兄在艺术和学术上的双重天分，耗在行政上，还不可惜？”
他的这些谈话，当时通过报纸广为流传。他称我“老兄”，其实我比他小了整整四十岁。但我已经没有时间与他开玩笑了，连犹豫的空间也不存在，必须走马上任，一耗六年。
这六年，我不断地重温着“可喜，可惜”这四个字。时间一久，后面这两个字的分量渐渐加重，成了引导我必然辞职的咒语。
六年过去，终于辞职成功。那一年，他已经八十五岁了；而我，也已经四十五岁。

sections.label: 六
paragraphs: 原以为辞职会带来轻松，我可以在长烟大漠间远行千里了。但实际情况并非如此。上海，从一些奇怪的角落伸出了一双双手，把我拽住了。
这是怎么回事？
原来上海一些文人聪明，想在社会大转型中通过颠覆名人来让自己成名。但他们又胆小，不敢触碰有权的名人。于是，等我一辞职，“有名无权”了，就成了他们的目标。正好，在职称评定中被我签字否决的申报者，也找到了吐一口气的机会。于是，我被大规模“围啄”。
我这个人什么也不怕，却为中国文化担忧起来。我们以前多少年的黑夜寻火、鞭下搏斗，不就是争取一种健康的文化环境吗，怎么结果是这样？
那天，我走进宿舍，在门房取出一些信件。其中有一封特别厚，我就拿起来看是谁寄来的。
一看就紧张了。寄自华东医院东楼的一张病床，而那字迹，我是那么熟悉！
这才想到，黄佐临先生住在医院里。我去探望过，却又有很长时间没去了。
赶快回家，关门，坐下，打开那封厚厚的信。
于是，我读到了——
秋雨：
去年有一天，作曲家沈立群教授兴致勃勃地跑到我家，上气不接下气地告诉我，有精品出现了！她刚从合肥回来，放下行李便跑来通报这个喜讯。她说最后一场戏，马兰哭得唱不下去了，在观众席看彩排的省委领导人哭得也看不下去了，而这场戏则是你老兄开了个通宵赶写出来的。
我听了高兴得不得了。兴奋之余，我与沈立群教授的话题便转到了我国今后歌剧的发展上来。沈说，京、昆音乐结构太严谨，给作曲家许多束缚，而黄梅戏的音乐本身就很优美，而且又给予作曲家许多发挥余地。今后我国新歌剧，应从这个剧种攻克。
对种种“风波”，时有所闻，也十分注意。倒不是担心你老兄——树大必招风，风过树还在；我发愁的乃是当前中国文化界的风气。好不容易出现一二部绝顶好作品，为什么总是跟着“风波”？真是令人痛心不已。
对于你老兄，我只有三句话相赠。这三句话，来自我的老师萧伯纳。一九三七年“七七事变”后三天我去他公寓辞别，亲眼看到他在壁炉上镌刻着的三句话：
他们骂啦，
骂些什么？
让他们骂去！
你能说他真的不在乎骂吗？不见得，否则为什么还要镌刻在壁炉上头呢？我认为，这只说明这个怪老头子有足够的自信力罢了。
所以我希望你老兄不要（当然也不至于）受种种“风波”的干扰。集中精力从事文化考察和写作，那才是真正的文化。
我这次住院，已经三个月了。原来CT后发现脑血管有黑点，经过三个疗程吊液后，已觉得好些。但目前主要矛盾是心脏（早搏、房颤），仍在治疗中。今年已经八十七岁，然而还不知老之将至，还幻想着要写一部书《世界最好的戏剧从来就是写意的》。你说，太“自不量力”不？
祝你考察和写作顺利。
佐临
华东医院东楼十五楼十六床
一九九三年五月二十一日
需要说明的是，他引用萧伯纳壁炉上的三句话，在信上是先写英文，再译成中文的。三句英文为：
They？have？said.
What said they？
Let？them？say！
这立即让我想到五十六年前他离开萧伯纳寓所时的情景，他在新加坡给我描述过。
几句话，漂洋过海，历尽沧桑，居然又被一个病榻上的老者捡起，颤颤巍巍地写给了我。我，承接得那么沉重，又突然感到喜悦。
Let them say！
这句简短的英文，成了我后来渡过重重黑水的木筏。从此，一路上变得高兴起来，因为这个木筏的打造者和赠送者，是萧伯纳和黄佐临。他们都是喜剧中人，笑得那么灿烂。
黄佐临先生在写完这封信的第二年，就去世了。
站在他的人生句号上一点点回想，谁都会发现，他这一生，实在精彩。
你看，我们不妨再归纳几句：
“七七事变”后第三天告别萧伯纳“赴国难”；
在国难中开创上海戏剧和中国戏剧的黄金时代；
二十年后，在另一番艰难岁月中发表了世界三大戏剧观的宏伟高论，震动国际；
等灾难过去，北上京城，在剧场里拷问知识分子的心灵；
最后，展开一个童心未泯、又万人钦慕的高贵晚年……
我想不出，在他之前或之后，还有哪一位中国艺术巨匠，拥有这么完满而美好的人生。
对他，我知道不能仅仅表达个人化的感谢。他让中国戏剧、中国艺术、中国文化、中国人，多了一份骄傲的理由。他是一座伟岸的高峰，让磕磕绊绊的中华现代文化大船，多了一支桅杆。这支桅杆，栉风沐雨，直指云天，远近都能看见。
现在，很多人已经不知道他的名字了，这不是他的遗憾。
我听从他的遗言，从来不对别人的说三道四稍作辩驳。但是，前两年，纪念中国话剧一百周年，几乎所有的文章都没有提黄佐临的名字，大家只把纪念集中在北京人艺和《茶馆》上，我就忍不住了。当然，《茶馆》这台戏也不错，尤其是第一场和最后结尾更好一点。但是，这可是纪念百年的风云史诗啊，怎么可以这样！
我终于写了文章，说：“看到一部丢失了黄佐临的中国话剧史，连焦菊隐、曹禺、田汉、老舍的在天之灵都会惊慌失措。历史就像一件旧家具，抽掉了一个重要环扣就会全盘散架。”
对不起，黄佐临先生，这一次我没有尊重您的遗言：Let them say！

sections.label: I
paragraphs: JULY 10, 1937. The house of George Bernard Shaw. More than two weeks later was Shaw’s eighty-first birthday. In those days, lots of people came for congratulations in advance, and he was annoyed.

As early as twelve years ago, when he had won the Nobel Prize, he had complained that the prize came late. He could often not find any help during his hardest time, but when he no longer wanted to strive again, the prize came.
“Until now, I’ve been struggling to the other side—now you throw the life buoy,” he said.
Obviously, then, he felt that “the other side” had been reached, and the end of his life was near.

However, who could imagine that twelve years would pass from then on, and he could also celebrate his birthday, without any sign of leaving the world. He liked to laugh at himself and felt that the balance of life he stole was too long; even he himself was embarrassed by it.
What was more, it was during his long stage of “life balance” he stole that he won the most respect.

At that point he seemed to have high prestige, and every corner of society was proud of bothering him. He tried to put them off, but some requests were difficult to refuse, for example, for donations. He was not stingy, and had already donated all 80,000 pounds gained from the Nobel Prize for literature to Sweden’s poor writers. However, he did not like someone to convey a bit of moral blackmail in it. In this regard, he wanted to clarify his position.

Exactly, one women’s association wrote a letter and asked him for a donation, with a very specific amount. Shaw replied immediately, saying that he knew nothing about the event, and was not interested in it, so he would not donate.

After the reply, he thought that no matter what you said, it was okay. He did not expect to receive their letter of thanks in a few days, which said they had auctioned off his letter, and the funds they got greatly exceeded the number they originally requested.
“I was involved, finally,” he shrugged.
As for various persons coming to his home directly, the servants rightly blocked them out. Therefore, the house was a bit quiet.
However, he heard the bell ring, and somebody entered. Soon the servant reported: “Mr. Huang from China, whom you agreed to receive, has come.”

Mr. Huang was Huang Zuolin, who had studied business in the United Kingdom in 1925, but soon learned drama through George Bernard Shaw and created Substance and Chinese Tea, which were appreciated by Shaw very much. Huang Zuolin had returned to China, and then went to the United Kingdom again with his wife two years earlier to study Shakespeare in the Imperial College, University of Cambridge, and learn directing in the London Academy of Dramatic Art. Currently he would probably be in his early thirties. It was a bit sudden for Shaw, this anxious meeting, but he quickly guessed the reason.

According to his experience, this student did not come to wish him a happy birthday. It would be associated with an event: in this case the Times had reported that Japan had officially triggered the war of aggression against China three days earlier, on July 7.

Shaw thought that if China and Japan fought a battle, Huang’s motherland would become a battlefield and he could never go back, so Mr. Huang might ask him if he could help him obtain a job in the United Kingdom for permanent residence. Of course, it would be better if it were theater work.
While thinking about that, Shaw went into the living room. He saw that this young man was looking at the sentence inscribed in the fireplace, which was a quotation from Shaw.
Immediately after Huang Zuolin heard footsteps, he came back and said hello to his teacher George Bernard Shaw.
Sitting down, Shaw immediately started: “I know what happened on July 7.”
“So, I come and say farewell to you,” Huang Zuolin said.
“Farewell? Where will you go?” George Bernard Shaw was very surprised.
“My motherland,” Huang Zuolin said.
“Your motherland?” Shaw was even more surprised, paused, and said, “There has been a battle, and the war will be worse and worse. You’re not a general, nor a soldier; why do you go back?”

Huang Zuolin was unable to explain a heavy concept of Chinese culture in English: “Defend the country.” He would only say: “Most of our Chinese people will go back once encountering this sort of thing. I am not a general, but I am a soldier.”
Shaw looked at Huang Zuolin, and did not speak for quite a while.

“What can I help you with then?” Shaw asked. “I had made a statement about what happened in China yesterday. I was there four years ago, know Soong Chingling, Lin Yutang, and their English is good. I also saw a lesser-known writer, Lu Xun.”
Huang Zuolin nodded and said: “I may not come back this time. Could you write me a few words again like last time?”
“The last time?” Shaw apparently had forgotten it.

“The last time, you wrote: Ibsen is not Ibsen-style, he is Henrik Ibsen; I’m not Shaw-style, I am George Bernard Shaw; if Mr. Huang wants to accomplish something, do not be the disciple of anyone, you must be original.” Huang Zuolin recited those few words.
“I remember!” Shaw laughed. “That is what I said.”
While speaking, Huang Zuolin had opened a new autograph book and placed it in front of Shaw, saying: “Give me a lifetime souvenir.”
Picking up his pen, raising his head, and thinking for a while, Shaw began to write. Huang Zuolin went behind him.
The first sentence George Bernard Shaw wrote was: “Come on, China! The future of the Eastern world is yours.”
After that, he turned to take a look at Huang Zuolin. Huang Zuolin was touched deeply and nodded. On the third day of the “Marco Polo Bridge Incident,” this sentence would move all the Chinese.
George Bernard Shaw continued: “If you have the willpower and courage, then it will be the Chinese Opera that makes the event much more spectacular in the future.”
Huang Zuolin made a bow to Shaw, put the autograph book away, and then left.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: THE ABOVE SCENE WAS TOLD in Singapore by Mr. Huang Zuolin when he was eighty. At that time I was lecturing at Singapore; an international theater workshop was being held there. Representatives participating in the preparatory events heard that the most authoritative of Asian drama masters Huang Zuolin, the disciple of George Bernard Shaw, was still alive, and so they boldly attempted to invite him to participate. This was just a fantasy, but if it became true, the seminar would have remarkable import.

The famous Singaporean dramatist Kuo Pao Kun made a special trip to Shanghai for personal invitation and arrangement. Some dramatists from several countries had also repeatedly knocked at my apartment door, hoping I could promote it a little.
They were right, because I was his “cross-age friend.” To this end, I talked with Mr. Huang Zuolin long distance. He said he hesitated slightly, not because of his body, but its “inner strength.”
I said, “It has been tested, come on.” He came accompanied by his daughter Huang Xiaoqin.
This sent shockwaves through the International Conference, also being held in Singapore.
The Singapore foreign minister visited him respectfully and asked: “When did you last come to Singapore?”
Mr. Huang Zuolin replied, “Sixty years ago.”
The foreign minister was very young, and he heard “sixty years ago” as “1960s.” This made him feel very far away, saying: “Nineteen sixties? Over twenty years ago, that’s too long!”
Mr. Huang Zuolin smiled and said, “Please push that back again forty years.”
The minister was confused, but thought the old man was the one confused. I then explained: “Mr. Huang went to the United Kingdom for study in 1925, passing through Singapore.”
“Sixty years ago?” The minister finally figured it out, but got scared actually.

I went on saying: “He went to the United Kingdom and studied with George Bernard Shaw. At that time, the writer had just been awarded the Nobel Prize for literature. When they said farewell, Shaw was eighty-one years old.”

The minister was still a bit confused. It was my intention, since Singapore official discourse is always too rigid, to make the conversation livelier. Even though the contents of what I threw out were, after all, correct.

Mr. Huang Zuolin made a speech at the International Conference. When the host called his name, the audience rose to applaud. He ascended to the podium, tall, with silver-white hair and robust carriage, manifesting a world-class elegance.

He began the lecture with standard London English, not very fast, but employing elegant words, with mildly humorous elements, mellow timbre, and gentle majesty. The auditorium grew silent, as if listening to instructions from heaven.

In high academic culture circles, people value the speaker himself but not his nationality. Those famous cultural giants in the West: we all knew their works, schools, and views, but often were not sure what nationality they were. For example, Mr. Huang Zuolin’s mentor, Shaw, where on earth did he come from, Ireland or Britain? Picasso was from Spain or France? Einstein? Culturally, the greatness always crossed boundaries. With this thought, I then turned around to look at the audience, and I actually found that everyone regardless of nationality had became a pious student of this elegant elder onstage. Who could believe that this elder had just returned from China’s disastrous Cultural Revolution?
Then please listen to a few words freely:
After Brecht, the absurdist drama pushed its grand philosophies into one alley after another, which seemed impassable, but were finally walked through…
He said this quietly, and the audiences recorded it carefully.

In the performance mode, please pay attention to the “poor theater” that followed the “total theater” by Gordon Craig. I also thought highly of Gradoffski. In recent years, theater anthropology has had the most academic output. Its center transferred to America from the United Kingdom and Poland. Richard Schechner from New York University discussed it well, but his experiment could not compare with Europe…

The audiences could not write things down as fast as he said them, he discovered, so he smiled and said: some terminologies and spellings of the names, I would entrust the Secretariat will distribute to you all.

Please note that theater study in the West since the end of World War II appears to be confused and messy, but it could integrate with the classical Oriental Theater, so there’s a huge potential for combination and creative space. Traditional Japanese drama was protected well, but too rigidly. China also wanted to combine tradition and innovation, but mostly there was administrative- and theory-oriented frame of mind, a lack of participation space for truly great artists. India had not been conscious…
Everyone was still working hard taking notes.

In short, this elegant elder had almost no time or space limitations. He spoke in that modern a fashion and shared professional knowledge that was not possessed even by a new generation of peer scholars in their twenties.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: THE YEAR MR. HUANG ZUOLIN SAID GOODBYE to Shaw, he went back to China, setting foot on the heavily bombed and devastated land. Finally, he settled down in Shanghai. After careful thought, he realized what he could do for the “national calamity” was still the drama.

Shanghai at that time was in a very special position. Its surroundings had been occupied by Japanese invaders, but since the inception of Shanghai, it had gradually formed an influence sphere with the United Kingdom, France, and the United States—the “concession,” Japan had not yet completely turned against these countries, so those places had become “islands.” In the “islands,” the artists who had escaped from the bloodbath got together and burst into an unprecedented level of social responsibility and creative passion. Until the outbreak of the Pacific War, when the “islands” were occupied, many works were banned, and authors were arrested, everyone still held on. Among them, Huang Zuolin was the main representative in theater circles.

Who would have thought it? Amid such great catastrophe, China ushered in its golden age of drama. Among these plays, some were united against Japan, some exposed the brutality, some criticized the darkness, and some focused on social reform and spiritual rehabilitation. Most of them explored internationalization and nationalization. Because Huang Zuolin had received excellent training in the United Kingdom, each show had a lively plot and high profile, and was embraced by a large audience. From the bits of information I had occasionally come into contact with, a not-too-important play, Inspection Commissioner, was played 77 times within 40 days. The audiences for other performances during the show were also surprising.
So many audiences crowded into the theater who were suffering distress at that time. The important mission of art was to warm the heart against those cold years.

Art must gather real energy to warm the heart. The artistic level of these performances, from the records of old artists, reached a point the descendants found difficult to surpass. To say the least, Shi Hui, the most commonly used actor by Mr. Huang Zuolin, was known as the “drama king” at that time. We can see from some of the surviving images that it might still be unsurpassable today. In addition to Shi Hui, the art team for Mr. Huang Zuolin was huge, and the list of names for each play could be very long.
Several old artists with good critical sense said: “those plays could not be better”; or “among the plays I saw in my life, those at that time had been amazing.”

This once again proved my point: the noblest art did not necessarily come from huge investment, authority concerns, and media operations, but on the contrary, often were the direct answer to a harsh environment. The best background for art is not gold but black.

Now, let’s scan the artistic achievements of Huang Zuolin at that time: Border Town Story, Small Town Story, Miaofeng Mountain, Metamorphosis, Lie Cover-Up, The True Story of Ah Q, Castaway, The Circus, The Burglar, Heroes in the Turbulent Days, Autumn, Jin Xiaoyu, Dragnet, Unchain My Heart, and Inspection Commissioner…these might actually be incomplete.

If an example were needed for art history written in the international community, that would state clearly that man can create the most wonderful art in a troubled world, I would suggest Shanghai at that time, and particularly Huang Zuolin.

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: MR. HUANG ZUOLIN finally accepted the year 1949. For the revolution, for the new regime, an artist full of romantic fantasy and with a long backlog of demands for social reform would accept almost anything without any resistance. He was active, positive, wanted to rehearse some plays for the new regime, and would not even care if it had something in it of “propaganda.”

However, something about it all made him so sad. In his later years, what he talked of most with me was those things. When talking, he was always apart from the crowd in a corner, waiting to talk for a long time. I knew it was this topic again.

In fact, his theater activities since coming back from the United Kingdom were not fully accepted by the Communist Party underground. He knew, of course, that the Communist Party underground also organized similar cultural activities, and there were also some decent intellectuals. He saw them as cultural fellows, but he himself was reluctant to engage in the political spectrum, not only in the Communist Party, but also the KMT.

I do not know how much work the Communist Party underground did in order to get him, but it seemed not to have an effect, as an underground Party member Li Delong “hid” in his troupe. Many years later, Li Delun, already a renowned music conductor, confessed: “I did not win him over; he won me by his personality and artistic charm.”

After 1949, the intellectuals of the Communist Party underground at that time of course had become the leaders of Shanghai and the national cultural circles, and they were all impressive for the long focus on “only for war, regardless of political party; only for art, not a tool.” Therefore, no matter how active he was, Huang Zuolin just regarded him as a “fellow traveler,” not “one of us.”

This way of thinking even extended to the new period after the Cultural Revolution. Many articles in the collections of historical materials, modern theater history, anti-Japanese war cultural history, and history of Shanghai have little to say about the significance of Huang Zuolin, and even belittle him in a roundabout way. Some revolutionary intellectuals we esteemed were involved.

Mr. Huang Zuolin had whispered to me: “Xia Yan is broad-minded and is nice to me. Yu Ling and his fellow soldiers, including Mr. Wang Yuanhua, the head of the propaganda department after the Cultural Revolution, adhered to those principles during their underground struggle, relatively indifferent to me.”

In addition to this history problem, he also encountered a worse environment. In Chinese drama circles after 1949, “Jiao for north and Huang for south” was commonly accepted as a slogan for directors. “Jiao for north” referred to Mr. Jiao Juyin from Beijing Art Theater. Due to the concentration of many high-profile culture intellectuals in Beijing, the cultural atmosphere was healthy; Jiao Juyin’s efforts, in collaboration with dramatists such as Lao She, Cao Yu, and Guo Moruo, yielded many fruits. “Huang for south” meant Huang Zuolin in Shanghai, but he encountered the “ultra-Left thought trend syndrome” of Ke Qingshi, the supreme leadership in Shanghai, and his capable persons in the propaganda and cultural fields Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan.
Director Xie Jin said that one time Ke Qingshi came to watch a play, but he stood up and went away with a livid face before the end, and Huang Zuolin was at a loss.

Another time, Huang Zuolin directed a drama written by a worker-author; the play was very ordinary, but the directorial approach was brilliant; unexpectedly, after an instruction by Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan immediately dictated to the newspapers: only the author was to be publicized, not the director.
Therefore, when “Jiao in north” became very famous, “Huang in south” became actually “yellow.”
After suffering injustice again and again, Huang Zuolin asked himself: “Where are these grievances coming from?” The answer: “Why do I care about politics again!”
Thus he recovered the dignity he had back in the United Kingdom. “No matter what they say, I am returning to art.”

Huang Zuolin withdrew from the public eye. Shanghai newspapers were more willing to report on Jiao Juyin in Beijing, as well as the Shaoxing Opera, Shanghai Opera, and Huai Opera, which could not be thoroughly remolded according to the guidance of Mr. Huang Zuolin.
What was the true world-class artistic master to do? What did he think? The busy streets of the city were at a loss and did not want to know.
Just then, the Great Famine, caused by political fever and natural disasters, began. Shanghai, a hungry city, was brought low.
Would such decent artistic behavior appear in the famine? No one dared to imagine.

Totally unexpectedly, on April 25, 1962, a newspaper in Beijing published a long article on “Drama” by Huang Zuolin. The topic was a bit modest, but this was a milestone in the modern world of drama. Suddenly it stood in front of people, and everyone was astonished.
The conceptual framework established in this article was not completely compatible with the local cultural realities, but it drew immediate notice from the international academic field.
It was just as if the king of lions had risen and shocked the distant mountains, but the swallows and fish did not feel it.

One should know that most of the Chinese literati at that time were still talking about class warfare. As for dramatic concepts, only the proletariat and propertied class were included, which were referred to as “flowers” and “poisonous weeds.” Therefore, these characters written in simple vernacular writings by Mr. Huang Zuolin were read like a new threshold.
Well, I could not help but look at his theoretical achievements in light of international academic standards.
First, to sum up the human drama with “illusion creation” and “illusion breaking” was a kind of high refinement, making things simple, and was a first-class academic accomplishment.
Second, to divide the inner and outer side of “illusion” by the concept of “the fourth wall” by Roline from France resulted in visual conceptual support for this precise and intense refining.
Third, to elicit Brecht and his breaking through the “illusion” and “the fourth wall” raised the “innovation function” of this German playwright to a “historical cohort function.”

Fourth, to mark three drama concepts in the twentieth century by Stanislavsky, Brecht, and Mei Lanfang, whose theories were profound and broad, broached unprecedented topics, but was still very relevant to the practice of drama. Since the day they were put forward, there has been no significant international objection.

Fifth, to transition to “freehand drama” from these three concepts was a major aesthetic move. Now it has become a universal language in theatrical circles, which is a miracle in the construction of modern literary theory.
Taking a bird’s-eye view of the world, summing up the world, and being accepted by the world, such theoretical results have always been rare.
It was April 25, 1962. This was the day that the Philosophy God and Art God both watched over China and Shanghai.
I really could not remember any aspect of all Chinese art theory, no, all of China’s culture that could surpass it for decades.
I had asked many intellectuals and theoreticians. They thought for a long time, but finally shook their heads and said: “Not one could be found.”

So, I want to remind you, two weeks after this date, on May 9, 1962, another cultural giant, Ba Jin from Shanghai, would make a statement, “Courage and Responsibility of Writers,” which sharply pointed out that the major barrier to the development of Chinese literature was the “sticks.” The practice had proved a harbinger of the Cultural Revolution disaster.
In the late spring of 1962, Shanghai was so bright. Great creativity, great discovery, great judgment, and great foresight had all appeared together.
The powerful glow is still a bit dazzling even after half a century, so now we deliberately turn a blind eye, as if no such thing had happened.

If today’s media were asked: what kind of memorable cultural figures and cultural events were worthy of remembrance in this city fifty years ago? …the answer would probably be two widely known songs, three familiar librettos, and a bunch of well-known stars. And, of course, they might list a few supposedly knowledgeable professors who did not write to express their opinions. There would be no mention of an article written by Huang Zuolin or statement by Ba Jin.

sections.label: V
paragraphs: I DID NOT WANT TO SAY ANY MORE about the sufferings of Mr. Huang Zuolin in the Cultural Revolution, for he himself did not want to say much.

I had experienced much in this respect: those who suffered the most did not want to say, those who said a lot were sure not to have suffered much, and those with high profiles had to have others suffer.

There were also differences among those who did not want to speak. In my opinion, as for the tragedy of it, Ba Jin had turned it into the sublime, while Huang Zuolin had turned it into comedy. Or rather, Ba Jin refined tragedy, while Huang Zuolin saw through it, so he laughed.

Several of his daughters had told me of his mocking of rebels during the Cultural Revolution, but they did not know they were being mocked. Several times he was present but did not get involved in the conversation, and in fact he shook his head gently.

Anyway, his ultimate thinking regarding that disaster was very serious, which was about the torture to the intellectual soul. Shortly after the Cultural Revolution, he came to Beijing and directed Brecht’s masterpiece Life of Galileo (cooperating with Chen Yong).

At that time, in order to put things right, the National Science Conference was held, so the intellectuals could have a space for forays into business, but could they establish their dignity in the spirit? Life of Galileo raised this issue in a timely way, which shocked all of Beijing.

People said that they had never seen a play that could shock the inner soul of the people at a critical moment. Additionally, this was the sequel of the “Scientific Conference,” which was just being held in the heart of national intellectualism.
“Jiao for north” had gone, “Huang for south” had come to Beijing, and the people of Beijing were surprised—he really deserved his reputation!

From Beijing to Shanghai, Mr. Huang Zuolin resolved to intensify his efforts to promote the “national theater system” based on “impressionistic drama.” He eagerly learned and explored, implementing one after another of the most advanced art experiments, and people almost forgot that he was almost eighty years old.

In those years, I had seen a lot of “surviving” senior scholars, good-natured and steady, respectable, but their thoughts were seriously lagging behind. No one could still stand at the forefront of international art like Mr. Huang Zuolin, delving into a variety of new genres, with vibrant life, even youthful romance.
At that time, he became much more “handsome” than ever, and his whole body sent out a unique radiance.

His daughter the director Huang Shuqin said a Soviet woman, a middle-aged scholar named Nina, told her: “Oh, I’m falling in love with your father. Rare is the man as noble and graceful as him!” Nina seemed to love him, really, and therefore she declared it to others, which eventually reached the ears of Mr. Huang Zuolin. He replied: “That’s good. The Sino-Soviet relationship can improve!”
The older man became “handsome,” and he entered a beautiful creative period sufficient to could conclude his whole life.
My judgment that “old age is the age of poetry” in the book Frost Cold River mainly came from my long-term observations of him.

At that time, he would read each of my academic works in a very short time. I once estimated that he might be more receptive to my World Theater, A History of Chinese Drama, and the like, but might not approve of Audience Psychology (the name for the first edition was Drama Aesthetic Psychology). Because Audience Psychology almost denied a series of the most authoritative art doctrines in history, only to find its principles for creation in the psychology of audience acceptance, which bore a kind of subversive destructive power for senior artists. Unexpectedly, one month after this book was published, his daughter handed me a long letter he wrote.

He happily said in his letter: “After reading this book, I know I have groped toward crowd psychology all my life. In The Would-Be Gentleman, Molière had already written how was a native person who wanted to be noble invited teachers to teach literature and knew that the writing without rhyme was called prose. Finally he exclaimed: I’ve been speaking prose every day!”
He said, “I am the native, and accidentally satisfy audience psychology.” Then he had made a detailed discussion on some art points.
This old man was too attractive; how could I not try my best to interact with him much?

He was also willing to stay with me. Even the foreign artists came, or someone else sent crabs or some other dish, and he would invite me for dinner. He finally knew I could cook at the dinner table, and did a good job, so he repeatedly urged me to open a “Professor Yu Restaurant,” dedicated to Shanghai culture circles. He “came” every day for a week, and if the business was not very good, he continued coming every day.

Later, he cheerfully told me a new idea of “play parade plan.” Twenty of the best dramas were selected and arranged in twenty large trucks for performance in one city and another. Each time he told me of this plan, he flushed with excitement.

He said that theater was dead, but the truck was alive; ancient Greece had no motor vehicles, but we now did, and this had been done in many European cities before. However, when I threw cold water on it, that there could be no “twenty best dramas” simply by choice, he thought for a moment, nodded his head, and was distressed. This process was repeated many times, which made me believe that great artists are children.
Even when our contacts were more frequent, the real “close cooperation” occurred only once.

That was in the mid-1980s. Shanghai cultural circles had also begun to comment on “title.” This was very troublesome, and officials were afraid to set foot in these matters. But they wanted to participate by finding two persons who could deal with them. These two were Mr. Huang Zuolin and me.

After multilateral coordination, we two were together named “dual directors” of “Shanghai Culture Senior Title Review Board.” I said the “dual directorship” could not be implemented, could only be led by Mr. Huang Zuolin, and I would take the deputy directorship. But Mr. Huang Zuolin explained that he was in cultural circles, while I could be viewed as in educational circles, and also was responsible for the review of the professors of liberal arts at the university, and so could be relatively objective. Thus the “dual directors” proposal was his.
During the review, Mr. Huang Zuolin showed his character sufficiently. He spoke rarely, but understood everything in his heart.

For example, regarding the so-called “tricky brains” in previous political campaigns after 1949, no matter how high their ranks and fames, he was not in favor of giving senior titles. A “president” from the Yan’an times, very old, eligible, and of high rank, also came for his declaration. As a general rule, his would be passed, but many members were silent. During discussion, Mr. Huang Zuolin only said, gently echoing Hamlet: “Work creation or people’s trickery, that is the question?” After the voting, he was not approved.

The Shanghai cultural circle was small, and the people eligible to declare senior titles were known by everyone. As for the rebel leaders and activists in the Cultural Revolution, what could we do? Mr. Huang Zuolin said: “We are not political censors, only doing our jobs. However, how is the art separated from the personality?”

I said, “If they repent past mistakes, and their business capability is very strong, we can also consider that in the future. But for now, enough time for observation has not passed.” As a result, such people in our first review were all not approved.

As for the actors in the “revolutionary model opera,” Mr. Huang Zuolin felt that there was no need to review them now. “They were not to blame for the extreme views of that decade. But they should know that when their peers are suffering, they cannot pretend not to see,” he said.

For the employees in local dramas, Mr. Huang Zuolin and I advocated they could not be given special care in professional evaluations. In his view, these actors had already had many honors, and they could not have everything. This was the evaluation of professional titles, so cultural standards and innovation levels had to be weighed.

In my view, the overall level of Shanghai local drama was not high, and the style was lacking. The so-called “genres” were only the individual performance characteristics of some young artists, and some of those were actually shortcomings. If our thinking was disorderly, it would be more and more disorderly in the future, and might become our “heritage.”

In those days, the cultural reasoning was clear, the art level could be distinguished, and we still missed it. Unexpectedly, many intellectuals we did not consider at that time had already been upgraded to “art masters,” the “city backbone.” I thought the soul of Mr. Huang Zuolin was reciting Hamlet again:
“Mastery or silliness? That is the question.”
“Backbone or trick? That is the question.”
Shortly after the professional evaluation, the National Ministry of Culture implemented three “polls” at the Shanghai Theater Academy. I was ranked first each time, so I was named president.
After hearing this, Mr. Huang Zuolin issued famous words to the media immediately: “gratifying, and unfortunate!”
The reporter from Shanghai TV Qi Ming asked him: “What is gratifying?”

He said, “Ten years of ‘Cultural Revolution’ had torn human relationships. After ten years, this guy is the only one to rank in the first place in the three polls. It is indeed heartening. The Ministry of Culture finally respects the public opinion, and it is all heartening.”
The reporter asked again, “What is unfortunate?”

He said, “This is a great administrative position, department level, but only suitable for those who know something of art but do not quite understand, who know a bit of theory, but are not sure enough. This guy doubles artistic and academic talent, so it is wasted on administration, isn’t it?”

His talk was widely circulated via newspapers. He called me “kiddo,” but in fact I was forty years younger than him. But I had no time to joke with him, and even no room for hesitation, for I had to assume the office, and that lasted six years.
For six years I kept pondering “gratifying, unfortunate.” As time went by, the latter word weighed much more significantly, which became a guiding mantra: I must resign.
Six years later, I finally quit. He was already eighty-five years old, while I was forty-five.

sections.label: VI
paragraphs: I ORIGINALLY THOUGHT THE RESIGNATION would bring ease and I could travel thousands of miles of desert. But this was not the case. Shanghai grabbed me with a pair of hands stretching out from some strange corners.
What was going on?

Actually, some of the Shanghai literati were smart, and wanted to become famous via the subversion of the celebrated in the transformation of society. However, they were timid and dared not touch those with power. So I was famous but without power after resignation, and therefore became their target. Now the declarers rejected by me in the evaluation of professional titles would have a chance to blow off steam. So I was massively “surrounded and pecked.”

I was afraid of nothing, but worried about Chinese culture. We had encountered fire at night, whipped and wrestled with it for many years, which was just to strive for a healthy cultural environment, and the result was this?
On that day, I went into the dormitory and took out some letters from the porter. One of them was particularly thick, and I picked it up to see who it was from.
I was nervous. It was from a hospital bed in the east building of Huadong Hospital, and the handwriting was so familiar to me!
I assumed Mr. Huang Zuolin was in the hospital. I once went to visit him, but had not gone for a long time.
I hurried home, closed the door, sat down, and opened the thick letter.
So, I began to read:
Qiuyu:

One day last year, the composer and professor Shen Liqun cheerfully came to my house and breathlessly told me: she had quality work! She had just come back from Hefei, and ran to share the happy news after putting down her luggage. She said that the last scene could not even be sung anymore because Malan had cried so much, and the provincial leaders watching the rehearsal also cried profusely. This was the play you wrote so hurriedly all night long.

I was thrilled. Besides the excitement, Professor Shen Liqun and I began to talk about the development of Chinese opera in the future. Shen said the Beijing and Kun Operas had stringent musical structures, which constrained the composers very much, but Huangmei Opera music was very beautiful, and the composers were given lots of room for development. China’s new opera in the future could derive from this kind of drama.

All kinds of “disturbances” have been heard and noticed by me. I am not worried about you—a tall tree catches the wind, but the tree is still there after the wind; what I worry about is China’s current cultural atmosphere currently. It is so difficult to put forth even one or two extremely good works—then why follow it with “disturbance”? It is painful really.

For you, I only have three sentences, which are from my teacher, George Bernard Shaw. Three days after the “Marco Polo Bridge Incident” in 1937, I went to his apartment for farewell, and saw these words engraved over the fireplace:
They have said.
What said they?
Let them say.
Can you say he does not care? Not likely; otherwise why would he engrave it above the fireplace? I think this only shows that the strange old man had plenty of confidence.
So I hope you aren’t (or are undeservedly) disturbed by them. Focus on the literary investigation and writing, which is the real culture.

I am hospitalized for three months. CT scans showed a black spot in my cerebral vascular system, and I feel better after three courses of infusion. But the principal problem is in the heart (premature beats, and atrial fibrillation), and I am still under treatment. This year I am eighty-seven years old, but I still dream of writing a book, The Best Drama in the World Has Always Been Impressionistic. I always overestimate myself?
May your investigations and writing succeed!
Zuolin
No.16, Building 15, East Building of Huadong Hospital

It was necessary to point out that these three lines he quoted in the fireplace of George Bernard Shaw were in English at first, and then translated into Chinese. The three lines of English were as follows:
They have said.
What said they?
Let them say.
This immediately made me think of fifty-six years ago when he left the home of George Bernard Shaw, which he had described to me in Singapore.
A few words, across the sea, out of great suffering, were finally picked up by an old man on his sickbed, and written to me in trembling hand. I undertook them so heavily, and suddenly felt joyful.
Let them say.

This brief English phrase became a raft for crossing through a lot of dark waters later. Along the way I became happy again, due to the makers and presenters of this raft, separately George Bernard Shaw and Huang Zuolin. They were writers of comedy, smiling so brightly.
Mr. Huang Zuolin died in the second year after writing this letter.
Reflecting and recalling this man little by little at the end of his life, everyone would discover that his life was truly wonderful.
We now sum it up in a few words:
On the third day of the “Marco Polo Bridge Incident,” he said goodbye to George Bernard Shaw, and cited “defense of the country”;
He created the golden age of Shanghai drama and national drama in China;
Twenty years later, he published a significant speech on three plays from other tough years, shaking the world;
After the disasters, he went to Beijing and tortured the hearts of intellectuals in the theater;
Finally, he developed a noble sunset style with a playful spirit to people’s admiration…
I could not think of another Chinese artistic master before or after him who had such a complete and happy life.

To him, I knew I could not just express personal gratitude. He gave reason for pride to Chinese opera, Chinese art, Chinese culture, and the Chinese people. He stalwartly provided one more mast for the ship of modern Chinese culture. This mast suffered great winds and rain, but was always pointing to the sky, visible far and near.
Now a lot of people did not know his name, but that was not for him to regret.

I listened to his last words, and never disputed comments by any of the others. However, two years ago, on the hundredth anniversary of Chinese drama, when almost no article mentioned Huang Zuolin, but only concentrated on the memorial in Beijing people’s art theatre and Teahouse, I could not help it. Of course, this show Teahouse was also good, especially the first and last acts. However, this was an epic commemoration of centuries, how could you pick this!

I finally wrote an article stating: “As for the Chinese drama history without Huang Zuolin, even the souls of Jiao Juyin, Cao Yu, Tian Han, and Lao She would be in a panic. History is like a piece of old furniture; the removal of a key piece will make the furniture fall apart.”
Let them say?
I was sorry, Mr. Huang Zuolin, but this time I did not respect your words: “Let them say!”

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 二十世纪末，最后那个冬天。我考察人类古文明四万公里，已由中东抵达南亚、中亚之间。处处枪口，步步恐怖，生命悬于一线。
那天晚上，在巴基斯坦、阿富汗边境，身边一个伙伴接到长途电话。然后轻声告诉我，国内有一个也姓余的北大学生，这两天发表文章，指控我在“文革”时期参加过一个黑帮组织，叫石什么。
“石什么？”我追问。
“没听清，电话断了。”伙伴看我一眼，说，“胡诌吧，那个时候，怎么会有黑帮组织，何况是您……”
还没说完，几个持枪的男人走近了我们。那是这里的黑帮组织。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 终于活着回来了。
各国的邀请函件多如雪片，要我在世纪之交去演讲亲眼所见的世界，尤其是恐怖主义日渐猖獗的情况。
但在国内，多数报纸都在炒作那个北大学生的指控。我也弄清楚了，他是说我在“文革”中参加过一个叫“石一歌”的写作组，没说是黑帮组织，却加了一顶顶令人惊悚的大帽子。
“石一歌？”
这我知道，那是周恩来总理的事儿。

我在《四十年前》一文中写过，一九七一年十月，周恩来着手收拾“文革”的烂摊子，到上海启动文化重建，第一步是强令各大学复课。由于那年正好是鲁迅诞辰九十周年、逝世三十五周年，他要求中文系复课先以鲁迅作品为教材，写鲁迅传记，研究鲁迅。于是，上海先后成立了两个组，一是设在复旦大学的《鲁迅传》编写小组，二是设在作家协会的鲁迅研究小组，都从各个高校抽人参加。我被抽去参加过前一个小组，半途离开。“石一歌”，是后一个小组的名字。
我不清楚的是，这后一个小组究竟是什么时候成立的，有哪些人参加，写过哪一些研究鲁迅的文章。
我更不清楚的是，“石一歌”怎么突然变成了一个恶名，而且堆到了我头上，引起那么多报刊的声讨？
估计有人指挥，又契合了世纪之交的文化颠覆狂潮。
按照常理，我应该把事情讲清楚。但是，遇到了三大困难——
一、狂潮既起，自己必然百口莫辩，只能借助法律，但这实在太耗时间了。我考察人类各大文明得出的结论，尤其是对世界性恐怖主义的提醒，必须快速到各国发表，决不能因为个人的名誉而妨碍大事。
二、狂潮既起，真正“石一歌”小组的成员哪里还敢站出来说明？他们大多是年迈的退休教授，已经没有体力与那些人辩论。我如果要想撇清自己，免不了要调查和公布那个小组成员的名单，这又会伤着那些老人。
三、要把这件事情讲清楚，最后只能揭开真相：那两个小组都是根据周恩来总理的指示成立的。但这样一来，就会从政治上对那个北大学生带来某种终身性的伤害。其实周恩来启动文化重建的时候，他还是牙牙学语的孩童，现在只是受人唆使罢了。这一想，又心疼了。
于是，我放弃自辩，打点行李，应邀到各地讲述《各大文明的当代困境》。但是，不管是在我国台湾、日本、马来西亚，还是在美国、法国、匈牙利，前来听讲的华文读者都会问我“石一歌”的事情。
原来，围绕着这古怪的三个字，国内媒体如《南方周末》、《文学报》等等已经闹得风声鹤唳。各国读者都以为我是逃出去的，两位住在南非的读者还一次次转弯抹角带来好意：“到我们这儿来吧，离他们远，很安静……”
冒领其名几万里，我自己也越来越好奇，很想知道这三个字背后的内容。但是，那么多文章虽然口气狞厉，却没有一篇告诉我这三个字做过什么。
时间一长，我只是渐渐知道，发起这一事件的，姓孙，一个被我否决了职称申请的上海文人；闹得最大的，姓古，一个曾经竭力歌颂我而被我拒绝了的湖北文人；后期加入的，姓沙，一个被我救过命，却又在关键时刻发表极左言论被我宣布绝交的上海文人。其他人，再多，也只是起哄而已。
他们这三个老男人，再加上那个学生，怎么闹出了这么大的局面？当然是因为传媒。

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 好奇心是压抑不住的。
虽然我不清楚“石一歌”小组的全部成员，却也知道几个。我很想找到其中一两个聊聊天，请他们告诉我，这个鲁迅研究小组成立后究竟写过什么文章。
可惜，“石一歌”小组集中发表文章的时候，我都隐藏在浙江山区，没有读到过。记得有一次下山觅食，在小镇的一个阅报栏里看到一篇署有这个名字的文章，但看了两行发现是当时的流行套话，没再看下去。因此现在很想略作了解，也好为那些担惊受怕的退休教授们说几句话。
那次我从台湾回上海，便打电话给一位肯定参加过这个组的退休教授。教授不在家，是他太太接的电话。
我问：那个小组到底是什么时候成立的？当时有哪些成员？
没想到，教授太太在电话里用哀求的声音对我说：“那么多报刊，批判成这样，已经说不清。我家老头很脆弱，又有严重高血压，余先生，只能让您受委屈了。”
我听了心里一哆嗦，连忙安慰几句，就挂了电话，并为这个电话深感后悔。这对老年夫妻，可能又要紧张好几天了。
这条路断了，只能另找新路。
但是，寻“石”之路，并不好找。
要不，从进攻者的方向试试？
终于，想出了一个好主意。
我在报刊上发表了一个“悬赏”，堂而皇之地宣布：那几个进攻者只要出示证据，证明我曾经用“石一歌”的署名写过一篇、一段、一节、一行、一句他们指控的那种文章，我立即支付自己的全年薪金，并把那个证据在全国媒体上公开发表。同时，我还公布了处理这一“悬赏”的律师姓名。
这个“悬赏”的好处，一是不伤害“石一歌”，二是不伤害进攻者。为了做到这两点，我真是花了不少心思。

《南方周末》没有回应我的“悬赏”，却于二○○四年发表了一张据说是我与“石一歌”成员在一起的照片，照片上除了我还有两个人，其中一个就是那个姓孙的发动者。照片一发，《南方周末》就把“石一歌”的话题绕开，转而声言，这个姓孙的人“清查”过我的“文革问题”。于是，又根据他提供的“材料”进行“调查”，整整用了好几个版面，洋洋洒洒地发表。虽然也没有“调查”出我有什么问题，但是，读者总是粗心的，只是强烈地留下了我既被“清查”又被“调查”的负面影响，随着该报一百多万份的发行量，覆盖海内外。
寻“石”之路，居然通到了这么一个险恶的大场面。
按照中国的惯例，“喉舌”撑出了如此架势，那就是“定案”，而且是“铁案”。
但是，在英国《世界新闻报》出事之后，我觉得有必要向《南方周末》的社长请教一些具体问题。
这些问题，当初我曾反复询问过该报的编辑记者，他们只是简单应付几句，不再理会。据我所知，也有不少读者去质问过，其中包括一些法律界人士，该报也都不予回答。但是，今天我还是要劝你，尊敬的社长，再忙，也要听一听我下面提出的这些有趣问题。

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 第一个问题：贵报反复肯定那个孙某人的“清查”，那么请问，是谁指派他的？指派者属于什么机构？为什么指派他？他当时是什么职业？有工作单位吗？
第二个问题：如果真的进行过什么“清查”，这个人怎么会把“材料”放在自己家里？他是档案馆馆长吗？是人事局局长吗？如果是档案馆馆长或人事局局长，就能截留和私藏这些档案材料吗？
第三个问题：他如果藏有我的“材料”，当然也一定藏有别人的“材料”，那么，“别人”的范围有多大？他家里的“档案室”有多大？
第四个问题：这些“材料”放在他家里，按照他所说的时间，应该有二十七年了。这么长的时间，是谁管理的？是他一人，还是他家里人也参加了管理？有保险箱吗？几个保险箱？钥匙由谁保管？
第五个问题：我在上世纪八十年代担任高校领导很多年，级别是正厅级，当时上级机关考察和审查官员的主要标准，恰恰是“文革表现”，而且严之又严。他既然藏有“清查”的“材料”，为什么当时不向我的上级机关移送？是什么理由使他甘冒“包庇”、“窝藏”之罪？
第六个问题：他提供的“材料”，是原件，不是抄件？如果是原件，有哪个单位的印章吗？
第七个问题：如果是抄件，是笔抄，还是用了复写纸？有抄写者的名字吗？
第八个问题：这些“材料”现在在哪里？如果已经转到了贵报编辑部，能让我带着我的律师，以及上海档案馆、上海人事局的工作人员，一起来看一眼吗？
第九个问题：如果这些“材料”继续藏在他家里，贵报能否派人领路，让我报请警官们搜检一下？
先问九个吧，实在不好意思再问下去了。
我不知道社长是不是明白：这里出现的，从一开始就不是什么“历史问题”，而极有可能是刑事案件。因为伪造文书、伪造档案、盗窃档案，在任何国家都是重大的刑事犯罪。
说“伪造文书”、“伪造档案”，好像很难听，但是社长，你能帮我想出别的可能来吗？
我这样问有点不礼貌，但细看贵报，除了以“爆料”的方式宣扬那次奇怪的“清查”外，还“采访”了很多“证人”来“证明”我的“历史”。但是这么多“证人”，为什么没有一个是我熟悉的？熟悉我的人，为什么一个也没有采访？这种事，总不能全赖到那个姓孙的人身上吧？
据一些熟悉那段历史的朋友分析，第一次伪造，应该发生在十一届三中全会否定“文革”之后，他们匆忙销毁了大量的材料，只能用伪造来填补；第二次伪造，应该发生在我出任上海市教授评审组组长一再否决了他们的职称申请之后；第三次伪造，应该发生在不少文人和媒体突然都要通过颠覆名人来进行自我表演的时候。当然，如果贵报涉嫌参与，不会是第一、第二次。
除了这件事，贵报十几年来还向我发起过好几拨规模不小的进攻，我都未回一语。今天还想请社长顺便查一查，这些进攻中，有哪几句话是真实的？如果查出来了，哪怕一句两句，都请告诉我。

sections.label: 五
paragraphs: 在“石一歌事件”上，比《南方周末》表现得更麻辣的，是香港的《苹果日报》。
香港《苹果日报》二○○九年五月十五日A19版发表文章说：“余秋雨在‘文革’时期，曾经参加‘四人帮’所组织的写作组，是‘石一歌’写作组成员，曾经发表过多篇重大批判文章，以笔杆子整人、杀人。”
这几句密集而可笑的谎言，已经撞击到四个严重的法律问题，且按下不表。先说香港《苹果日报》为什么会突然对我失去理智，又给我戴上了“石一歌”的破帽？细看文章，原来，他们针对的是我在汶川“5·12”地震后发表的一段话。我这段话的原文如下——
有些发达国家，较早建立了人道主义的心理秩序，这是值得我们学习的，但在大爱和至善的集体爆发力上，却未必比得上中国人。我到过世界上好几个自然灾害发生地，有对比。这次汶川大地震中全民救灾的事实证明，中华民族是人类极少数最优秀的族群之一。
“5·12”地震后，正好有两位美国朋友访问我。他们问：“中国的‘5·12’，是否像美国的‘9·11’，灾难让全国人民更团结了？”
我回答说：“不。‘9·11’有敌人，有仇恨，所以你们发动了两场战争。‘5·12’没有敌人，没有仇恨，中国人只靠爱，解决一切。”
开始我不明白，为什么这段话会引起香港和内地那么多中国文人的排斥。很快找到了一条界线：我愿意在中国寻爱；他们坚持在中国寻恨。
与此同时，我在救灾现场看到有些遇难学生的家长要求惩处倒塌校舍的责任者。我对这些家长非常同情，却又知道这种惩处在全世界地震史上还没有先例，难度极大，何况当时堰塞湖的危机正压在头顶，便与各国心理医生一起，劝说遇难学生家长平复心情，先回帐篷休息。这么一件任何善良人都会做的事情，竟然也被《苹果日报》和其他政客批判为“妨碍请愿”。
对此，我不能不对某些香港文人说几句话。你们既没有到过地震现场，也没有到过“文革”现场，却成天与一些内地来的骗子一起端着咖啡杯指手画脚，把灾难中的高尚和耻辱完全颠倒了。连你们，也鹦哥学舌地说什么“石一歌”！

sections.label: 六
paragraphs: 写到这里，我想读者也在笑了。
一个不知所云的署名，被一个不知所云的人戴到了我的头上，就怎么也甩不掉了。连悬赏也没有用，连地震也震不掉！这，实在太古怪了。
有人说，为别人扣帽子，是中国文人的本职工作。现在手多帽少，怎么可能摘掉？
但是，毕竟留下了一点儿遗憾：戴了那么久，还不知道“石一歌”究竟写过什么样的文章。
终于，一个阳光明媚的日子来到了。
二○一○年仲夏的一天，我在河南省郑州市的一个车站书店，随手翻看一本山西出版的杂志《名作欣赏》（总第318期）。开始并不怎么在意，突然眼睛一亮。
一个署名“祝勇”的人，在气愤地批判“石一歌”几十年前的一次“捏造”。
“捏造”什么呢？原来，一篇署名“石一歌”的文章说，鲁迅在住处之外有一间秘密读书室，在那里阅读过马克思主义著作。
这个人断言，“石一歌”就是我，因此进行这番“捏造”的人也是我。
不仅如此，这个人还指控我的亡友陈逸飞也参与了“捏造”，因为据说陈逸飞画过一幅鲁迅读书室的画。那画，我倒是至今没有见到过。
任何人被诬陷为“捏造”，都不会高兴，但我却大喜过望。
十几年的企盼，就想知道“石一歌”写过什么。此刻，我终于看到了这个小组最让人气愤的文章，而且是气愤到几十年后还不能解恨的文章，是什么样的了。
我立即买下来这本杂志，如获至宝。
被批判为“捏造”的文章，可能出现在一本叫《鲁迅的故事》的儿童读物里。在我印象中，那是当时复旦大学中文系按照周恩来的指示复课后，由“工农兵学员”在老师指导下写的粗浅作文，我当然不可能去读。但是，如果有哪篇文章真的写了鲁迅在住处之外有一间读书室，他在里面读过马克思主义的著作，那可不是“捏造”。
因为，那是鲁迅的弟弟周建人公开说过多次的，学员们只是照抄罢了。
周建人会不会“捏造”？好像不会。因为鲁迅虽然与大弟弟周作人关系不好，却与小弟弟周建人关系极好，晚年在上海有频繁的日常交往。周建人又是老实人，不会乱说。何况，周建人在“文革”期间担任着浙江省省长、全国人大副委员长，学员们更是没有理由不相信。
其实，那间读书室我还去参观过，很舒服，也不难找。鲁迅时代的中国知识分子，读马克思主义著作很普遍，鲁迅也读了不少。他连那位担任过中共中央主要负责人、又处于通缉之中的瞿秋白都敢接到家里来，还怕读那些著作吗？
原来，这就是“石一歌”的问题！

sections.label: 七
paragraphs: 我悬了十几年的心放了下来，觉得可以公布“石一歌”小组的真实名单了。但我还对那个电话里教授太太的声音保持着很深的记忆，因此决定再缓一缓。
现在只能暂掩姓名，先粗粗地提几句：
一九七二年根据周恩来指示在复旦大学中文系成立的《鲁迅传》编写小组，组长是华东师范大学教师，副组长是复旦大学教师，组内有复旦大学六人，上海社会科学院一人，上海艺术研究所一人，华师大附中一人，上海戏剧学院一人即我，半途离开。由于人员太散，该组又由正、副组长和复旦大学一人、上海艺术研究所一人，组成“核心组”。

后来根据周恩来指示在上海市巨鹿路作家协会成立的“石一歌”鲁迅研究小组，成立的时间我到今天还没有打听清楚，组长仍然是华东师范大学教师，不知道有没有副组长，组内有华东师范大学二人，复旦大学三人，上海社会科学院二人，华师大附中一人。由于都是出于周恩来的同一个指示，这个小组与前一个小组虽然人员不同，却还有一定的承续关系，听说还整理过前一个小组留下的鲁迅传记。在这个小组正式成立之前，复旦大学中文系的部分学员也用过这个署名。
这些事，已经过去整整四十年了。
对于今天的批判者，我无话可说，只有一个劝告：凭着天良，最好不要再去伤害已经去世，因此不能自辩的大艺术家，如陈逸飞。

sections.label: 八
paragraphs: 好了，寻“石”之路大体已到尽头，我也不想写下去了。
石头已经寻得。穿过密密层层的藜棘，终于得到了与这三个字相关的文章和名单。
最后，我不能不说一句：对“石一歌事件”，我要真诚地表示感谢。这三个字，给我带来了好运。
我这么说，不带任何讽刺。
第一，这三个字，给了我真正的轻松。

本来，我这个人，是很难摆脱各种会议、应酬而轻松的，但是这个可爱的谣言救了我。当今官场当然知道这是谣言，却又会百般敬畏造谣者，怕他们在传媒上再次闹事而妨害社会稳定。这一来，官场就尽量躲着我。例如我辞职二十多年，从未见过所在城市的每一任首长，哪怕是在集体场合。其实，这对我是天大的好事，使我不必艰苦推拒，就可以从各种头衔、职务中脱身而出，拥有了几乎全部自由时间。这么多年来我种种成绩的取得，都与此有关。貌似弃我，实为惠我。国内噪声紧随，我就到国外讲述中华文化。正好，国际间并不在乎国内的什么头衔。总之，我摸“石”过河，步步敞亮。
第二，这三个字，让我认知了环境。

当代中国文化界的诸多人士，对于一项发生在身边又延续多年的重大诬陷，完全能够识破却不愿识破。可能是世道不靖，他们也胆小了吧，同行的灾难就成了他们安全的印证，被逐的孤鹜就成了他们窗下的落霞。面对这种情景，我彻底放弃了对文化舆论的任何企盼，因全方位被逐而独立。独立的生态，独立的思维，独立的话语，由至小而至大，因孤寂而宏观。到头来，反而要感激被逐，享受被逐。像一块遗弃之石，唱出了一首自己的歌。这，难道不正是这三个字的本意吗？
第三，这三个字，使我愈加强健。

开始是因为厌烦这类诽谤，奉行“不看报纸不上网，不碰官职不开会，不用手机不打听”的“六不主义”，但这么一来，失去了当代敏感渠道的我，立即与自然生态相亲，与古代巨人相融。我后来也从朋友那里听说，曾经出现过一拨拨卷向我的浪潮，但由于我当时完全不知，居然纤毫无损。结果大家都看到了，我一直身心健康，神定气闲。这也就在无意中提供了一个社会示范：真正的强健不是呼集众人，追随众人，而是逆反众人，然后影响众人。“大勇似怯”，“大慈无朋”。
由于以上三个原因，我认真考虑了很久，终于决定，把“石一歌”这个署名正式接收下来。
然后，用谐音开一间古典小茶馆叫“拾遗阁”，再用谐音开一间现代咖啡馆叫“诗亦歌”。或者，干脆都叫“石一歌”，爽利响亮。
不管小茶馆还是咖啡馆，进门的墙上，都一定会张贴出各种报刊十几年来的诽谤文章，证明我为什么可以拥有这个名号。
如果那一批在这个名号后面躲了很多年的退休老教授们来了，我会免费招待；如果他们要我把这个名号归还给他们，我就让他们去找《南方周末》、《苹果日报》。但他们已经年迈，要去广州和香港都会很累，因此又会劝他们，不必多此一举了。
我会端上热茶和咖啡，拍拍他们的肩，劝他们平静，喝下这四十年无以言表的滋味。
我也老了，居然还有闲心写几句。我想，多数上了年纪的人都会像那些退休老教授，听到各种鼓噪绝不作声。因此，可怜的是历史，常常把鼓噪写成了课本。

sections.label: I
paragraphs: AT THE END OF THE TWENTIETH CENTURY, and in its final winter, I studied ancient civilizations for 40,000 kilometers, and arrived from the Middle East in the place between South Asia and Central Asia. Guns everywhere, horrors at every step, my life hanging by a thread.

That night, at the border of Pakistan and Afghanistan, a partner received a long-distance call. Then he told me softly that there was a student from Peking University surnamed Yu who was publishing articles these days accusing me of participating in the mafia organization called “Shi” during the Cultural Revolution.
“What?” I asked.
“I couldn’t hear. The phone was cut off.” The partner took a look at me and said, “It’s a fabrication. There was no triad gang at that time, not to mention you—”
He could not finish, as several armed men had approached us. For there was a real “triad gang” right here.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: FINALLY we came back alive from our journey.
Invitations poured in from all around the world for me to give a speech about the world at the turn of the century, especially its rampant terrorism.

However, in China, most newspapers speculated over the allegation by that Beijing University student. I had also figured out that what he said was that I once took part in a writing team named “Shi Yige” during the Cultural Revolution—no triad gang, but a group wearing many horrible hats.
“Shi Yige?”
I knew that was related to Premier Zhou Enlai.

In my Forty Years Ago, which I wrote in October 1971, Zhou Enlai set out to clean up the awful mess of the Cultural Revolution; he started the culture reconstruction in Shanghai and its first step was to force the universities to reopen. Because that year was the ninetieth anniversary of the birth of Lu Xun and the thirty-fifth anniversary of his death, he demanded that the resumption of the Chinese Department begin with Lu Xun’s works, writing biographies of him and studying him. Thus Shanghai had set up two groups; one was the writing committee for the Lu Xun Biography, located in Fudan University, while the second was the Lu Xun research team based at the Writers Association, and the teachers from various colleges and universities attended. I was selected to participate in the first group, but left halfway through. “Shi Yige” was the name of the latter group.
What I did not know was who took part in the latter group when it was founded and the articles they wrote about the research of Lu Xun.
What I also did not know was why “Shi Yige” suddenly turned into an insult, piled on my head and causing denunciation by so many newspapers and magazines.
Perhaps that had been controlled by someone following the cultural subversion frenzy at the turn of the century.
According to common sense, I would need to make things clear. However, I encountered three difficulties.

First, the frenzy that arose. My stance be beyond dispute, and the law was the only way to do that, but this was time-consuming. My conclusions drawn from my investigations of major human civilizations, especially the cautions regarding worldwide terrorism, had to be conveyed quickly to various countries, and could not be obstructed by matters of my personal reputation.

Second, how could the real members in “Shi Yige” stand up and state things clearly? Most of them were elderly retired professors, and had no strength to debate. If I wanted to distance myself, the members of that group would inevitably be investigated and publicly identified, which in turn would hurt the elderly.

Third, if the matter was made clear, the truth would be revealed: those two groups were established under the instruction of Premier Zhou Enlai. But politically this would bring some kind of permanent damage to that student. When Zhou Enlai started culture reconstruction, this student was just a babe in the woods, and so he was put up to it by others. This distressed me. So I gave up on self-defense, put the article into my briefcase, and was invited to talk about the Contemporary Dilemma of Major Civilizations. However, no matter whether I was in Taiwan, Japan, Malaysia, the United States, France, or Hungary, the Chinese readers all asked me about “Shi Yige.”
“Shi Yige?”
“Shi Yige?”

In fact, in focusing on it, domestic media such as Southern Weekly and Literature Newspaper had been too jittery. Readers from various countries all thought I had escaped China, and two readers living in South Africa made an oblique reference to conferring on me their kindness again and again: “Here is far away from them, very quiet…”

Its reputation was falsely claimed for tens of thousands of miles, I myself was more and more curious, wanting to know the facts behind it. However, so many ferocious articles did not tell me what these words in fact meant.

As time went by, I gradually learned that the person who had launched this effort was surnamed Sun, a Shanghai scholar whose title application I had rejected; the person who expanded it was surnamed Gu, a Hubei scholar who had tried to praise me before but was refused by me; the person who later joined in was surnamed Sha, a Shanghai scholar whose life was saved by me, but made clear he was breaking off his relationship with me through his far-left comments in key moments. Others were just booing on the sidelines.
These three old men, coupled with that student, how could they make such a big problem? That, of course, was because of the media.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: CURIOSITY was irrepressible.

Although I was not sure of all the members in the “Shi Yige” team, I also knew some. I wanted to chat with one or two of them, and let them tell me what articles they wrote after the establishment of the Lu Xun research team.

Unfortunately, when the “Shi Yige” team was publishing articles intensively, I was hiding in the Zhejiang mountains and had not read about them. One time I found food in the foothills and saw an article affixed with this name on the newspaper fence in a small town, but I did not read it anymore for it was merely the popular clichés at that time. So now I wanted to learn a bit and also speak a little with those fearful retiring professors.
After I went back to Shanghai from Taiwan, I called up a retired professor who had participated in the group before. The professor was not at home, and his wife answered the phone.
I asked: when was that group founded? What members were in it at that time?

Unexpectedly, his wife said to me on the phone with a pleading voice: “So many newspapers have picked up these criticisms, and I am at a loss to explain. My husband is fragile, with severe hypertension. Mr. Yu, I am sorry for your grievance.”

My heart trembled while I listened, I hastened to comfort her with a few words, and just hung up the phone, but I still felt deeply sorry for this phone call. That elderly couple might be nervous for several days.
That path was a dead end, and I could only look for another one.
However, the path to “Shi Yige” was not easy.
Or, was it easily taken from the direction of the attackers?
Finally, I came up with a good idea.

I grandly announced a “reward” in the newspapers: as long as those attackers presented evidence to prove that I had ever used the signature “Shi Yige” to write an article, paragraph, section, row, or even a line as they alleged, I would immediately pay my annual salary and publish the evidence in the national media. Also, I published the name of a lawyer who would handle this “reward.”
The purpose of this “reward” was not to harm “Shi Yige” at first, and also not harm the attacker. I really put a lot of thought into those two points.

Southern Weekly did not respond to my “reward,” but it published a photo of me and the members of “Shi Yige” in 2004; beside me were two others, and one of them was the one who had started it all, Mr. Sun. After that Southern Weekly steered clear of the “Shi Yige” topic, and said the man named Sun had “checked” into my problems in the Cultural Revolution. Therefore, it had “investigated” based on the “material” provided, and published the articles, which took up several pages. Although there was no problem involved in being thus investigated, the readers always ignored that, given the strong negative impact of being “checked” and “investigated.” With a circulation in the millions, this newspaper was read both at home and abroad.
So the path to “Shi Yige” led to a very nasty spectacle.
In accordance with China’s practice, “the mouthpiece” launched that position, and that had to be a “verdict,” and also a “definite verdict.”

However, after the incident with News of the World in the United Kingdom, I felt I must be obliged to ask the president of Southern Weekly some specific questions. These questions I repeatedly asked the editors and reporters of this newspaper, but they simply offered a few words and did not pay attention. As far as I knew, many readers chose tough questions, including some lawyers, and the paper also made no response. However, today I was going to say, “Dear president, I know you are very busy, but you have to listen to my interesting questions below.”

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: THE FIRST QUESTION: you reaffirmed the “check” by Sun, so I want to ask, who appointed him? What institute does the appointed person belong to? Why did they appoint him? What did he do at the time? Did he have a working unit?

The second question: If the “check” was carried out, how could he bring the “material” home? Was he the curator of the archives? Was he the general of the Personnel Bureau? If he was, could he intercept and possess these archival materials?
The third question: If he possessed my “material,” and of course, he must possess some others’ material as well, what did this encompass? How big was his “archive”?

The fourth question: These “materials” in his home would be twenty-seven years old, according to the timeline he mentioned. Who managed them for such a long time? Was he alone, or did his family also attend to their management? Was there a safe? How many? Who kept the keys?

The fifth question: I assumed the leading department-level position at the university in the 1980s for many years; at that time, the main standards for higher organs investigating and reviewing officials was “performance in the Cultural Revolution,” which was very strict. Since he hid the “materials” for “checking,” why did he not transfer them to the higher organ? What reasons made him risk the crimes of “sheltering” and “harboring”?
The sixth question: Was the “material” he provided the original or a copy? If it was the original, did it bear the seal of the unit?
The seventh question: If it was a copy, was it copied by pen or through carbon paper? Did it include the name of the scribe?

The eighth question: Where were these “materials” now? If they were transferred to your newsroom, could I bring my lawyer and the staff of the Shanghai City Archives and Shanghai Personnel Bureau for a look?
The ninth question: If these “materials” were still hidden in his home, could you send someone there so police officers could examine them?
These nine were sufficient, and I was truly reluctant to ask any more.

I did not know whether the president understood: the incident here was, from the outset, not a “historical issue,” but most likely a criminal case, for the document forgery, archive falsification, and record theft were the major criminal offenses in any country. It seemed very harsh to say “document forgery” and “archive falsification,” but dear president, could you help me think of another possibility?

It was a bit impolite to ask, but looking at your paper, besides that strange “check” in the way of “disclosure,” you also “interviewed” many “witnesses” to “prove” my “history.” However, why were these “witnesses” all unfamiliar to me? Why did you not interview anyone who was familiar with me? Such a thing could not be all attributed to that man named Sun, right?

According to the analysis of some friends familiar with that period of history, the first occurrence of falsification could have been after the Cultural Revolution was denied by the third session of the Eleventh Congress. They rushed to destroy a large number of materials, and could only replace them with forgeries; the second time falsification could have occurred was after I took the leadership of Shanghai City Professor Review Group and repeatedly rejected the accusers’ title applications; the third time might have been when many scholars and media suddenly wanted to improve their standing by subverting other scholars. Of course, if your newspaper was involved in it, it would not be the first or second time.

Besides this matter, your newspaper also launched several small-scale attacks within a dozen years, but I did not reply. Today, I also would like to invite the president to check which sentences in these attacks were true. If you look it up, and even if it is just one or two sentences, please let me know.

sections.label: V
paragraphs: AS FOR THE “SHI YIGE EVENT,” what was a much spicier presentation than that of Southern Weekly was from the Apple Daily in Hong Kong.

Hong Kong’s Apple Daily published an article in its A19 edition on May 15, 2009: “Yu Qiuyu once participated in the writing group organized by the ‘Gang of Four’ during the ‘Cultural Revolution,’ as a member of the writing group ‘Shi Yige,’ who had published many significant critical articles to trick and kill people with the pen.”

These intensive and ludicrous lies had raised four serious legal problems. First, I wanted to ask why Apple Daily in Hong Kong would suddenly lose its head over me, and then put the wrongheaded stigma of “Shi Yige” on me? After a careful review, it turns out that they directed it at the statement issued after the Wenchuan earthquake on May 12. The original text was as follows:

Some developed countries set up a humanitarian order earlier, which is worth our study, but as for the collective power of love, they may not be comparable to the Chinese. I have been to several places where natural disasters occurred in the world. The national disaster relief in Wenchuan earthquake proved that the Chinese nation was one of the very best ethnic groups in this kind of effort.
After the “5/12” earthquake, two friends from the United States visited me. They asked: “The Chinese ‘5/12,’ the United States ‘9/11,’ does the disaster make the whole nation more united?”
I replied: “No. ‘9/11’ provoked enmity and hatred, so you had waged two wars. ‘5/12’ had no enemy or hatred, and Chinese people solved all problems with love.”

At the beginning, I did not understand why this should cause so much repulsion in Hong Kong and among mainland Chinese scholars. Soon I found a line: I like to find love in China; they stick to finding hate in China.

Meanwhile, I saw on the website that some parents of the dead children demanded punishment of those responsible for the collapsed school buildings. I had had great sympathy for them, but knew that there was no such precedent in the history of global earthquakes; it was very difficult, so I and national psychologists persuaded parents to calm down and go back to their tents for needed rest. Such a thing would be done by any kind person, but even this was criticized by Apple Daily and other politicians as “petition obstructing.”

In this regard, I could not fail to say some words about certain Hong Kong scholars. You had never been to the earthquake site, nor experienced the Cultural Revolution, but found fault with some mainland Chinese “crooks” by holding coffee cups, overturning the noble and humble alike in the wake of disaster. You even came after them to say “Shi Yige” just like a parrot!

sections.label: VI
paragraphs: WHEN I WROTE THIS, I thought the readers were also smiling.
An unintelligible signature was put on my head by an unintelligible person, and it could not be thrown away no matter how, even by a reward, even by an earthquake! It was very weird.
Someone said that it was the job of Chinese scholars to label others. Now there were more hands but fewer caps, and how could they be removed?
However, a little regret was left after all: I was labeled so long, but still did not know what kinds of articles “Shi Yige” actually wrote.
Finally, a break came.

On a summer day in 2010, I was in a bookstore at the station in Zhengzhou, Henan Province, and I casually flipped through a magazine, Masterpiece Appreciation (No. 318), published by Shanxi. I did not care at the beginning, but suddenly my eyes lit up.
A person signed “Zhu Yong” indignantly criticized a “fabrication” about “Shi Yige” decades before.
What did they “fabricate”? It turned out that an article named “Shi Yige” had stated that a secret reading room was set aside for Lu Xun outside his residence, where he read Marxist works.
This person asserted that “Shi Yige” was me, so the person who fabricated this was also me.

Not only that, but this man also alleged that my dead friend Chen Yifei was also involved in the “fabrication,” because Chen Yifei was said to have painted a picture of Lu Xun’s reading room, which I had never seen until now.
Any person being framed in a “fabrication” would not be pleased, but I was overjoyed.

A dozen years of hope, and I only wanted to know what “Shi Yige” had written. At this point, I finally saw the most irritating article in this group, which could not be disposed of even after decades.
I immediately bought the magazine, as if I had found a treasure.

The article criticized as “fabrication” might have appeared in a children’s book called The Story of Lu Xun. In my mind, that was the shallow composition written by “worker-peasant-soldier students” under the guidance of teachers after the resumption of the Chinese Department in Fudan University in accordance with the instruction of Zhou Enlai, and of course I would not be able to read it. However, if any article really claimed there was a reading room outside of Lu Xun’s apartment where he read the works of Marxism, that was not “fabrication.”
The reason is that that was said publicly many times by the younger brother of Lu Xun, Zhou Jianren, and the students simply copied it.

Would Zhou Jianren “fabricate”? That seemed unlikely. For the relationship between Lu Xun and his big brother Zhou Zuoren was not very good, but that between Lu Xun and his younger brother Zhou Jianren was, with frequent daily contact in his later years in Shanghai. Zhou Jianren was honest and did not talk nonsense. What was more, Zhou Jianren served as the governor of Zhejiang Province and vice chairman of the national People’s Congress during the Cultural Revolution, and the participants had no reason not to believe it.

In fact, I also visited that reading room, which was very comfortable and easy to find. Chinese intellectuals in the era of Lu Xun commonly read Marxist works, and Lu Xun also read a lot. He even received Qu Qiubai, who served as the principal of the CPC—was he afraid to read those books?
That turned out to be the question of “Shi Yige”!

sections.label: VII
paragraphs: MY HEART FELT RELIEVED after hanging in fire for a dozen years, and I thought it was time to release the true list of “Shi Yige.” But I also maintained a deep memory of that voice of the professor’s wife, so I decided to slow down.
Now I had to mask the names temporarily and here just mention a few:

In 1972, the writing group of Lu Xun Biography was founded in the Chinese Department of Fudan University according to the instruction of Zhou Enlai, whose head was the teacher of East China Normal University; deputy head was the teacher of Fudan University; and the group members included six persons from Fudan University, one from Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, one from Shanghai Art Research Institute, one from the affiliated high school of East China Normal University, and one from Shanghai Theater Academy—that was me, but as I said earlier, I left halfway through. Since the staff was too scattered, the “core group” was founded by the head, the deputy head, the one from Fudan University, and the one from Shanghai Art Research Institute.

Later, according to the instruction of Zhou Enlai, the “Shi Yige” Lu Xun research team was founded in the Shanghai Writers Association at Julu Road, Shanghai City, but its founding date was not ascertained until now, and its head was still the teacher of East China Normal University. I did not know whether that was the deputy leader, and its group members included two persons from East China Normal University, three from Fudan University, two from Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, and one from affiliated high school of East China Normal University. Since these two groups were all founded according to the same instructions by Zhou Enlai, they had a certain continuity, even if the group members were different, and I heard the latter one also finished off the Lu Xun Biography left by the first group. Before the formal establishment of this group, some students in the Chinese Department of Fudan University had also used this signature.
These had been the facts throughout the past forty years.

For today’s critics, I had nothing to say but this advice: if you have any conscience, it is best not to hurt the great artists who have died and therefore cannot defend themselves, such as Chen Yifei.

sections.label: VIII
paragraphs: WELL, THE PATH TO “SHI YIGE” had basically come to an end, and I did not want to write anymore.
It had been found. Through the thick chenopodium weeds, I finally obtained the articles and lists related to those words.
Finally, I had to say: As for the “Shi Yige event,” I would like to sincerely express my gratitude. It brought me good luck.
It was without any irony that I said so.
First, these words gave me real ease.

Originally, I found it difficult to get out of meetings, to entertain myself and relax, but this lovely rumor saved me. The official circle today, of course, knew that it was a rumor, but they would revere the rumormongers, for they were afraid of a riot again in the media that would harm social stability. Thus the official circle would also elude me as far as possible. For example, for over twenty years, I had never seen any head of each city, even in collective gatherings. In fact, it was very good for me, so I had no need to be pushy about it, and could get out of various titles and positions, so as to have nearly all my time to myself. Various accomplishments over the years all derived from this. It seemed an abandonment, but actually was a benefit. Domestic noise pushed me abroad to speak of Chinese culture. The title I might have had was not cared for much in the international arena. In short, I crossed the river by feeling my way over the stones, step by spacious step.
Second, these words helped me perceive the environment.

Many people in contemporary Chinese cultural circles could completely see though the great slander that lasted for many years, but they did not want to. Maybe due to the desperate times, they were timid; the disasters of their peers became confirmations of their security; the expulsion of birds became a lonely sunset under their windows. Facing this scenario, I completely gave up any hope in terms of public cultural opinion and became totally independent upon my full expulsion. The ecology of independence, independent thinking, and independent words grew and emerged from solitude to the wider world. Finally, I was grateful to be expelled, and also enjoyed it, just like a deserted rock singing a song of its own. Could that not be the true meaning of those words?
Third, these words made me stronger.

At the beginning, I adhered to “six nots”—“no newspaper, no Internet, no title, no meetings, no cell phone, and no curiosity”—because of the boredom of such defamations, and by shutting out the contemporary noise, I was instantly intimate with a more natural ecology and became one with ancient giants. I later heard from friends that tides were turning for me, but I still had my integrity, for I knew nothing. Now the result was that I was always in good health, calm, and relaxed. Unintentionally, I offered a social model: the real robustness was not to call up people and follow the crowd, but rebel and influence them. “The real courage was calm and composed” and “the people too kind were without friends.”
Due to these three reasons, I thought for a long time and finally decided to receive the signature of “Shi Yige” officially.

Then I opened a classic little teahouse named “pavilion of deficiency supplements,” and then opened a modern coffee shop called “song poems,” or simply “Shi Yige,” efficiently and loudly. Whether on the little teahouse or on the café, on the door would be posted the defamatory articles from all the newspapers over a dozen years, to prove why I could have this name.
