paragraphs: 感谢诸位，来与我们一起，送别亲爱的妈妈。
我妈妈于一九二二年一月六日出生，于二○一二年十二月九日凌晨去世，在这个世界上生活了整整九十年，也算高龄了。妈妈在最后的日子里没有任何痛苦，只因老年性的心血管系统疾病失去了意识。我们这些晚辈一天天都轮流陪在她身边，她走得很安详。
因此，我要求几位弟弟，在今天的追悼会上不要过于悲伤，更不要失声痛哭。
悲伤和痛哭，容易进入一种共同模式，这是妈妈不喜欢的。记得十年前我们也在这里追悼爸爸，从头到尾，妈妈一直都没有哭，大家以为她过度悲痛而失神了。但是，回到家里，在爸爸那个小小的写字台前，她突然号啕大哭，哭得像一个小女孩一样。马兰抱住她，抚摸着她的背，她哭了很久很久。从此，整整十年，直到她自己去世，她不再哭过一声，不再流一滴眼泪。她此生的哭声和眼泪，全都终止于爸爸。
妈妈拒绝一切群体化的悲伤，避过一切模式化的情感。我们今天，也要顺着她。那就让我们在心底，为这独一无二的生命，唱一首独一无二的送别之歌。
妈妈的独一无二，可以从一件小事说起。几天前，我们守在妈妈床边，为她服务了十年之久的保姆小许动情地说，整整十年，没有听到过她的一句责备，一句重话。
我说：“你只有十年，我是她的大儿子，多少年了？从小到大，也没有听到过。”
其实，今天到场的舅舅、舅妈和所有年长的亲友都可以证明，在你们漫长的人生记忆里，有没有留下一丝一毫有关我妈妈稍稍发火的记忆？
我看到你们全在摇头，对，肯定没有。我一生见到的妈妈，永远只是微笑，只是倾听，只是腼腆，最多，只是沉默。直到半年前一起吃饭，我说她毛笔字写得比我好，她还腼腆得满脸通红。
但是，我要告诉今天在场的年轻人，不要小看了微笑和腼腆。你们眼前的这位老人，还留下了一系列艰深的难题。
对于这些难题，我曾多次当面问过妈妈，她只是三言两语匆匆带过。每次，我总以为还有机会细问。也许在一个没有旁人的安静下午，让她一点点地回答我。但是，这个机会再也没有了，她把一切答案都带走了。
于是，我心中的难题，也就成了永远的难题，无人可解。
第一个难题。她这么一个大城市的富家之女，为了在战争年月支撑一个小家庭，居然同意离别在上海工作的丈夫，到最贫困的乡村度过自己美丽的青春，一切生活细节都回到她完全不熟悉的原始起点。对她来说，就像一下子跌进了石器时代。这，怎么可能？
第二个难题。回去的乡村，方圆多少里只有她一个人识字，她却独自挑起了文明启蒙的全部重担。开办识字班，为每家每户写信、读信、记柴账、谷账……她每天忙得不可开交，却没有任何人要她这么做，也没有得到过任何报酬。这，又怎么可能？
第三个难题。她和爸爸，这对年轻夫妇，当初是怎么冒险决定的，让他们刚刚出生的大儿子，我，在如此荒昧的农村进入至关重要的早期教育？在那所极其简陋的小学开办之前，是由妈妈独自承担吗？在我七岁的时候，妈妈又果断地决定，我每天晚上不再做功课、写作业，而是替代她，来为所有的乡亲写信、记账。她作出这个决定，显然是为了培养我的人生责任感，但她难道完全不考虑我的学业了吗？
第四个难题。有些亲友曾经认为，妈妈是在瞎碰瞎撞中很偶然地完成了对我的早期教育。这确实很有可能。但是，我到上海读中学后，很快获得了全市作文比赛第一名和数学竞赛大奖，原因是我为乡亲写过几百封信，又记了那么多账。妈妈知道我获奖的消息后，居然一点儿也不感到惊讶。难道，她不是瞎碰瞎撞，而是早有预计？

第五个难题。到上海后，遇到了饥荒和“文革”。全家遭受的最大困顿就是吃饭，这事全由妈妈一人张罗。“文革”中，一切被“打倒”人员的全部生活费，是每月每家二十六元人民币，而当时我家，是整整八口人，其中包括一名因失去父母而被收养的孩子。家里早就没有任何余钱，所有稍稍值钱的东西也都已经卖完。那么，二十六元，八口人，这道完全无解的算术题，妈妈到底是怎么一天天算下来的？我们看到的只是一个结果，那就是全家都没有饿死。这究竟是如何做到的？
与前面几个难题不同的是，这个难题出现时我已经长大，留下了一些片段记忆。
例如，“文革”灾难中的一天，妈妈步行到我所在的学院，找到了已经很久没有吃过一顿饱饭的我。在一片吵闹的高音喇叭声中，她伸出温热的手掌紧紧贴在我的手掌上。我感觉到，中间夹了一张纸币。她说，还要立即赶到关押爸爸的地方去。我一看手掌，那是一张两元钱的纸币。这钱是从哪里来的？我百思不得其解。
但是，过几天我就侦查到了。原来妈妈与几个阿姨一起，在一家小工厂洗铁皮。那么冷的天还赤着脚，浑身上下都被水浇湿了。几元钱，就是这么挣来的。
前几天，妈妈已经失去知觉，我坐在病床边长时间地握着她的手掌。突然如迅雷闪电，记起了那年她贴着两元钱纸币握住我手掌时的温热。还是这个手掌，现在握在我手上。然后，我又急急地去抚摸她的脚，四十多年前的冷水铁皮，让我今天还打了个寒颤。
妈妈的手，妈妈的脚，我们永远的生命支架。难道，这些天要渐渐地冷却了吗？
我一动妈妈的手脚，她肩头的被子就有点滑落，马兰赶忙去整理。肩头，妈妈的肩头，更是我家的风雨山脊。
有关妈妈肩头的记忆，那就更多了。例如，我曾写过，“文革”中有一次我从农场回家，吃惊地看到一张祭祖的桌子居然在自动移位。细看之下才发现妈妈一个人钻在桌子底下，用肩在驮桌子。家里的人，有的被关押了，有的被逼死了，有的被流放了，没有一双手来帮她一把，她只能这样。
“文革”结束后，公道回归，被害的家人均获平反，我也被选拔为全国最年轻的高校校长。但是，不管声名如何显赫，我的衣食负担还是落在妈妈肩上。直到今天，集体宿舍的老邻居们还都记得，我妈妈每隔几天就肩背一个灰色的食物袋来为我做饭，后面还跟着爸爸。
现在，很多当年同事仍在美言我在那个年代的工作效能，不少出版社也在抢着出版我那时写的学术著作。但是只有我知道，这一切的一半分量，都由一副苍老的肩膀扛着，直到马兰的出现。
说到这里，我想大家都已明白，妈妈一生的微笑和腼腆，绝不是害怕、躲避、无能、平庸。恰恰相反，她完成了一种特殊的强大。
妈妈让我懂得，天地间有另一种语言。记得当年爸爸单位的“革命群众”每隔几天就会来威胁妈妈，说爸爸如果再不交代“反党罪行”就会“死无葬身之地”。妈妈每次都低头听着，从不反驳一句，心里只想着下一顿饭能找一些什么来给孩子们吃。后来叔叔在安徽被逼死，妈妈陪着祖母去料理后事，当地的“革命群众”又在一旁厉声训斥，妈妈只是捧着骨灰盒低头沉默，随便他们说什么。
几十年过去，现在我们都知道了，妈妈的沉默是对的。那些“革命群众”不值得辩论。一辩论就进入他们的逻辑系统，必定上当。妈妈固守的，是另一套做人的基本道理，也就是天道天理。只有沉默，才能为天道天理让出位置，才能为历史裁判留下空间。
妈妈心中的天道天理，比我们常说的大是大非还要高。妈妈并不否认大是大非，例如，在“文革”灾难中，她和我都知道，只要我去与造反派疏通一下，表示服从，爸爸的处境也许会改变，但我坚决不去疏通，她也赞成我这么做。又如，她知道我曾经到一个出版社单独与“工总司”暴徒对峙，又冒险悄悄地主持了上海唯一的周恩来追悼会，她都没有阻止我，只说“做事不大声，做完就走人”。
但是，这些事，还不是她心中的终点。她的终点听起来很平常：不管别人怎么闹，都要好好活下去。
在这一点上，妈妈显然高于爸爸。爸爸是典型的儒家，相信“修身、齐家、治国、平天下”那一套，成天要为正义挺身而出，为此受尽折磨。直到十年前，还被广州、上海、天津的三份诬陷我的报刊活活气死。他临终床头那几份报刊上的颤抖笔画，便是生死遗命。其实爸爸和妈妈同龄，妈妈能够多活十年，原因之一，是她压根儿不听那些恶言。因此，这些恶言只能折腾爸爸，却无伤妈妈。
针对这个对比，我曾经说过，我是中国人，当然忘不了杀父之仇；但我又是妈妈的儿子，懂得绝不能让自己受恶言操控。我想，朋友们都会认同，我受妈妈的影响更深一些。
很多读者都奇怪，我为什么受到媒体间那么多谣言的一次次围攻而从不解释，从不反驳？只要见过我妈妈，就明白了。
最后，我想用一件远年往事，作为这个悼词的归结。

在我六岁那年，一个夏天的傍晚，妈妈翻过两座山，吴石岭和大庙岭，到上林湖的表外公家去了，当夜必定回来。我为了让妈妈惊喜，就独自翻山去接妈妈。那时山上还有很多野兽，我却一点儿也不害怕。后来在第二座山的山顶遇到栖宿在破凉亭里的一个乞丐家庭，他们还劝我不要再往前走，但我还是没听他们的。终于，我在翻完第二座山的时候见到了妈妈。现在想来，妈妈也是够大胆的，那么年轻，那么美貌，独自一人，走在黑夜山路上。然而，更有趣的是，妈妈在山路上见到我，竟然不吃惊，不责怪，不盘问，只是高兴地说一句“秋雨来了”，便一把拉住我的手，亲亲热热往回走。这情景，正合得上布莱希特的一个剧名：《大胆妈妈和她的孩子们》。
是的，我毕生的大胆，从根子上说，都来自于妈妈。十几年前我因贴地冒险数万公里考察了密布着恐怖主义危险的人类古文明遗迹，被国际媒体誉为“当今世界最勇敢的人文教授”。其实那每一步，还是由妈妈当年温热的手牵着。
妈妈，您知道，我为您选定的归息之地，就在那条山路边上。爸爸已经在那里安息，山路的另一侧，则安息着祖父、祖母、叔叔，以及您的父亲——我们的外公。因此，您不会寂寞。
您先在上海度过这个寒冷的冬天，明年春天，我会领着弟弟们，把您送到那里。
妈妈，这是我们的山路，我们的山谷。现在，野兽已经找不到了，山顶上的凉亭早就塌了，乞丐的家也不见了。剩下的，还是那样的山风，那样的月亮，那样的花树。
妈妈，我真舍不得把您送走。但是，更舍不得继续把您留在世间。这世间，对您实在有点说不过去。整整九十年，越想越叫人心疼。那就到那里去休息吧，妈妈。
谢谢大家，陪我和妈妈说了这么多话。
二○一二年十二月十三日下午四时三十分，在妈妈的追悼会上。

sections.label: main
paragraphs: THANK YOU ALL FOR COMING and joining us, to say farewell to my dear mother.

My mother was born on January 6, 1922, and died in the early morning of December 9, 2012, living exactly ninety years in this world, and she grew to advanced age. My mother had no pain at her end of days, only lost the consciousness due to age-related diseases in her cardiovascular system. We the younger generations all took turns to accompany her every day, and she went peacefully.
Therefore, I ask my younger brothers not to be too sad at today’s memorial service, not to burst into tears.

Sadness and tears easily enter into a common pattern, which our mother did not like. Ten years ago, when we here mourned for our father, from beginning to end, our mother never cried; everybody thought she was in too much grief and absence. However, once going back home, at the little desk of our dad, she suddenly cried, cried like a little girl. Ma Lan held her, stroked her back, and she cried for a very long time. From then on, for a decade, until her own death, she did not cry anymore. Her cries and tears all ended with our dad.
Mom refused all group sadness, and evaded all the patterned feelings. We today also follow her. Let’s sing a unique song of farewell for this unique life in our hearts.

The uniqueness of mother can be derived from one small thing. A few days ago, as we waited at our mother’s bed, the nanny Xu, who served Mom for over ten years, said with emotion that no reproach or harsh word was heard from her for ten years.
I said, “You have only ten years. I am her older son, how many years? I have never heard it since my childhood.”
In fact, uncles, aunts, and all older relatives here can attest to it: in your lifelong memories, can you remember a trace of Mom’s anger?

I see you all shake your heads. No, absolutely not. Mom, I see all my life, is always smiling, just listening, just shy, at most she is just silent. Until six months ago we had dinner together. I said her calligraphy was better than mine, and she blushed with a shy look.
However, I want to tell young people here today, don’t underestimate the smile and shyness. This old woman in front of you also leaves a number of puzzles.

For these puzzles, I had repeatedly had to ask Mom, but she hurried over it with a few words. Each time, I always thought there was a chance to ask in detail. Maybe she could reply in a quiet afternoon without anyone else around. However, I had no chance, and she has taken them all away.
In this way, the puzzles in my mind have become eternal puzzles, with no solution.

The first puzzle. She was such a rich daughter of a big city; however, in order to support a family in wartime, she agreed to leave her husband working in Shanghai and went to the most impoverished countryside for their beautiful youth, with all details of life returning to an original starting point she was unfamiliar with. For her, it was like all of a sudden she fell into the Stone Age. How is this possible?

The second puzzle. In the village, she was the only literate person for many miles, but she alone took on the whole burden of civilization and enlightenment. She ran the literacy classes, wrote letters, read letters, inventoried the firewood, and the cereal. She was terribly busy, but nobody wanted her to do it, and she never received any remuneration. How is this possible?

The third puzzle. How did she and my father, this young couple, make the the crucial decision to let me, their eldest son, enter my critical early education in this ignorant rural area? As for the launching of a very shabby elementary school, was it undertaken by mother alone? When I was seven years old, Mom made a decision not to let me do my lessons or homework every night, but alternatively, to write letters or keep accounts for all the folks. Such a decision was apparently aimed at developing my sense of responsibility, but could she never take into account my studies?

The fourth puzzle. Some relatives believe that Mom completed my early education by accident. It is possible. However, after I arrived in the middle school in Shanghai, I soon won first place in a citywide essay contest and math contest awards because I had written hundreds of letters and kept so many accounts for folks. When Mom heard such news, she was not surprised at all. Actually, it was not by accident, but was expected.

The fifth puzzle. Shanghai faced famine and the Cultural Revolution. The biggest difficulty facing the whole family was food, which was entirely dealt with by Mom. In the Cultural Revolution, the living cost for all persons was 26 yuan per family per month, while my family consisted of eight people, including an adopted child. No extra money was left at home, and all valuables had already been sold. So, 26 yuan, eight people, an arithmetic problem without solution; how did Mom count it down day by day? What we saw was that no one starved to death. How could she do it?
Unlike the above puzzles, when this puzzle appeared, I had grown up and was left some fragments of memory.

For example, one day during the Cultural Revolution disaster, Mom walked to the school where I was in and found I hadn’t had a full meal for a long time. Amid the loud, high horns, she pressed her warm palm on mine. I felt banknotes in the middle. She said she had to hurry to my dad immediately. I glanced at my palm, and there was a two-yuan banknote. Where did the money come from? I could not comprehend.

However, I found the answer in a few days. My mother and several aunts washed iron sheets in a small factory. They were barefoot even on cold days, and wet throughout. They earned only a little money in this way.

A few days ago, my mother lost consciousness, and I held her hands while sitting at the bedside for a long time. Suddenly, like thunder and lightning, I remembered the warmth when she put the two-yuan banknote in my hand that year. The same palm was now held by me. Then, I hurried to touch her feet; the iron sheets of over forty years ago still made me shiver today.
Mom’s hand, Mom’s feet, our eternal life support. Do these days gradually cool?
Once I moved her hands and feet, the quilt at her shoulders slid down a bit, and Ma Lan rushed to finish it. The shoulders, Mom’s shoulders, were the storm ridge of our family.

The memories of Mom’s shoulders were much more. For example, I once wrote when I came home from the farm in the Cultural Revolution, I was surprised to see a table for worshipping was shifting by itself. I looked at it in detail and found my mother was under the table to shoulder it alone. People in my family were imprisoned, forced to die, or exiled. No one helped her, so she could only do it in this way.

After the Cultural Revolution, justice returned, the blasted family member was vindicated, and I was chosen as the youngest university president in the country. However, no matter how eminent my reputation was, my life burden still fell on the shoulders of my mother. Until today, old neighbors in the dormitory have recalled that my mom came to cook for me every couple of days with a gray shoulder bag, followed by my dad.

Now a lot of colleagues still praise my work performance at that time, and many publishing houses are rushing to publish my academic books. However, only I know that half of it was carried by a pair of old shoulders, until the emergence in my life of Ma Lan.
Here, I thought we all knew that; her smile and lifelong shyness never came from fear, evasion, disability, and mediocrity. Instead, it expressed and fulfilled a special strength.

From my mom, I know another language exists between heaven and earth. I still remember the “revolutionary masses” of my father would threaten my mom every few days, and they said my dad would “die without a burial place” if the “anti-Party crime” was not explained clearly. Mom bowed and listened all the time, never refuting, and only thinking about the next meal for her children. When my uncle was forced to die in Anhui, Mom made arrangements for a funeral with her grandmother; the local “revolutionary masses” sharply reprimanded her, but Mom just held the urn silently, just let them talk.

Several decades have passed, and we all know by now that her silence was right. Those “revolutionary masses” were not worth debating. The debate would make you enter into their logical system, and inevitably be fooled. What Mom clung to is another basic season, or natural justice. Only silence can leave space for natural justice and historical arbitration.

Natural justice, we used to say, was much more profound than right and wrong. Mother did not deny right and wrong; for example, in the disaster of Cultural Revolution, both she and I knew that as long as I got past it with the rebels, showing obedience, the situation of my father might be changed, but I was determined not to, and she agreed with me. Another example: she knew that I had confronted the “worker revolution headquarters” in a publishing house alone, and quietly presided over the only memorial service for Zhou Enlai in Shanghai; she did not stop me, just said “do not be loud; finish and go soon.”
However, these things were not the goal in her heart. Her aim sounded very common: regardless of others, she was always going to survive.

In this regard, Mom was apparently greater than Dad. Dad was a typical Confucian, believing in “self-cultivation, family harmony, country management, and world peace,” so he always stood up for justice and was tortured much. A decade ago, he died due to three newspapers framing me in Guangzhou, Shanghai, and Tianjin. The quivering strokes on that bunch of newspapers and magazines beside his bed were the testament of life and death. In fact, my father and mother were of the same age; Mom would live ten more years than Dad, because she resolutely did not listen to those abusive words. Therefore, they could defeat Dad, but not Mom.

In regard to this comparison, I have said that I am a Chinese, and of course could not forget to avenge the murder of my father; but I am the son of my mother, and know never to be controlled by abusive words. I think my friends will agree that I am influenced more by my mother.
Many readers will wonder, why do you never explain or refute so many rumors besieging you again and again in the media? You will understand from seeing my mother.
Finally, I would like to conclude this eulogy with a past event.

When I was six years old, on a summer evening, Mom traveled over two mountains, Wushi Ridge and Damiao Ridge, and went to the house of Grandpa, but said she would come back that night. To surprise her, I crossed over the mountains alone to pick up my mother. There were many wild animals in the mountains at that time, but I was not afraid at all. Later I met a beggar family roosted on the top of the second mountain, and they advised me not to go, but I still did not listen to them. Finally, I saw Mom when I crossed over the second mountain. Now I thought, Mom was bold enough, she was so young, so beautiful, but she dared to cross over the mountains at night alone. However, what was more interesting was that Mom was not surprised to see me on the mountain road; she even did not blame or question me, but said gladly, “Qiuyu is coming,” then she took my hand, and we went back in a completely familial way. The scene was the same as in the drama of Brecht: Mother Courage and Her Children.

Yes, the courage in my life has its roots in my mom. A dozen years ago, I passed through tens of thousands of kilometers to study ancient ruins, lands bristling with risks of terrorism and other dangers, and I was praised as “the bravest humanities professor in the world today” by the international media. Every step was in fact still guided by the warm hands of my mom.

Mom, you know your resting place that I have selected for you is just on the roadside of that mountain. Dad is already resting there. On its other side rests our grandparents, aunts, uncles, and your father—our grandfather. Therefore, you will not be lonely.
You first spend this cold winter in Shanghai, and then I will take you there together with my brothers next spring.

Mom, this is our mountain, our valley. Now, the beast has been unable to find it, the hilltop pavilion has collapsed, and the beggar family has gone. There remains the mountain wind, moon, and flowers as usual.

Mom, I really could not bear to send you away. However, I am much more reluctant to keep you in the world continuously. Such a world is a little unreasonable to you. For the whole ninety years, it distressed us more and more. Just go to the mountain and your rest, Mom.
Thank you for accompanying me to say so much to my mom.
—4:30 p.m., December 13, 2012, at my mother’s memorial service.

zh.title: 祭笔
intro: 《秋雨合集》二十卷，在除夕的爆竹声中终于编成了，我轻轻放下手上的笔。
放下又捡起，再端详一番：笔。
人的一生会触碰到很多物件，多得数也数不清。对我来说，最重要的物件，一定是笔。
我至今还没有用电脑，一切文字都用笔写出，被出版界誉为稀世无多的“纯手工写作”。会不会改变？不会。虽然我并不保守，但一个人的生命有限，总需要守住几份忠贞，其中一份，就是对笔。
也许很多人会笑我落伍，但只要读了我下面的片断记忆，一定就会理解了。

sections.label: 一
paragraphs: 我人生的第一支笔，是一支竹杆小毛笔。妈妈在代村民写信，我用这支小毛笔在边上模仿，那时我才三岁。第二年就被两个新来的小学老师硬生生地从我家桌子底下拖去上学了，妈妈给我换了一支好一点的毛笔。我一上课就黏得满脸是墨，惹得每个老师一下课就把我抱到小河边洗，洗完，再奔跑着把我抱回座位。
七岁时，妈妈给了我一支比毛笔还长的蘸水笔，外加一瓶蓝墨水，要我从此代她为村民写信、记账。把笔头伸到墨水瓶里蘸一次，能写七个字。笔头在纸上的划动，吸引着乡亲们的一双双眼睛。乡亲们几乎不看我，只看笔。
这也就是说，妈妈在我很小的时候就已经有意无意地告诉我，这笔，对乡亲们有一种责任。
九岁小学毕业到上海读中学，爸爸狠狠心为我买了一支“关勒铭”牌的钢笔，但很快就丢了，爸爸很生气。后来知道我得了上海市作文比赛第一名和数学竞赛大奖，爸爸气消了，但再也不给我买好钢笔。我后来用的，一直是别人不可能拿走的那种廉价钢笔。我也乐意，因为轻，而好钢笔总是比较重。

sections.label: 二
paragraphs: 我第一次大规模地用笔，是从十九岁到二十一岁，替爸爸写“交代”。那是“文革”灾难的初期，爸爸被“革命群众”揭发有政治问题和历史问题，立即“打倒”，停发工资，而我们家有八口人要吃饭。爸爸希望用一篇篇文字叙述来向“革命群众”说明事实真相，因此一边擦眼泪一边写，很快眼睛坏了，就由他口述，由我代笔。一开始他还没有被关押，天天晚上在家里他说我写。后来被“革命群众”上纲上线为“反对伟大领袖”，不能回家了。他告诉当权者说自己已经不能写字，必须由我代笔。因此，还能几天放回一次，但不能在家里过夜。
我一共为爸爸写了六十多万字的“交代”。我开始时曾劝爸爸，没有必要写，但后来写着写着，知道了从祖父和外公开始的很多真实往事，觉得很有历史价值和文学价值，便写了下去。而且，又主动追问了爸爸很多细节，再从祖母、妈妈那里核实。这一切，就是我后来写作《吾家小史》的起点。这书，断断续续写了四十多年。
当时为爸爸写“交代”，用的是圆珠笔。一根塑料直杆，每支三角钱，我写完了很多支。用这种圆珠笔，要比用钢笔使力，笔杆又太细，写着很不舒服。但爸爸要求，在写的材料下面必须垫一张蓝紫色的“复写纸”，使材料交上去之外还留个底，因此只能用这种圆珠笔。写一阵，手指发僵，而中指挨着食指的第一节还有深深的笔杆印。再写下去，整个手掌都会抽搐，因为实在写得太急、太多了。

sections.label: 三
paragraphs: 再怎么说，我爸爸都不应该是“文革”斗争的重点。他不是干部，不是资本家，也不是知识分子。“打倒”他，是出于“革命群众”的嫉妒。嫉妒他什么呢？只有一条，生了四个儿子，属于“人丁兴旺”。那年月，“人丁兴旺”必然食不果腹，但“革命群众”不管，只在他平日与同事聊天中收集到几句似乎“不满”的言语，便“打倒”了，长时间关押。

“文革”的真正重点，倒是与我的专业有关。戏剧，成了社会灾难的引爆点。整个“文革”，开始于批判吴晗的《海瑞罢官》——那是戏剧；“文革”的旗帜，是几部所谓“革命样板戏”——那也是戏剧。人类历史上从未有这样的事：很多人只因为说了一两句与戏剧相关的话，便身陷铁窗，或丧失生命。我考上的上海戏剧学院戏剧文学系，是学习戏剧理论和戏剧写作的，这专业一下子成了颠倒黑白、美丑、善恶的“集中营”。我决定退出，折笔改行。
在上海戏剧学院，我是反对“文革”的“保守派三座大山”之一。在爸爸已经被“打倒”的情况下，我的这种反对，在当时就是一种悲壮的自毁行为。就像我的叔叔余志士先生以连续三次的割脉自杀来抗议“文革”一样，我捧着他的骨灰盒接过了他的遗志。
正在这时，一场更大的灾难降临，全国城里的学生必须断学废学，上山下乡，不准回城。上海学生，有不少更是被惩罚性地发配到了遥远的边疆。出发前，所有的家长和学生都必须去看一台彻底否定教育和文化的戏剧《边疆新苗》。天哪，仍然是戏剧！我看过这台戏剧后去农场时，把所有的笔都丢进了垃圾桶，包括为爸爸写“交代”的圆珠笔。当时，爸爸的“罪行”加重，不能离开关押室了，我也就无法再为他代笔。
为什么要把笔丢进垃圾桶？首先是一种抗议性决裂。“革命样板戏”和《边疆新苗》使我产生了一种专业性耻辱。其次，是因为发现没有机会写字了。到农场后给谁写信？爸爸那里不准通信，如果给妈妈写信，她又能用什么样的话语回信？而且，我打听到，我们劳动的地方根本没有邮局，寄信要在休息的日子步行很远的路才能找到一个小镇，但实际上并没有休息的日子。由于这两个原因，理所当然，折笔、弃笔、毁笔、葬笔。
实际情况比预料的更糟。我们在农场自搭茅草屋，四根竹子撑一块木板当床，睡着睡着就陷到泥淖里去了。用笔的地方完全没有，用笔的时间也完全没有。永远是天不亮下田，天全黑才回，累得想不起字，想不起笔，想不起自己是一个能写字的人。

sections.label: 四
paragraphs: 一九七一年的一个政治事件使周恩来总理突然成了中国的第二号人物，他着手领导复课，试图局部地纠正“文革”灾难。这就使很多濒临灭绝的“边疆新苗”有可能回城读书了，也使我们有机会回上海参与一点教材编写。我被分配到“鲁迅教材编写组”，这又拿起了笔。记得那笔是从静安寺百乐商场买的，一元钱左右的吸墨水钢笔。当时的钢笔也已经有了几个“国内名牌”，像“英雄”、“金星”什么的，那就要二三元钱一支了，我买不起。
编教材，我分到的事情很少，几天就写完了。但是，复课、编教材这件事虽然由周恩来直接布置，却仍然受到主张废学停课的极左派反对，认为是“右倾翻案”，时时准备反击。他们正忙着张罗让刚刚回课堂的学生再看一遍《边疆新苗》这样的戏，“重返边疆再革命”。这让我又一次愤怒，既为教育愤怒，又为戏剧愤怒。但是，由于当时已经出现了恢复教育的势头，我的愤怒也就变成了学术勇敢。

我拿起那支一元钱的笔，开始行动。那时为了复课，各大学的图书馆重新开放。我利用上海戏剧学院图书馆一个早就熟悉的职工蔡祥明，偷偷摸进了当时还视为禁地的外文书库，开始了《世界戏剧学》的写作。我的笔，大量抄写外文原文，再借着各种词典的帮助一段段翻译。同时还要通览大量背景材料，最后汇集起全世界十三个国家的全部戏剧学理论。这件事，在工作量上非常巨大，因为这些内容直到四十几年后的今天还没有被完整翻译过来。我当时居然凭一人之力，在密闭的空间，以笔为杖，步步潜行。更不容易的是，当时在外面，一窗之隔，只要说一句不利于“革命样板戏”的话，就会有牢狱之灾。为此，我不能不对那支一元钱的钢笔表示敬意，对自己的青年时代表示敬意。
当时完全无法设想这部长达六十八万言的艰深学术著作能够出版，当然更无法预料，这书居然在几十年后一直成为全国在这一重大学科上的唯一教材，未被替代。
可见，那支笔，那支帮我偷偷潜行的拐杖，在黑暗泥泞中描划出了一个庞大的学术构建。
与这个学术构建相比，我后来完成的很多学术著作，虽然更为著名，却失去了一份不惜赴死的生命力度。

sections.label: 五
paragraphs: 由于我在灾难中的表现，灾难过去之后全院三次民意测验均名列第一，被破格提升为院长。
连一个小组长也没有做过，却成为国家重点艺术高校的第一领导者，这似乎像是坐了“火箭”，但却是十年的信任沉淀。全院的教师和职工看了我整整十年，有的事当时没有看明白，后来也终于明白了，例如，我一次次鬼鬼祟祟地消失在外文书库的原因。
灾难中的形象往往会传播得很广，当时我的社会声望已远远超出学院，被选为整个上海市的中文专业教授评审组组长，兼艺术专业教授评审组组长。每次评审，我们对那些在灾难岁月投机取巧、丧失天良的文人都断然予以否定。于是，我又拿起了那支笔，一次次重重地写下了否定结论，又浓浓地签上自己的名。那支笔在当时，几乎成了法官敲下的那个锤子，响亮、果敢、权威、无可争议。
这就是二十世纪八十年代，我那时说得上仕途畅达，官运亨通。已经是全国最年轻的高校校长，却还常有北京和上海的高官竭力要把我拉进更高的权力圈子，这在当时很容易。于是，有了一次次长谈，一次次规劝。这些高官，后来都成了非常显赫的领导人。但是，我太明白我的笔的秉性。它虽然也有能力继续成为更大法官的锤子，但它显然并不愿意。
于是，我在上上下下的万分惊愕中辞职了。辞了二十三次，才被勉强批准。然后，穿上一件灰色的薄棉袄，去了甘肃高原，开始踏访公元七世纪的唐朝。
当年寻找古迹，需要长时间步行，而那些路并不好走。在去阳关的半道上，我几度蹲下身去察看坟丘密布的古战场，把我插在裤袋口上的旧钢笔弄丢了。那支旧钢笔不值什么钱，但正是它，我在辞职前反复搓弄，它总是顽强地告诉我，只愿意把我的名字签在文章上，而不是文件上。
既然它对我有点重要，我还在沙原上找了一会儿。但那地方太开阔、太芜杂了，当然找不到。转念一想也释然了：这支笔是陪了我很久的老朋友，从现在起，就代表我陪陪一千多年前的远戍将士和边塞诗人吧。
我考察的习惯，不在现场抄录什么，只在当天晚上回到旅舍后才关起门来专心写作。记得在兰州我曾长时间住在一个极简陋的小招待所里，简陋到上厕所要走很远的路。当地一位年长的文人范克峻先生读过我的不少学术著作，又看到我行李简薄，便送来了一支圆珠笔和两叠稿纸。这种圆珠笔的笔杆较粗，比我为爸爸写“交代”的那一种更好用。只不过那稿纸太薄，一写就穿，落笔要小心翼翼。
我把白天的感觉写成一篇篇散文，寄给在《收获》杂志做编辑的老同学李小林。邮局找不到，就塞到路边一个灰绿色的老邮筒里。这时才觉得范克峻先生给我送薄稿纸算是送对了。稿纸薄，几篇文章叠在一起也能塞得进那邮筒。
写了就及时寄走，是怕在路上丢失。有的地方连路边邮筒也找不到，那就只能将写好的文章随身带了。随身带，又要求稿纸越薄越好。由此我养成了习惯，只用薄稿纸。即使后来可以用较好的稿纸了，也选择薄稿纸。这一来，那种容易划破薄稿纸的圆珠笔，就需要更换了。

当然，写起来最舒服的还是吸墨水的钢笔。但这对我这个不断赶路的旅行者来说，就很不方便，因为必须带墨水瓶。墨水瓶都是玻璃做的，夹在行李里既容易洒，又容易碎。据说过去安徒生旅行时是把墨水瓶拴根绳子挂在脖子上的，那就不会洒，也不会碎了。但我不会模仿他，因为那样不仅难看，而且有显摆自己“很有墨水”的嫌疑。安徒生旅行时还肩扛一大圈粗麻绳，那是准备在旅馆万一失火时可以滑窗而逃。可见，他走得比我还麻烦，但我走得比他远得多，时间也长得多。
后来我还是学了安徒生的一半，随身带墨水瓶，但不挂在脖子上。选那种玻璃特别厚的瓶子，瓶口拧紧处再垫一个橡胶圈。但这样还是不保险，因为几经颠簸后，瓶盖易裂。所以再加一个笨办法，在瓶盖外再包一层塑料纸，用细麻绳绕三圈扎紧。行李本来就很小，把墨水瓶安顿在衣服中间。
我从甘肃路边邮筒寄出的一叠叠薄稿纸，如果有可能发表，似乎应该起个总题目。因此，在寄出第三叠时，我在信封背后加了一句：“就叫《文化苦旅》吧”。后来，路还在一直走，风餐露宿，满身烟尘，却永远带着那支钢笔，那瓶墨水。我想应该对笔表示一点什么了，因此为接下来的文集起名时加了一个“笔”字，叫《山居笔记》。

sections.label: 六
paragraphs: 笔之大难，莫过于在北非、中东、南亚、中亚的极端恐怖地区了。
我写了那么多中华文明遗迹，为了对比，必须去寻找同样古老或更古老的其他文明。但那路，实在太险峻、太艰难、太无序、太混乱了。我必须贴地而行，不能坐飞机，因此要经过无数关口。查啊查，等啊等，翻啊翻，问啊问。他们在问我，我却永远问不清，前面可以在哪里用餐，今晚可以在哪里栖宿。
由于危机天天不断，生命朝不保夕，因此完全不能靠事后记忆了，必须当天写下日记。但写日记的地方在哪里？在废弃的战壕边，在吉普的车轮上，在岗亭的棚架下。这一来，笔又成了问题。显然不能带墨水瓶，如果带了，那些人很可能会让我当场喝两口看看是不是危险物品。圆珠笔他们也查得仔细，又拧又拆，要判断那是不是特制的微型手枪。
好在，这时世界上已流行一种透明塑料杆的轻型墨水笔，一支可以写好几天，不必吸墨水。沿途见不到超市、文具店，因此我不管入住什么样的小旅馆，只要见到客房里有这种笔，立即收下，以防哪一天写日记时突然接不上。
在行经伊拉克以及伊朗、巴基斯坦、阿富汗、尼泊尔那漫长的边界地区时，一路上黑影幢幢、堡垒隐隐、妖光熠熠、枪口森森，我把已写好的日记手稿包在一个塑料洗衣袋里紧抱在胸前，手上又捏着一支水笔。我想，即使人被俘虏了，行李被抢走了，我的纸笔还在，还能写作。当然更大的可能是不让写，那我也要尽最大努力，为自己保留一丝最后的机会，为笔保留一丝最后的机会。
这种紧抱稿子紧捏笔的情景，我一直保持到从尼泊尔入境西藏的樟木口岸。
那支水笔，连同我在历险行程中一直藏在行李箱中一支较好的钢笔，很快被一个慈善机构高价拍卖，所得款项全部捐献，以补充北京市残障儿童的乳品供应。
后来我在进一步研究中国文明与世界现代先进文明的差距时，又考察了欧洲九十六座城市。虽然也非常辛苦，但那种悬生命于一线的危险没有了，而且一路上也比较容易得到顺手的笔。

当我考察完世界那么多地方之后，从联合国开始，很多国际机构和著名大学纷纷邀请我作主题演讲。所谓主题，大多是“全球背景下的中国文明”、“一个中国学者眼中的当代世界文化”、“五万公里五千年”、“全球面临的新危机”等等。华盛顿国会图书馆、联合国世界文明大会、哈佛大学、耶鲁大学、哥伦比亚大学、纽约大学等等都去了，还应邀在我国香港、澳门、台湾长期授课。我想，既然沿途用了那么多笔，现在正该用一支更好的笔把考察成果系统地写出来了。
但是，万万没有想到，遭遇了意想不到的情况。

sections.label: 七
paragraphs: 正是在我基本完成对中国文明和世界文明的长时间考察之际，我周围的文化格局发生了整体性蜕变。简单说来，八十年代由“反思、创新”组成的文化主题全线失落，居然由大规模的“联欢”和“联谤”组成了新世纪文化的二元结构。前者标榜“盛世国粹”，后者标榜“言论自由”，中西合璧，烈烈扬扬。其他文化当然也有，但最热闹的却是它们。
这个二元结构使我和妻子走投无路。妻子马兰，那么优秀的表演艺术家，由于九度婉拒了一次据说是“顶级重要的联欢会”，被地方官员“冷冻”，失去了工作；而我，则不知为什么成了文化诽谤的第一焦点，“文革派”、“自由派”和官方一些媒体亲密合作，联手造谣，我即便无声无息，也永远浊浪滚滚。这就是说，我们夫妻两人，正好被“二元结构”齐齐地开除了。我们又不愿向权力求助，因此注定无处可去。
照理应该移民，但我们没有条件，只能逃到广东省一个几乎不在意文化的城市，躲了很多年。国内无人理会，国际间却一直在热心地寻找我们，邀请演讲和演出。台湾更把我当作了中华文化的主要演讲者，邀请尤其殷切。这使我产生了一个矛盾：要不要继续凭着冒死考察的成果，系统地来阐释中国文化？
还是以前遇到过的老问题：是折笔、弃笔、毁笔、葬笔，还是再度拾笔、执笔、振笔、纵笔？
相比之下，要剥夺我妻子的演出权利是容易的，因为她已经离开了地区依赖性很强的创作群体；但是，要剥夺我的笔却不很容易，因为这只是个人的深夜坚守，没有地域性限定，除非我自己觉得没有意思了。
到底自己觉得有没有意思呢？妻子一次次无言地看着我，我玩弄着笔杆一次次摇头。还去阐释中国文化？请看报刊上永远在喷泻的千百篇诽谤我的文章，用的全是中国汉字、中国语法、中国恶气、中国心计。而且，所有的诽谤只要稍作调查就能立即识破，但整整二十年，没有任何一个文化机构和文化团体，作过一丝一毫的调查，发过一丝一毫的异议。这些报刊、机构和团体，都不是民间的。
民间，也好不到哪里去。我妻子的观众，我自己的读者，在数量上都曾经长期领先全国，在热度上更是无以复加；但一夜之间，听说被官员冷冻了，被媒体围殴了，大家也就立即转变立场，全都乐滋滋地期待着新的拳脚。
这与我在“文革”时期对民众的观察，一模一样。
因此，我除了摇头，还是摇头。

后来，突然发现了几个奇怪的材料，我才开始改变态度。第一个材料告诉我，我遭受的多数诽谤的运作中枢，居然是上海几十年前鼓吹断学废学的戏剧《边疆新苗》的炮制者；第二个材料告诉我，其他几次针对我的全国性造谣事件，策划者也是当年上海造反派司令部的两个首领；第三个材料告诉我，在上海积极响应诽谤和造谣的，主要是被我否决教授职称申请的那些文人和他们的学生。这一下子就前后贯通了，我只惊讶，他们已经年岁不小，却还如此老当益壮，徒众如云。
这几个发现让我默然良久。我父亲的十年关押，我叔叔的三度割脉，我全家的濒临饿死，我岳父的当街批斗，全都一一浮现在眼前。原来，我要不要重新拾笔，并不仅仅关及我目前的处境，而是牵涉到很大的时空坐标。

一切文化孽力都会以文化的方式断灭文化。简单说来，也就是“以笔夺笔”。因此，我作为可怜长辈的后代，还应该担负一点守护文化的责任。事实证明，我的守护并不会被当代中国文化乐意接受，但我不能光看它的脸色。我不仅还要执笔，而且也可以不再拒绝国际间的演讲邀请。我当然不会控诉我们夫妻俩的遭遇，但当我说清楚了中国文化的千年脉络、万里对比，也许会有一些中外读者对二十年来由“联欢”和“联谤”组成的文化二元结构产生一点怀疑，开始认识到那未必是中国文化的真正魂魄。
因此，我又郑重地执笔了。执笔之时给自己定下了一个最严格的规矩：时间不多，笔墨珍贵，不能有一点一滴浪费在对诽谤的反驳上。
于是，在诽谤声依然如狂风暴雨的一个个夜晚，在远离无数“文化盛典”的僻静小屋，由失业很久的妻子陪伴着，我一笔笔地写出了一批书籍。它们是：《中国文脉》、《何谓文化》、《君子之道》、《北大授课》、《极端之美》、《吾家小史》，以及它们的部分初稿《寻觅中华》、《摩挲大地》、《借我一生》……此外，还精选了几部中国文化经典，全都用当代散文作了翻译。以前的那些“文化大散文”文集和学术著作，也都认真地整理了出来。
至此，我不敢说对得起中国文化，却敢说我对得起自己的笔了。当然，笔也对得起我。
我还可以像老朋友一样对笔开一句玩笑：你耗尽了我的一生，我却没有浪费你太多的墨水。
不仅没有浪费太多的墨水，也没有浪费什么社会资源。这二十卷书，每一卷都没有申请过一元钱的资助。据说现在国家有钱，这样的资助名目非常之多，诸如研究基金、创作补助、项目经费、学术津贴、考察专款、资料费用、追加资金……每项都数字惊人。我始终没有沾染分毫，只靠一支笔。
有了笔，一切都够了。

sections.label: 八
paragraphs: 在行将结束此文的时候，突然冒出来一个回忆，觉得有意思再说几句。
记得那一次考察欧洲，坐船过英吉利海峡，正遇风急浪高，全船乘客颠得东倒西歪、左仰右合。只有我，生来就不晕船，居然还在船舱的一个咖啡厅里写作。有两位英国老太太也不晕船，发现我与她们同道，高兴地扶着栏杆走到了我身后。我与她们打过招呼之后继续埋头书写，随即传来这两位老太太的惊叹声：“看！多么漂亮的中国字！那么大的风浪他还握得住笔！”
这两位老太太完全不懂中文，因此她们说漂亮不漂亮，只是在指一种陌生的文字记号的整齐排列，不足为凭。但是，我却非常喜欢她们的惊叹。不错，漂亮的中国字，那么大的风浪还在写。这一切，不正是有一点象征意义么？
我是一个握笔之人，握在风浪中，竟然还能写那么多，写得那么整齐。
写的目的，不完全是为了读者。写到后来，很大一部分是为了那风浪，为了那条船，为了那支笔。甚至，为了那些愿意赞赏汉字外型美的外国老太太，或者老大爷。
其实，更主要是为了自己。看看过了那么多年，这个七岁就为乡亲们代写书信的小男孩，还能为乡亲们代写点什么；这个二十岁左右就为父亲代写“交代”的青年人，还能为中国文化向国际社会“交代”点什么。
看自己，并不是执着于“我”，而是观察一种生命状态，能否扩展和超脱。这是佛教的意思。
于是，谨此祭笔。
且拜且祭，且忆且思，且喜且泣。
癸巳除夕至甲午春节。

en.title: Pen Memories
intro: TWENTY VOLUMES OF QIUYU COLLECTIONS were finally completed amid the firecrackers on New Year’s Eve. I gently put down the pen.
I put it down, but then picked it up, and then looked at it: pen.
In a human life, many objects will be touched; we cannot count them. For me, the most important thing must be the pen.

Until now, I have not used the computer, and all my articles have been written out, which was praised as the rare “pure handwriting” by the publishing world. Will this change? No. Although I am not a conservative, a person’s life is limited, and always needs to keep a few fidelities, and one of them is the pen.
Maybe a lot of people will laugh at me, but if you read my pieces of memory, you must understand.

sections.label: I
paragraphs: THE FIRST PEN IN MY LIFE was a small bamboo brush. Mom wrote letters on behalf of the villagers, and I imitated her with this small brush at the edge; at that time I was three years old. Next year I was forcefully dragged to go to school from my desk by two new elementary school teachers, and Mom gave me a good brush. In the class, my face was stained with ink, so the teacher had to take me to the river for washing once the class was over, and then they took me back to my seat.

At the age of seven, Mom gave me a dip pen longer than the brush, together with a bottle of blue ink, and requested me to write letters and keep accounts on her behalf for the villagers. Once dipping in the bottle, I could write seven words. The slide of the pen drew the eyes of folks. They almost did not look at me, just the pen.
That is to say, Mom told me when I was very young, intentionally or unintentionally, that the pen has a responsibility to the folks.

When graduating from elementary school when I was nine years old, I went to middle school in Shanghai and my dad bought me a “Guanleming” pen, but soon it was lost, and Dad was very angry. Later, when he knew I had won first place in the Shanghai essay contest and mathematics contest, Dad did not get angry but he no longer bought me a nice pen. Later I always used cheap pens others will not take away. I was happy, for they were light and the good pens were always a bit heavy.

sections.label: II
paragraphs: I WAS TWENTY OR SO YEARS OLD when I used a pen on a large scale for the first time, to write a “confession” for Dad. That was the beginning of the disastrous “Cultural Revolution.” Dad was accused of political and historical problems by “revolutionary masses.” He was “struck down” at once, found his wages suspended, but we eight people had to eat. Dad wanted to use an article to elucidate the facts to the “crowds,” so he wiped away tears while writing—and soon his eyes were hurting, so I wrote on his behalf from his dictation. At the beginning he had not been imprisoned, and we wrote at home every night. Later he was brazenly said by “the revolutionary masses” to be against “the great leader” and could not go home. He told authorities that he could not write and I must be used. Therefore, he could go home every few days, but could not stay overnight.

I wrote over 600,000 words of “confession” for my father. At the beginning, I tried to persuade my father that there was no need to write, but I knew many memories about my grandfather and grandfather, which I felt had great historical and literary values, so he wrote them down. Moreover, I asked many details of my father and verified them from my grandmother and mother. This was the start of my work History of My Family, a book written in sections over forty years.

I used a ballpoint pen when I wrote the “confession” for my father. A plastic straight bar cost me three jiao, and I used up a lot of them. Such pens wasted more energy than other pens; its pen holder was too thin, very uncomfortable. But my father required blue-purple carbon paper under the written materials, in order to leave one copy after handing over the material, so only the ballpoint pen could be used. After a while, my fingers became stiff, with deep pen imprints left in the first quarter of my middle finger next to the index finger. Then I continued, but the whole palm was cramped, because I wrote too much and too hastily.

sections.label: III
paragraphs: NO MATTER WHAT, my dad should not be the focus for the struggle of the Cultural Revolution. He was not a member of a cadre, not a capitalist, not an intellectual. “Striking him down” was completely due to the jealousy of the “crowds.” What were they jealous of? Only one thing: he had four sons and had a large family. In those days, a large family had to have insufficient food, but “revolutionary masses” considered nothing, just collected some “unsatisfied” words from his usual chats with colleagues, so he was “struck down” and imprisoned for a long time.

The real focus of the Cultural Revolution was associated with my major: drama itself became the tipping point of social disaster. The whole Cultural Revolution began with the criticism of Hai Rui Dismissed from Office, by Wu Han—that was the drama; the banner of Cultural Revolution was several so-called “revolutionary model operas”—that was also drama. Never in human history has there been such a thing: so many people imprisoned or killed just from words associated with drama. I went to the Literature Department of Shanghai Theatre Academy, learning the theory of drama and dramatic writing, but this profession suddenly became a “concentration camp” reversing right and wrong, beauty and ugliness, good and evil. I decided to leave and change my profession.

At Shanghai Theater Academy, I was one of “three mountains of conservatives” against the Cultural Revolution. My dad had been “struck down,” and my objection at the time was a tragic act of self-destruction, just like my uncle, Mr. Yu Zhishi, who slit his wrist for three consecutive times to protest against the Cultural Revolution. I held his cinerary casket and took over his unfulfilled wish.

But then a bigger catastrophe came: the national students had to waste their studies to go and work in the countryside, and were not allowed to return to the city. Most students in Shanghai were sent to the remote frontier as punishment. Before their departure, all the parents and students were required to watch a drama, Promising Youth in Frontier, completely denying their education and culture. Oh my God, it was still drama! When I went to the farm after seeing this drama, I threw all my pens in the waste bin, including the ballpoint pen I used writing a “confession” for dad. At that time, his “crime” had increased, and he could not be imprisoned in the detention room, so I could no longer write for him. Why did I put the pen in the trash? It was first of all a kind of protest. The “revolutionary model opera” and Promising Youth in Frontier subjected me to professional humiliation.

Second, I found no chance to write. Whom would I write to? Dad was not allowed to write letters; if I wrote to Mom, how could she reply to me? Moreover, I heard there was no post office in my workplace, and when I posted a letter, I would have to walk long distances to a town during the day for rest, but in fact there was no day for rest. Due to these two reasons, I of course broke the pen, abandoned the pen, destroyed the pen, buried the pen.

It was much worse than we expected. We set up the cottage on the farm; a plank supported by four bamboo branches was the bed, and the mire would be gradually stick to us as we slept. There was no time or place to use the pen. We went to the farm before dawn and left at the end of dusk all the time. You would be so tired you could not think of words or pen. You’d even forget you were a man who could write.

sections.label: IV
paragraphs: A POLITICAL EVENT IN 1971 suddenly made Premier Zhou Enlai the number-two figure in China. He set out to lead the classes, and tried to correct the Cultural Revolution disaster locally, so as to allow many endangered “promising youth in the frontier” the chance to return to study, giving us the opportunity to return to Shanghai to participate in the preparation of textbooks. I was assigned to the “Lu Xun textbook compiling group,” so I picked up the pen again. I remembered that pen was bought from Baile Shop of Jing’an Temple, an ink pen costing about one yuan. At that time, several “national brands,” such as “hero” and “Venus,” had been manufactured, but they cost two or three yuan, which I could not afford.

As for the preparation of textbooks, I got a few assignments, and finished within a few days. However, even though Zhou Enlai directly arranged the resumption of class and textbook work, it was still opposed by ultraleftists advocating the suspension of classes; they thought it was a “rightist reverse” and were always ready to fight back. They were busy preparing to replay dramas like Promising Youth in Frontier to students, “returning to the borderland for revolutions.” It made me angry again, both for education and drama. However, since the momentum of education restoration had grown, my anger turned to scholarly bravery.

I picked up that one-yuan pen and started taking action. At the time, the university library reopened in order to restore education. With the help of a friendly worker, Cai Xiangming, in the Shanghai Theater Academy library, I sneaked into the section on foreign language books, then still considered off-limits, and began writing about world drama. My pen copied a large number of texts in foreign languages, and then with the help of various dictionaries, I translated the sentences one by one. Meanwhile, I browsed through a large amount of background material, and finally brought together all of the theories of drama in thirteen countries around the world. It was a huge workload, for they could not be translated completely within forty years. I (it was actually only me) was in such a confined space, moving forward step by step with the pen. What was more difficult was that outside the window one might be imprisoned for saying oneword against “revolutionary model opera.” In this regard, I could not fail to pay tribute to that one-yuan pen and my youth.

At that time, I was totally unable to imagine that the 680,000 characters of abstruse academic work could be published, of course, and more unpredictably, that it would actually become the only textbook on this important subject for decades, never to be replaced.
Thus, that pen, that walking stick, helped me secretly describe a huge academic edifice in the dark mud.
Compared with that edifice, many academic works I completed later were much more well-known, but they did not have the power of a life braving death.

sections.label: V
paragraphs: BECAUSE OF MY PERFORMANCE IN THE DISASTER, I was ranked first place three times in various polls, so I was promoted to president.

Never having been a group leader before, I became the first leader of the main national art college, which seemed like a “rocket,” but it was because of trust that had grown over ten years. Teachers and staff in the college had looked at me for a full decade; they did not understand something at that time, and only later did they understand, for example, the reason I had secretly disappeared into the foreign-language books.

My image in the disaster continued to spread widely. At that time, my social reputation extended far beyond the college, and I was chosen as leader of a Chinese professor review team in Shanghai and of the art professor review team. In each review, we denied with great resolve the opportunistic literati who had lost their consciences in the disaster. So I picked up the pen, wrote the negative conclusion heavily, and signed my name deeply. The pen at that time nearly became a gavel for the judge: loud, bold, authoritative, and indisputable.

In the 1980s, I had a successful career. I was already the nation’s youngest university president, and even the officials in Beijing and Shanghai tried their best to draw me into higher power circles, which at that time was easy for me. So there were talks and persuasions again and again. These senior officials afterward became very prominent leaders. However, I knew little about the mettle of my pen. Although it also had the ability to be the gavel of a bigger judge, it clearly was not willing to be so.

Therefore, I resigned, to the dismay of all members. Twenty-three times I was narrowly approved. Then, wearing a gray thin jacket, I went to the Gansu plateau to begin my tour of the Tang Dynasty of the seventh century AD.

I needed to walk long and hard at that time when hunting for historical sites, and the road was not good. On the way to Yangguan, I squatted down several times to see the ancient battlefields covered by tombs, but I lost my old pen that I’d stuck in my pocket. The old pen was not worth any money, but it was this pen that I rubbed repeatedly with my hands before quitting; it always told me sternly that it was only willing to sign my name to the articles, not the files.

Now that it was of a little importance to me, I looked for it in the sand for a while. But the land was too wild and disordered, and of course I could not find it. Then I thought: this pen, this old friend of mine, had accompanied me for a long time, and from now on, on my behalf, could accompany the garrison troops and frontier fortress poets going back one thousand years.

My investigative habit was not to copy anything in the scene, but only to concentrate on writing when going back to the hotel and closing the door. Once I lived in a very simple and small hostel in Lanzhou for a long time; even the bathroom was far away. A local senior scholar, Fan Kejun, had read my many academic works; upon seeing my simple luggage, he sent me a ballpoint pen and two piles of paper. Its pen holder was thick, which was much more useful than the one I wrote the “confession” with for my father. But the paper was too thin, so I had to use great care.

I wrote some essays about my feelings during the day and sent them to my old classmate Li Xiaolin, the editor of the journal Harvest. I could not find the post office, so I put them into a gray-green old mailbox. Then I really appreciated the thin paper sent by Mr. Fan Kejun. It was just because of the thin paper that several articles stacked together could be crammed into that mailbox.

In order to avoid losing it on the road, I posted the article away immediately. In some places, there was even not a mailbox at the roadside, and I could only take them along, so thinner paper was much better. Due to this, I made it a habit to use thin paper. Even though I could use good paper later, I still even then chose the thin kind. In this way, I had to change the ballpoint pen, which easily cut through the thin paper.

Of course, the ink pen was still the most comfortable. But this was very inconvenient to me, a constant traveler, for a bottle of ink has to be carried. It was made of glass, easy to leak or break in the luggage. It was said that during the trip, Andersen tied an ink bottle on a rope around his neck, so it would not be spread or broken. But I would not imitate him, for it was not only very unsightly, but also seemed like showing off. Moreover, Andersen also carried a large circle of coarse twine, so as to slide from the window of a hotel in case of a fire. Therefore, he took more trouble than me, but I went much further than him, for a longer time.

Later, I learned half from Andersen, carrying the ink bottle, but not hanging it around my neck. A kind of glass bottle with a special thickness was selected, with a rubber ring put at the mouth of the bottle. But this was still not safe, for the bottlecap cracked easily on a bumpy road. Therefore, another way was devised: to cover a layer of plastic wrap outside the bottle cap, and then tie three knots with fine twine. My luggage was small, and I put it in the middle of my clothes.

I mailed piles of thin paper from the roadside mailboxes in Gansu Province. If it was possibly for publishing, a named would be given. Therefore, when sending out the third pile, I added a sentence on the back of envelope: “Just call it A Bittersweet Journey Through Culture.” Later, the tour continued, and I was exposed to deprivation and hunger, covered with soot, but I always carried that pen and bottle of ink. I thought I should express something to my pen, so I added a character of “pen” as a character for my next collection, named Pen Note About Mountain Life.

sections.label: VI
paragraphs: THE GREAT DISASTER OF THE PEN OCCURRED in the extreme terror-prone regions of North Africa, the Middle East, South Asia, and Central Asia.

I had written about so many sites in Chinese civilization, so I had to go and find other civilizations of the same age for contrast. However, that road was too steep, too difficult, too chaotic, too confusing. I had to walk, but could not fly, so I had to pass through numerous checkpoints. I was continuously checked, made to wait, detained, and interrogated. They always asked me questions, but I never asked about a place for a meal and a place for rest.

Due to such continued crises day after day, life was precarious, so I could not rely on memory and had to write in a diary each day. But where could I write a diary? On the side of abandoned trenches, on the jeep wheels, or under the scaffolding of a booth? However, the pen was a problem. Obviously the ink bottle could not be taken along, for they might make me drink a little to prove it was not dangerous. Even the ballpoint pens would be checked carefully by them to determine whether it was not a special pistol.

Fortunately, at this time a sort of transparent plastic pole-light ink pen was popular, and one could write for days without blotting. Along the way I would not see any supermarkets or stationery stores, so I would stock up on such pens upon seeing them in the hotel, to avoid any interruptions when writing in the diary.

Passing through the long border regions in Iraq, Iran, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Nepal, there were dark buildings, fortresses, a sense of foreboding and the muzzles of many guns. I wrapped the diary manuscripts that had been written in a plastic laundry bag tightly against my chest, with a pen in hand. I thought, even if I was captured, and my luggage was snatched away, my pen and paper would still be there, and I could still write. Of course it would be more likely that I could not write, but I would try my best to keep the slightest last chance for me and my pen.
Such was my situation holding pen and manuscripts when we entered the Zhangmu port into Tibet from Nepal.

That pen, along with a better pen hidden in the boot during my adventure travel, was soon auctioned at high price by a charity; all proceeds were donated to supplement the dairy products of handicapped children in Beijing.

Then when I further studied the gap between Chinese civilization and the world’s modern civilizations, I investigated another ninety-six cities in Europe. Although it was very hard, the life-threatening risk had gone, and pens were easily obtained along the way.

After I investigated so many places in the world, many international institutions and famous universities, beginning with the United Nations, invited me to give keynote speeches. Most so-called keynotes referred to “Chinese civilization within the global context,” “contemporary world culture in the eyes of a Chinese scholar,” “50,000 miles & 5,000 years,” “the new global crisis,” and so on. I had been to the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., the United Nations World Conference on Civilization, Harvard University, Yale University, Columbia University, and New York University, and was still being invited for long-term teaching in Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan of China. I thought I had used up so many pens along the way, and now a better pen should be used to write the findings systematically.
However, an unthinkable situation arose.

sections.label: VII
paragraphs: WHEN I BASICALLY COMPLETED the long-term investigation to China and world civilizations, the cultural situation around me changed suddenly and totally. Simply speaking, the culture theme composed of “reflection and innovation” in the 1980s had declined completely, and a dual structure of culture had formed in the new century. The former one boasted of the “heyday quintessence,” the latter one of “freedom of speech,” which was supposed to be a triumphant combination of Chinese and Western elements. There were other cultures of course, but they were the most popular.

This dual structure drove me to desperation. My wife, Ma Lan, an excellent performing artist, lost her job after nine times refusing a so-called “highest-level get-together” and was “frozen” by local officials. I became the first focus of cultural slander somehow: the “Cultural Revolution party,” “freedom party,” and some official media cooperated closely, teamed up to spread disinformation, and even I was silenced. These were turbulent times. In other words, we as a couple were fired by a “dual structure.” We did not want to seek help from the powers-that-be, and therefore we were destined to have nowhere to go.

We felt we should emigrate, but we had no qualifications, so we could only flee to a city in Guangdong Province that did not care about culture, and hide there for a number of years. Nobody noticed me in China, but the people abroad had been eagerly seeking me for lectures and performances. Taiwan regarded me as a major speaker on Chinese culture, offering steady invitations. A paradox was generated: should I continue to explain Chinese culture systematically based on my achievements while risking my life?

Also, there was the question encountered previously: break the pen, abandon the pen, destroy the pen, and bury the pen, or once again pick up the pen, write with the pen, move swiftly with the pen, and release the pen?

In contrast, it was easy to deprive my wife’s performance rights, for she had already left her group and was greatly dependent on the local area, but it was difficult for them to deprive me of my pen, for that was mine alone to hold at night, without geographical bounds, unless I felt it had lost all meaning.

Was it meaningful? My wife looked at me again and again wordlessly, but I played with my pen and shook my head. Did I still interpret Chinese culture? Thousands of articles slandering me forever in the newspapers were all written in Chinese characters, in Chinese grammar, with Chinese evil spirit, intent on Chinese shenanigans. Moreover, all these defamations could be seen through immediately with only a brief effort, but for twenty years no cultural institution or association made the slightest investigation or voiced a shred of dissent. These newspapers, agencies, and other bodies lacked any sense of civil duty.

In so-called civil society, it was not much better. My wife’s audiences and my own readers were long in the leading position of audiences in China and could grow no more; however, overnight, once we were said to be frozen by officials and beaten down by the media, everyone immediately shifted their loyalties and looked forward contentedly to new initiatives.
This was exactly what I had observed in the Cultural Revolution.
Therefore, I could only shake my head.

I suddenly noticed a few strange texts, and began to change my attitude. The first text told me that the center of most of the slanders I suffered was actually the makers of the drama Promising Youth in Frontier, who had advocated the interruption and waste of education in Shanghai several decades earlier; the second text told me that the planners for other national disinformation events were two leaders of the Shanghai Rebel Headquarters at that time; the third batch of material told me that the persons actively fomenting the slander and disinformation in Shanghai were mainly scholars whose title applications had been rejected by me, along with their students. I understood suddenly, and I was surprised that, though they had grown old, they were still so vital and strong, with hordes of followers.

These discoveries made me silent for a long time. Ten years of my father’s detention, my family’s starving to death, and the street criticism of my father-in-law all emerged one by one in front of me. Originally, whether I picked up the pen again did not just involve my current situation, but also was related to a great deal of such yardsticks of space and time.

All evil forces of culture would be stopped only in a cultural way. Simply speaking, that was “to seize the pen via the pen.” Therefore, I, as the descendant of poor elders, should also be responsible for protecting the culture. Facts proved that my protection was not to be accepted by contemporary Chinese culture, but I could not only consider that attitude. Along with writing, I would no longer reject the international invitations. Certainly, I would be defensive about the sufferings of me and my wife, but when I made the millennial assessment and comparison of Chinese culture some readers at home and abroad would surely doubt the dual culture structure, and begin to realize that might not be the real soul of Chinese culture.
Therefore, I solemnly wrote, and set the most rigorous rules for myself: there was not much time, and the ink was precious, so nothing could be wasted on the refutation of slander.

Thus, in nights full of defamation, in a quiet cabin away from the numerous “cultural festivals,” I wrote batches of books with the help of my wife, who was unemployed for a long time. They were: Evolution of Chinese Culture, What Is the Culture, Way to Be a Gentleman, Teaching in Peking University, Extreme Beauty, History of My Family, as well as portions of the preliminary first drafts of Quest for Chinese Culture, Touch on the Earth, and Take My Life. In addition, I also selected some Chinese cultural classics and translated them into modern prose. The prior “cultural essays” and academic works were also sorted out carefully.
At this point, I dared not to say that I treated the Chinese culture fairly, but I was worthy of my pen. Of course, the pen was also worthy of me.
Like an old friend, I also played a joke on the pen: you run out of my life, but I do not waste too much ink.

I not only wasted little ink, but also few social resources. Not one volume out of twenty involved applications for one yuan of funding. It was said that now the country was rich, and there were many kinds of financing—for example, research funding, creation allowances, project funding, academic allowance, investigation funds, information costs, additional funds…each was startling, but I never required anything, just a pen.
The pen was enough for me.

sections.label: VIII
paragraphs: AT THE END OF WRITING THIS ARTICLE, a memory suddenly surfaced, so I have a few more words.

Once, as I was investigating Europe and sailed across the English Channel, the sea ran high, and the whole ship of passengers reeled left and right. Only I, the born sailor, still wrote in a coffee shop of the cabin. Two British women did not feel seasick, and they found me similarly resilient, so they came behind me holding the handrail with very pleasant expressions. I greeted them and continued writing, and then an amazing sound came from them: “Look! What beautiful Chinese characters! He can still hold the pen tightly in such big waves!”

They did not understand Chinese, so the beauty they referred to was the neat arrangement of strange word marks. Not enough to go on—however, I was very happy for their amazed statement. Good, beautiful Chinese characters, the way I kept writing in such a big storm. Was not this a bit of symbolism?
I was a man holding a pen, holding it in the storm, writing so many characters, writing so neatly.

My purpose was not solely for the readers. Later, a large part of it was for the storms, for the ship, for the pen, even for those foreign old women and men who were willing to appreciate the appearance of Chinese characters.

In fact, it was mainly for me. After so many years, what that seven-year-old boy who wrote letters for the folks also wrote for folks, period; that young man who transcribed a “confession” for his father at about twenty years old also “confessed” to the international community about Chinese culture.
I myself was not obsessed with “me,” but wanted to observe a state of life, whether it could be expanded or detached. This was the meaning of Buddhism.
Therefore, I would memorialize my pen.
I worshipped and memorialized it, recalled and missed it, happily and tearfully.
—From New Year’s Eve in Guisi Year to Spring Festival in Jiawu Year
